title: A Cross-Modal Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensate Material Properties and Cellular Function Across Species and Perturbations
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates formed by phase separation are quintessential mesoscale structures whose emergent material properties (viscosity, elasticity, interfacial tension, aging) shape gene regulation, signaling, and stress responses. Yet the field remains fragmented: biophysical measurements are reported in disparate experimental systems, while large-scale imaging, proteomics, and genetics datasets rarely connect condensate material state to cellular outcomes. This working group will synthesize publicly available datasets to build a unified, cross-species map linking condensate composition and sequence features to emergent material properties and downstream phenotypes.

We will integrate (i) curated condensate component databases (e.g., LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS), (ii) protein sequence/structure annotations (AlphaFold DB, InterPro, disorder predictors, prion-like domain catalogs), (iii) high-content microscopy repositories and segmentation-ready image sets (Cell Painting, Image Data Resource, Human Protein Atlas subcellular localization, yeast GFP collections), (iv) proteomics and interactomics (PRIDE, BioGRID, HuRI), and (v) perturbation-response resources (DepMap CRISPR screens, GEO/ArrayExpress transcriptomics, LINCS). We will extract quantitative condensate phenotypes from images using reproducible pipelines (CellProfiler/napari + deep learning segmentation) and harmonize them with reported rheology/FRAP-derived metrics from the literature via text-mining and manual curation.

The core scientific questions are: (1) Which molecular features (valency, charge patterning, aromatic content, disorder architecture, multimerization) best predict condensate material state across contexts? (2) Do distinct “material property regimes” correspond to conserved functional outputs (e.g., transcriptional bursts, stress granule-mediated translation control) and pathological transitions (e.g., solidification in neurodegeneration)? (3) Can we identify universal versus lineage-specific design principles for mesoscale organization?

Methodologically, we will develop multimodal machine learning models that jointly embed sequence/structure, interaction networks, and image-derived condensate morphology to predict material properties and phenotypic consequences. We will emphasize interpretable models (e.g., graph neural networks with attention over interaction motifs; sparse additive models over sequence features) to generate testable hypotheses. Benchmark tasks and open evaluation sets will be released to spur community contributions.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated expertise spanning polymer physics, cell biology, computer vision, NLP-based literature mining, and statistical learning, plus the infrastructure to host community curation sprints and model hackathons. The working group will include experimentalists who understand assay biases, data scientists to build harmonization pipelines, and theorists to connect emergent properties to mesoscale physics.

Training will be embedded via trainee-led “data carpentry” modules on image analysis, reproducible ML, and open curation, culminating in a public, versioned knowledge graph of condensate properties and an open-source toolkit to relate condensate material state to cellular function. Outputs will follow open science practices: containerized workflows, FAIR metadata schemas, and pre-registered analysis plans to ensure reproducibility and broad reuse.
background_and_significance:
Biomolecular condensates formed via liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) and related demixing processes are now recognized as pervasive mesoscale structures that organize biochemical reactions in space and time. At the scale between single macromolecules and organelles, condensates exhibit emergent material properties—viscosity, elasticity, surface tension, permeability, and aging/solidification—that are not trivially predictable from individual components. These properties govern key cellular functions including transcriptional regulation (e.g., enhancer/promoter hubs), RNA metabolism (stress granules and P-bodies), signal transduction (e.g., T cell receptor proximal assemblies), and chromatin organization. Condensate material state can tune reaction rates, buffering capacity, selectivity, and responsiveness to stress. Conversely, aberrant material transitions (e.g., maturation into gels or solids) are implicated in neurodegeneration and myopathies, highlighting the need for principles linking composition and sequence to functional material states.

Despite rapid growth, the field remains fragmented along methodological and organismal boundaries. Biophysical measurements of condensate material properties are often reported for a limited set of proteins in specific in vitro conditions or specialized live-cell assays, and are described using heterogeneous metrics (FRAP half-times, apparent diffusion coefficients, rheology-derived moduli, coarsening rates). In parallel, cell imaging repositories contain millions of microscopy images capturing puncta, granules, and subcellular localization patterns across cell types and perturbations, yet these data are rarely connected to quantitative material-state measurements. Proteomics and interactomics resources provide deep coverage of interaction partners, stoichiometry proxies, and post-translational modifications (PTMs) that influence phase behavior, but are typically analyzed independently from imaging phenotypes. Functional genomics screens and transcriptomic perturbation datasets reveal cellular dependencies and downstream consequences, yet do not explicitly encode condensate material properties.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that unifies these disparate data modalities to address fundamental questions about emergence at the mesoscale. The proposed working group leverages only publicly available datasets and requires transdisciplinary expertise—polymer physics to formalize material regimes, cell biology to interpret assay context and biases, computer vision to quantify condensate morphology, natural language processing (NLP) to extract material metrics from literature, and statistical learning to integrate heterogeneous evidence. No single laboratory can feasibly curate cross-species condensate component knowledge, harmonize imaging-derived phenotypes with literature rheology, and build interpretable multimodal models at the necessary scale.

A synthesis effort is timely because (i) condensate component databases (LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS) have matured; (ii) structural resources (AlphaFold DB) enable systematic treatment of folded domains and multimerization interfaces; (iii) high-content imaging (Cell Painting, Image Data Resource, Human Protein Atlas, yeast GFP libraries) supports quantitative, perturbation-rich phenotyping; and (iv) functional genomics resources (DepMap, LINCS, GEO/ArrayExpress) provide mechanistic readouts. Integrating these sources can reveal conserved versus lineage-specific design rules, identify material-property regimes associated with distinct cellular outcomes, and produce generalizable, testable hypotheses about how molecular features scale into emergent mesoscale behaviors.

By producing an open knowledge graph, benchmark datasets, and community-vetted analytical workflows, this project will transform condensate biology from a collection of case studies into a predictive, quantitative science of mesoscale emergence, aligned with NCEMS’s mission to synthesize public data, develop innovative analytics, and train a data-savvy workforce.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group focuses on how molecular-scale features and interaction architectures give rise to emergent condensate material properties and how those properties map to cellular functions and dysfunction. We will treat “material state” as a latent but inferable property supported by multiple evidence types (e.g., FRAP recovery, droplet morphology and dynamics, sensitivity to perturbations, and signatures of aging). Our questions are designed to be answerable via synthesis of existing public data across species, cell types, and perturbation contexts.

RQ1: Which molecular features best predict condensate material properties across contexts?
H1.1: Multivalency and interaction-network topology (degree, clustering, motif enrichment for modular binding domains) will be stronger predictors of viscoelastic regimes than any single sequence feature alone.
H1.2: Charge patterning (e.g., κ-like measures), aromatic content, and low-complexity/disorder architecture will predict liquid-like behavior (fast recovery, spherical morphology) versus gel/solid-like behavior (slow recovery, irregular morphology), but these relationships will be modulated by the presence of folded oligomerization domains and coiled-coils.
H1.3: PTM potential (phosphorylation-rich segments, arginine methylation motifs, SUMOylation sites) will systematically shift predicted material state toward more dynamic regimes, consistent with “tunable stickers-and-spacers” models.

RQ2: Do distinct material-property regimes correspond to conserved functional outputs across species and perturbations?
H2.1: Condensates inferred to be more liquid-like will associate with rapid, reversible stress responses (e.g., translational repression and recovery) and high responsiveness to kinase/phosphatase perturbations, whereas more arrested regimes will associate with long-lived transcriptional programs or pathological proteostasis signatures.
H2.2: Across eukaryotes, stress granule-like assemblies will occupy a conserved region of material-state space characterized by moderate viscosity, high compositional turnover, and strong coupling to RNA-binding protein features; deviations from this region will correlate with disease-associated mutations and aging signatures.
H2.3: Material regimes will predict downstream phenotypes beyond localization—e.g., essentiality dependencies (DepMap), drug sensitivities, and transcriptomic modules—after controlling for expression level and baseline localization.

RQ3: What is universal versus lineage- or compartment-specific in condensate design principles?
H3.1: Universal principles will emerge at the level of coarse-grained features (valency, sticker density, interaction modularity), while lineage-specificity will appear in the particular molecular implementations (e.g., prion-like domains enriched in fungi; expanded intrinsically disordered regions in metazoan regulators).
H3.2: Nuclear condensates (transcription/splicing) will show stronger dependence on aromatic and arginine-rich motifs and chromatin-associated interaction networks; cytoplasmic condensates will show stronger coupling to translation machinery interactions and stress-responsive PTMs.

RQ4 (methodological): Can multimodal models that integrate sequence/structure, networks, images, and perturbation responses infer material state and predict functional consequences in a transferable way?
H4.1: Joint embeddings learned from multiple modalities will outperform unimodal predictors for both material-state inference and phenotype prediction, particularly when transferring across cell types and species.
H4.2: Interpretable architectures (attention over interaction motifs; sparse additive models over curated biophysical features) will identify mechanistically meaningful predictors that align with polymer-physics expectations and known disease mutations.

Together, these questions test a central premise of mesoscale emergence: that condensate material properties are an integrative phenotype arising from the interplay of molecular grammar, interaction networks, and cellular context, and that these properties causally constrain cellular function.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will execute a community-scale synthesis in four coordinated workstreams: (WS1) data assembly and harmonization, (WS2) image-derived condensate phenotyping, (WS3) literature mining and material-metric curation, and (WS4) multimodal modeling and interpretation. All work uses publicly available data; no new experiments will be performed.

WS1: Cross-modal data assembly and entity resolution. We will compile a unified registry of condensates, components, and contexts by integrating LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, and related curated resources. We will standardize identifiers (UniProt, Ensembl, gene symbols), species mapping (orthogroups via OrthoDB/eggNOG), and contextual metadata (cell type, stress/perturbation, compartment). We will construct a knowledge graph with nodes for proteins, condensates, PTMs, interactions, assays, images, and phenotypes, using a versioned schema (e.g., RO-Crate + JSON-LD) and explicit provenance.

WS2: Quantitative condensate phenotypes from public images. We will leverage segmentation-ready or high-content repositories (Image Data Resource, Cell Painting, Human Protein Atlas, yeast GFP collections). Using reproducible pipelines (CellProfiler/napari) and deep learning segmentation when needed (e.g., U-Net variants), we will extract features capturing condensate morphology and spatial organization: puncta count, size distribution, circularity, texture, intensity enrichment, co-localization proxies, and cell-to-cell heterogeneity. For datasets with time-lapse or repeated measures, we will compute dynamic proxies (appearance/disappearance rates, coarsening-like changes). We will implement rigorous QC: plate/batch correction, illumination normalization, and negative/positive control anchoring where available. Outputs will be stored as feature tables linked to image provenance.

WS3: Material-property extraction from literature and databases. We will create a curated corpus of condensate material measurements (FRAP half-times, mobile fractions, diffusion estimates, rheology-derived moduli, viscosity estimates, aging timescales). NLP pipelines (scientific language models + rule-based extraction) will identify candidate measurements, units, conditions, and constructs; expert curators will validate and annotate assay type, temperature, salt, crowding agents, and in vivo/in vitro status. We will harmonize metrics by mapping to a latent “material state” representation (e.g., probabilistic factor model) that accounts for assay-specific biases and uncertainty.

WS4: Multimodal modeling, benchmarking, and interpretation. We will build models that map from (i) sequence/disorder features (IUPred/ESpritz, prion-like scores, charge patterning, sticker density), (ii) AlphaFold-derived structural features (domain boundaries, oligomerization interfaces, confidence-weighted exposure), (iii) interaction networks (BioGRID, HuRI; graph motifs; community structure), and (iv) image-derived phenotypes to predict (a) curated material metrics and (b) downstream functional readouts (DepMap dependencies, LINCS/GEO transcriptional modules). We will compare: elastic net and GAM baselines; gradient-boosted trees; graph neural networks with attention; and multimodal fusion (late fusion and joint representation learning). We will prioritize interpretable outputs: feature attributions, motif-level attention, and partial dependence plots, and we will test transfer across species/cell types via domain adaptation and hierarchical modeling.

Validation without new experiments will rely on internal consistency checks (held-out assays/datasets), replication across independent sources, and concordance with known perturbation effects (e.g., kinase inhibition shifting stress granule dynamics). We will preregister primary analyses, define benchmark splits, and release evaluation sets to enable community comparison.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific products. (1) A public, versioned knowledge graph linking condensate components, sequence/structure features, interaction networks, imaging-derived morphology, curated material measurements, perturbations, and functional outcomes across species. (2) Harmonized “material state” labels and uncertainty-aware latent representations that reconcile heterogeneous assays (FRAP, rheology, morphological proxies). (3) Benchmark datasets and tasks for predicting condensate material properties and phenotypic consequences from multimodal inputs, with standardized train/validation/test splits and baselines. (4) Interpretable multimodal models that identify molecular and network determinants of liquid-like versus arrested regimes and that predict which perturbations shift condensates between regimes.

Biological insights. We expect to uncover conserved material-property regimes associated with shared cellular functions (e.g., stress granule-mediated translation control) and to identify lineage- or compartment-specific design strategies (e.g., fungal prion-like enrichment versus metazoan modular domain architectures). By integrating perturbation-response data, we anticipate mapping which signaling pathways and PTM programs tune condensate material state, and which genetic dependencies are selectively associated with more arrested or more dynamic condensates.

Impact on mesoscale emergence. The project advances NCEMS’s mission by converting disparate public datasets into a coherent synthesis that explains how emergent mesoscale material properties arise from molecular features and interaction architectures, and how these properties constrain higher-order cellular phenotypes. The resulting resources will enable researchers to (i) generate testable hypotheses about disease-associated mutations and pathological aging, (ii) prioritize candidate regulators that modulate condensate dynamics, and (iii) systematically compare condensate behaviors across organisms and conditions.

Community and workforce impact. The open benchmarks, code, and curation protocols will lower barriers for new entrants (including trainees and researchers from adjacent fields such as ML, physics, and network science) to contribute to condensate biology. By emphasizing reproducible workflows and interpretability, the project will also establish community standards for quantitative, integrative analysis of condensate material properties from existing data.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS resources and justification. The project requires NCEMS support because it is beyond a single lab’s capacity: it combines large-scale cross-modal data integration, community curation, and benchmarking that benefit from a neutral synthesis center to convene diverse experts, host working meetings, and support shared infrastructure. NCEMS will provide convening support (working group meetings, virtual collaboration infrastructure), facilitation for cross-disciplinary coordination, and access to computational resources appropriate for large-scale image feature extraction and model training.

Budget categories (high-level). (1) Personnel support: partial support for a project manager/data steward to coordinate curation, metadata standards, and releases; and support for trainee participation (graduate students/postdocs) via NCEMS training activities and working sessions. (2) Computing and storage: cloud/HPC credits for image processing at scale, model training, and hosting of intermediate artifacts; persistent storage for derived feature tables and knowledge-graph versions. (3) Working group convenings: travel and lodging for multi-institutional participants for 2–3 in-person meetings (including accessibility support), plus funds for virtual workshops and hackathons. (4) Software and services: costs for collaboration tooling where needed (e.g., project management, annotation platforms) while prioritizing open-source options.

Team composition and collaboration plan. The working group will include: polymer/soft-matter physicists (material-state theory and latent variable design), cell biologists with condensate expertise (assay interpretation and bias control), computer vision specialists (segmentation and feature engineering), NLP/text-mining experts (literature extraction), network scientists (interactome modeling), and statisticians/ML researchers (multimodal fusion and interpretability). We will intentionally include members across career stages, institutions (R1, PUIs), and geographies, with defined roles and rotating trainee leadership opportunities.

Feasibility and timeline. Months 0–6: schema, entity resolution, initial curation and image pipelines. Months 6–12: scaled feature extraction, literature metric harmonization, first benchmark release. Months 12–18: multimodal models, interpretability analyses, cross-species transfer tests. Months 18–24: final knowledge-graph release, manuscripts/preprints, community challenge and training modules. All milestones are achievable using existing data and NCEMS-enabled coordination and compute.

title: Emergent Principles of Organelle Contact Sites: A Synthesis of Proteomics, Imaging, and Genetic Interaction Data
abstract:
Membrane contact sites (MCS) between organelles (ER–mitochondria, ER–endosome, mitochondria–lysosome, etc.) are mesoscale hubs for lipid transfer, calcium signaling, and organelle dynamics. Despite rapid discovery of tethering proteins and lipid transporters, fundamental questions remain: What network architectures make MCS robust? Which molecular features predict contact specificity? How do contacts rewire under stress and disease? Addressing these requires synthesis across proteomics, imaging, and functional genomics—data that exist publicly but are rarely integrated.

This working group will assemble and harmonize diverse datasets: (i) proximity labeling proteomics (BioID/APEX datasets in PRIDE) targeting organelle membranes and known MCS components, (ii) subcellular localization and co-localization imaging (Human Protein Atlas, IDR, yeast GFP libraries), (iii) organelle morphology and dynamics from high-content screens (Cell Painting, Mitobank-like imaging sets), (iv) genetic interaction maps (yeast GI networks, DepMap coessentiality), and (v) lipidomics and metabolomics studies that report contact-dependent flux phenotypes (Metabolomics Workbench). We will create a standardized ontology for contact site types, experimental modalities, and confidence levels, enabling cross-study comparisons.

Scientific aims: (1) Infer a conserved “contactome” by building probabilistic networks of MCS proteins and their organelle-pair specificity across species. (2) Identify emergent network motifs (redundant tethers, modular lipid-transfer units, stress-inducible adapters) that confer robustness to perturbations. (3) Link MCS network states to higher-order phenotypes such as mitochondrial fission/fusion balance, lysosomal positioning, and unfolded protein responses, using integrated imaging and transcriptomic readouts.

Analytically, we will develop multi-layer network models that combine physical proximity evidence (proximity proteomics), functional coupling (genetic interactions/coessentiality), and spatial co-localization (image-derived metrics). We will apply community detection and dynamic network inference to detect condition-specific rewiring. To address heterogeneity and batch effects, we will use hierarchical Bayesian models and domain adaptation methods for imaging features. Interpretability will be prioritized to yield mechanistic hypotheses (e.g., predicting which tethers compensate for loss of a lipid transporter in specific cell states).

NCEMS resources are critical to convene organelle biologists, mass spectrometrists, imaging experts, network scientists, and statisticians to agree on standards, curate metadata, and build shared pipelines. The project exceeds single-lab capacity because it requires cross-modal harmonization, extensive curation of experimental context, and robust benchmarking across organisms and cell types.

Deliverables will include an open, queryable MCS knowledge graph; reproducible workflows for integrating proximity proteomics with imaging and genetics; and a set of predictive models linking contact-site composition to organelle phenotypes. Training components will include trainee-led annotation jamborees, tutorials on network inference and image feature extraction, and open challenges to engage new talent. All code, derived datasets, and documentation will be released under permissive licenses with full provenance tracking.
background_and_significance:
Membrane contact sites (MCS) are stable yet dynamic zones where two organelles approach within tens of nanometers without fusing. At this mesoscale—between individual proteins and whole organelles—MCS enable functions that neither organelle can execute alone: non-vesicular lipid exchange, rapid Ca2+ transfer, localized metabolite channeling, and coordination of fission, fusion, and motility. MCS have expanded from a handful of canonical examples (ER–mitochondria, ER–plasma membrane) to a dense web of contacts involving endosomes, lysosomes, peroxisomes, lipid droplets, and Golgi. This expansion has created a central challenge in molecular and cellular biology: understanding how emergent cellular behaviors arise from a distributed, multi-organelle interaction network.

Despite major experimental advances, MCS biology remains fragmented across subfields and modalities. Proximity labeling proteomics (BioID/APEX/TurboID) has revealed extensive candidate tether and transporter repertoires, yet these datasets are often context-specific and difficult to compare due to differing baits, labeling radii, cell types, and statistical thresholds. Imaging resources—from the Human Protein Atlas and Image Data Resource (IDR) to yeast GFP libraries and high-content morphological screens—provide spatial context, but are rarely integrated with proteomics at scale. Functional genomics adds a third perspective: genetic interaction maps in yeast and coessentiality patterns in DepMap can distinguish physical proximity from functional coupling, and can reveal redundancy and buffering—properties expected to underlie robustness. Finally, lipidomics and metabolomics studies provide phenotypic readouts of fluxes that are frequently attributed to contact-dependent pathways, but are not systematically connected to MCS composition.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that unifies these disparate public data streams into a coherent “contactome” framework. The project directly addresses emergence: MCS are mesoscale structures whose system-level properties (robustness, specificity, rewiring under stress) cannot be inferred from single-gene studies alone. The availability of vast public datasets across organisms and perturbations makes MCS an ideal testbed for NCEMS’s vision of leveraging AI and data science to discover unexpected principles.

A synthesis is needed for three reasons. First, contact specificity is poorly understood: why do certain proteins preferentially operate at ER–mitochondria versus ER–endosome contacts, and what molecular features (domains, topology, lipid-binding motifs) encode this specificity? Second, robustness is a hallmark of contact-mediated processes: cells often tolerate loss of individual tethers, implying redundancy and compensatory pathways. Determining the network architectures that enable this buffering requires integrating physical and functional evidence across many perturbations. Third, MCS are dynamic: stress, nutrient state, and disease mutations rewire contacts, but we lack generalizable models linking compositional changes to higher-order phenotypes such as mitochondrial fragmentation, lysosome repositioning, or unfolded protein responses.

By synthesizing public proteomics, imaging, genetic interaction, and metabolomics resources within an open, standardized framework, this working group will deliver a mechanistic, predictive understanding of MCS as emergent mesoscale networks. The outputs will serve as broadly reusable infrastructure for organelle biology, systems biology, and disease research, while training a data-savvy workforce in integrative, reproducible science.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will pursue three tightly linked scientific questions about emergent principles of organelle contact sites (MCS). Each question is framed to be answerable via synthesis of publicly available datasets and to yield testable, mechanistic hypotheses.

Question 1: What is the conserved, probabilistic architecture of the “contactome” across organelle pairs, organisms, and conditions?
Hypothesis 1A: MCS composition is best represented as a probabilistic multilayer network in which edges reflect distinct evidence types (physical proximity, spatial co-localization, functional coupling), and conserved cores emerge as high-confidence intersections across layers.
Hypothesis 1B: Contact specificity is encoded by a combination of (i) membrane topology (single-pass vs multi-pass), (ii) domain composition (SMP, PH, FFAT, C2, START-like), and (iii) contextual co-occurrence with organelle identity markers; these features will predict organelle-pair assignment better than any single modality.
Hypothesis 1C: Orthologous proteins will preserve “contact roles” (tether, lipid-transfer module, regulatory adaptor) even when specific partners differ, implying evolutionary conservation of mesoscale functions.

Question 2: Which network motifs and redundancies confer robustness of MCS-mediated functions to perturbation?
Hypothesis 2A: Robust MCS are characterized by redundant tethering motifs (multiple parallel edges connecting the same organelle pair) and modular lipid-transfer units (transporters plus regulators) that form semi-independent subgraphs.
Hypothesis 2B: Negative genetic interactions and coessentiality will enrich for pairs of proteins occupying parallel paths (functional redundancy), while positive interactions will enrich within modules (shared pathway). Integrating these patterns with proximity proteomics will identify compensatory tether/transfer relationships.
Hypothesis 2C: Disease-associated genes and stress-response genes will disproportionately occupy “bridge” positions (high betweenness) connecting modules, making them key determinants of failure modes when buffering is exceeded.

Question 3: How do MCS networks rewire under stress and disease-relevant states, and how does rewiring relate to higher-order organelle phenotypes?
Hypothesis 3A: Stress conditions (e.g., ER stress, oxidative stress, nutrient deprivation) induce state transitions in the contactome—detectable as changes in edge weights and community structure—rather than uniform up/down regulation.
Hypothesis 3B: Distinct rewiring programs map to specific phenotypic signatures in imaging-derived features: for example, increased ER–mitochondria tethering modules will associate with mitochondrial fragmentation and altered cristae-related proxies; increased mitochondria–lysosome coupling will associate with lysosome repositioning and mitophagy-like morphological states.
Hypothesis 3C: A small set of latent “contact states,” inferred from integrated multi-omics and imaging, will predict downstream transcriptomic stress responses (UPR, ISR, inflammatory programs) more accurately than single-gene markers.

Across all questions, we will explicitly test whether integrating modalities yields qualitatively new insights (emergent motifs, state transitions, conserved cores) that are not recoverable from any single dataset. The guiding hypothesis is that MCS function emerges from network organization and context-dependent rewiring, and that these properties can be inferred through rigorous synthesis of existing public data.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. The project will be executed as an NCEMS working group with coordinated subteams for (i) data acquisition/curation, (ii) ontology/standards, (iii) modeling and inference, (iv) benchmarking/validation via cross-dataset concordance, and (v) training and dissemination. No new experimental data will be generated; all analyses will rely on publicly available datasets.

Data sources and harmonization. We will aggregate five data classes: (1) proximity labeling proteomics (BioID/APEX/TurboID) from PRIDE and companion repositories, focusing on baits at organelle membranes and known MCS components; (2) subcellular localization and co-localization imaging from Human Protein Atlas, IDR, and yeast GFP collections; (3) high-content morphological screens (e.g., Cell Painting and organelle-focused imaging datasets) providing quantitative features for mitochondria, ER, lysosomes, peroxisomes, and lipid droplets; (4) functional genomics: yeast genetic interaction networks and human coessentiality (DepMap), plus curated CRISPR screen metadata; (5) lipidomics/metabolomics from Metabolomics Workbench and related public studies with perturbations tied to contact-dependent pathways.

We will implement a metadata-first pipeline: standardize identifiers (UniProt/Ensembl/SGD), map orthology (e.g., via OrthoDB/InParanoid resources), and normalize experimental context (cell type, perturbation, bait, labeling enzyme, imaging channel, segmentation method). Batch effects will be tracked rather than erased: we will store study-level covariates and propagate uncertainty.

Ontology and knowledge graph. We will create an MCS ontology covering organelle pairs, subtypes (e.g., ERMES-like vs VAP-FFAT mediated), evidence modalities, and confidence scoring. Entities (proteins, complexes, organelles, phenotypes, conditions) and relations (physically proximal, co-localized, genetically buffering, condition-induced) will be represented in a versioned knowledge graph (KG). The KG will support queries such as “proteins with strong ER–mitochondria proximity evidence and negative GI with lipid-transfer genes.”

Multi-layer network inference. We will build a multilayer contactome where each layer encodes an evidence type: proteomics-derived proximity edges (bait–prey and prey–prey via co-enrichment), imaging-derived co-localization edges (protein–organelle and protein–protein spatial co-occurrence), and functional coupling edges (GI/coessentiality). Edge weights will be modeled with hierarchical Bayesian approaches that incorporate study-specific noise, false discovery rates, and missingness. We will integrate layers using probabilistic graphical models and network fusion methods (e.g., similarity network fusion adapted to evidence layers), producing posterior probabilities for protein membership in specific organelle-pair contacts.

Motif discovery and robustness analysis. We will quantify network motifs (parallel tether redundancy, bow-tie modules, bipartite tether–lipid-transfer assemblies) and relate them to robustness signatures from GI/coessentiality. Community detection (multilayer Leiden/Infomap variants) will identify modules; centrality and controllability analyses will highlight bridge proteins predicted to govern failure modes.

Dynamic rewiring and phenotype linkage. Condition-specific networks will be inferred by stratifying datasets by perturbation/stress annotations and by applying dynamic network models (state-space or change-point formulations on edge weights). Imaging features will be harmonized via domain adaptation (e.g., CORAL-like alignment; hierarchical mixed models) to enable cross-study phenotype embeddings. We will link inferred contact states to phenotypes using interpretable models (sparse regression, additive models) and cross-validated prediction.

Benchmarking and quality control. We will benchmark against curated MCS gene sets, known complexes (e.g., ERMES, VAP–OSBP axes), and orthogonal evidence (literature co-mentions, curated databases). Robustness will be assessed via leave-one-study-out analyses, calibration of posterior probabilities, and sensitivity to thresholds. All pipelines will be containerized and executed in reproducible workflows.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific products. (1) A conserved, probabilistic “contactome” across major organelle pairs, with explicit uncertainty and evidence provenance. This will move the field beyond static lists of candidate tethers toward a quantitative, integrative network view. (2) Identification of emergent network motifs that explain robustness—e.g., redundant tether architectures and modular lipid-transfer units—derived from joint analysis of physical proximity and functional coupling. (3) A set of inferred condition-dependent contact states and rewiring programs, linked to higher-order organelle phenotypes such as mitochondrial fragmentation, lysosome repositioning, and ER stress signatures.

Methodological advances. The project will deliver generalizable methods for multimodal synthesis at the mesoscale: multilayer network fusion with hierarchical uncertainty, domain adaptation for integrating imaging features across heterogeneous experiments, and interpretable models that map network states to phenotypes. These approaches will be reusable for other mesoscale systems (e.g., phase-separated condensates, cytoskeletal hubs).

Community resources. We will release an open MCS knowledge graph and accompanying “contactome atlas” with interactive queries, downloadable tables, and documentation. Reproducible workflows will enable other groups to add new public datasets as they appear, ensuring longevity beyond the working group.

Impact on molecular and cellular biosciences. By revealing organizing principles that govern contact specificity, robustness, and rewiring, the project will provide a mechanistic foundation for understanding how cells coordinate metabolism, signaling, and organelle dynamics through distributed mesoscale interfaces. The results will inform disease research by prioritizing bridge proteins and modules likely to be vulnerable in neurodegeneration, metabolic disorders, and infection, while remaining strictly synthesis-based (no new experiments). Finally, the working group will train trainees in rigorous, open, cross-disciplinary data synthesis—directly advancing NCEMS goals of cultivating a data-savvy workforce and catalyzing community-scale discovery.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support rationale. The project requires intensive, coordinated synthesis across proteomics, imaging, genetics, and metabolomics—work that is beyond a single lab due to the scale of curation, the need for cross-domain standards, and the computational and collaborative overhead of building reusable community infrastructure. NCEMS resources are essential to convene multidisciplinary experts, support trainee participation, and provide a neutral venue for standards-setting and open dissemination.

Working-group meetings and collaboration. We request support for 2–3 in-person working meetings hosted by NCEMS (or hybrid), plus regular virtual sprints. Funds will cover travel, lodging, and per diem for a geographically diverse team, prioritizing participation from trainees, early-career investigators, and researchers from institutions with limited resources.

Personnel effort (synthesis-focused). Budget will support partial effort for a project coordinator/data curator (metadata harmonization, ontology management, repository deposition), and limited analyst support (workflow engineering, KG implementation, benchmarking automation). Faculty PIs will contribute in-kind scientific leadership and domain expertise. Trainees will be supported through travel and dedicated training time during sprints.

Computational resources. We will leverage NCEMS-supported compute where available and/or cloud credits for scalable processing of imaging features and network inference. Anticipated costs include storage for derived feature matrices and KG artifacts, compute for containerized workflows, and hosting for an interactive portal (or deployment on existing NCEMS infrastructure).

Community products and dissemination. Funds will support documentation, tutorial production, and maintenance of a public repository/website for the contactome atlas and knowledge graph. We will allocate resources for accessibility (captioning recorded tutorials) and for open workshops that broaden participation.

Budget principles. All expenditures directly enable synthesis (curation, integration, modeling, training, dissemination). No funds will be used for new experimental data generation. The budget will be managed to maximize reusable outputs (standards, pipelines, KG) and durable community impact aligned with NCEMS’s mission.

title: A Pan-Cell Atlas of Cytoskeletal Self-Organization: Integrating Live-Cell Imaging, Proteomics, and Biophysical Models
abstract:
The cytoskeleton is a paradigmatic emergent system: local interactions among actin, microtubules, motors, and crosslinkers generate mesoscale structures (stress fibers, asters, cortical networks) that determine cell shape, division, and migration. While thousands of imaging experiments and perturbation datasets exist, we lack a synthesis that connects molecular composition and regulation to emergent cytoskeletal architectures across cell types and conditions.

This working group will integrate publicly available resources spanning (i) live-cell imaging repositories (Image Data Resource, Cell Image Library) containing actin/microtubule reporters and perturbations, (ii) high-content morphological profiling (Cell Painting) that captures cytoskeleton-dependent shape features, (iii) proteomics of cytoskeletal fractions and interactomes (PRIDE, BioGRID), (iv) phosphorylation and signaling datasets relevant to cytoskeletal regulation (PhosphoSitePlus, CPTAC), and (v) CRISPR/RNAi perturbation screens affecting migration, adhesion, and cytokinesis (DepMap, genome-wide RNAi datasets). We will build standardized pipelines to extract quantitative descriptors of cytoskeletal organization from images (filament orientation fields, network anisotropy, bundle thickness, dynamic instability proxies) using computer vision and biophysical feature engineering.

Key questions: (1) What molecular “control knobs” (motor abundance, crosslinker type, post-translational modifications) most strongly determine emergent cytoskeletal patterns? (2) Are there universal low-dimensional “states” of cytoskeletal organization shared across cell types, or are patterns strongly context-specific? (3) Can we predict transitions between states (e.g., lamellipodial to contractile) from upstream signaling and protein composition?

We will develop integrative models that combine image-derived cytoskeletal metrics with omics features using representation learning and causal inference. A central methodological contribution will be bridging data-driven embeddings with mechanistic active gel and polymerization models: we will fit simplified biophysical models to observed mesoscale patterns, enabling interpretable parameters (effective contractility, polymerization rate, crosslinking strength) to be inferred from imaging at scale. This “mechanistic latent space” will allow cross-dataset comparisons even when imaging modalities differ.

NCEMS support is needed to coordinate multidisciplinary expertise—cell biophysicists, imaging analysts, ML researchers, and statisticians—to create community standards for cytoskeletal feature extraction and to host collaborative model-fitting sprints. The scale of harmonizing diverse imaging modalities and linking them to proteomic and perturbation data exceeds typical lab capabilities.

Outputs will include an open Cytoskeletal Self-Organization Atlas with harmonized features, metadata, and embeddings; containerized workflows for image-to-physics parameter inference; and predictive models linking molecular perturbations to emergent architectures and cellular behaviors. Training will be delivered through hands-on workshops on reproducible imaging analysis, mechanistic modeling, and multimodal data integration, with trainees leading benchmark dataset creation and documentation. All results will be disseminated openly, enabling broad reuse and accelerating discovery of general principles of cytoskeletal emergence.
background_and_significance:
The cytoskeleton exemplifies emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences: nanoscale interactions among actin and tubulin polymers, motors (myosins, kinesins, dynein), and crosslinkers (α-actinin, fascin, filamin, MAPs) give rise to mesoscale architectures such as lamellipodial branched networks, contractile stress fibers, microtubule asters, and cortical shells. These patterns are not encoded by any single molecule; rather, they arise from collective dynamics—polymerization, force generation, crosslinking, and turnover—coupled to boundary conditions (adhesion geometry, confinement) and regulatory signaling. Mesoscale cytoskeletal structures, in turn, control higher-level outcomes including cell polarity, migration modes, cytokinesis, mechanosensing, and tissue morphogenesis. Understanding how molecular composition and regulation map onto emergent cytoskeletal organization is therefore a fundamental problem at the core of NCEMS’s mission.

Despite decades of work, the field lacks a unifying, cross-context synthesis. The literature contains thousands of live-cell imaging experiments with fluorescent reporters of actin and microtubules, plus perturbations (drug treatments, knockdowns, optogenetic activations) that elicit striking reorganizations. In parallel, large-scale proteomics and interactomics have cataloged cytoskeletal components and their binding partners across cell lines, tissues, and conditions, while phosphoproteomics has documented signaling-dependent post-translational modifications that tune polymerization and contractility. Functional genomics screens (CRISPR and RNAi) have identified genes influencing migration, adhesion, and division. Yet these datasets remain siloed: imaging studies are hard to compare due to differences in microscopy modalities, labels, and analysis; omics data often lack direct links to cytoskeletal phenotypes; and mechanistic models are typically fit to small, bespoke datasets rather than community-scale observations.

A synthesis approach is now feasible and timely because (i) public repositories have matured (Image Data Resource, Cell Image Library, PRIDE, BioGRID, PhosphoSitePlus, CPTAC, DepMap), (ii) standardized morphological profiling (Cell Painting) provides a bridge between molecular perturbations and cell shape states that strongly reflect cytoskeletal organization, and (iii) modern computer vision and multimodal learning can extract quantitative descriptors from heterogeneous images and align them with omics features. Importantly, the key scientific opportunity is not simply to “predict phenotypes,” but to identify general principles—low-dimensional state spaces, conserved control parameters, and transition rules—that characterize cytoskeletal self-organization across diverse biological contexts.

This proposal directly targets NCEMS priorities. It leverages only existing, publicly available data and integrates distinct modalities at a scale beyond any single laboratory. It requires a transdisciplinary working group combining cell biophysics (to define interpretable mesoscale features and mechanistic models), imaging/data science (to build robust extraction pipelines), machine learning/statistics (to develop representation learning and causal inference), and domain experts in cytoskeletal regulation (to interpret control knobs and signaling logic). The resulting Pan-Cell Atlas will serve as a community resource for hypothesis generation, benchmarking, and mechanistic inference, enabling new insights into how emergent cytoskeletal patterns arise and how they are rewired in disease, development, and environmental adaptation.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will address three overarching questions linking molecular-level regulation to emergent mesoscale cytoskeletal organization across cell types, perturbations, and imaging modalities.

Question 1: What molecular “control knobs” most strongly determine emergent cytoskeletal patterns?
Hypothesis 1A (modular control): A small set of molecular modules—(i) actin nucleation/branching (Arp2/3, WAVE/WASP), (ii) actin bundling/crosslinking (fascin, α-actinin, filamin), (iii) myosin-II contractility and regulators (ROCK, MLCK, phospho-myosin), (iv) microtubule dynamics and stabilization (EB proteins, MAPs, stathmin), and (v) adhesion coupling (integrins, talin, vinculin)—explain most variance in cytoskeletal organization metrics across datasets.
Hypothesis 1B (PTM gating): Phosphorylation states of key regulators act as switches that shift cells between distinct organizational regimes (e.g., high myosin light chain phosphorylation promotes contractile bundles; high cofilin phosphorylation stabilizes actin networks), and these effects are detectable as consistent shifts in mechanistic latent parameters.

Question 2: Are there universal low-dimensional “states” of cytoskeletal organization shared across cell types, or are patterns strongly context-specific?
Hypothesis 2A (shared state manifold): Across cell lines and conditions, cytoskeletal architectures occupy a low-dimensional manifold with recurrent states such as (i) protrusive/lamellipodial, (ii) isotropic cortical, (iii) stress-fiber/contractile, (iv) rounded/mitotic, and (v) polarized microtubule aster/centrosomal states. These states can be recovered from image-derived features and remain stable under dataset harmonization.
Hypothesis 2B (contextual warping): While the manifold is shared, cell type and environment (substrate stiffness proxies, adhesion patterns, epithelial vs mesenchymal programs) warp state occupancy and transition probabilities. Thus, “universal states” exist, but their accessibility is modulated by context-dependent constraints.

Question 3: Can we predict transitions between cytoskeletal states from upstream signaling and protein composition, and identify likely causal drivers?
Hypothesis 3A (predictable transitions): Transitions (e.g., lamellipodial → contractile; cortical → stress fiber; interphase → cytokinetic ring) are predictable from combined features: proteomic abundances, phosphosite activities, and genetic perturbation signatures. Predictive performance will generalize across datasets when using mechanistically grounded representations.
Hypothesis 3B (causal asymmetry): Integrating perturbation data (CRISPR/RNAi, small molecules) with observational omics will reveal directional dependencies: certain regulators act as upstream causes of state changes, while others are downstream responders. Causal inference will identify a subset of robust drivers whose inferred effects are consistent across independent datasets.

Cross-cutting methodological hypothesis (mechanistic latent space): Fitting simplified active-gel and polymerization models to image-derived statistics yields interpretable latent parameters (effective contractility, polymerization rate, crosslinking strength, microtubule dynamic instability proxies) that (i) align heterogeneous imaging modalities, (ii) improve out-of-domain prediction, and (iii) enable mechanistic interpretation of learned embeddings.

Together, these questions and hypotheses aim to transform cytoskeletal biology from a collection of context-specific observations into a synthesis of generalizable, testable principles of emergence at the mesoscale.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will run an NCEMS-style synthesis working group with coordinated “integration sprints” and “analysis sprints,” each producing open datasets, code, and manuscripts. All analyses will use only publicly available data; no new experiments will be performed.

Data sources and cohort definition. We will assemble a curated corpus spanning: (i) live-cell and fixed-cell imaging with actin/microtubule reporters and perturbations from Image Data Resource (IDR) and Cell Image Library; (ii) Cell Painting morphological profiles linked to genetic and chemical perturbations (e.g., Broad Institute Cell Painting); (iii) proteomics and cytoskeletal fraction datasets from PRIDE, plus protein interaction networks from BioGRID; (iv) phosphoproteomics and signaling annotations from PhosphoSitePlus and CPTAC; and (v) functional genomics screens (DepMap CRISPR, genome-wide RNAi) for migration/adhesion/cytokinesis-related phenotypes. We will define inclusion criteria (metadata completeness, channel identity, perturbation annotation, cell line mapping) and create a harmonized sample index keyed by cell line, perturbation, and assay.

Image processing and feature extraction. We will develop standardized, containerized pipelines for: segmentation (Cellpose/StarDist where applicable), cytoskeletal enhancement (ridge filters, steerable filters), and quantitative descriptors capturing mesoscale organization: filament orientation fields, nematic order parameters, anisotropy, bundle thickness distributions, actin edge enrichment, stress-fiber density proxies, microtubule radiality/aster scores, texture features, and dynamic proxies from time series (autocorrelation, speckle-like turnover metrics, plus tracking of EB comets where available). We will benchmark against curated “gold sets” annotated by experts and trainees.

Multimodal integration and representation learning. We will align imaging-derived features with omics and perturbation features using: (i) joint embeddings via variational autoencoders or contrastive learning with modality-specific encoders; (ii) batch and modality correction (e.g., Harmony-like approaches, domain-adversarial training) to reduce dataset-specific artifacts; and (iii) graph-informed regularization using BioGRID interaction networks to encourage biologically plausible feature sharing.

Mechanistic latent space inference. We will connect data-driven embeddings to simplified mechanistic models: active gel theory for actomyosin contractility and polymer network alignment; polymerization models for actin branching vs bundling; and microtubule dynamic instability parameterizations. We will fit model parameters to image summary statistics using approximate Bayesian computation or simulation-based inference, producing interpretable parameters (effective contractility, crosslinking strength, polymerization rate, catastrophe frequency proxies). This enables cross-dataset comparison even when raw imaging differs.

Causal inference with perturbations. We will integrate CRISPR/RNAi and chemical perturbation metadata to estimate causal effects on cytoskeletal state variables. Approaches will include: (i) meta-analysis of perturbation effects across studies; (ii) causal graph discovery constrained by known signaling pathways; and (iii) instrumental-variable style analyses where perturbations serve as interventions. We will assess robustness via sensitivity analyses and replication across independent datasets.

Validation and evaluation (within synthesis constraints). We will validate by (i) cross-dataset generalization (train on one repository, test on another), (ii) held-out perturbations and cell lines, (iii) agreement with known biology (e.g., ROCK inhibition reducing contractility parameters), and (iv) uncertainty quantification for mechanistic parameters.

Deliverables will be produced iteratively: a harmonized feature table, embeddings, mechanistic parameter estimates, and predictive models, all versioned and documented for community reuse.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Primary outcome: an open Cytoskeletal Self-Organization Atlas that links mesoscale cytoskeletal organization to molecular composition, post-translational regulation, and genetic/chemical perturbations across cell types and conditions. The Atlas will include harmonized metadata, image-derived cytoskeletal descriptors, learned multimodal embeddings, and mechanistic latent parameters inferred from active-gel/polymerization models.

Scientific impact. The project will yield generalizable principles of cytoskeletal emergence by (i) identifying a small set of molecular control modules that explain major axes of cytoskeletal variation, (ii) mapping universal versus context-warped cytoskeletal state manifolds, and (iii) quantifying transition rules between states and their likely causal drivers. These results will address long-standing puzzles—why similar perturbations yield different architectures across cell types, and which regulatory levers most reliably shift organization.

Methodological impact. We will deliver community standards for cytoskeletal feature extraction and a practical bridge between data-driven vision models and interpretable biophysical parameters. The “mechanistic latent space” will provide a portable representation that enables comparisons across microscopy modalities and laboratories, supporting reproducible synthesis beyond this project.

Predictive utility. The resulting models will enable in silico prediction of how perturbations (gene knockouts, kinase activity changes, drug classes) shift cytoskeletal organization and associated behaviors (migration, adhesion, cytokinesis proxies). This can accelerate hypothesis generation in cell biology, mechanobiology, and disease contexts (e.g., metastasis, cardiomyopathies, ciliopathies) without requiring new experiments.

Community and workforce impact. The working group will cultivate a cross-disciplinary network of biophysicists, cell biologists, statisticians, and ML researchers, and will train trainees in reproducible multimodal synthesis. By producing benchmark datasets and open workflows, we will lower barriers for new investigators to enter cytoskeletal emergence research and for the broader community to test new algorithms and models on shared standards.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated, community-scale synthesis across heterogeneous datasets and disciplines, plus shared compute and convening resources that exceed typical single-lab capacity.

Budget categories (indicative, aligned to NCEMS working-group model).
1) Working group convenings and collaboration: Support for 2–3 in-person meetings at NCEMS (or NCEMS-supported venue) plus monthly virtual sprints. Funds cover travel, lodging, and per diem to ensure participation across geographic regions and institution types, including primarily undergraduate institutions and resource-limited settings.
2) Trainee participation and training: Stipends/travel awards for graduate students and postdocs to attend meetings and lead curation/benchmarking tasks; support for workshop logistics and instructional materials. This directly advances NCEMS’s workforce-training mission.
3) Research coordination and project management: Partial support for a project coordinator to manage data manifests, meeting agendas, milestone tracking, and cross-team integration; this is critical for timely delivery of interoperable outputs.
4) Computing and data infrastructure: Allocation of NCEMS compute for image processing and model training; storage for derived feature datasets; and support for maintaining a public data portal (or deposition to appropriate repositories such as Zenodo/OSF with mirrored access). We will optimize pipelines for scalable execution and provide lightweight subsets for users without large compute.
5) Software engineering and reproducibility support: Time for maintaining containerized workflows, CI testing, and documentation; support for code review and security best practices.

Resource needs and justification. Harmonizing imaging modalities and extracting cytoskeletal metrics at scale requires substantial compute and coordinated standards-setting. Mechanistic model fitting via simulation-based inference is compute intensive and benefits from shared infrastructure. Convenings are necessary to align biological interpretation, define consensus feature sets, and resolve cross-dataset mapping challenges.

Non-NCEMS contributions. Participating labs will contribute in-kind expertise, existing code, and domain knowledge; however, the integrative coordination, shared compute, and community-facing dissemination require NCEMS resources to achieve the intended scale, rigor, and openness.

title: Emergent Chromatin Domains at the Mesoscale: Synthesizing Hi-C, Imaging, and Epigenomic Data to Explain 3D Genome Function
abstract:
Chromatin folds into mesoscale structures—loops, topologically associating domains (TADs), compartments, and transcriptional hubs—that exhibit emergent behavior not predictable from individual DNA-binding events. Although vast public datasets exist (Hi-C and derivatives, ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, imaging), fundamental puzzles persist: Which molecular mechanisms are necessary and sufficient for domain formation? How do domains relate to transcriptional variability, replication timing, and genome stability across cell types and species?

This working group will synthesize (i) 3D genome conformation datasets (4D Nucleome, GEO Hi-C/Micro-C, Capture-C), (ii) super-resolution and multiplexed imaging of chromatin organization (4DN imaging, IDR), (iii) epigenomic profiles (ENCODE/Roadmap ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq), (iv) single-cell multi-omics (scATAC+scRNA, scHi-C where available), and (v) perturbation datasets targeting cohesin/CTCF, chromatin remodelers, and transcription machinery (CRISPR screens, degron time courses in GEO). We will harmonize metadata (cell cycle state, differentiation stage, perturbation timing) and implement standardized processing pipelines to generate comparable domain calls and imaging-derived spatial metrics.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify conserved versus context-specific rules linking epigenomic patterns to emergent 3D domains. (2) Quantify how perturbations shift domain boundaries and compartmentalization, and how these shifts propagate to gene expression variability and replication timing. (3) Test competing mechanistic models—loop extrusion, compartmental phase separation, transcription-driven clustering—by fitting them to cross-modal observations and evaluating predictive performance.

Methodologically, we will build a model comparison framework in which mechanistic simulations (polymer models with extrusion and compartment interactions) are calibrated using summary statistics derived from Hi-C and imaging. We will pair this with machine learning predictors that map 1D epigenomic tracks to 3D organization, using interpretable architectures (e.g., attention over regulatory elements, graph models over genomic bins). A key innovation will be integrating imaging constraints to reduce identifiability issues inherent in Hi-C-only inference.

NCEMS support is essential because the work requires coordinated expertise in polymer physics, genomics, imaging, and statistics, plus community agreement on standards for cross-study domain comparisons. The project’s scale—processing hundreds of datasets, curating perturbation metadata, and running model-fitting pipelines—demands dedicated synthesis infrastructure and collaborative working sessions.

Deliverables will include an open benchmark suite for 3D genome model evaluation; harmonized, analysis-ready matrices and imaging-derived metrics; and a public “Mechanisms of Chromatin Domains” resource with reproducible workflows. Training will be incorporated through trainee-led reproducibility audits, tutorials on 3D genome processing, and open-source contributions to simulation and ML toolkits. The synthesis will yield deeper, more generalizable insights into how mesoscale chromatin organization emerges and controls nuclear function.
background_and_significance:
Genome function is inherently three-dimensional. Regulatory elements separated by tens to hundreds of kilobases in 1D can be proximal in 3D, enabling enhancer–promoter communication, insulation, and coordinated transcription. Yet chromatin organization is not simply a sum of local binding events; it exhibits mesoscale emergent structures—loops, TADs, compartments, and transcriptional hubs—whose properties depend on collective interactions across many loci and molecular actors. Understanding how these mesoscale domains arise, how robust they are to perturbation, and how they influence cellular phenotypes remains a central challenge in molecular and cellular biology.

Over the past decade, the field has produced a vast body of publicly available data that, in principle, enables synthesis-driven progress. Bulk and single-cell Hi-C, Micro-C, and Capture-based assays map contact frequencies genome-wide across many cell types, developmental stages, and perturbations. Orthogonal imaging modalities (multiplexed DNA FISH, Oligopaint, live-cell labeling, super-resolution microscopy) provide direct spatial distances, cell-to-cell heterogeneity, and dynamic behavior. Epigenomic maps (histone modifications, transcription factor occupancy, chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation) annotate the biochemical state of the same genome. Finally, increasingly systematic perturbation datasets (acute cohesin/CTCF degradation, transcription inhibition, chromatin remodeler knockdowns, CRISPR screens) provide quasi-causal leverage. Despite this richness, key puzzles persist because datasets are siloed, processed using inconsistent pipelines, and rarely compared across modalities.

Three long-standing questions motivate this working group. First, what molecular mechanisms are necessary and sufficient for domain formation? Loop extrusion models explain many features of loops and TAD boundaries, while compartmentalization and phase-separation-like interactions explain long-range segregation of active and inactive chromatin. Transcriptional clustering and nuclear landmarks add further complexity. Each mechanism has empirical support, but their relative contributions—and when one dominates—remain unclear. Second, how do chromatin domains relate to functional outcomes such as transcriptional variability, replication timing, and genome stability? Empirical links are often correlative and cell-type specific; generalizable rules have not emerged. Third, why do different assays sometimes disagree (e.g., strong Hi-C domains without clear imaging compaction, or vice versa), and what does that imply about identifiability and model adequacy?

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that addresses these questions at the mesoscale. The proposed project aligns with NCEMS’s emphasis on emergence: chromatin domains represent collective properties arising from many weak interactions, constrained by nuclear geometry and dynamic processes. The mesoscale focus is essential because it bridges molecular mechanisms (protein binding, nucleosome modifications) and cellular outcomes (gene expression programs, replication, genome maintenance). Progress requires integrating disparate public datasets, harmonizing metadata (cell cycle, differentiation, perturbation timing), and establishing shared benchmarks for model evaluation—tasks beyond any single laboratory.

By convening experts in polymer physics, 3D genomics, imaging, epigenomics, and statistics/ML, this working group will produce a unified, testable framework for chromatin domain emergence. The synthesis will not generate new experimental data; instead, it will unlock the latent value of existing community resources, providing reproducible pipelines, cross-modal standards, and mechanistic insight that can guide future experimentation and theory. In doing so, it will help resolve foundational uncertainties about how 3D genome architecture emerges and how it shapes nuclear function across contexts and species.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will address three integrated research questions that map directly onto the emergence of mesoscale chromatin domains and their functional consequences. Each question is paired with falsifiable hypotheses designed to be testable using only publicly available data across modalities.

RQ1: What rules connect 1D epigenomic state to emergent 3D domains, and which of these rules are conserved across cell types and species?
H1.1 (conserved boundary grammar): TAD boundaries are best predicted by a conserved “boundary grammar” combining architectural protein occupancy (CTCF/cohesin when available), promoter-associated marks (H3K4me3), and local chromatin accessibility, with species- and lineage-specific tuning primarily affecting boundary strength rather than boundary position.
H1.2 (compartment state sufficiency): A/B compartment identity can be predicted from a low-dimensional epigenomic embedding dominated by transcriptional activity and repressive marks (e.g., H3K27ac/H3K4me1 vs H3K9me3/H3K27me3), and this mapping is conserved across contexts, while compartment switching is associated with coordinated changes in multiple marks rather than any single factor.
H1.3 (imaging-constrained heterogeneity): Imaging-derived distance distributions will reveal that loci with similar Hi-C compartment scores can differ substantially in spatial variability; this variability is explained by epigenomic “microstate diversity” (heterogeneity in accessibility/TF binding in single-cell data) rather than mean epigenomic levels.

RQ2: How do perturbations to architectural proteins, chromatin state regulators, and transcription machinery propagate through mesoscale organization to affect gene expression variability, replication timing, and genome stability proxies?
H2.1 (differential sensitivity): Acute cohesin depletion preferentially weakens loops and TAD insulation with limited immediate effect on compartmentalization, whereas transcription inhibition preferentially reduces active compartment clustering and transcriptional hubs with smaller effects on boundary positions.
H2.2 (functional coupling via insulation): Changes in boundary insulation (not merely contact frequency) predict changes in gene expression variability (cell-to-cell dispersion in scRNA-seq) by altering enhancer–promoter competition and regulatory neighborhood mixing.
H2.3 (replication timing mediation): Perturbation-induced compartment switching and/or hub dissolution mediates shifts in replication timing, with late-replicating heterochromatin showing higher structural robustness than early-replicating active regions.

RQ3: Which mechanistic models (loop extrusion, compartmental/phase-separation-like interactions, transcription-driven clustering) best explain cross-modal observations, and can a unified model predict unseen datasets?
H3.1 (model identifiability improvement): Incorporating imaging constraints (distance distributions, radial positioning, hub counts) into model calibration will reduce parameter non-identifiability present in Hi-C-only fitting and improve out-of-sample prediction across cell types.
H3.2 (context-dependent model dominance): No single mechanism explains all contexts; instead, model comparison will show that extrusion dominates TAD-scale statistics in interphase cycling cells, while compartmental interactions dominate megabase-scale segregation, and transcription-driven clustering is required to explain hub-like features and their perturbation sensitivity.
H3.3 (predictive sufficiency of hybrid models): A hybrid mechanistic model combining extrusion plus compartment interactions will predict bulk Hi-C and imaging statistics, but explaining single-cell variability and hub formation will require an additional stochastic clustering component linked to transcriptional state.

Collectively, these hypotheses convert a fragmented literature into a coherent synthesis agenda: discover conserved rules, quantify causal propagation using perturbations, and adjudicate competing mechanisms using rigorous cross-modal model comparison.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will execute a community-scale synthesis in four coordinated workstreams: (W1) data inventory and metadata harmonization; (W2) standardized processing and feature extraction for Hi-C/Micro-C, imaging, and epigenomics; (W3) cross-modal integration and predictive modeling; (W4) mechanistic model calibration and comparison. The project uses only publicly available datasets and will be organized around iterative NCEMS working sessions to converge on standards, benchmarks, and shared analyses.

W1: Dataset selection and metadata harmonization. We will curate a tiered corpus: Tier A “gold standard” datasets with matched modalities in the same cell type/condition (e.g., 4D Nucleome cell lines with Hi-C + imaging + ChIP/ATAC); Tier B datasets with partial overlap; Tier C perturbation time courses (degron, inhibitor, CRISPR). Metadata fields will be normalized using controlled vocabularies: cell type/lineage, species/build, cell cycle state, differentiation stage, perturbation target, dose, and time post-perturbation. We will implement a machine-readable schema (JSON/YAML) and use programmatic validation to flag inconsistencies.

W2: Standardized processing and feature extraction.
Hi-C/Micro-C: Reprocess raw or uniformly processed contact matrices when available; otherwise ingest standardized matrices (e.g., .cool/.mcool). Apply consistent normalization (e.g., ICE/VC or alternative with sensitivity analysis). Call loops (where resolution allows), TADs/boundaries (multiple callers), and compartments (eigenvectors) across resolutions. Extract summary statistics: insulation profiles, boundary strength, contact decay, compartment strength, and distance-dependent scaling.
Imaging: From multiplexed DNA FISH and super-resolution datasets, extract locus-pair distance distributions, radial positioning, domain compaction metrics, and hub statistics (cluster counts/sizes). Map probes to genomic coordinates and harmonize to reference builds.
Epigenomics and single-cell: Ingest ENCODE/Roadmap ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq tracks; compute binned features aligned to Hi-C bins. For scATAC/scRNA, compute cell-state embeddings and variability metrics (e.g., gene expression dispersion controlling for mean) aligned to genomic neighborhoods.

W3: Cross-modal integration and ML prediction. We will train interpretable predictors mapping 1D features to 3D outcomes (boundary probability, compartment score, hub propensity). Candidate models include attention-based sequence/track models and graph neural networks over genomic bins with edges informed by linear adjacency and known regulatory links. Evaluation will use strict train/test splits by chromosome and by dataset (leave-one-cell-type-out) to assess generalization. Imaging-derived constraints will be used as auxiliary losses or calibration targets to prevent Hi-C-only overfitting.

W4: Mechanistic modeling and model comparison. We will implement a common interface for polymer simulations incorporating: (i) loop extrusion with tunable loading, processivity, and barrier parameters; (ii) compartment interactions parameterized by epigenomic state; (iii) optional transcription-driven clustering terms. Models will be calibrated to match multi-objective summary statistics from Hi-C and imaging using Bayesian optimization or approximate Bayesian computation. We will compare models using predictive likelihood on held-out datasets and posterior predictive checks, emphasizing falsifiable discrepancies (e.g., correct Hi-C but incorrect distance distributions).

Feasibility and risk mitigation. Key risks are heterogeneity in data quality and assay differences. We address this via tiered datasets, sensitivity analyses across callers/normalizations, and explicit uncertainty propagation (bootstrap across replicates, hierarchical models across studies). The NCEMS working-group format is essential for consensus on standards, coordinated code development, and rapid cross-disciplinary iteration.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific outcomes. (1) A quantitative, cross-context “rulebook” linking epigenomic patterns to mesoscale chromatin domains, separating conserved determinants (shared across lineages/species) from context-specific modifiers (cell cycle, differentiation, perturbation timing). (2) A causal propagation map showing how perturbations to cohesin/CTCF, chromatin regulators, and transcription machinery alter boundary insulation, compartment strength, and hub organization—and how these structural changes relate to gene expression variability and replication timing. (3) A rigorous adjudication of mechanistic hypotheses through cross-modal model comparison, clarifying when loop extrusion is sufficient, when compartmental interactions dominate, and when additional clustering mechanisms are required to explain imaging and single-cell variability.

Methodological outcomes. (4) A public benchmark suite for 3D genome model evaluation, including standardized datasets, summary statistics, and scoring protocols that incorporate both Hi-C and imaging constraints. (5) Harmonized, analysis-ready resources: uniformly processed contact matrices (or standardized ingestions), domain calls with uncertainty estimates, imaging-derived spatial metrics mapped to genomic coordinates, and matched epigenomic feature matrices. (6) Open-source, modular workflows for reprocessing, feature extraction, ML prediction, and mechanistic simulation calibration, enabling other groups to extend analyses to new datasets without reinventing pipelines.

Impact on the molecular and cellular sciences. This synthesis will transform fragmented evidence into generalizable principles of chromatin domain emergence at the mesoscale, directly advancing NCEMS’s mission to explain unexpected system-level properties arising from many interacting components. By integrating orthogonal modalities, the project will reduce ambiguity in interpreting Hi-C, improve identifiability of mechanistic models, and provide a shared foundation for future experimental design (e.g., which perturbations best discriminate models, which imaging readouts resolve uncertainties). The deliverables will lower barriers for new entrants, support reproducible cross-study comparisons, and accelerate discovery in genome regulation, development, and disease contexts where 3D genome organization is implicated.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS working-group support needs. This project requires coordinated, multi-lab synthesis that exceeds the capacity of any single group due to (i) the scale and heterogeneity of public 3D genome and imaging datasets, (ii) the need for consensus standards and shared benchmarks, and (iii) the computational burden of uniform processing and mechanistic model calibration. NCEMS resources are essential to convene the team, provide collaborative infrastructure, and support trainee-driven integration work.

Requested budget categories (illustrative, aligned to typical synthesis-center mechanisms).
1) Working meetings and collaboration: Support for 3–4 in-person working sessions at NCEMS (or NCEMS-supported venues) plus monthly virtual sprints. Costs include participant travel, lodging, and meeting logistics to ensure participation across geographic regions and institution types.
2) Personnel time for synthesis: Partial support for a project coordinator/data steward (metadata schema, dataset tracking, releases), plus limited support for research software engineering to harden workflows, containers, and benchmarking infrastructure. This is crucial for producing community-grade, reusable deliverables.
3) Trainee support and training activities: Travel and subsistence for graduate students/postdocs to attend working sessions; support for trainee-led reproducibility audits, tutorial development, and office-hour style community onboarding.
