4) Computing and storage: Cloud or institutional compute credits for large-scale reprocessing of contact matrices, ML training, and simulation-based calibration; storage for intermediate artifacts and cached public data downloads. We will minimize costs by prioritizing tiered datasets and using efficient data formats (cooler/zarr/parquet).

In-kind contributions and leveraged resources. Participating labs will contribute domain expertise, existing open-source tools, and institutional compute where feasible. We will leverage public repositories (4DN, ENCODE, GEO, Roadmap) and existing community standards (e.g., cooler formats, 4DN metadata conventions) while extending them for cross-modal integration.

Budget justification (why NCEMS). The primary value of NCEMS funding is catalytic: enabling intensive, structured collaboration, shared infrastructure, and workforce training to produce benchmarked, reproducible synthesis products that the broader community can adopt and extend.

title: A Unified Synthesis of Protein Complex Stoichiometry and Assembly Pathways from Structural, Proteomic, and Ribosome Profiling Data
abstract:
Cells rely on thousands of protein complexes whose emergent functions depend on correct stoichiometry and assembly order. Despite abundant public data—structures, interaction maps, quantitative proteomics, and translation dynamics—we lack an integrated understanding of how assembly pathways and dosage constraints shape complex composition across conditions and species. This working group will build a synthesis framework to infer complex stoichiometry control principles and predict assembly vulnerabilities.

We will integrate (i) structural repositories (PDB, AlphaFold DB, EMDB) to define interfaces and assembly intermediates, (ii) curated complex catalogs (CORUM, Complex Portal), (iii) quantitative proteomics across tissues and perturbations (PRIDE, CPTAC), (iv) ribosome profiling and translation initiation datasets (GWIPS-viz-linked studies in GEO), (v) chaperone interaction and co-translational assembly evidence (BioGRID, proximity labeling proteomics), and (vi) genetic dependency/interaction data (DepMap, yeast GI). Harmonization will include mapping orthologs, standardizing protein identifiers, and annotating complex membership confidence.

Core questions: (1) What global rules govern complex stoichiometry—are there conserved “dosage buffering” strategies across complex types (ribosomes, proteasomes, membrane complexes)? (2) Can we infer assembly order from co-translational interaction signals, interface topology, and translation timing, and how does this differ across organisms? (3) Which complexes are most sensitive to subunit imbalance, and can we predict disease-relevant vulnerabilities (e.g., haploinsufficiency, aneuploidy effects)?

Analytical approach: We will develop probabilistic models that combine structural interface graphs with quantitative abundance and translation-rate data to infer latent assembly pathways and stoichiometric constraints. Network flow and Bayesian structure learning will be used to rank plausible assembly orders consistent with co-translational evidence. We will also build predictive models linking inferred imbalance sensitivity to genetic dependency patterns and proteostasis stress signatures.

NCEMS support is required because the project spans structural biology, proteomics, translation biology, and statistical modeling, and demands coordinated curation and scalable computation. No single lab typically has access to the breadth of expertise needed to reconcile structural interface information with proteome-wide quantitative constraints.

Deliverables: (i) an open “Complex Assembly Atlas” with inferred stoichiometries, assembly pathway hypotheses, and confidence scores; (ii) reproducible pipelines for integrating structure, proteomics, and ribosome profiling; (iii) benchmarks for assembly inference methods; and (iv) case studies on medically relevant complexes (mitochondrial OXPHOS, spliceosome, chromatin remodelers). Training will include workshops on proteomics harmonization, structural data parsing, and Bayesian modeling, with trainees leading curation of specific complex families. All outputs will be released openly with versioned datasets and transparent provenance, enabling the community to test and refine emergent principles of complex assembly.
background_and_significance:
Protein complexes are the primary functional units of the cell, enabling emergent behaviors—catalysis, transport, signaling, and genome regulation—that cannot be predicted from isolated subunits. These emergent properties depend critically on two coupled features: (i) stoichiometry, the relative dosage of each subunit available for assembly, and (ii) assembly pathways, the ordered sequence of binding events and intermediates that yield a mature complex. Failures in either dimension generate toxic orphan subunits, proteostasis stress, altered interaction networks, and disease phenotypes, including haploinsufficiency syndromes, aneuploidy-associated vulnerabilities, neurodegeneration, and cancer dependencies.

Despite decades of biochemical and structural work, our understanding remains fragmented. Structural repositories (PDB, EMDB) and predicted models (AlphaFold DB) capture interfaces and plausible quaternary arrangements for many complexes, but they rarely encode the kinetics or order of assembly. Curated catalogs such as CORUM and Complex Portal define membership and functional annotation, yet they do not quantify condition-specific stoichiometry. Quantitative proteomics resources (PRIDE, CPTAC) provide large-scale abundance measurements across tissues, perturbations, and disease states, but abundance alone does not reveal which subunits are limiting or buffered, nor how abundance aligns with actual assembled complex levels. Ribosome profiling datasets in GEO (discoverable via GWIPS-viz) provide translation initiation and elongation dynamics that can reveal co-translational assembly signatures and timing offsets between subunits, but these signals are rarely integrated with structural interface topology. Finally, interaction and dependency resources (BioGRID, proximity labeling proteomics, DepMap, yeast genetic interaction maps) contain evidence for chaperone involvement, transient intermediates, and fitness consequences of subunit perturbation, yet they are typically analyzed separately from structural and translational constraints.

This proposal addresses a central synthesis gap: we lack a unified, quantitative framework that reconciles structural interface architecture with proteome-wide dosage constraints and translation dynamics to infer assembly pathways and predict which complexes are vulnerable to imbalance. Filling this gap directly aligns with NCEMS’s focus on mesoscale emergence. Protein complexes occupy the mesoscale between molecules and organelles, and their collective behaviors—buffering, cooperative assembly, and quality-control routing—create system-level properties such as robustness to dosage variation and conditional fragility under stress.

The opportunity is uniquely ripe because the necessary data already exist publicly at community scale, but integration requires coordinated expertise and infrastructure beyond a single laboratory. Mapping identifiers and orthologs across modalities, curating complex definitions, extracting interface graphs from heterogeneous structural sources, normalizing proteomics across studies, and harmonizing ribosome profiling signals into comparable translation-timing features are each nontrivial. Moreover, the conceptual integration—linking interface topology and translation timing to plausible assembly orders, then connecting inferred assembly constraints to genetic dependencies—demands a transdisciplinary team spanning structural biology, proteomics, translation regulation, network science, and Bayesian/statistical modeling.

By synthesizing these data, the working group will produce generalizable principles of stoichiometry control and assembly, a community resource (“Complex Assembly Atlas”), and validated analytical strategies for mesoscale inference. The resulting insights will help explain long-standing puzzles such as why some complexes tolerate subunit imbalance while others collapse, how co-translational interactions shape assembly trajectories, and which complexes become liabilities in disease contexts characterized by dosage perturbation.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will address three interconnected scientific questions about emergent properties of protein complex formation. Each question is paired with testable hypotheses that can be evaluated using only publicly available data integrated across modalities.

Question 1: What global rules govern complex stoichiometry across conditions and species?
Hypothesis 1A (dosage buffering classes): Complexes fall into conserved “buffering regimes” that can be inferred from multi-study proteomics: (i) tightly buffered complexes where subunit abundances co-vary to preserve stoichiometry, (ii) partially buffered complexes with one or a few limiting subunits that set assembly capacity, and (iii) weakly buffered complexes where excess subunits are tolerated via degradation or alternative complex membership.
Hypothesis 1B (topology–stoichiometry coupling): Interface topology predicts buffering regime. Specifically, complexes with high interface centralization (hub subunits with many contacts) will exhibit stronger dosage control on hub abundance and stronger signatures of orphan-subunit degradation for peripheral partners.
Hypothesis 1C (conservation of limiting subunits): Across orthologous complexes, the identity of limiting subunits (as inferred from abundance ratios and dependency patterns) is conserved more often than expected by chance, reflecting evolutionary optimization of assembly control.

Question 2: Can assembly order be inferred from co-translational interaction evidence, interface architecture, and translation timing, and how does it differ across organisms?
Hypothesis 2A (co-translational precedence): Subunits that engage in co-translational interactions (e.g., nascent chain binding detected by proximity labeling or curated evidence) are earlier in assembly order than subunits lacking such evidence, conditional on interface exposure timing.
Hypothesis 2B (interface accessibility constraint): Assembly steps preferentially occur when the relevant interfaces are structurally accessible in intermediates; thus, assembly order can be constrained by a directed acyclic graph derived from interface occlusion/creation across plausible subcomplexes.
Hypothesis 2C (translation-timing coordination): Ribosome profiling-derived initiation rates and elongation profiles predict temporal coordination among interacting subunits; interacting pairs with strong co-translational assembly evidence will show reduced timing offsets compared to non-interacting pairs, after controlling for expression level and subcellular localization.
Hypothesis 2D (organismal divergence): While high-level assembly motifs (e.g., scaffold-first vs. modular subassembly) are conserved, specific ordering and co-translational signatures differ between yeast and human for complexes with expanded paralogy or additional regulatory subunits.

Question 3: Which complexes are most sensitive to subunit imbalance, and can we predict disease-relevant vulnerabilities?
Hypothesis 3A (imbalance sensitivity signature): Complexes with (i) strong stoichiometric buffering, (ii) high interface centralization, and (iii) extensive co-translational assembly evidence are more sensitive to perturbation of specific subunits, reflected in DepMap dependency strength and yeast genetic interaction severity.
Hypothesis 3B (haploinsufficiency and aneuploidy linkage): Subunits predicted to be limiting and early-assembling are enriched for haploinsufficient genes and show stronger negative fitness consequences under copy-number loss or dosage imbalance contexts.
Hypothesis 3C (proteostasis coupling): Complexes predicted to generate many orphan subunits under imbalance will correlate with proteostasis stress signatures (e.g., chaperone engagement, unfolded protein response markers) in perturbation proteomics datasets.

Together, these questions aim to reveal emergent mesoscale principles: how structural constraints, translational dynamics, and cellular quality control jointly shape robust yet conditionally fragile complex formation across the tree of life.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will execute a community-scale synthesis pipeline that integrates structural, proteomic, translational, interaction, and dependency data into unified probabilistic models. The working group will include domain leads for (i) structural interface extraction, (ii) proteomics normalization, (iii) ribosome profiling feature engineering, (iv) statistical/Bayesian modeling, and (v) biological interpretation and benchmarking. All analyses will use only publicly available datasets.

1) Data assembly and harmonization.
Complex definitions: Start from CORUM and Complex Portal; create a consensus complex set with membership confidence scores (e.g., agreement across catalogs, evidence codes). Map proteins to UniProt accessions; propagate to Ensembl/RefSeq where needed.
Orthology mapping: Use public orthology resources (e.g., Ensembl Compara/OMA) to connect yeast–human and other model organisms for conserved complexes.
Structural interfaces: For each complex, extract interface graphs from PDB biological assemblies and EMDB-derived models when available; supplement missing structures with AlphaFold DB multimer predictions or monomeric models combined with known interaction pairs. Compute residue–residue contact maps and derive subunit–subunit interface weights (area, predicted confidence, conservation).
Proteomics: Aggregate quantitative proteomics from PRIDE and CPTAC with standardized processing metadata. Harmonize to comparable abundance units via within-study normalization and cross-study scaling using shared reference proteins/housekeeping sets; annotate tissue/condition.
Ribosome profiling: Curate ribo-seq datasets via GEO/GWIPS-viz links; compute gene-level initiation/elongation proxies, translation efficiency, and condition-specific timing features. Where available, extract subcellular fraction or stress condition labels.
Co-translational and chaperone evidence: Integrate BioGRID interactions, curated co-translational assembly reports, and proximity labeling proteomics; encode as edge priors on subunit pairs and as chaperone association scores.
Genetic dependency/interaction: Use DepMap CRISPR dependency profiles and yeast GI networks; map to complex membership and orthologs.

2) Stoichiometry inference and buffering regimes.
For each complex and condition, estimate relative stoichiometry by comparing subunit abundance ratios to catalog stoichiometries where known. Use hierarchical Bayesian models to separate measurement noise, batch effects, and true condition effects, yielding posterior distributions over subunit ratios and a “buffering index” capturing how tightly ratios are maintained across conditions.

3) Assembly pathway inference.
Construct a constrained assembly search space: nodes are subcomplex states; edges are allowed binding events consistent with interface topology (e.g., a subunit can bind only if its interface partner is present and interface is exposed). Incorporate priors from co-translational evidence (favor early binding), translation timing (favor temporally proximal subunits), and chaperone associations (allow otherwise unfavorable steps).
Apply (i) Bayesian structure learning to infer directed assembly graphs and (ii) network flow/shortest-path formulations to rank high-probability assembly routes. Output a posterior over assembly orders and key intermediates with confidence scores.

4) Predicting imbalance sensitivity and disease relevance.
Train predictive models (regularized regression, gradient boosting, and Bayesian additive models) linking inferred features—buffering index, limiting-subunit probability, interface centralization, co-translational priors, and orphan burden estimates—to DepMap dependencies and yeast GI severity. Evaluate enrichment for haploinsufficiency and copy-number sensitivity using public gene-constraint metrics.

5) Benchmarking and case studies.
Benchmark against complexes with experimentally characterized assembly (proteasome, ribosome subassemblies, OXPHOS, spliceosome modules). Perform ablation studies (remove one modality) to quantify the marginal value of each data type. Produce deep-dive case studies emphasizing medically relevant complexes and cross-species comparisons.

NCEMS enablement. NCEMS support will provide the convening power for cross-domain curation standards, coordinated compute for scalable interface extraction and ribo-seq processing, and an iterative working-group model to align methods, validate outputs, and deliver community-facing resources beyond single-lab capacity.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Primary products. (1) Complex Assembly Atlas: an open, versioned resource containing (i) harmonized complex definitions and orthology links, (ii) inferred condition-specific stoichiometry distributions, (iii) predicted limiting subunits and buffering regimes, (iv) probabilistic assembly pathway hypotheses with intermediate states, and (v) vulnerability scores indicating sensitivity to imbalance. Each entry will include provenance, confidence metrics, and links to underlying public datasets.

Methodological advances. We will deliver validated synthesis methods that integrate structural interface graphs with proteomics and translation dynamics—an analytical strategy broadly applicable to mesoscale emergence problems. Key advances include: (i) hierarchical models that quantify stoichiometric buffering across heterogeneous proteomics studies, (ii) assembly-order inference under explicit structural constraints with probabilistic priors from co-translational evidence, and (iii) predictive linking of assembly/stoichiometry features to genetic dependency landscapes.

Scientific insights. The project will generate general principles describing how cells achieve robust complex formation despite fluctuating expression and how that robustness breaks under perturbation. Expected insights include identifying conserved buffering regimes across complex classes, revealing when co-translational assembly is a dominant organizing principle, and clarifying which structural topologies produce high orphan-subunit burden and proteostasis stress.

Broader impacts for disease and biotechnology. Vulnerability predictions will help prioritize complexes and subunits likely to be dosage sensitive in aneuploidy, copy-number variation, and haploinsufficiency contexts, providing hypotheses for mechanistic follow-up by the community (without generating new data in this project). The Atlas will also support synthetic biology and protein engineering by highlighting assembly bottlenecks and stoichiometric constraints relevant to reconstituting complexes.

Workforce and community impact. Trainees will gain portable skills in data harmonization, reproducible pipelines, Bayesian modeling, and responsible AI/data science. By publishing benchmarks and transparent workflows, we will lower barriers for new groups to contribute improvements, extend to additional organisms, and test emergent mesoscale theories of complex formation.
budget_and_resources:
Budget rationale (NCEMS working-group model). The project’s primary costs are personnel time for cross-domain synthesis, convening and coordination, compute for large-scale public-data processing, and trainee-centered training activities. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation.

1) Personnel support. Funds will support partial effort for a cross-institutional team including: (i) a project manager/data steward to coordinate data governance, identifier mapping, and releases; (ii) a research software engineer to build and maintain containerized workflows, CI, and the Atlas API; (iii) quantitative scientists to implement Bayesian and network-flow models; and (iv) domain experts (structural biology, proteomics, translation) contributing curated rules and validation. Trainees (graduate students/postdocs) will be supported for focused curation/modeling sprints and will lead documentation and tutorial development.

2) Convening and collaboration resources. NCEMS support is essential to convene 2–3 intensive working meetings plus regular virtual sessions, enabling rapid iteration across disciplines. Budget includes travel and lodging for geographically distributed participants, with explicit support for early-career researchers and participants from institutions with fewer resources.

3) Compute and storage. Large-scale interface extraction from structural repositories, reprocessing/feature extraction from ribosome profiling datasets, and cross-study proteomics harmonization require scalable compute and storage. Funds will cover cloud/HPC allocations, data egress where unavoidable, and long-term archival storage for derived, shareable datasets and model artifacts.

4) Training and dissemination. Budget supports hands-on workshops (hybrid where possible), tutorial materials, and mini-hackathons focused on (i) proteomics harmonization, (ii) structural interface graph construction, and (iii) probabilistic modeling for assembly inference. We will also allocate resources for accessibility (captioning, recorded sessions) and for maintaining a public documentation site.

5) NCEMS value-add beyond a single lab. The scope demands coordinated standards, shared infrastructure, and sustained cross-lab integration. NCEMS resources will enable neutral convening, shared compute, and professional data stewardship, ensuring the Atlas and pipelines are community-grade, maintained, and broadly reusable.

title: Mesoscale Metabolic Channeling: Synthesizing Spatial Proteomics, Metabolomics, and Enzyme Complex Data to Map Functional Microdomains
abstract:
Metabolism is often depicted as a well-mixed network, yet growing evidence suggests enzymes form mesoscale assemblies and microdomains that enable metabolic channeling—emergent behavior where spatial organization alters flux, noise, and regulation. Public datasets now include spatial proteomics, organelle proteomes, metabolomics, and interaction maps, but they are rarely integrated to test when and where channeling occurs and what design principles govern it.

This working group will synthesize (i) spatial proteomics and subcellular fractionation datasets (Human Protein Atlas spatial proteomics, PRIDE fractionation studies), (ii) proximity labeling proteomics for metabolic enzymes (PRIDE), (iii) metabolomics across compartments and perturbations (Metabolomics Workbench, HMDB-linked studies), (iv) protein complex and interaction data (CORUM, BioGRID), (v) imaging-based localization for metabolic enzymes (IDR, HPA immunofluorescence), and (vi) genome-scale metabolic models and flux datasets (BiGG, published 13C MFA datasets with shared raw data). We will curate evidence for enzyme co-localization, complex formation, and condition dependence.

Scientific questions: (1) Which pathways exhibit strongest signatures of channeling (e.g., glycolysis, purine synthesis, TCA-associated metabolons), and are these conserved across taxa? (2) How do stress, cell cycle, or differentiation alter metabolic microdomain organization? (3) Can spatial organization explain discrepancies between enzyme abundance and observed metabolite levels or fluxes?

Methodological innovations will include constructing “spatially annotated metabolic networks” where edges are weighted by co-localization and complex evidence, enabling simulations that compare well-mixed versus microdomain-constrained flux. We will develop statistical tests for channeling signatures using metabolite covariance patterns and perturbation responses, and integrate imaging/proteomics priors to constrain model space. Machine learning will be used to predict microdomain formation propensity from enzyme features (oligomerization, disorder, membrane association) and interaction network context.

NCEMS support is essential to convene metabolomics experts, systems biologists, proteomics specialists, and biophysicists to align on standards for spatial evidence and to build interoperable pipelines across omics modalities. The project’s scope—harmonizing metabolomics metadata, mapping metabolites across platforms, and integrating with localization and interaction data—requires dedicated synthesis infrastructure.

Deliverables will include an open atlas of candidate metabolic microdomains with evidence scores; reproducible workflows for mapping metabolites and spatial proteomics into compartment-resolved models; and a set of community benchmarks for detecting channeling from public data. Training will be provided through hands-on modules on metabolomics normalization, network modeling, and FAIR data practices, with trainees leading pathway-focused curation efforts. The synthesis will advance understanding of emergent metabolic behavior arising from mesoscale spatial organization.
background_and_significance:
Metabolism is traditionally represented as a set of reactions connected by diffusible intermediates in a well-mixed cytosol and organelles. This abstraction underpins genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs), flux balance analysis, and many interpretations of metabolomics. Yet cells are not well-stirred reactors: they are crowded, structured, and dynamically reorganized. Increasing evidence indicates that enzymes can assemble into mesoscale complexes (“metabolons”), associate with membranes or cytoskeletal scaffolds, partition into phase-separated condensates, or co-localize within organelle subdomains. These spatial organizations can produce metabolic channeling—preferential transfer of intermediates between sequential enzymes—an emergent property where collective spatial arrangement alters system-level behavior such as flux control, noise filtering, and responsiveness to perturbations.

Despite decades of biochemical observations, channeling remains difficult to establish and generalize across pathways, cell types, and conditions. Classical demonstrations rely on specialized assays (e.g., isotope dilution, transient time analysis, enzyme tethering) that are not easily scaled, and they often focus on a small number of pathways. Meanwhile, modern data resources have exploded: spatial proteomics and subcellular fractionation provide quantitative localization patterns; proximity labeling identifies neighborhood proteomes around bait enzymes; curated complex databases catalog stable assemblies; imaging repositories provide single-cell localization and co-occurrence; and metabolomics plus 13C flux datasets quantify pathway outputs under perturbations. However, these datasets are typically analyzed in isolation, using incompatible identifiers, variable metadata quality, and differing spatial resolutions. The result is a missed opportunity to test, at community scale, when spatial organization is necessary to explain metabolic phenotypes.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze synthesis research on mesoscale emergence. The mesoscale—between individual biomolecules and organelles—is precisely where metabolons, enzyme clusters, and microdomains operate, and where emergent metabolic behaviors can arise from collective interactions. A synthesis effort can leverage publicly available data to infer microdomain candidates, quantify evidence for co-localization and complex formation, and connect spatial organization to flux and metabolite patterns. Importantly, such integration requires expertise spanning proteomics, metabolomics, imaging, systems biology, biophysics of organization, and statistical/machine learning—well beyond the capacity of any single lab.

Understanding metabolic channeling has broad significance. First, it provides a mechanistic explanation for persistent discrepancies between enzyme abundance and metabolite levels, and for why GEMs sometimes fail to predict flux rerouting under stress or differentiation. Second, it reframes metabolic regulation as an emergent property of spatial organization, potentially revealing design principles (e.g., pathway topology, intermediate instability, thermodynamic driving forces, or toxicity) that favor microdomain formation. Third, it has translational relevance: many diseases involve metabolic rewiring and altered organelle structure; if channeling is condition-dependent, it may represent an underappreciated layer of vulnerability or robustness. Finally, establishing interoperable pipelines and benchmarks for detecting channeling from public data will empower the broader community to incorporate spatial constraints into metabolic modeling and hypothesis generation.

This working group will address these needs by synthesizing multiple public modalities into a unified, evidence-scored atlas of candidate metabolic microdomains and a set of reproducible computational tools to test channeling hypotheses across pathways, taxa, and conditions.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will pursue three tightly linked research questions aimed at identifying when metabolic channeling is likely, how it changes across contexts, and whether it resolves long-standing modeling inconsistencies. Across all questions, we define “channeling signature” operationally as convergent evidence that (i) sequential enzymes are co-localized beyond expectation, (ii) physical association or shared neighborhood is supported, and (iii) metabolite/flux behavior is better explained by constrained intermediate exchange than by a well-mixed assumption.

RQ1: Which metabolic pathways exhibit the strongest and most reproducible signatures of channeling, and are these signatures conserved across taxa?
Hypothesis 1A (pathway propensity): Pathways with unstable, reactive, or toxic intermediates (e.g., aldehydes, acyl-phosphates), high local demand for throughput, or strong thermodynamic coupling will show stronger microdomain evidence than pathways with stable, freely diffusing intermediates.
Hypothesis 1B (topology and stoichiometry): Linear pathways with high-flux sequential steps (e.g., glycolysis segments), or branched pathways with committed steps (e.g., purine biosynthesis), will exhibit higher co-localization/complex scores than highly distributed networks.
Hypothesis 1C (conservation): Core bioenergetic and nucleotide pathways will show conserved microdomain candidates across eukaryotes, while specialized pathways will show lineage- and compartment-specific organization.

RQ2: How do stress, cell cycle, and differentiation alter metabolic microdomain organization?
Hypothesis 2A (stress-induced reorganization): Oxidative stress, nutrient limitation, and heat shock will increase assembly of channeling-prone pathways by promoting enzyme clustering, membrane association, or condensate formation, yielding higher co-localization and proximity-labeling evidence under stress than in baseline conditions.
Hypothesis 2B (cell-state specificity): Differentiation and cell-cycle transitions will rewire microdomain organization in ways that align with changing biosynthetic demands (e.g., S-phase nucleotide synthesis), producing predictable shifts in microdomain scores and compartmentalization.
Hypothesis 2C (organelle coupling): Conditions that alter organelle morphology (e.g., mitochondrial dynamics, ER stress) will modulate microdomains at organelle contact sites, increasing evidence for spatial coupling between pathways distributed across compartments.

RQ3: Can spatial organization explain discrepancies between enzyme abundance and observed metabolite levels or fluxes?
Hypothesis 3A (model mismatch reduction): For selected pathways, incorporating spatially constrained intermediate transfer into GEM-derived simulations will reduce residual error between predicted and observed flux/metabolite responses to perturbations compared to well-mixed models.
Hypothesis 3B (covariance fingerprints): Channeling will manifest as characteristic metabolite covariance and perturbation-response patterns—specifically, reduced intermediate pool variability relative to upstream/downstream metabolites and dampened accumulation under partial inhibition—consistent across datasets when microdomain evidence is high.
Hypothesis 3C (predictable determinants): Enzyme intrinsic features (oligomerization propensity, intrinsically disordered regions, membrane-binding motifs) and network context (interaction degree, complex membership) will predict microdomain formation propensity, enabling generalization beyond well-studied examples.

Together, these questions test whether mesoscale spatial organization is a widespread, condition-tunable determinant of metabolic behavior and provide falsifiable, data-driven criteria for when channeling must be invoked to explain emergent metabolic phenotypes.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working group structure. We will run an NCEMS-style synthesis project organized into three integrated thrusts: (T1) Data harmonization and evidence scoring; (T2) Spatially annotated metabolic network construction and simulation; (T3) Statistical and machine-learning tests for channeling signatures. Each thrust will be co-led by investigators from different disciplines, with trainees embedded as pathway curators and pipeline developers.

T1: Data ingestion, harmonization, and spatial evidence scoring. We will compile public datasets spanning: spatial proteomics/subcellular fractionation (Human Protein Atlas spatial proteomics; PRIDE fractionation studies), proximity labeling proteomics (PRIDE), curated complexes/interactions (CORUM, BioGRID), imaging localization (HPA immunofluorescence; IDR), metabolomics (Metabolomics Workbench; HMDB-linked studies), and flux datasets/models (BiGG models; public 13C MFA datasets with raw data and metadata). Harmonization will include identifier mapping (UniProt/Ensembl/gene symbols; metabolite identifiers via InChIKey/SMILES/HMDB/KEGG), compartment ontology alignment (GO cellular component; Uberon/Cell Ontology where relevant), and metadata normalization (cell type, perturbation, time, platform). We will compute per-enzyme localization probability vectors across compartments using Bayesian/empirical Bayes models that combine fractionation and imaging evidence, with uncertainty estimates.

We will define an “enzyme-pair spatial association score” integrating: (i) co-localization similarity (e.g., cosine similarity of localization vectors with uncertainty propagation), (ii) proximity labeling co-enrichment (effect sizes and FDR across studies), and (iii) complex/interaction support (binary/weighted evidence from CORUM/BioGRID). Scores will be calibrated against negative controls (random enzyme pairs matched for abundance and annotation depth) and positive controls (known stable complexes).

T2: Spatially annotated metabolic networks and microdomain-constrained simulation. Starting from curated pathway maps and GEMs (BiGG), we will build spatially annotated reaction graphs where edges connect sequential reactions and are weighted by enzyme-pair spatial association. We will derive candidate “microdomains” as subnetworks with high internal spatial association and coherent compartment assignment, using community detection and constrained clustering.

To test functional consequences, we will implement two comparative modeling regimes: (i) baseline well-mixed models (standard FBA/parsimonious FBA or kinetic proxy models where available), and (ii) microdomain-constrained models where intermediate exchange between specific reaction pairs is restricted/biased according to spatial scores (implemented as additional constraints or effective channeling parameters). Where 13C MFA fluxes are available, we will evaluate model fit via likelihood-based comparison and cross-validation.

T3: Statistical tests and ML prediction of channeling propensity. We will develop statistical signatures from metabolomics: covariance structure across perturbations, intermediate accumulation patterns, and response linearity under enzyme inhibition or nutrient shifts. We will test whether these signatures correlate with microdomain evidence scores, controlling for confounders (expression level, pathway size, measurement platform). For prediction, we will train interpretable models (regularized logistic regression/gradient boosting) to predict high-evidence microdomain membership from enzyme features (domain architecture, oligomerization annotations, disorder predictions, membrane association, PTM sites) and network context (interaction degree, complex membership, pathway centrality). Performance will be assessed via nested cross-validation and held-out taxa/cell types.

Milestones. (M1) Harmonized multi-omics knowledge graph and scoring schema; (M2) Atlas of candidate microdomains with evidence and uncertainty; (M3) Benchmarked tests linking spatial evidence to metabolite/flux behavior; (M4) Open pipelines and training modules.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Primary scientific products. (1) An open, evidence-scored atlas of candidate metabolic microdomains (“metabolon candidates”) across pathways, compartments, and conditions, including uncertainty estimates and provenance links to underlying datasets. (2) Spatially annotated metabolic network representations that integrate enzyme localization, proximity neighborhoods, and complex membership, enabling community reuse in modeling and hypothesis generation. (3) Quantitative benchmarks and statistical tests for detecting channeling signatures from public metabolomics and perturbation datasets, with guidance on when inference is reliable given data sparsity and platform differences.

Mechanistic insights. By comparing well-mixed versus microdomain-constrained simulations against public 13C flux and metabolomics observations, we expect to identify pathways where spatial organization is necessary to reconcile enzyme abundance with metabolite/flux behavior. We anticipate that high-confidence channeling candidates will be enriched for pathways with labile/toxic intermediates and high-flux sequential steps, and that stress or cell-state transitions will systematically modulate microdomain evidence.

Methodological impact. The project will deliver interoperable pipelines for cross-modal identifier mapping, compartment ontology alignment, and evidence integration—recurring bottlenecks in synthesis biology. Our spatial scoring framework and model-comparison approach will provide a general template for studying other mesoscale emergent phenomena where spatial organization shapes function.

Community and workforce impact. The working group will train graduate students and postdocs in FAIR data practices, reproducible multi-omics integration, and spatially informed metabolic modeling. By producing reusable data structures, code, and tutorials, we will lower barriers for diverse labs—including those without experimental infrastructure—to contribute to and extend mesoscale metabolic research.

Long-term significance. Establishing when and why metabolic channeling occurs will refine core assumptions in systems biology, improve predictive metabolic models, and open new avenues for understanding disease-associated metabolic rewiring as an emergent property of mesoscale organization rather than solely gene expression changes.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS working group support rationale. The proposed synthesis requires intensive cross-disciplinary coordination, shared standards, and substantial computation for multi-omics harmonization and model comparison—beyond the capacity of a single lab or existing bilateral collaborations. NCEMS resources are essential to convene domain experts, support trainee-driven curation, and provide synthesis infrastructure.

Budget categories (high-level). (1) Working group convenings: support for multiple in-person meetings at NCEMS (or NCEMS-supported venue) plus regular virtual meetings, enabling rapid iteration on standards, integration decisions, and joint interpretation. Travel support will prioritize broad participation across geography, institution types, and career stages. (2) Personnel support: partial support for trainees (graduate students/postdocs) and/or research software engineers for pipeline development, dataset curation, and documentation. Trainees will be embedded across thrusts and mentored by multi-PI teams. (3) Computing and data infrastructure: allocation for storage and compute to run containerized workflows, host intermediate harmonized datasets, and perform cross-validation/model fitting at scale. (4) Dissemination and training: resources for producing training materials, maintaining public repositories, and hosting community webinars/hack sessions.

Resource plan and roles. The team will include (i) proteomics/spatial proteomics experts to interpret fractionation and proximity labeling; (ii) metabolomics experts to address platform-specific normalization and metabolite ID mapping; (iii) systems biologists to implement GEM integration and constraint-based modeling; (iv) biophysicists to translate mesoscale organization concepts into testable constraints; and (v) statisticians/ML researchers to develop calibrated evidence scores and predictive models. NCEMS staff support (facilitation, data science consultation, and open-science guidance) will be leveraged to maintain momentum and ensure interoperability.

Feasibility and timeline. A 18–24 month working group timeline is feasible: months 1–6 harmonization and scoring; months 7–14 atlas and modeling; months 15–24 benchmarking, manuscripts, and training releases. All work relies exclusively on existing public data and will be delivered as reusable open resources.

title: Emergent Robustness in Gene Regulatory Networks: A Synthesis of Single-Cell Perturbation Atlases Across Cell Types
abstract:
Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) display emergent robustness: stable cell identities persist despite molecular noise and many perturbations, yet can switch catastrophically under others. Single-cell perturbation technologies have generated large public datasets (CRISPRi/a Perturb-seq, CROP-seq, multimodal readouts), but the field lacks a cross-study synthesis to identify universal robustness motifs and context-specific vulnerabilities.

This working group will integrate publicly available single-cell perturbation datasets from GEO, ArrayExpress, and dedicated portals (e.g., scPerturb resources), including CRISPR-based knockdowns/activations with scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, and protein readouts (CITE-seq). We will harmonize gene identifiers, perturbation efficacies, cell state annotations, and batch effects using standardized pipelines. We will also integrate transcription factor binding/epigenomic priors (ENCODE) and protein interaction networks (BioGRID) to constrain GRN inference.

Key questions: (1) What network motifs (feedback loops, redundant regulators, feedforward motifs) repeatedly underlie robustness across diverse cell types? (2) Which perturbations cause state transitions versus buffered responses, and can we predict this from network topology and chromatin context? (3) How do emergent properties like multistability and criticality vary across differentiation trajectories and disease states?

Analytical plan: We will infer GRNs using a combination of causal inference methods tailored to perturbation data (e.g., conditional independence with intervention labels, dynamical latent variable models) and compare inferred networks across datasets via alignment techniques. We will quantify robustness using metrics such as response sparsity, attractor stability, and variance amplification. A methodological deliverable will be a benchmarking framework that evaluates GRN inference methods on real perturbation data with standardized gold-standard proxies (e.g., TF binding, curated pathways) and reproducible splits.

NCEMS support is required because meaningful synthesis demands coordination across many datasets with heterogeneous protocols and readouts, and requires expertise spanning single-cell genomics, statistics, dynamical systems, and computational infrastructure. The working group format enables community consensus on metadata standards (perturbation annotation, efficacy reporting) and fosters broad participation.

Deliverables will include: (i) a harmonized cross-study perturbation atlas with unified cell state labels; (ii) an open library of robustness metrics and visualization tools; (iii) a catalog of conserved robustness motifs and predicted “tipping-point” regulators; and (iv) tutorials and reproducible notebooks for trainees. Training will focus on best practices for single-cell data integration, causal modeling, and open science workflows. By synthesizing intervention-rich datasets, the project will reveal emergent principles governing stability and change in cellular regulatory systems.
background_and_significance:
Cell identity is remarkably stable: differentiated cells maintain coherent transcriptional programs despite stochastic gene expression, cell-cycle fluctuations, and environmental variation. This stability is widely attributed to gene regulatory networks (GRNs)—interacting transcription factors (TFs), chromatin regulators, and signaling pathways that implement feedback, feedforward, and redundancy. Yet robustness is not absolute. Some perturbations are buffered with minimal phenotypic consequences, while others trigger abrupt state transitions (e.g., lineage switching, dedifferentiation, apoptosis) that resemble tipping points in dynamical systems. Understanding when and why GRNs absorb perturbations versus undergo catastrophic reconfiguration is a central question in molecular and cellular biology and an archetype of emergence: system-level stability and multistability arise from many interacting molecular components.

The last five years have produced an unprecedented volume of single-cell perturbation data. CRISPRi/a Perturb-seq, CROP-seq, and related methods couple targeted genetic interventions to single-cell transcriptomes; newer studies add chromatin accessibility (scATAC-seq), protein abundance (CITE-seq), and multiplexed perturbations. These datasets are publicly available across GEO, ArrayExpress, and dedicated portals, but remain fragmented. Each study uses distinct cell types, perturbation libraries, multiplicities of infection, guide designs, readout modalities, time points, and analysis pipelines. As a result, the field lacks consensus answers to basic questions: Are there universal robustness motifs shared across cell types? Are certain TF architectures consistently associated with buffering? Can we predict which regulators are “tipping-point” nodes whose perturbation drives state transitions, and how does this depend on chromatin context?

A synthesis effort is now timely for three reasons. First, perturbation atlases are intervention-rich, enabling causal inference that is difficult with observational single-cell atlases alone. Second, the diversity of cell types and conditions across studies creates a natural laboratory for identifying conserved versus context-specific principles of robustness. Third, the emergence focus of NCEMS—particularly mesoscale organization between molecules and organelles—maps directly onto GRNs as mesoscale control systems that integrate molecular interactions into cell-level phenotypes.

However, extracting generalizable principles requires integration beyond the scope of any single lab. Harmonization must reconcile heterogeneous metadata (guide sequences, target genes, perturbation modality, efficacy), batch effects, and cell-state annotations. Robustness itself must be operationalized with consistent metrics that can be computed across modalities and experimental designs. Finally, GRN inference from perturbation data remains methodologically unsettled: approaches differ in assumptions (linearity, sparsity, time dependence), and benchmarking on real-world perturbation datasets is limited.

This proposal establishes a community-scale working group to synthesize public single-cell perturbation datasets into a harmonized atlas and a comparative framework for GRN robustness. By integrating perturbation readouts with TF-binding and epigenomic priors (ENCODE) and protein interaction networks (BioGRID), we will constrain inferred networks and quantify emergent properties such as multistability, criticality, and variance amplification. The outcome will be a shared resource and a set of testable, cross-system principles that link network architecture to the emergent stability of cell identity, with direct relevance to differentiation, regeneration, and disease states such as cancer and immune dysfunction.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group addresses how emergent robustness arises in GRNs across cell types and conditions, leveraging intervention-based single-cell datasets to move from correlation to causation. We organize the research around three interconnected questions, each paired with explicit hypotheses and falsifiable predictions.

Question 1: What GRN motifs repeatedly underlie robustness across diverse cell types?
Hypothesis 1A (Conserved buffering motifs): Robust cell identities are supported by conserved motif families—mutual inhibition with self-activation (toggle-like circuits), multi-layer negative feedback, and redundant parallel regulators—that recur across immune, epithelial, and stem/progenitor systems.
Predictions: (i) Across datasets, perturbations to nodes embedded in high-redundancy or negative-feedback motifs will yield sparse transcriptional responses (few differentially expressed genes per cell) and low state-transition probability; (ii) motif enrichment will be consistent after controlling for node degree and expression level.
Hypothesis 1B (Mesoscale modularity): Robustness is primarily a property of mesoscale modules (gene programs) rather than individual edges.
Predictions: Perturbations within the same inferred module will produce similar response signatures even when targeting different genes; module-level connectivity will be more conserved across cell types than edge-level connectivity.

Question 2: Which perturbations cause state transitions versus buffered responses, and can we predict this from topology and chromatin context?
Hypothesis 2A (Tipping-point regulators): A minority of regulators act as tipping-point nodes whose perturbation pushes cells across attractor boundaries.
Predictions: (i) These nodes will show high causal influence (large average treatment effect on module scores) and high control centrality in inferred networks; (ii) their perturbation will increase transcriptional variance and multimodality (state splitting) before a transition.
Hypothesis 2B (Chromatin-gated vulnerability): Vulnerability is gated by chromatin accessibility and TF occupancy at target enhancers/promoters.
Predictions: Perturbations will be more likely to induce state transitions when the perturbed regulator has accessible binding sites in the starting state (scATAC-seq/CITE-seq-informed) and when ENCODE priors indicate strong occupancy; conversely, closed chromatin contexts will attenuate responses even for topologically central nodes.

Question 3: How do emergent properties like multistability and criticality vary across differentiation trajectories and disease states?
Hypothesis 3A (Trajectory-dependent criticality): Cells near fate bifurcations exhibit signatures of criticality—variance amplification, slowing down (persistence of perturbation effects), and increased susceptibility to transitions.
Predictions: Along pseudotime/differentiation trajectories, robustness metrics will show non-monotonic patterns with peaks in variance and state-transition probability near branch points.
Hypothesis 3B (Disease rewiring of robustness): Disease states (e.g., cancer cell lines, inflammatory immune states) alter robustness by rewiring feedback and redundancy, creating both fragility (new tipping points) and hyper-robustness (resistance to perturbation).
Predictions: Compared to matched non-disease contexts, disease networks will show altered motif composition (e.g., strengthened positive feedback) and shifted tipping-point sets; these differences will be reproducible across independent datasets of similar states.

Collectively, these hypotheses connect network architecture and chromatin context to emergent stability and switching, yielding generalizable, testable principles and predictive models of perturbation outcomes.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will execute a synthesis-only project using publicly available datasets and priors. The working group will include expertise in single-cell perturbation genomics, statistical causal inference, dynamical systems, network science, epigenomics, and software engineering. Activities are organized into four technical aims with iterative, in-person/virtual sprints supported by NCEMS.

Aim 1: Assemble and harmonize a cross-study perturbation atlas. We will curate Perturb-seq/CROP-seq/CRISPRi/a datasets from GEO/ArrayExpress and portals (e.g., scPerturb), prioritizing (i) diverse cell types, (ii) availability of guide sequences and assignment methods, (iii) inclusion of controls, and (iv) multimodal readouts when available (scRNA, scATAC, CITE-seq). Harmonization steps: (1) standardized gene identifiers (HGNC/Ensembl), guide-to-target mapping, and perturbation modality labels; (2) uniform QC, doublet filtering, and ambient RNA correction using community tools; (3) batch-aware integration within and across studies using scVI/totalVI or comparable methods, with explicit preservation of perturbation signal; (4) unified cell-state annotation via reference mapping to public atlases plus within-study marker validation; (5) perturbation efficacy estimation using target knockdown signatures, guide-level effects, and (where available) direct measurements, producing an efficacy score and uncertainty.

Aim 2: Causal GRN inference constrained by external priors. We will infer directed regulatory effects using complementary methods appropriate for intervention data: (i) conditional independence/graphical models with intervention labels to orient edges; (ii) regularized regression/DoWhy-style causal effect estimation for perturbation-to-gene/module impacts; (iii) latent dynamical models (e.g., variational state-space) to capture time-dependent responses when time points exist. Priors: ENCODE TF binding and chromatin marks will define candidate TF→target edges; BioGRID/STRING protein interactions will inform regulator-regulator coupling. We will evaluate sensitivity to priors by running “prior-free” and “prior-constrained” variants.

Aim 3: Define and compute robustness and tipping metrics across datasets. We will operationalize robustness at three levels: (a) gene-level response sparsity and effect-size distributions; (b) module-level stability using gene program scores and perturbation-induced shifts; (c) state-level attractor stability using transition probability between annotated states and energy-landscape proxies (e.g., potential from diffusion maps). Additional emergent metrics include variance amplification, multimodality (mixture models), and early-warning indicators of criticality (autocorrelation/slowing down in time-course datasets).

Aim 4: Cross-dataset network alignment and benchmarking. To identify conserved motifs, we will align inferred GRNs across cell types using module-based matching, graph kernels, and motif-frequency comparisons with degree-preserving null models. We will build a benchmarking suite: standardized train/test splits within datasets (held-out perturbations), cross-study transfer tests, and evaluation against gold-standard proxies (ENCODE edges, curated pathways, known TF hierarchies). Performance will be assessed for (i) edge recovery, (ii) causal effect prediction, and (iii) tipping-point prediction accuracy.

All analyses will be implemented as reproducible pipelines (Nextflow/Snakemake), containerized, and executed on shared compute resources coordinated through NCEMS.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific outcomes. (1) A harmonized, cross-study single-cell perturbation atlas spanning multiple cell types and modalities with standardized metadata (perturbation identity, efficacy, cell-state labels) and interoperable formats. (2) A quantitative, multi-level definition of GRN robustness—gene, module, and state—implemented as an open software library with validated metrics. (3) A catalog of conserved robustness motifs (e.g., negative feedback, redundancy, feedforward control) and a complementary catalog of context-specific vulnerabilities, including predicted tipping-point regulators whose perturbation induces state transitions.

Methodological outcomes. (4) A community benchmarking framework for GRN inference from perturbation data that evaluates not only edge recovery but also predictive utility (forecasting transcriptional responses and state transitions). This will clarify when different causal/dynamical methods are appropriate and how strongly conclusions depend on epigenomic and protein-interaction priors. (5) Practical standards for reporting perturbation experiments in public repositories (minimum metadata, efficacy estimation, control definitions), developed through working-group consensus and disseminated to the community.

Impact on emergence in molecular and cellular sciences. By synthesizing intervention-rich datasets, the project will reveal how mesoscale network architecture gives rise to emergent stability and switching—linking molecular interactions and chromatin context to cell-level phenotypes. The results will inform fundamental biology (principles of cell fate control), disease mechanisms (how robustness is rewired in cancer/immune dysfunction), and therapeutic strategies (identifying regulators likely to overcome pathological robustness or avoid unintended tipping). Because all outputs are derived from public data and released openly, the work will accelerate downstream research, enable reproducible comparisons across new perturbation atlases, and provide a durable platform for training data-savvy scientists in causal inference and network biology.
budget_and_resources:
Budget philosophy and NCEMS need. This project is synthesis-only but compute- and coordination-intensive. NCEMS support is essential to convene a multidisciplinary team, provide neutral infrastructure for community standards, and sustain collaborative engineering beyond a single lab’s capacity.

Requested resources (illustrative categories aligned with NCEMS working-group support).
1) Working-group convenings and collaboration: Support for 2–3 in-person meetings plus regular virtual sprints, including travel for geographically distributed participants, with prioritized support for trainees and participants from under-resourced institutions. Funds will also cover meeting facilitation, accessibility services, and collaborative planning.
2) Personnel support for synthesis and training: Partial support for a project coordinator/data steward (metadata curation, repository management, compliance with open-science policies) and for trainee participation (graduate students/postdocs) to develop pipelines, benchmarking, and documentation. Faculty salaries are not required beyond allowable effort; emphasis is on enabling cross-lab integration work.
3) Computational resources: Cloud/HPC credits for reprocessing large single-cell datasets, running integration models (e.g., scVI/totalVI), and performing repeated GRN inference/benchmarking across splits. Storage is required for intermediate objects, cached downloads, and reproducible containers.
4) Software engineering and dissemination: Support for maintaining robust, tested codebases; DOI-backed releases (Zenodo); and creation of training materials (tutorial notebooks, recorded lectures, example datasets). Minimal funds are allocated for publication costs where open-access fees are necessary.

In-kind contributions. Participating labs will contribute domain expertise, existing code modules, and mentorship for trainees. NCEMS will provide convening infrastructure, project management support, and alignment with center-wide standards for open, team, and reproducible science.

Deliverable-linked spending. Expenditures are explicitly tied to deliverables: (i) harmonized atlas release, (ii) robustness metric library, (iii) benchmarking suite, and (iv) training curriculum, each with scheduled milestones and public releases.

title: A Community Synthesis of Mesoscale Protein Quality Control: Integrating Proteostasis Networks, Aggregation Data, and Stress Responses
abstract:
Protein quality control (PQC) is an emergent cellular system spanning chaperones, proteasomes, autophagy, and stress granules. Failures in PQC lead to aggregation and disease, yet we lack a unified synthesis connecting proteostasis network states to aggregation propensity and cell fate across organisms and stressors. Public datasets now include proteome-wide aggregation measurements, chaperone interactomes, stress transcriptomics, and imaging of aggregates—ripe for integrative analysis.

This working group will synthesize (i) proteomics datasets quantifying insoluble/aggregated fractions under stress (PRIDE), (ii) interactomes for chaperones and ubiquitin ligases (BioGRID, HuRI), (iii) transcriptomic responses to heat shock, oxidative stress, and proteasome inhibition (GEO), (iv) imaging datasets of aggregate formation and clearance (IDR, Cell Image Library), (v) genetic screens for proteostasis factors (DepMap, yeast screens), and (vi) sequence/structure features (AlphaFold, disorder predictions, aggregation propensity predictors). We will curate stress conditions, time courses, and cell types to enable comparative analyses.

Scientific questions: (1) Can we define discrete, reproducible “proteostasis states” that predict whether cells route misfolded proteins to degradation, sequestration, or refolding? (2) Which network configurations confer resilience (rapid recovery) versus vulnerability (runaway aggregation)? (3) How do mesoscale assemblies (stress granules, aggresomes) interact with PQC pathways to create emergent thresholds and hysteresis?

Methodologically, we will develop integrative models combining network biology and time-series analysis. Latent state models will infer proteostasis regimes from multi-omics signatures. We will link these regimes to aggregate imaging phenotypes and insoluble proteome composition. Causal discovery approaches leveraging perturbation screens will identify key control nodes. A specific methodological product will be an open pipeline for harmonizing “insoluble proteome” assays and mapping proteins across studies with standardized confidence metrics.

NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis spans many data types and requires deep domain expertise to interpret assay-specific biases (e.g., detergent solubility differences). The collaboration will include neurodegeneration experts, proteomics analysts, imaging scientists, and computational modelers to ensure robust integration.

Deliverables: an open Proteostasis Emergence Atlas cataloging stress conditions, proteostasis states, aggregate compositions, and predicted control nodes; reproducible workflows for integrating insoluble proteomics with imaging and transcriptomics; and community benchmarks for predicting aggregation outcomes from sequence and network context. Training will include trainee-led curation of stress datasets, workshops on reproducible proteomics and imaging analysis, and open-source contributions. The project will illuminate emergent PQC behavior and identify general principles of cellular resilience.
background_and_significance:
Protein quality control (PQC) is a canonical example of biological emergence: coordinated behaviors arise from the coupled actions of chaperones, ubiquitin ligases, the proteasome, autophagy, and phase-separated assemblies that collectively maintain proteome integrity. At the mesoscale—between individual proteins and whole organelles—PQC organizes misfolded proteins into dynamic assemblies (stress granules, aggresomes, JUNQ/IPOD-like compartments) and routes them toward refolding, sequestration, or degradation. These collective behaviors exhibit thresholds, nonlinearity, and memory (hysteresis): modest increases in misfolded protein load can trigger abrupt transitions to persistent aggregation, while recovery can lag despite stress removal. Such emergent properties are central to aging, neurodegeneration, and proteotoxic stress responses, yet our understanding remains fragmented across assays, organisms, and subfields.

Over the past decade, the community has generated extensive publicly available datasets that, if integrated, can resolve longstanding puzzles in PQC. Proteomics studies quantify “insoluble” fractions or detergent-resistant aggregates across stressors and time courses (e.g., heat shock, oxidative stress, proteasome inhibition) in diverse cell types and model organisms. Large interaction resources map chaperone-client relationships and ubiquitin-system wiring (BioGRID, HuRI), while transcriptomic compendia capture stress programs and proteostasis remodeling (GEO). Imaging repositories contain rich phenotypes of aggregate nucleation, growth, subcellular localization, and clearance (IDR, Cell Image Library). Genetic perturbation screens in yeast and human cells identify resilience and vulnerability factors (yeast deletion/overexpression screens; DepMap CRISPR dependencies). Finally, sequence/structure resources (AlphaFold, disorder predictors, aggregation propensity scores) provide mechanistic priors on which proteins are likely to misfold, phase-separate, or become aggregation seeds.

Despite this abundance, synthesis is hindered by heterogeneity in experimental definitions (e.g., “insoluble” depends on extraction chemistry and centrifugation), inconsistent annotation of stress intensity and timing, incomplete mapping between gene/protein identifiers across species, and the need to align molecular readouts with mesoscale imaging phenotypes. Individual laboratories typically specialize in one modality (proteomics, imaging, genetics, computational modeling) and cannot, alone, harmonize biases across modalities and organisms while developing robust integrative models. NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale effort that combines domain expertise, AI/data science, and open science practices to generate a coherent, reusable synthesis.

This working group targets a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biology: how do distributed PQC components collectively generate discrete cellular regimes (proteostasis “states”) and state transitions that determine cell fate under proteotoxic stress? Answering this requires integrating multi-omics, networks, and imaging to connect molecular composition (which proteins aggregate), system configuration (which PQC modules are engaged), and mesoscale organization (where aggregates form and how they are processed). A synthesis that identifies reproducible states and control nodes would provide unifying principles for resilience versus collapse, explain why similar stressors yield different outcomes across cell types, and reveal general mechanisms by which mesoscale assemblies regulate global proteostasis. Beyond immediate biological insight, the project will produce community resources—curated datasets, harmonization pipelines, benchmarks—that enable future mechanistic and therapeutic work without generating new experimental data, fully aligned with NCEMS’s mission to leverage existing public data for transformative understanding of emergence in molecular and cellular systems.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This project is organized around the premise that PQC is best understood as a stateful, mesoscale system: cells occupy discrete, reproducible proteostasis regimes defined by coordinated changes in network activity, aggregate composition, and spatial organization. We will test this premise with three interlocking research questions and associated hypotheses that are explicitly tractable using publicly available data.

RQ1: Do cells occupy discrete, reproducible “proteostasis states” across stressors, time, and species?
Hypothesis 1A (state discreteness): Multi-omics signatures (stress transcriptomics, insoluble proteome composition, and PQC interaction/network features) cluster into a small number of recurrent latent states rather than forming a continuum. These states will be conserved at the level of pathway logic (e.g., HSF1-driven chaperone upregulation vs ISR activation vs autophagy engagement) even when specific genes differ by species.
Hypothesis 1B (state predictability): A state inferred from early time points (or mild stress) will predict later mesoscale outcomes—aggregate burden, persistence, and clearance kinetics—better than any single modality alone.

RQ2: Which network configurations confer resilience versus vulnerability to runaway aggregation?
Hypothesis 2A (network redundancy vs bottlenecks): Resilient states are characterized by distributed capacity (multiple chaperone systems engaged; balanced ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy flux proxies), whereas vulnerable states show bottlenecks—over-reliance on a narrow set of chaperones or E3 ligases and reduced network controllability.
Hypothesis 2B (client spectrum reshaping): Resilience involves a stress-dependent reshaping of chaperone-client and ubiquitin-target spectra toward high-risk proteins (high disorder, high aggregation propensity, metastable domains), observable as concordance between predicted aggregation propensity and measured insolubility changes.
Hypothesis 2C (genetic causal support): Nodes identified as bottlenecks by integrative network analysis will be enriched among essentiality/fitness modifiers in DepMap and yeast genetic screens under proteotoxic contexts, indicating causal leverage rather than mere correlation.

RQ3: How do mesoscale assemblies (stress granules, aggresomes, quality-control compartments) generate emergent thresholds and hysteresis in PQC?
Hypothesis 3A (threshold behavior): Imaging-derived features (nucleation rate, number/size distributions, subcellular localization) will exhibit nonlinear transitions as a function of inferred proteostasis state and misfolded-protein load proxies, consistent with phase-transition-like behavior.
Hypothesis 3B (hysteresis and memory): For matched stressors with recovery time courses, cells will show state-dependent hysteresis: the path into aggregation differs from the path out, reflected by delayed reversal of insoluble proteome composition and persistent mesoscale assemblies despite transcriptomic normalization.
Hypothesis 3C (assembly–pathway coupling): Specific assemblies act as regulators, not just sinks: stress granule engagement will correlate with altered translation/ISR programs and selective sequestration of PQC factors, while aggresome formation will couple to microtubule/HDAC6 pathways and autophagy engagement; these couplings will appear as reproducible cross-modal dependencies.

Across all questions, we will evaluate conservation and context-dependence by stratifying analyses by organism (yeast, fly, worm, human), cell type (neuronal vs non-neuronal), and stressor class. The unifying hypothesis is that emergent proteostasis behavior can be captured by a limited set of latent regimes and transition rules, and that these regimes can be mechanistically interpreted via integrated network structure, genetic perturbation evidence, and mesoscale imaging phenotypes.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will conduct a community-scale synthesis using only publicly available datasets. The working group will include expertise in proteomics, imaging analysis, stress biology, neurodegeneration, network science, causal inference, and reproducible software engineering. Activities are organized into four technical aims with shared curation standards and cross-validation.

Aim 1: Curate and harmonize proteostasis-relevant datasets across modalities.
1) Insoluble/aggregated proteomics: Systematically identify PRIDE studies measuring detergent-insoluble fractions, aggregate-enriched pellets, or thermal/proteome stability proxies under defined stressors. Extract metadata (cell type, organism, stressor dose, time, lysis/extraction chemistry, MS quantification method). Develop a harmonization schema that maps assay types to a common “aggregation evidence” scale with confidence metrics (e.g., extraction harshness, replicate structure, peptide coverage).
2) Interaction and pathway networks: Download chaperone-client and ubiquitin-system interactions from BioGRID/HuRI and curated complexes (CORUM). Annotate edges with evidence type and context when available.
3) Transcriptomics: Curate GEO time courses for heat shock, oxidative stress, proteasome inhibition, ER stress, and recovery. Process uniformly (recount/DESeq2 where possible; batch correction; gene set scores for HSR/ISR/UPR/autophagy).
4) Imaging: Identify IDR/Cell Image Library datasets with aggregate markers (e.g., polyQ, ubiquitin, p62, TDP-43, Hsp104 in yeast). Extract or compute standardized features (puncta count, size, intensity, spatial distribution, co-localization with organelle markers; clearance kinetics).
5) Genetics: Integrate DepMap dependencies and available stress-relevant CRISPR screens; incorporate yeast genetic interaction and deletion sensitivity datasets.
6) Sequence/structure priors: Compute disorder, low-complexity, prion-like domains, predicted aggregation propensity, and AlphaFold-derived features (pLDDT, domain architecture).

Aim 2: Infer latent proteostasis states from multi-omics.
We will fit latent variable/state-space models that integrate transcriptomic signatures, insoluble proteome shifts, and network activity proxies. Candidate approaches include multi-view factor analysis (MOFA+), dynamic Bayesian/hidden Markov models for time series, and variational autoencoders with modality-specific encoders. We will assess state robustness via: (i) held-out studies (leave-one-study-out), (ii) perturbation labels (stressor class) as external validity, and (iii) stability under metadata-stratified resampling.

Aim 3: Link states to mesoscale imaging phenotypes and emergent transitions.
We will map imaging datasets into a shared feature space and align them to molecular states using matched conditions (stressor/time/cell type) when direct matching exists, and probabilistic matching when it does not (metadata-driven priors). We will test for nonlinearities by fitting generalized additive models and change-point models relating state coordinates and misfolded-load proxies to imaging outcomes. Hysteresis will be evaluated using paired stress/recovery trajectories when available, comparing forward vs reverse mappings between state and phenotype.

Aim 4: Identify control nodes using perturbation evidence and causal discovery.
We will integrate genetic perturbation screens with network structure to prioritize candidate control nodes. Methods include causal discovery on perturbation-annotated datasets (e.g., invariant causal prediction across contexts), network controllability/centrality measures, and mediation-style analyses linking perturbation → state shift → phenotype. Candidates will be ranked by multi-evidence scoring (genetic effect size, cross-dataset reproducibility, network position, and consistency with known biology).

Quality control and feasibility.
We will predefine inclusion criteria, metadata minimums, and confidence scoring to prevent over-integration of incompatible assays. All models will be benchmarked against simple baselines (single-modality predictors; random networks) and evaluated with transparent uncertainty estimates. The output will be an integrated, queryable Proteostasis Emergence Atlas and a validated, reusable pipeline for insoluble-proteome harmonization and cross-modal state inference.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Primary scientific outcomes. (1) A data-driven taxonomy of proteostasis states: a compact set of latent regimes that recur across datasets and capture coordinated engagement of chaperones, ubiquitin-proteasome pathways, autophagy, and stress programs. Each state will be annotated with characteristic molecular signatures (gene sets, interaction modules, insoluble-proteome fingerprints) and mesoscale phenotypes (aggregate burden, localization, clearance kinetics). (2) Quantitative transition rules: models describing when and how cells cross thresholds into persistent aggregation, including evidence for nonlinear change points and hysteresis during recovery. (3) Mechanistic hypotheses for resilience and collapse: prioritized control nodes (e.g., specific chaperone systems, E3 ligases, co-factors, trafficking/aggresome components) supported by convergent evidence from network structure, perturbation screens, and cross-context invariance.

Community resources. We will deliver an open Proteostasis Emergence Atlas that links stress conditions, time courses, cell types, and organisms to inferred states and predicted outcomes. The Atlas will include harmonized insoluble-proteome datasets with standardized confidence metrics and a transparent mapping of assay differences. We will also provide benchmark datasets and evaluation tasks for predicting aggregation outcomes from sequence, network context, and early stress responses, enabling method development beyond this project.

Broader impacts aligned with NCEMS. The project directly advances NCEMS’s focus on mesoscale emergence by connecting molecular networks to mesoscale assemblies and cell-level outcomes. By synthesizing only public data at community scale, it will resolve long-standing fragmentation in PQC research, provide a unifying framework for interpreting disparate stress and aggregation studies, and generate reusable analytical strategies for other emergent cellular systems (e.g., phase separation, organelle biogenesis). Training components (curation sprints, reproducible analysis workshops, trainee-led software contributions) will build a data-savvy workforce skilled in integrating proteomics, imaging, and network biology under open science practices. Finally, the resulting principles and resources will accelerate downstream translational efforts by clarifying which PQC configurations are most predictive of vulnerability in disease-relevant contexts, without requiring new experimental data within the scope of this working group.
budget_and_resources:
Budget philosophy and NCEMS need. This is a community-scale synthesis spanning proteomics, imaging, transcriptomics, networks, and genetics. NCEMS support is essential to convene a multidisciplinary team, provide collaborative space/time for intensive integration, and supply professional support for data engineering, reproducible workflows, and training—capabilities beyond a single lab or a typical bilateral collaboration.

Requested resources (categories). (1) Working group convenings: support for 2–3 in-person meetings at NCEMS (or NCEMS-supported venue) plus regular virtual meetings.
