Funds cover travel, lodging, and per diem for participants across career stages and institutions, with explicit inclusion of trainees and researchers from under-resourced institutions. (2) Personnel effort for synthesis: partial support for a project manager/data curator and a research software engineer (RSE) to maintain pipelines, metadata standards, and releases; modest support for trainee participation (e.g., summer salary/stipends) focused on curation, benchmarking, and documentation. (3) Computing: cloud/HPC allocations for large-scale reprocessing (imaging feature extraction; multi-omics model fitting) and storage for intermediate derivatives; funds also cover persistent hosting of the Atlas artifacts and backups. (4) Training and dissemination: workshop materials, tutorial development, and small grants for trainee-led open-source contributions (e.g., adding modules, writing vignettes), plus publication costs for open-access dissemination when appropriate.

Leveraged, no-cost resources. We will rely exclusively on publicly available datasets (PRIDE, GEO, BioGRID, HuRI, IDR, Cell Image Library, DepMap, AlphaFold) and open-source software ecosystems (Python/R, scverse, Bioconductor). Participating labs will contribute in-kind expertise, existing scripts, and domain knowledge to interpret assay-specific biases.

Budget governance and feasibility. A steering committee will track milestones (curation completeness, pipeline releases, model benchmarks, Atlas versions) and align expenditures with deliverables. The budget prioritizes durable community infrastructure (curated datasets, validated pipelines, training materials) over transient analyses, ensuring that NCEMS investment yields long-lived, reusable outputs consistent with the Center’s mission.

title: Emergent Cell Polarity from Molecular Interactions: Synthesizing Spatial Transcriptomics, Proteomics, and Imaging Across Epithelia
abstract:
Cell polarity is an emergent property in which local molecular interactions generate stable, large-scale spatial organization (apical–basal domains, tight junctions) that enables tissue function. While many polarity regulators are known, we lack a cross-tissue synthesis connecting molecular composition and signaling to emergent polarity architectures, especially across development, disease, and species. Public spatial omics and imaging datasets now make this synthesis feasible.

This working group will integrate (i) spatial transcriptomics datasets (10x Visium and other platforms with public releases in GEO and portals), (ii) single-cell RNA-seq atlases with epithelial annotations (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens), (iii) proteomics of junctional complexes and membrane domains (PRIDE), (iv) imaging datasets of epithelial polarity markers (Human Protein Atlas, IDR), and (v) perturbation datasets affecting polarity (CRISPR screens, organoid perturbation transcriptomics). We will focus on harmonizing epithelial cell type ontologies and spatial coordinate frameworks to compare polarity programs across tissues.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify conserved “polarity modules” (gene/protein sets) and quantify their spatial segregation across epithelia. (2) Determine how emergent polarity breaks down in cancer, inflammation, and infection by comparing spatial organization signatures. (3) Link molecular modules to mesoscale structures such as tight junction continuity, lumen formation, and planar cell polarity patterns.

Analytical approach: We will develop computational methods to infer polarity axes and domain boundaries from spatial transcriptomics and multiplex imaging, using spatial statistics and graph-based segmentation. Multi-omic factor models will integrate RNA, protein, and imaging features to define polarity states. We will also incorporate known interaction networks to interpret modules mechanistically. A methodological contribution will be an open “polarity scoring” toolkit that quantifies polarity strength and organization from diverse spatial datasets.

NCEMS support is required to convene developmental biologists, epithelial physiologists, spatial omics experts, and computational scientists to align on ontologies, quality control, and cross-platform integration. The project goes beyond a single lab due to the breadth of tissues, platforms, and the need for rigorous standardization.

Deliverables will include a cross-tissue Polarity Synthesis Atlas with harmonized spatial datasets, polarity scores, and module annotations; reproducible pipelines for spatial data integration; and a catalog of disease-associated polarity disruption signatures. Training will be embedded through workshops on spatial data analysis, open annotation of epithelial structures, and reproducibility practices. This synthesis will advance understanding of how mesoscale polarity emerges from molecular networks and how its disruption drives pathology.
background_and_significance:
Epithelia line organs, form barriers, and create specialized interfaces for absorption, secretion, and signaling. Their function depends on cell polarity: the stable partitioning of molecular components into apical, basal, and lateral domains, coupled to tissue-scale organization such as lumen formation, planar cell polarity, and continuous tight junction belts. Polarity is a canonical emergent phenomenon: nanometer-scale interactions among scaffolds, lipids, cytoskeletal regulators, and trafficking machinery generate micron-scale domains and multicellular architectures that are robust to noise yet plastic during morphogenesis and repair. Despite decades of mechanistic work identifying polarity complexes (PAR, Crumbs, Scribble), junctional components (claudins, occludin, ZO proteins, cadherins), and signaling pathways (Rho GTPases, Hippo, Wnt/PCP), we still lack a synthesis framework that connects molecular composition and interaction topology to emergent mesoscale polarity patterns across tissues, developmental stages, and disease contexts.

This gap persists for three reasons. First, polarity is typically studied in a small number of model epithelia (MDCK, Drosophila epithelia, intestinal organoids), and findings are often generalized without a quantitative, cross-tissue comparison. Second, polarity readouts span modalities—transcripts, proteins, post-translational modifications, subcellular localization, and morphology—yet most analyses are confined to a single data type. Third, polarity is inherently spatial: the same genes may be expressed broadly, but their localization and co-association determine functional domains. Traditional bulk omics and even single-cell RNA-seq lose spatial context, making it difficult to infer domain boundaries, axes, and junction continuity.

Public data resources now enable a community-scale synthesis that was previously infeasible. Spatial transcriptomics (e.g., Visium and other platforms) provides tissue context for epithelial compartments; large single-cell atlases (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens) provide cell-type resolution and developmental trajectories; proteomics repositories (PRIDE) contain junctional and membrane-domain enrichments and interaction partners; imaging repositories (Human Protein Atlas, Image Data Resource) provide localization of polarity markers across tissues; and perturbation datasets (CRISPR screens, organoid perturbation transcriptomics) reveal causal links between genes and polarity phenotypes. However, these datasets are heterogeneous in coordinate systems, resolution, annotation standards, and quality metrics. Without harmonized ontologies and robust integrative methods, the field cannot extract general principles of how polarity emerges or fails.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze this synthesis at the mesoscale, bridging molecules to organelle- and cell-scale organization. The proposed working group directly addresses NCEMS priorities by (i) using only existing public data; (ii) requiring cross-lab expertise in epithelial biology, spatial omics, imaging analysis, proteomics, and AI/data science; and (iii) producing broadly reusable analytical tools and an openly accessible Polarity Synthesis Atlas. By quantifying polarity as a set of conserved modules and spatial organization signatures, we will move beyond descriptive marker lists toward predictive, testable models of emergent epithelial architecture. This synthesis has high biomedical relevance: polarity loss and junction disruption are hallmarks of carcinoma progression, inflammatory barrier failure, and pathogen invasion. A rigorous cross-tissue, cross-disease polarity framework will therefore advance fundamental cell biology and provide a shared quantitative language for diverse communities.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This project is organized around the central question: How do molecular interaction networks and regulatory programs give rise to conserved mesoscale polarity architectures across epithelia, and how do distinct perturbations disrupt those architectures in disease?

Research Question 1: What molecular “polarity modules” are conserved across epithelial tissues, species, and developmental stages, and how are they spatially segregated into apical, basal, and lateral domains?
Hypothesis 1A: Conserved polarity modules exist as partially independent, recurrent gene/protein sets corresponding to (i) apical trafficking and membrane identity, (ii) tight junction assembly/maintenance, (iii) adherens junction–actin coupling, and (iv) basal adhesion/ECM sensing, and these modules show consistent patterns of spatial segregation even when absolute expression varies by tissue.
Hypothesis 1B: The degree of module segregation (not simply module abundance) is a quantitative proxy for “polarity strength” and will correlate with morphological indicators such as lumenization and continuous junction belts.

Research Question 2: Can polarity axes and domain boundaries be inferred reproducibly from spatial transcriptomics and multiplex imaging across platforms and resolutions?
Hypothesis 2A: A shared latent polarity coordinate system can be inferred from spatial gradients and neighborhood graph structure, enabling alignment of datasets with different section orientations, sampling densities, and marker panels.
Hypothesis 2B: Integrating imaging-derived localization features (e.g., apical enrichment of EPCAM/Crumbs, junctional ZO-1 belts) with transcript-derived module scores will substantially improve boundary detection and reduce platform-specific artifacts.

Research Question 3: How does emergent polarity break down in cancer, inflammation, and infection, and are there distinct, convergent “disruption signatures” across etiologies?
Hypothesis 3A: Polarity breakdown is not monolithic; it decomposes into separable failure modes—junctional fragmentation, apical–basal mixing, basal detachment/ECM remodeling, and planar polarity disorganization—that can be detected as changes in module segregation, boundary sharpness, and spatial autocorrelation.
Hypothesis 3B: Different diseases converge on a limited set of disruption signatures despite distinct upstream drivers (e.g., EMT programs in carcinoma, cytokine-driven barrier remodeling in inflammation, pathogen-mediated junction targeting in infection).

Research Question 4: Which molecular interaction subnetworks best explain transitions between polarity states and disruption modes?
Hypothesis 4A: Network-constrained multi-omic factor models will identify interpretable regulatory axes (e.g., Rho/actomyosin tension, endocytic recycling, Hippo/YAP mechanosensing) that map onto mesoscale structural outcomes.
Hypothesis 4B: Perturbation datasets (CRISPR screens, organoid perturbation transcriptomics) will enrich for specific modules and network hubs whose effects on polarity are context-dependent but predictable from tissue-specific module coupling.

Research Question 5 (methodological): Can we define a community-adoptable, quantitative “polarity scorecard” that is robust across datasets and useful for benchmarking new methods?
Hypothesis 5A: A small set of standardized metrics—module segregation index, boundary continuity score, axis coherence, and junctional network integrity—will be sufficient to summarize polarity organization across epithelia.
Hypothesis 5B: These metrics will generalize across platforms and will enable meta-analyses that identify outlier tissues or conditions revealing new biology (e.g., specialized epithelia with unconventional polarity architectures).

Together, these questions and hypotheses operationalize emergence: they link local molecular modules and interaction networks to global, measurable spatial organization, and they explicitly test whether a shared quantitative framework can unify diverse epithelial systems and disease contexts using only public data.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will execute a community-scale synthesis using only publicly available datasets. The working group will include: epithelial/developmental biologists (domain knowledge and phenotypic interpretation), spatial transcriptomics experts (platform nuances, preprocessing), imaging scientists (segmentation, feature extraction), proteomics/network biologists (complex composition, interaction priors), and statisticians/ML researchers (factor models, benchmarking). NCEMS support will be used to convene iterative in-person/virtual meetings focused on ontology alignment, method benchmarking, and deliverable integration.

Data acquisition and inclusion criteria. We will curate datasets across multiple epithelia (intestine, kidney, lung, mammary, skin, liver bile ducts, reproductive tract) and conditions (healthy, development, cancer, inflammation, infection). Sources include GEO/SRA and portal releases for spatial transcriptomics; Human Cell Atlas and Tabula Sapiens for scRNA-seq; PRIDE for junctional/membrane proteomics and interactomes; Human Protein Atlas and IDR for immunofluorescence and multiplex imaging; and public perturbation datasets (DepMap/CRISPR screens where polarity-related readouts exist, organoid perturbation scRNA-seq/spatial where available). Inclusion requires: public access, sufficient metadata, epithelial annotation or markers enabling epithelial compartment identification, and licensing compatible with redistribution of derived products.

Harmonization: cell types, tissues, and spatial coordinate frameworks. (1) Ontologies: map epithelial cell types to Cell Ontology terms and tissue context to UBERON; create a polarity-structure annotation schema (apical domain, basal domain, tight junction, adherens junction, lumen boundary, planar polarity axis) with clear definitions and examples. (2) Cross-dataset alignment: standardize gene identifiers, protein accessions, and antibody targets; harmonize imaging channels/markers via controlled vocabularies. (3) Spatial coordinates: represent each dataset as a spatial graph (spots/cells as nodes; adjacency edges by physical proximity) with optional layer annotations (e.g., basal lamina, lumen-facing boundary) when available.

Aim 1 methods: identify conserved polarity modules and quantify segregation. We will compute within-dataset module candidates using integrated approaches: (i) co-expression/co-abundance modules (WGCNA-like on spatially smoothed expression; multi-omic correlation across matched tissues), (ii) network-informed modules using known polarity/junction interactions (STRING, BioGRID, CORUM, curated polarity complex lists), and (iii) transfer learning from scRNA-seq to spatial data via label transfer and deconvolution. Module conservation will be assessed by cross-tissue reproducibility metrics (module overlap significance, stability under resampling) and by functional enrichment (GO, cellular component).

Aim 2 methods: infer polarity axes and domain boundaries. We will develop a “polarity scoring” toolkit with four core computations: (1) Axis inference: estimate dominant polarity direction using spatial gradients of apical vs basal module scores and graph Laplacian eigenvectors; align axes across samples by maximizing correspondence to anatomical landmarks (lumen/basement membrane when annotated) or by unsupervised axis coherence. (2) Boundary segmentation: graph-based segmentation (community detection/Markov random fields) on combined features (module scores, neighborhood composition, imaging-derived localization) to delineate domains. (3) Junction continuity: quantify tight junction belt integrity using imaging skeletonization where available or spatial autocorrelation/edge-density proxies where imaging is absent. (4) Polarity strength: compute segregation indices (e.g., Moran’s I for module scores, mutual information between domain labels and module scores, boundary sharpness).

Aim 3 methods: disease/disruption signatures and perturbation integration. We will assemble condition-labeled cohorts and perform meta-analysis using hierarchical models that account for tissue, platform, and batch. Disruption signatures will be defined as shifts in the polarity scorecard relative to matched healthy references. Perturbation datasets will be integrated by mapping perturbed genes to modules and networks; enrichment and causal prioritization will use gene set enrichment, network propagation, and (where phenotype readouts exist) supervised models predicting disruption mode.

Benchmarking and validation (computational). Because no new experiments are allowed, validation will rely on: (i) internal consistency (replication across datasets and platforms), (ii) concordance between modalities (RNA vs protein vs imaging localization), (iii) recovery of known biology (e.g., apical markers enriched luminally; claudin-specific patterns in epithelia), and (iv) sensitivity analyses (downsampling, marker ablation, alternative adjacency definitions). All methods will be packaged with unit tests and documented benchmarks on representative datasets.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Primary products. (1) Polarity Synthesis Atlas: a harmonized, cross-tissue resource linking epithelial cell types, spatial coordinates, polarity modules, and polarity scorecard outputs across healthy, developmental, and disease contexts. The Atlas will include dataset-level metadata, standardized annotations, and derived features (module scores, inferred axes, domain segmentations, disruption signatures) that can be queried and reused. (2) Open-source “Polarity Scoring Toolkit”: reproducible pipelines and APIs to compute polarity metrics from spatial transcriptomics and/or multiplex imaging, with reference implementations for common platforms and clear guidance on required inputs. (3) Catalog of polarity disruption signatures: a structured taxonomy of failure modes (e.g., junction fragmentation vs apical–basal mixing) with associated molecular modules and network hubs, enabling cross-study comparisons.

Scientific advances. The synthesis will produce a quantitative, testable framework for emergence in epithelial polarity by explicitly connecting molecular modules and interaction subnetworks to mesoscale organization metrics. We expect to identify a conserved core of polarity modules shared across epithelia, alongside tissue-specialized modules that explain functional diversity (e.g., absorptive vs secretory surfaces). We also expect to find that diverse diseases converge onto a limited set of disruption modes, clarifying which aspects of polarity are most fragile and which are robust.

Broader impacts. The resulting tools and Atlas will lower barriers for researchers to analyze spatial datasets in a polarity-aware manner, improving interpretability of spatial omics studies and providing benchmarks for AI methods that claim to infer spatial organization. Clinically relevant impacts include improved mechanistic stratification of epithelial cancers and barrier diseases based on polarity organization rather than single markers. Workforce impacts include training trainees in integrative spatial analysis, ontology-based annotation, and reproducible synthesis workflows—skills aligned with NCEMS’s goal to develop data-savvy molecular and cellular scientists.

Why NCEMS. These outcomes require coordinated, community-scale standardization and integration across modalities, tissues, and analytic traditions; they are not achievable by a single lab. NCEMS convening, computational support, and open-science infrastructure will accelerate consensus building and dissemination, maximizing reuse and long-term value.
budget_and_resources:
Budget rationale (NCEMS working group model). The project is synthesis-only and relies on convening expertise, supporting trainee participation, and providing shared computational infrastructure for harmonization and benchmarking. We request NCEMS support for:

1) Working group meetings and collaboration (largest need). Funds will support multiple structured meetings over the project period: an initial scoping/ontology summit, two integration/benchmarking meetings, and a final synthesis and dissemination meeting. Support includes participant travel (with attention to geographic diversity), lodging, meeting space, and hybrid participation infrastructure to include members who cannot travel. These meetings are essential for consensus on polarity definitions, annotation standards, and cross-platform QC—tasks that cannot be completed effectively by asynchronous collaboration alone.

2) Personnel support for synthesis and training. Modest support is requested for a cross-institutional coordination role (project manager or research software engineer fraction) to maintain repositories, manage data inventories, implement workflow automation, and ensure documentation. Support for trainees (graduate students/postdocs) will enable them to lead specific deliverables (e.g., module curation, imaging feature extraction, benchmarking notebooks) and participate in training activities.

3) Computing and data management resources. Although data are public, processing spatial omics and imaging at scale is computationally intensive. Funds will support cloud/HPC compute allocations, storage for intermediate and derived artifacts, and costs associated with persistent hosting of the Polarity Synthesis Atlas (e.g., static site, object storage, DOI minting). We will prioritize efficient representations (compressed feature matrices, tiled image features rather than raw images when licensing limits redistribution).

4) Dissemination and training materials. Budget will support creation of tutorials, workshops, and documentation (technical writing, video captioning, accessibility), and potentially small subawards for community contributors to improve adoption.

NCEMS-specific resource needs. NCEMS convening capacity, facilitation of multidisciplinary consensus, and access to center-supported data-science expertise are required to integrate modalities and standardize ontologies beyond what existing single-lab efforts can achieve. The budget is designed to maximize reusable community products rather than new data generation, fully aligning with NCEMS funding requirements.

title: A Synthesis of Mitochondrial Network Emergence: Linking Morphodynamics, Proteostasis, and Bioenergetics Across Cell Types
abstract:
Mitochondria form dynamic networks whose emergent morphology—fragmented, tubular, or hyperfused—reflects the balance of fission, fusion, transport, and mitophagy. Although many public datasets measure mitochondrial morphology, gene dependencies, proteomics, and respiration, they remain siloed. This working group will synthesize these resources to uncover general principles linking molecular regulation to emergent mitochondrial network states and cellular outcomes.

We will integrate (i) high-content imaging datasets with mitochondrial stains/reporters (Cell Painting, IDR), (ii) curated mitochondrial protein resources (MitoCarta), (iii) proteomics and phosphoproteomics under metabolic and stress perturbations (CPTAC, PRIDE), (iv) CRISPR dependency data for mitochondrial genes (DepMap), (v) transcriptomic responses to metabolic shifts (GEO), and (vi) publicly available bioenergetic measurements where raw data are shared (Seahorse-style outputs in supplementary repositories). Image analysis pipelines will extract network features (branch length distributions, connectivity, fragmentation indices) and, where time-lapse exists, morphodynamic rates.

Scientific questions: (1) Are there conserved, low-dimensional mitochondrial “network states” that recur across cell types and perturbations? (2) Which molecular programs (post-translational modifications of DRP1/OPA1, proteostasis pathways, lipid metabolism) drive transitions between states? (3) How do emergent network states predict higher-order phenotypes such as apoptosis sensitivity, ROS handling, and differentiation potential?

Analytically, we will build multimodal models that link omics signatures to image-derived network states, using domain adaptation to handle different imaging conditions. We will combine mechanistic modeling (balance equations for fission/fusion/turnover) with data-driven inference to estimate effective rates from snapshots and limited time series. We will also identify genetic interaction patterns that reveal compensatory pathways stabilizing network morphology.

NCEMS support is essential due to the scale of imaging harmonization and the need to integrate across modalities and institutions. The working group will bring together mitochondrial biologists, quantitative microscopists, ML experts, and systems biologists to establish community standards for mitochondrial network quantification.

Deliverables include an open MitoNetwork Emergence Atlas with standardized morphology features, inferred network states, and linked molecular predictors; reproducible image analysis and integration workflows; and a set of prioritized hypotheses about regulators that control state transitions across contexts. Training will include trainee-led development of annotation sets for benchmarking segmentation, tutorials on reproducible image analytics, and open science practices. The synthesis will clarify how mesoscale mitochondrial organization emerges and impacts cellular physiology.
background_and_significance:
Mitochondria are not static “beans” but dynamic, self-organizing networks whose mesoscale organization emerges from local molecular events—membrane fission and fusion, cytoskeletal transport, organelle contact sites, and selective turnover via mitophagy. Network morphology is tightly coupled to function: fragmented mitochondria are frequently associated with stress, mitophagy priming, and altered redox balance; elongated or hyperfused networks can support oxidative phosphorylation, resist autophagic turnover, and buffer transient insults. Yet the field lacks a unifying, quantitative framework that connects molecular regulation to reproducible, cross-context “network states” and to downstream cellular phenotypes.

A central challenge is that evidence is dispersed across modalities and experimental systems. High-content microscopy has produced thousands of images with mitochondrial dyes or reporters across genetic and chemical perturbations, but these datasets are typically analyzed with assay-specific metrics (e.g., “fragmentation score”) and are difficult to compare across imaging platforms. In parallel, large-scale proteomics and phosphoproteomics under metabolic shifts and stress (e.g., hypoxia, nutrient deprivation, ROS) have cataloged extensive post-translational regulation of mitochondrial proteins and fission/fusion machinery. Genome-wide CRISPR screens identify dependencies and genetic interactions involving mitochondrial pathways, while transcriptomic compendia capture adaptive programs that remodel metabolism. Bioenergetic measurements (e.g., oxygen consumption rate, spare respiratory capacity) offer functional grounding but are rarely integrated with morphology at scale. The result is a patchwork of mechanistic narratives without a synthesis that reveals general principles of emergence.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that is beyond any single laboratory: harmonizing heterogeneous imaging datasets, extracting standardized network features, linking them to multi-omics signatures, and inferring effective dynamical parameters requires coordinated expertise in mitochondrial biology, quantitative image analysis, machine learning, and systems modeling. Critically, this project uses only existing publicly available data, aligning with NCEMS’s mission to unlock new knowledge from the “data already in the world.”

The scientific significance is threefold. First, mitochondria are a canonical example of mesoscale emergence: network-level properties (connectivity, percolation, heterogeneity, spatial distribution) arise from molecular-scale events and feed back to cellular-scale outcomes (cell fate decisions, stress tolerance, differentiation). Second, mitochondrial dysregulation is implicated across cancer, neurodegeneration, cardiometabolic disease, and aging; identifying conserved network states and their regulators could unify disparate disease observations and improve interpretability of perturbation datasets. Third, developing robust, transferable computational strategies for mitochondrial network quantification and multimodal integration will generalize to other organelles and mesoscale assemblies (ER networks, endolysosomal systems, stress granules).

By synthesizing imaging-derived morphodynamics with proteostasis and bioenergetics across diverse cell types, this working group will move the field from qualitative descriptors to a quantitative “state-space” view of mitochondrial organization. The outcome will be an open, reusable atlas and analysis framework that enables the community to test mechanistic hypotheses, compare results across laboratories, and understand how mitochondrial network emergence constrains and enables cellular physiology.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will address how mitochondrial networks exhibit emergent mesoscale states, what molecular programs govern transitions among those states, and how those states predict higher-order cellular outcomes. We focus on questions that require synthesis across imaging, omics, genetic dependency, and functional bioenergetic data—an integration not feasible within single-lab datasets.

RQ1: Do conserved, low-dimensional mitochondrial network states recur across cell types and perturbations?
Hypothesis 1A: Despite heterogeneous imaging conditions and cell-specific morphologies, mitochondrial networks occupy a small number of conserved latent states characterized by combinations of connectivity, branch length distributions, puncta density, and spatial dispersion.
Hypothesis 1B: These states are better captured by multivariate feature manifolds (graph/topology + texture + spatial statistics) than by single “fragmentation” metrics, and will be reproducible across independent datasets after domain adaptation.
Hypothesis 1C: Time-resolved datasets will reveal that apparent continuum variation in snapshots decomposes into state dwell times and transition rates, indicating metastable attractor-like behavior.

RQ2: What molecular programs drive transitions between network states?
Hypothesis 2A: Transitions are governed by coordinated modules rather than single regulators: (i) fission/fusion machinery and its PTMs (e.g., DRP1 phosphorylation states; OPA1 processing), (ii) proteostasis and quality control (mitochondrial ribosome, chaperones, AAA proteases, UPRmt), and (iii) lipid metabolism and membrane remodeling (cardiolipin synthesis/remodeling; ER-mito contact regulators).
Hypothesis 2B: Proteostasis stress signatures (e.g., elevated mitochondrial unfolded protein response components) predict fragmentation-to-clearance trajectories, whereas lipid remodeling signatures predict tubular-to-hyperfused stabilization.
Hypothesis 2C: Specific phosphosites and proteoforms act as “switches” that bias the effective fission/fusion balance, detectable as consistent predictors of inferred transition probabilities across contexts.

RQ3: How do emergent network states relate to bioenergetics and cellular phenotypes?
Hypothesis 3A: Network state is predictive of bioenergetic capacity beyond gene expression alone: hyperfused/tubular states associate with higher spare respiratory capacity and coupling efficiency, while fragmented states associate with reduced maximal respiration and increased glycolytic compensation.
Hypothesis 3B: Network states modulate stress outcomes: fragmented states correlate with higher basal ROS and heightened apoptosis sensitivity under additional insults; intermediate connected states maximize resilience by balancing distribution and quality control.
Hypothesis 3C: In differentiating systems and lineage models, transitions toward more connected networks precede (and partially predict) commitment and metabolic rewiring, serving as a mesoscale biomarker of differentiation potential.

RQ4 (methodological): Can we infer effective dynamical parameters of mitochondrial morphodynamics from heterogeneous snapshots and limited time series?
Hypothesis 4A: A hybrid approach combining mechanistic balance models (fission, fusion, turnover) with probabilistic state-space inference can estimate effective rates that are consistent across datasets and predict observed state occupancy.
Hypothesis 4B: These inferred parameters will align with independent genetic dependency patterns (e.g., cells dependent on fusion machinery will exhibit low inferred fusion capacity and high fragmentation propensity).

Together, these questions and hypotheses create a cohesive synthesis agenda: define states, map molecular drivers, connect to function, and infer dynamics—producing generalizable principles of mitochondrial network emergence at the mesoscale.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will execute a community-scale synthesis using only publicly available datasets, organized into four integrated work packages (WPs) spanning data curation, image-derived network phenotyping, multimodal integration, and mechanistic inference. The team will include mitochondrial biologists (interpretation and priors), quantitative microscopists (feature validity), ML/data scientists (domain adaptation and multimodal modeling), and systems biologists (state-space and rate inference). NCEMS support is essential for convening, cross-institution compute coordination, and establishing community standards.

WP1: Data discovery, selection, and harmonization. We will curate imaging datasets with mitochondrial stains/reporters from Cell Painting repositories and the Image Data Resource (IDR), prioritizing experiments with perturbation metadata (compound, dose, time; CRISPR/ORF; stress conditions). We will map gene identifiers to MitoCarta and annotate perturbations to pathways (GO, Reactome). Proteomics/phosphoproteomics will be drawn from CPTAC and PRIDE with explicit sample annotations; transcriptomics from GEO (metabolic shifts, stress, differentiation); dependency data from DepMap (CRISPR gene effect, co-dependency). Bioenergetic readouts will be extracted from repositories where raw OCR/ECAR tables are shared (supplementary files, Zenodo, Figshare), standardizing units and assay phases. Harmonization will include consistent cell line identifiers (DepMap IDs), treatment ontologies, and time alignment where possible.

WP2: Standardized mitochondrial network feature extraction. We will implement reproducible pipelines (containerized) to segment mitochondria and quantify network properties. For segmentation, we will benchmark classical (adaptive threshold + skeletonization) and deep-learning approaches (pretrained U-Net variants), selecting methods per dataset based on staining quality and resolution. Features will include: (i) morphology/texture (area, aspect ratio, intensity heterogeneity), (ii) skeleton/graph metrics (total branch length, node degree distribution, largest connected component, loop counts), (iii) fragmentation/connectivity indices, (iv) spatial organization (perinuclear vs peripheral distribution; anisotropy), and (v) when time-lapse exists, morphodynamic rates (event frequencies, persistence, autocorrelation). Trainees will generate small expert-annotated sets for benchmarking segmentation and skeleton fidelity.

WP3: Learning conserved network states across datasets. We will learn low-dimensional representations using variational autoencoders or contrastive learning on feature vectors and/or image embeddings, then define discrete or continuous states via mixture models/HMMs. To address batch effects and imaging heterogeneity, we will apply domain adaptation (e.g., CORAL, adversarial alignment, or Harmony-like integration on embeddings) using shared controls and weak supervision from known perturbations (e.g., DRP1 activation → fragmentation). State reproducibility will be evaluated by cross-dataset transfer: train on one dataset, predict states in another, and test concordance of known biological perturbations.

WP4: Multimodal integration and mechanistic inference. We will link state occupancy to omics using multi-view models (MOFA+, regularized canonical correlation, and supervised approaches such as elastic net, gradient boosting, and multimodal transformers where appropriate). We will prioritize interpretability: pathway-level predictors, phosphosite modules, and proteostasis signatures. For dynamics, we will fit mechanistic balance equations describing effective fission, fusion, and turnover, embedding them in a probabilistic state-space model to infer rates from snapshot distributions and limited time series. We will triangulate inferred drivers using DepMap co-dependency networks and genetic interaction patterns, identifying compensatory modules stabilizing morphology.

Validation within synthesis constraints. We will perform internal validation via held-out datasets, sensitivity analyses (segmentation method, feature sets), negative controls (non-mitochondrial stains), and robustness to metadata uncertainty. No new experimental data will be generated; all conclusions will be supported by cross-dataset replication and transparent uncertainty quantification.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific products. The primary deliverable will be an open “MitoNetwork Emergence Atlas” that defines reproducible mitochondrial network states across cell types and perturbations, accompanied by standardized quantitative features, state assignments with uncertainty, and linked molecular predictors (genes, pathways, phosphosite modules, proteostasis and lipid programs). The atlas will include crosswalks among datasets (imaging, proteomics, transcriptomics, dependency, bioenergetics) and a documented schema for metadata harmonization.

Conceptual advances. We expect to establish whether mitochondrial morphology is best described as a small set of conserved mesoscale states and to identify the dominant molecular axes controlling transitions (e.g., PTM-regulated fission/fusion, proteostasis capacity, membrane lipid remodeling). By integrating bioenergetics, we will quantify how network emergence constrains functional outputs such as spare respiratory capacity, coupling efficiency, and stress resilience, providing a state-space framework that unifies previously siloed observations.

Methodological advances. We will deliver validated, transferable pipelines for mitochondrial network segmentation and graph-based quantification, plus domain-adaptation strategies enabling cross-platform comparison—an enabling technology for the community. Hybrid mechanistic/data-driven inference will provide estimated effective rates of fission/fusion/turnover, offering a bridge between molecular perturbations and emergent network behavior.

Community impact. The working group will produce prioritized, testable hypotheses about regulators and compensatory pathways that stabilize or destabilize network states, guiding future experimental work (outside this synthesis project). Standards for reporting mitochondrial network metrics and recommended benchmarking datasets will improve reproducibility across laboratories.

Workforce and training impact. Trainees will gain experience in open, team-based data synthesis, imaging analytics, and multimodal modeling, directly advancing NCEMS’s goal of training a data-savvy molecular and cellular workforce. Overall, the project will clarify how mesoscale mitochondrial organization emerges and why it matters for cellular physiology, disease-relevant stress responses, and differentiation.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS working-group support rationale. This project requires coordinated, community-scale synthesis across imaging, omics, dependency, and bioenergetics data, including harmonization of heterogeneous metadata and compute-intensive image processing and representation learning. These needs exceed what a single lab can accomplish and benefit directly from NCEMS convening power, cyberinfrastructure, and open-science expertise.

Major budget categories (illustrative, aligned with typical synthesis-center working groups).
1) Meetings and collaboration: Support for 2–3 in-person working meetings at NCEMS (or hybrid), including travel, lodging, and per diem for a geographically distributed team; dedicated time for structured hackathons and integration sprints; accessibility support to broaden participation.
2) Personnel time (as allowed by NCEMS mechanisms): Partial support for a project manager/data curator to coordinate dataset intake, metadata standards, and releases; and support for trainee participation (graduate students/postdocs) through stipends or travel awards to attend working sessions and lead tutorial development.
3) Compute and storage: Cloud or NCEMS-managed compute credits for large-scale image processing, embedding training, and model fitting; storage for intermediate artifacts and derived feature tables; and costs for long-term archiving (e.g., Zenodo deposition is free, but curation time is not).
4) Software engineering and reproducibility: Resources for containerization, workflow automation, CI setup, and documentation; optional consultation with NCEMS data/software staff to ensure best practices.

Resource plan and roles. Participating labs will contribute complementary expertise and in-kind effort: mitochondrial biology interpretation and priors; quantitative microscopy and segmentation benchmarking; ML/domain adaptation; systems modeling and state-space inference. NCEMS resources will be used to (i) convene and coordinate the team, (ii) provide neutral infrastructure for shared pipelines and data products, and (iii) ensure outputs meet gold-standard open, reproducible science expectations.

Deliverable-driven milestones. Budget allocations will be tied to milestones: curated dataset registry and schema (release 1), standardized feature extraction and benchmarking set (release 2), cross-dataset state model and predictors (release 3), and final atlas + training materials (release 4).

title: Emergent Signaling Specificity: Integrating Single-Cell Phospho-Proteomics, Kinase Networks, and Imaging to Decode Pathway Crosstalk
abstract:
Cell signaling pathways exhibit emergent specificity: shared kinases and second messengers can yield distinct outcomes depending on context, timing, and spatial organization. Public datasets now include mass cytometry, single-cell phospho-proteomics, kinase-substrate maps, and live-cell imaging reporters, yet we lack a synthesis that explains how mesoscale organization and network context generate specific phenotypes.

This working group will integrate (i) single-cell phospho-signaling datasets (CyTOF and CITE-seq phospho panels with public deposition), (ii) bulk phosphoproteomics time courses (CPTAC, PRIDE), (iii) curated kinase-substrate relationships (PhosphoSitePlus, SIGNOR), (iv) protein interaction networks (BioGRID), (v) imaging datasets of signaling dynamics (IDR), and (vi) perturbation-response resources (LINCS, CRISPR screens). We will harmonize stimulation conditions, time points, and antibody/peptide mappings to comparable signaling features.

Scientific questions: (1) What network motifs and baseline states determine whether signals propagate linearly, saturate, oscillate, or bifurcate into distinct cell fates? (2) How does spatial compartmentalization (membrane microdomains, endosomes, nucleus) shape emergent pathway crosstalk? (3) Can we predict context-specific drug responses from integrated signaling state representations?

Methodologically, we will develop dynamical models that integrate time-resolved phosphoproteomics with single-cell heterogeneity. We will use latent variable ODE models and neural differential equations constrained by known kinase-substrate graphs to infer effective signaling circuits. Imaging-derived spatial features (e.g., nuclear translocation dynamics) will serve as additional constraints. A major deliverable will be a standardized benchmark for signaling model inference across modalities and a set of open tools for harmonizing phospho datasets.

NCEMS support is required because cross-modal integration of phospho data is technically challenging (inconsistent identifiers, variable coverage) and demands collaboration among proteomics experts, signaling biologists, statisticians, and ML researchers. The project’s community-scale nature includes building shared standards for metadata and reproducible pipelines.

Deliverables will include an open Signaling Specificity Atlas with harmonized datasets, inferred context-specific circuits, and predictive models of perturbation outcomes; reusable workflows for phosphoproteomics processing and integration; and tutorials for trainees on dynamical modeling and reproducible analysis. By synthesizing diverse public data, the project will uncover emergent principles explaining how cells achieve specific decisions using shared signaling components.
background_and_significance:
Cells reuse a limited set of signaling components—kinases, phosphatases, adaptors, and second messengers—to control a vast repertoire of outcomes including proliferation, differentiation, migration, and apoptosis. A central unsolved problem is signaling specificity: how do shared pathways (e.g., MAPK, PI3K/AKT, JAK/STAT, NF-κB) produce distinct phenotypes across cell types and stimuli? Specificity is increasingly understood as an emergent property arising from mesoscale organization (complexes, scaffolds, condensates, membrane microdomains), network context (feedback/feedforward motifs, pathway crosstalk), and heterogeneous baseline states across cells. Yet mechanistic accounts remain fragmented, often derived from individual pathways, single modalities, or bespoke experimental systems.

NCEMS’ focus on emergence at the mesoscale aligns directly with this challenge. Signaling decisions are rarely encoded by a single phosphorylation event; instead, they emerge from coordinated patterns across many sites and proteins, integrated over time and space. For example, ERK can drive proliferation or differentiation depending on pulse duration and amplitude; NF-κB can encode inflammatory programs via oscillatory nuclear translocation; and AKT/mTOR outputs depend on compartment-specific activation and nutrient state. These behaviors reflect dynamical regimes (linear propagation, saturation, oscillation, bistability) that are properties of networks rather than individual molecules.

The last decade has produced a wealth of publicly available data that could, in principle, resolve these emergent principles. Single-cell phospho-profiling by mass cytometry (CyTOF) and phospho-CITE-seq captures heterogeneous signaling states across thousands of cells under diverse perturbations. Bulk phosphoproteomics time courses in CPTAC and PRIDE provide deep coverage of phosphorylation dynamics, often with multiple time points and drug/stimulus conditions. Curated causal knowledge bases (PhosphoSitePlus, SIGNOR) and interaction networks (BioGRID) provide mechanistic constraints. Imaging repositories (IDR) include live-cell reporters of translocation and activity, offering direct readouts of spatial organization and temporal encoding. Perturbation-response resources (LINCS) and CRISPR screens provide phenotypic consequences of modulating signaling nodes.

Despite this abundance, the field lacks a community-scale synthesis that harmonizes these modalities into a coherent, reusable framework for inference and prediction. Major barriers include inconsistent identifiers (protein isoforms, phosphosites, antibody epitopes), variable coverage and missingness across platforms, differences in stimulation protocols and time scales, and the absence of standardized benchmarks for model inference. Most analyses either remain within one modality or treat prior knowledge bases as static annotations rather than constraints on dynamical models.

This working group addresses a long-standing puzzle—how specificity emerges from shared signaling components—by integrating existing datasets into a unified “Signaling Specificity Atlas” and developing graph-constrained dynamical modeling approaches that connect mesoscale organization to phenotypic outcomes. The project is beyond the capacity of a single laboratory because it requires coordinated expertise in proteomics processing, single-cell analysis, imaging feature extraction, causal network biology, and modern AI/ODE modeling, as well as community standards for metadata and reproducibility. By leveraging NCEMS resources to convene and support a diverse team, we will create broadly useful tools and principles that generalize across pathways, cell types, and perturbations, advancing molecular and cellular biosciences through synthesis rather than new experiments.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal is organized around three scientific questions that target emergent signaling specificity as a mesoscale phenomenon. Each question is paired with testable hypotheses that can be evaluated using only publicly available datasets integrated across modalities.

Question 1: What network motifs and baseline states determine whether signals propagate linearly, saturate, oscillate, or bifurcate into distinct cell fates?

Hypothesis 1A (motif–regime mapping): Dynamical regimes are predictable from a compact set of network motifs embedded in kinase–substrate and protein interaction graphs. Specifically, negative feedback with appropriate delay predicts oscillatory or adaptive responses (e.g., NF-κB, ERK), positive feedback predicts bistability and fate bifurcation, and incoherent feedforward predicts pulse generation and adaptation. We will test whether motif scores computed from curated causal graphs (SIGNOR/PhosphoSitePlus + BioGRID) explain observed time-course features extracted from bulk phosphoproteomics and single-cell trajectories.

Hypothesis 1B (baseline-state gating): Pre-stimulus signaling states (e.g., basal phosphorylation, receptor abundance, cell cycle state) gate which dynamical regime is realized after stimulation. We predict that heterogeneity in baseline nodes upstream of key motifs (e.g., phosphatase levels, scaffold availability) will stratify cells into distinct response classes with different downstream phenotypes. This will be tested by linking baseline single-cell phospho profiles (CyTOF/phospho-CITE-seq) to subsequent inferred dynamics and to perturbation outcomes where available.

Question 2: How does spatial compartmentalization shape emergent pathway crosstalk and specificity?

Hypothesis 2A (compartment-specific coupling): Pathway crosstalk is mediated by compartment-specific coupling terms—effective interactions that appear only when proteins co-localize in membrane microdomains, endosomes, nucleus, or condensates. We predict that models incorporating spatial features (e.g., nuclear translocation kinetics, endosomal residence proxies) will require fewer “ad hoc” edges and will better generalize across contexts than purely cytosolic, well-mixed models.

Hypothesis 2B (spatiotemporal code reuse): Shared components encode different outputs via differences in spatial routing and timing rather than changes in network topology. For example, ERK nuclear entry dynamics and AKT membrane recruitment dynamics will explain condition-specific transcriptional and phenotypic responses even when phosphorylation of core nodes appears similar in bulk. We will test this by integrating imaging-derived features from IDR with phospho time courses and assessing improvements in predicting downstream signatures (LINCS) and viability/fitness phenotypes (CRISPR screens).

Question 3: Can context-specific drug responses be predicted from integrated signaling state representations?

Hypothesis 3A (latent state sufficiency): A low-dimensional latent “signaling state” learned from integrated phospho, network, and imaging constraints is sufficient to predict drug response classes (sensitive, resistant, adaptive) across cell types and perturbations better than gene expression alone.

Hypothesis 3B (mechanism-aware transfer): Graph-constrained neural ODE models will transfer across datasets (e.g., from deep bulk time courses to sparse single-cell panels) by leveraging mechanistic priors, enabling prediction under new combinations of stimuli and inhibitors without retraining from scratch.

Collectively, these hypotheses operationalize emergence: specificity is not encoded in single measurements but arises from motif-driven dynamics, baseline heterogeneity, and spatial routing. The working group will evaluate these hypotheses through pre-registered analyses and benchmarks built from harmonized public data.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and team science structure. We will run an NCEMS Working Group with coordinated sprints across data harmonization, feature extraction, modeling, and benchmarking. All work uses publicly available data; no new experiments will be performed. The approach is organized into four technical aims.

Aim 1: Assemble and harmonize a cross-modal signaling compendium. We will curate representative datasets spanning: (i) single-cell phospho signaling (CyTOF, phospho-CITE-seq panels with public deposition), (ii) bulk phosphoproteomics time courses (CPTAC, PRIDE), (iii) kinase–substrate and causal edges (PhosphoSitePlus, SIGNOR), (iv) protein interactions (BioGRID), (v) live-cell imaging reporters (IDR), and (vi) perturbation outcomes (LINCS signatures, public CRISPR screens). Harmonization tasks include: identifier normalization (UniProt accessions, gene symbols, isoforms), phosphosite mapping (PSP site IDs, peptide-to-site localization, antibody epitope mapping), condition ontology (stimulus, dose, inhibitor, cell line/type, time), and quality flags (missingness, batch, coverage). We will implement a “minimum information for phospho-signaling synthesis” metadata schema and provide converters for common formats.

Aim 2: Extract comparable signaling features across modalities. For time courses (bulk phosphoproteomics, some CyTOF time series), we will compute dynamical summaries: peak amplitude, time-to-peak, adaptation index, oscillation score, and bifurcation indicators via change-point detection and spectral methods. For single-cell data, we will infer pseudotime/trajectory structure where appropriate and compute baseline-state embeddings that capture pre-stimulus variation. For imaging, we will extract interpretable features such as nuclear/cytosolic ratio dynamics, translocation frequency, pulse width, and subcellular localization states using standardized pipelines (e.g., CellProfiler/napari-based workflows when available) applied to IDR-provided segmentations or raw images where permitted.

Aim 3: Build graph-constrained dynamical models linking motifs, space, and heterogeneity. We will develop and compare model classes:

(1) Latent variable ODE/state-space models: A low-dimensional latent state z(t) drives observed phospho features, with dynamics dz/dt = f(z, u, c) where u is stimulus/perturbation and c encodes context (cell type, baseline state). We will fit using variational inference and handle missingness explicitly.

(2) Neural differential equations constrained by kinase graphs: We will parameterize f using graph neural networks over kinase–substrate edges, with priors favoring known causal directions and sparsity. This enables mechanistic interpretability while retaining flexibility.

(3) Compartment-aware extensions: We will include coupled latent states for compartments (membrane/endosome/nucleus/cytosol) with exchange terms informed by imaging-derived constraints (e.g., nuclear entry rates). Where imaging is absent, we will use proxy annotations (e.g., GO cellular component) with uncertainty.

Aim 4: Benchmarking, validation, and prediction tasks. We will create standardized tasks and splits: (i) reconstruct held-out time points, (ii) predict single-cell response class from baseline, (iii) transfer across modalities (train on bulk, predict sparse panels), and (iv) predict drug/perturbation outcomes (LINCS signatures, CRISPR fitness) from inferred signaling states. Evaluation metrics include predictive log-likelihood, calibration, motif recovery, and out-of-domain generalization. We will perform sensitivity analyses to dataset selection and priors, and we will pre-register key comparisons to reduce researcher degrees of freedom.

Feasibility and NCEMS need. The work requires coordinated expertise (proteomics, antibody mapping, imaging analysis, causal networks, differential equation modeling) and substantial integration effort to produce reusable standards and benchmarks—precisely the community-scale synthesis mission of NCEMS.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific outcomes. The project will produce a synthesis-driven, cross-modal explanation of how signaling specificity emerges from shared components. We expect to identify motif–regime relationships that generalize across pathways (e.g., feedback-driven oscillations, feedforward-driven pulses) and quantify how baseline heterogeneity gates regime selection. By integrating spatial readouts, we anticipate demonstrating that compartment-specific routing accounts for a substantial fraction of apparent “crosstalk” and context dependence, reducing the need for overly dense, uninterpretable network models.

Methodological outcomes. We will deliver validated, graph-constrained dynamical modeling tools that integrate bulk time courses, single-cell heterogeneity, and imaging-derived spatial constraints. A key product will be a benchmark suite for signaling model inference across modalities, including curated datasets, standardized splits, and evaluation metrics. These resources will enable the community to compare methods transparently and accelerate development of mechanistic AI for molecular and cellular systems.

Community resources. The Signaling Specificity Atlas will provide harmonized datasets, mappings (antibody/peptide/phosphosite), inferred context-specific circuits, and predictive models of perturbation outcomes. The atlas will be designed for reuse: modular data packages, documented APIs, and example notebooks that support new datasets and new modeling approaches.

Broader impact. Predicting context-specific drug responses from signaling state representations can inform therapeutic strategies, including combination design and identification of adaptive resistance mechanisms, without requiring new experiments in early hypothesis generation. More broadly, the project advances NCEMS’ emergence agenda by linking mesoscale organization and network dynamics to cell-level decisions using synthesis of public data. Training activities embedded in the working group will produce a cohort of researchers fluent in open, reproducible, cross-modal data science for molecular and cellular biology.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support rationale. This is a community-scale synthesis effort requiring intensive, in-person and virtual coordination among multiple labs and disciplines, plus dedicated support for data harmonization and reproducible infrastructure. The work exceeds a single lab’s capacity because it spans proteomics processing, single-cell analysis, imaging feature extraction, causal knowledge integration, and dynamical ML modeling, and because it aims to produce community standards and benchmarks.

Requested NCEMS resources (typical Working Group needs). (1) Convening support: funds for multiple multi-day working meetings at NCEMS (or NCEMS-supported venue), enabling deep integration work, paired programming, and consensus building on standards. (2) Participant support: travel, lodging, and per diem for a geographically and institutionally diverse team, including investigators from R1 and non-R1 institutions and international participants when allowable. (3) Trainee support: travel awards and stipends for graduate students and postdocs to attend meetings, lead tutorials, and perform reproducibility audits. (4) Cyberinfrastructure: access to NCEMS-supported compute for model training and benchmarking (GPU/CPU as needed), shared storage for intermediate artifacts, and technical consultation on scalable, reproducible workflows.

Budget categories (high-level). Personnel time will be contributed in-kind by participating labs; NCEMS funds will primarily cover convening, participant support, trainee development, and compute. Anticipated categories include: meeting logistics; travel and lodging; trainee support; software engineering/curation support (part-time research software engineer or data curator, if allowed); and dissemination (workshops, documentation, long-term archiving fees).

Resource plan and governance. We will establish a steering committee (PIs + trainee representative) to prioritize datasets, approve schema changes, and manage deliverables. Milestones will be tied to meetings: (i) v1 harmonized compendium and schema, (ii) v1 benchmark suite, (iii) v1 atlas release with baseline models, (iv) manuscript and public training modules. All deliverables will be archived in long-term repositories (Zenodo/OSF) with DOIs, ensuring persistence beyond the award period.

title: A Comparative Synthesis of Ribosome Heterogeneity and Specialized Translation Across Tissues and Stress Conditions
abstract:
Ribosomes are often treated as uniform machines, yet accumulating evidence suggests ribosome composition and rRNA modifications vary, potentially enabling specialized translation—an emergent regulatory layer at the mesoscale. Public datasets include ribosome profiling, quantitative proteomics of ribosomal proteins, rRNA modification maps, and genetic perturbations, but they have not been synthesized to test whether ribosome heterogeneity systematically predicts selective translation programs.

This working group will integrate (i) ribosome profiling datasets across tissues, development, and stress (GEO), (ii) proteomics quantifying ribosomal protein paralogs and associated factors (PRIDE, CPTAC), (iii) rRNA modification and ribosome biogenesis datasets (public epitranscriptomic studies), (iv) single-cell RNA-seq atlases for tissue context (Tabula Sapiens, HCA), and (v) perturbation datasets targeting ribosomal proteins, snoRNPs, and biogenesis factors (CRISPR screens, DepMap). We will curate metadata on growth conditions, stressors, and cell types, and standardize processing of ribosome profiling to comparable translation efficiency metrics.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify reproducible axes of ribosome heterogeneity (protein composition, modification patterns, associated factors) across contexts. (2) Test whether specific heterogeneity signatures correlate with selective translation of mRNA subsets (e.g., IRES-containing, uORF-rich, mitochondrial-targeted). (3) Determine whether specialized translation is conserved across species and how it relates to stress adaptation and disease.

Analytical approach: We will build joint models linking ribosome composition proxies (from proteomics and expression of ribosomal paralogs/biogenesis factors) to translation efficiency changes inferred from ribosome profiling. We will use multivariate association methods with careful confounder control (growth rate, global translation shifts) and causal inference leveraging perturbation datasets. We will also develop motif-based and structure-aware predictors of mRNAs sensitive to ribosome state.

NCEMS support is essential because integrating ribosome profiling with proteomics and modification data requires specialized expertise and substantial curation; no single lab typically spans these domains. The working group will coordinate standards for reporting ribosome profiling processing and for mapping ribosomal protein isoforms across datasets.

Deliverables will include a Ribosome Heterogeneity Synthesis Resource with harmonized datasets, inferred heterogeneity axes, and candidate specialized translation programs; reproducible pipelines for ribosome profiling processing; and open benchmarks for detecting specialized translation. Training will be provided through workshops on ribosome profiling analysis, proteomics integration, and open science practices, with trainees leading curation of tissue- and stress-specific modules. The synthesis will clarify whether and how ribosome diversity yields emergent translational control.
background_and_significance:
Translation is a central determinant of cellular state, coupling gene expression programs to proteome composition, growth, and adaptation. The ribosome is traditionally modeled as a uniform molecular machine with fixed stoichiometry and function. However, multiple lines of evidence now indicate that ribosomes can vary in composition (e.g., tissue- or lineage-biased usage of ribosomal protein paralogs, differential incorporation of accessory factors, and variable occupancy of ribosome-associated proteins), in rRNA chemical modifications (e.g., 2′-O-methylation and pseudouridylation), and in biogenesis pathways that shape ribosome quality and specialization. These sources of ribosome heterogeneity occur at the mesoscale—between individual biomolecules and organelles—where ensembles of ribosomes collectively influence higher-order outcomes such as stress resistance, differentiation trajectories, and disease phenotypes.

A key unresolved question is whether ribosome heterogeneity is merely correlated with cellular context (a byproduct of transcriptional differences, growth rate, or biogenesis capacity) or whether it constitutes an emergent regulatory layer that causally reshapes which mRNAs are translated. “Specialized translation” hypotheses propose that certain ribosome states preferentially translate mRNA subsets with distinct 5′ leaders (e.g., IRES-like elements), upstream open reading frames (uORFs), codon usage biases, RNA structure features, or subcellular targeting signals (e.g., mitochondrial or ER-targeted transcripts). If true, ribosome heterogeneity would represent a generalizable mechanism for selectively implementing proteome programs without changing mRNA abundance, providing a powerful explanation for context-specific proteome remodeling during stress, development, and disease.

Public data relevant to this problem have grown dramatically: ribosome profiling provides codon-resolved footprints and translation efficiency estimates across hundreds of perturbations and tissues; quantitative proteomics measures ribosomal protein abundances and paralog usage; epitranscriptomic studies map rRNA modifications and snoRNA-guided modification machinery; single-cell atlases provide cell-type context and enable deconvolution of bulk measurements; and CRISPR screens and dependency maps offer perturbation-based constraints on ribosome components and biogenesis factors. Yet these resources remain siloed, processed with inconsistent pipelines, and described with incomplete metadata, preventing robust cross-study inference. Consequently, the field lacks a community-scale synthesis that can quantify reproducible axes of ribosome heterogeneity and test, with statistical rigor, whether those axes predict selective translation programs across contexts.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze this synthesis because (i) the question centers on emergence at the mesoscale, (ii) resolving it requires integration of heterogeneous molecular datasets and advanced AI/data-science methods, and (iii) the scale of curation, harmonization, and multi-modal modeling exceeds what a single laboratory can sustain. By assembling a multidisciplinary working group spanning ribosome biology, proteomics, epitranscriptomics, statistical genetics, causal inference, and machine learning, we will create a unified, reusable resource and analytical framework. This effort will address a long-standing puzzle—whether ribosome diversity systematically encodes selective translation—and will establish reproducible standards for future synthesis research in translational control.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will address whether ribosome heterogeneity constitutes a reproducible, predictive, and partially causal layer of translational regulation across tissues and stress conditions. We will focus on three overarching research questions, each with testable hypotheses that can be evaluated using only publicly available datasets.

Research Question 1: What are the dominant, reproducible axes of ribosome heterogeneity across biological contexts?
Hypothesis 1A (structured heterogeneity): Across tissues, developmental stages, and stressors, ribosome heterogeneity is not random noise but organizes into a small number of recurrent axes reflecting (i) differential abundance of ribosomal protein paralogs and select core proteins, (ii) variation in ribosome-associated factors (initiation/elongation modulators, quality control factors), and (iii) coordinated patterns of rRNA modification and biogenesis factor activity.
Hypothesis 1B (context specificity with conservation): While the magnitude of heterogeneity varies by context (e.g., proliferative vs. quiescent tissues; acute vs. chronic stress), the underlying axes are partially conserved across species (e.g., yeast, mouse, human) and across dataset modalities.

Research Question 2: Do specific ribosome heterogeneity signatures predict selective translation of defined mRNA subsets beyond global translational shifts?
Hypothesis 2A (selectivity beyond scaling): After controlling for confounders (growth rate proxies, total ribosome occupancy, global initiation/elongation changes, batch effects), certain ribosome states are associated with differential translation efficiency of mRNA subsets defined by mechanistic features: uORF-rich leaders, structured 5′ UTRs, IRES-like elements, specific codon usage patterns, signal peptide/mitochondrial targeting sequences, or stress-response regulons.
Hypothesis 2B (feature-mediated sensitivity): Translation sensitivity to ribosome state is mediated by interpretable mRNA sequence/structure features that can be learned by motif-based and structure-aware models and that generalize across datasets.

Research Question 3: Is there evidence consistent with causality between ribosome components/biogenesis pathways and specialized translation programs, and how does this relate to stress adaptation and disease?
Hypothesis 3A (perturbation consistency): Genetic perturbations of ribosomal proteins, paralogs, snoRNP components, and biogenesis factors produce translation changes that align with the inferred heterogeneity axes, supporting a causal relationship rather than mere correlation.
Hypothesis 3B (fitness and disease relevance): Ribosome states associated with selective translation correspond to differential fitness dependencies in DepMap/CRISPR screens and align with disease-relevant contexts (e.g., cancer lineages, ribosomopathies, neurodegeneration) where translation reprogramming is implicated.

Across all questions, we will explicitly test robustness to alternative processing pipelines and model specifications. We will treat “specialized translation” as an operational, falsifiable claim: a ribosome heterogeneity signature must predict mRNA-specific translation changes with reproducible effect sizes across independent datasets and must remain after accounting for global translation and transcriptional composition. These hypotheses directly target emergent mesoscale behavior—how ensembles of heterogeneous ribosomes yield system-level selectivity in protein synthesis.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will execute a community-scale synthesis organized around shared curation standards, harmonized processing pipelines, and multi-modal modeling. The team will be divided into cross-cutting task forces: (T1) ribosome profiling harmonization, (T2) proteomics and ribosomal protein isoform/paralog mapping, (T3) rRNA modification/biogenesis integration, (T4) single-cell context and deconvolution, and (T5) modeling/causal inference and benchmarking. All analyses will use existing public data only.

Data acquisition and inclusion criteria. We will compile ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) and matched RNA-seq from GEO/SRA and curated repositories, emphasizing datasets with clear metadata (tissue/cell type, stressor, time, species, replicate structure). Proteomics will be drawn from PRIDE and CPTAC with ribosomal protein quantification or whole-proteome coverage enabling extraction of ribosome-related features. rRNA modification datasets will include published maps of 2′-O-methylation and pseudouridylation, along with snoRNA/biogenesis factor perturbation studies where available. Single-cell atlases (Tabula Sapiens, Human Cell Atlas, mouse atlases) will provide cell-type composition references. Perturbation constraints will come from CRISPR screens and DepMap gene effect matrices.

Harmonized processing.
1) Ribo-seq: Standardized adapter trimming, rRNA/tRNA depletion filtering, alignment, P-site assignment, and footprint periodicity QC. Translation efficiency (TE) will be estimated with generalized linear models that incorporate RNA-seq abundance and library size, producing comparable TE effect sizes across studies. We will compute additional features: initiation vs. elongation proxies, ribosome occupancy along ORFs, and uORF translation where detectable.
2) Proteomics: We will build a ribosomal protein/paralog mapping table resolving gene symbols, isoforms, and shared peptides. Abundances will be normalized within study and transformed into composition signatures (e.g., relative paralog ratios; ribosome-associated factor modules).
3) rRNA modifications/biogenesis: We will represent modification landscapes as site-level or region-level scores and, when direct maps are absent, infer modification/biogenesis activity from expression of snoRNAs and modifying enzymes, with uncertainty estimates.
4) Cell-type context: For bulk tissues, we will deconvolve cell-type proportions using reference atlases and include composition covariates to reduce confounding.

Multi-modal integration and inference.
A) Axis discovery: We will learn latent “ribosome state” axes using multi-view factor models (e.g., MOFA-like frameworks) and regularized matrix factorization that jointly incorporate proteomics, modification proxies, and biogenesis factor expression. Stability will be assessed by bootstrap and replication across independent cohorts.
B) Association with selective translation: For each dataset, we will model gene-level TE changes as a function of ribosome state axes, controlling for stress class, growth proxies, batch, and global translation shifts. Meta-analysis will combine effects across studies with random-effects models.
C) Mechanism-aware mRNA sensitivity models: We will test enrichment of predicted sensitive mRNAs for 5′ UTR motifs, uORFs, RNA structure metrics, codon usage, and subcellular targeting. We will train interpretable predictors (motif/feature-based) and, where feasible, structure-aware sequence models with careful cross-study validation.
D) Causal triangulation: We will use perturbation datasets to test whether manipulating axis-loading genes (ribosomal proteins, snoRNPs, biogenesis factors) shifts TE in the predicted direction. Where matched perturbation Ribo-seq exists, we will apply difference-in-differences designs; otherwise we will triangulate using consistency across TE signatures, expression responses, and fitness dependencies.

Benchmarking and sensitivity analyses. We will run alternative TE estimation methods, evaluate confounder sets, and quantify reproducibility across pipelines. Negative controls (randomized axis assignments; housekeeping mRNAs) will be used to estimate false discovery rates and guard against overinterpretation.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Primary outcomes will be (1) a harmonized, multi-modal synthesis dataset spanning Ribo-seq, proteomics, rRNA modification/biogenesis proxies, single-cell context, and perturbation constraints; (2) a set of reproducible ribosome heterogeneity axes (“ribosome states”) with quantified uncertainty, cross-context prevalence, and cross-species conservation; and (3) rigorously validated associations between ribosome states and selective translation programs, including interpretable mRNA features that predict sensitivity.

We anticipate three classes of scientific conclusions. First, we will determine whether ribosome heterogeneity collapses into a small number of conserved axes or is largely context-idiosyncratic. Second, we will test whether any axis predicts mRNA-specific translation changes beyond global translation scaling, thereby providing strong evidence for or against specialized translation as a general phenomenon. Third, we will connect ribosome states to stress adaptation and disease relevance by integrating perturbation data and dependency maps, identifying candidate ribosome components or modification pathways that modulate translation programs linked to proliferation, mitochondrial function, proteostasis, or immune signaling.

The broader impact is a community-scale, NCEMS-aligned synthesis that advances understanding of emergent mesoscale regulation: how ensemble-level variation in a core molecular machine yields system-level selectivity. Methodologically, the project will establish best practices for cross-study Ribo-seq normalization, ribosomal protein paralog quantification from proteomics, and integration of modification maps with translation outputs. Practically, the Ribosome Heterogeneity Synthesis Resource will enable researchers to rapidly test new hypotheses, benchmark new algorithms for detecting specialized translation, and prioritize targets for future experimental validation (outside the scope of this synthesis award). Finally, the working group’s training activities will produce a cohort of trainees skilled in reproducible multi-omics synthesis, strengthening the future data-savvy workforce in molecular and cellular biosciences.
budget_and_resources:
This proposal is designed as a community-scale synthesis working group that requires NCEMS coordination, convening, and computational support beyond a single laboratory’s capacity. The budget will be structured to maximize collaborative integration, trainee participation, and open deliverables while using only publicly available data.

NCEMS resources requested.
1) Working group convenings: Support for 2–3 in-person meetings at NCEMS (or NCEMS-supported venues) plus regular virtual meetings.
