Budget categories (use aligned with typical NCEMS Working Group mechanisms). (1) Personnel support: partial support for a project manager/data curator to coordinate dataset tracking, metadata harmonization, and release management; and limited support for trainee participation (graduate students/postdocs) to conduct curation, reproducibility checks, and pipeline development under supervision. (2) Participant travel and meetings: funds for in-person working meetings at NCEMS (or equivalent) to accelerate integration decisions, resolve standards, and conduct hands-on hackathons; plus support for virtual collaboration tools. (3) Computing and storage: allocation for scalable compute (CPU/GPU where needed for imaging segmentation and model training), high-capacity storage for raw-data reprocessing (proteomics), and long-term hosting of derived products (mirrors on Zenodo plus a lightweight web portal). (4) Dissemination and training: workshop logistics, captioning/recording, documentation, and potential publication fees for open-access dissemination.

Resource plan and feasibility. We will leverage existing public repositories (PRIDE, GEO/SRA, IDR, Metabolomics Workbench, BioGRID) and NCEMS-supported compute to avoid new data generation costs. Each subteam will commit defined deliverables per quarter (curated dataset list, reprocessed proteomics compendium, imaging phenotype tables, integrated models, and guidelines). NCEMS convening power will be used to recruit diverse expertise (endosomal biology, EV methods, statistics, AI/data science) across institutions, career stages, and geographies, and to ensure outputs meet community needs through iterative feedback. The final products will be maintained as a versioned resource with clear governance for updates beyond the award period.

title: Emergent Mechanics of the Nucleus: Integrating Lamin Variants, Chromatin State, and Microscopy-Based Deformation Phenotypes
abstract:
Nuclear mechanics emerge from interactions between lamins, chromatin, and cytoskeletal coupling, influencing migration, genome stability, and differentiation. Public datasets include lamin isoform expression, chromatin state maps, high-content imaging of nuclear shape, and mechanical perturbation assays, yet they have not been synthesized to derive general principles linking molecular composition to emergent mechanical phenotypes.

This working group will integrate (i) imaging datasets quantifying nuclear morphology across perturbations (Cell Painting, IDR, HPA), (ii) transcriptomic and proteomic profiles of lamins and nuclear envelope components across tissues (GTEx-like expression resources, CPTAC), (iii) epigenomic maps reflecting chromatin compaction (ENCODE ATAC-seq/ChIP-seq), (iv) perturbation datasets altering lamins, chromatin modifiers, and LINC complex components (CRISPR screens, GEO), and (v) datasets reporting nuclear deformation under confinement or strain where raw imaging is public. We will standardize nuclear shape descriptors (eccentricity, blebbing, wrinkling) and infer mechanical proxies from deformation assays.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify molecular determinants of emergent nuclear stiffness and deformability across cell types. (2) Determine how chromatin compaction states interact with lamin composition to produce nonlinear mechanical responses and failure modes (rupture). (3) Link nuclear mechanical states to downstream outcomes such as DNA damage signatures, transcriptional changes, and migration phenotypes.

Analytical approach: We will build integrative models combining imaging-derived mechanical proxies with omics features. Mechanistic modeling will incorporate composite material concepts (lamina shell + chromatin core) to interpret data-driven relationships. We will use causal inference leveraging perturbations to disentangle lamin-driven versus chromatin-driven effects. A methodological deliverable will be an open toolkit for extracting standardized nuclear mechanics features from microscopy images.

NCEMS support is required because the synthesis spans mechanobiology, imaging analytics, epigenomics, and statistical modeling, and demands coordinated curation across diverse datasets. The working group will establish metadata standards for nuclear mechanics experiments and promote reusable analysis pipelines.

Deliverables will include a Nuclear Mechanics Emergence Atlas with harmonized imaging features, molecular predictors, and inferred mechanical regimes; reproducible workflows for nuclear shape and deformation analysis; and a catalog of candidate regulators of rupture susceptibility. Training will include workshops on quantitative image analysis, mechanistic modeling, and open science. The synthesis will elucidate how mesoscale nuclear mechanics emerge from molecular and chromatin organization.
background_and_significance:
The cell nucleus is a mesoscale structure whose mechanical behavior—stiffness, deformability, viscoelastic relaxation, and rupture propensity—emerges from coupled molecular components: the nuclear lamina (lamins A/C, B1/B2 and associated envelope proteins), chromatin organization (compaction, tethering, and phase-like organization), and force transmission through the LINC complex to the cytoskeleton. Nuclear mechanics is not merely a biophysical curiosity: it shapes cell migration through constricted environments, influences mechanotransduction and lineage commitment, modulates genome stability through nuclear envelope rupture and DNA damage, and contributes to disease phenotypes in laminopathies and cancer. Yet, despite extensive mechanobiology literature, we lack generalizable principles that map molecular composition and chromatin state to emergent mechanical phenotypes across cell types, perturbations, and contexts.

A key barrier is fragmentation of evidence across modalities. High-content microscopy captures nuclear morphology and texture changes across thousands of perturbations (e.g., Cell Painting and related image-based profiling), but these phenotypes are rarely linked quantitatively to mechanical parameters. Conversely, mechanical assays (micropipette aspiration, microfluidic constriction, AFM indentation, stretch devices) often produce interpretable deformation trajectories but in small, heterogeneous studies with inconsistent metadata and limited molecular profiling. Meanwhile, transcriptomic and proteomic resources describe lamin isoform abundance and nuclear envelope composition across tissues and cell lines (e.g., GTEx-like expression compendia, CCLE-style resources, CPTAC), and epigenomic maps (ENCODE ATAC-seq, histone ChIP-seq) quantify chromatin accessibility and marks linked to compaction. Perturbation datasets (CRISPR knockout/activation screens, RNAi, small-molecule epigenetic modulators) provide quasi-experimental variation that can support causal inference. Each dataset alone offers partial insight; synthesis is required to uncover emergent rules.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze such synthesis at the mesoscale—between biomolecules and organelles—where emergent properties arise from collective organization. Nuclear mechanics is an archetypal mesoscale emergence problem: a lamina “shell” and chromatin “core” interact nonlinearly, with thresholds and failure modes (blebbing, wrinkling, rupture) that cannot be predicted from single-component measurements. Public data are now sufficiently rich to attempt a community-scale integration that is beyond the scope of a single lab: harmonizing image-derived nuclear phenotypes across platforms; aligning them with molecular and epigenomic features; and using perturbations to disentangle lamin-driven versus chromatin-driven contributions.

The proposed working group addresses a long-standing puzzle: why similar lamin expression can yield different mechanical outcomes across contexts, and why chromatin decompaction sometimes softens nuclei but sometimes increases rupture susceptibility. By integrating diverse public datasets, we will build a Nuclear Mechanics Emergence Atlas that links molecular composition and chromatin state to deformation phenotypes and downstream outcomes. This synthesis will generate testable, general principles; provide open tools and metadata standards for the field; and train a data-savvy workforce at the interface of mechanobiology, imaging analytics, and integrative modeling.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This project is organized around three scientific questions that target emergence: how collective organization of lamins and chromatin produces nuclear mechanical regimes, how nonlinear interactions generate failure modes, and how mechanical states propagate to cellular outcomes. We emphasize hypotheses that can be evaluated using publicly available observational and perturbational datasets, with explicit attention to confounding, context dependence, and scale.

Research Question 1: What molecular features best predict emergent nuclear stiffness and deformability across cell types and perturbations?
Hypothesis 1.1 (lamin stoichiometry): The ratio and isoform balance of LMNA (A/C) to LMNB1/LMNB2, together with key envelope partners (e.g., emerin, SUN1/2, nesprins), predicts a substantial fraction of variance in nuclear deformability proxies derived from imaging and deformation assays. We predict that stoichiometry and co-expression modules outperform single-gene predictors.
Hypothesis 1.2 (contextual modifiers): The predictive value of lamin abundance is modulated by chromatin compaction state and by cytoskeletal coupling signatures. In particular, lamin A/C effects are amplified in cells with strong actomyosin contractility programs, whereas in low-contractility contexts chromatin features dominate.

Research Question 2: How do chromatin compaction and lamin composition interact to generate nonlinear mechanical responses and rupture susceptibility?
Hypothesis 2.1 (composite material nonlinearity): Nuclear mechanics exhibits regime behavior consistent with a composite shell–core model: (i) a lamina-dominated regime where deformation is limited and shape irregularities reflect shell buckling/wrinkling; (ii) a chromatin-dominated regime where accessibility/heterochromatin marks predict stiffness; and (iii) an interaction regime where intermediate lamina integrity plus decompacted chromatin yields high deformability but elevated rupture risk.
Hypothesis 2.2 (tethering and boundary conditions): Chromatin–lamina tethering (inferred from lamina-associated domain proxies, heterochromatin marks, and expression of tethering factors) shifts the transition thresholds between regimes, producing discontinuous changes in blebbing/rupture phenotypes under confinement.

Research Question 3: How do emergent nuclear mechanical states relate to downstream outcomes (genome stability, transcriptional programs, and migration phenotypes)?
Hypothesis 3.1 (damage linkage): Mechanical regimes characterized by high deformability under confinement and high predicted rupture propensity are associated with increased DNA damage signatures (e.g., γH2AX-related transcriptional modules, DNA repair pathway activation) and with micronuclei/aberrant morphology features in imaging.
Hypothesis 3.2 (transcriptional coupling): Mechanical state is coupled to reproducible transcriptional programs beyond stress responses, including differentiation-associated chromatin remodeling and mechanotransduction pathways (YAP/TAZ targets). We predict that models incorporating mechanical proxies improve prediction of these programs relative to molecular features alone.
Hypothesis 3.3 (migration trade-off): Cells in the interaction regime (moderate lamina, decompacted chromatin) show enhanced predicted migratory capacity through constrictions but pay a genome stability cost, consistent with an emergent trade-off surface.

Cross-cutting methodological question: Can we derive standardized, comparable mechanical proxies from heterogeneous imaging and deformation datasets?
Hypothesis M (latent mechanics): A shared latent “mechanics” representation can be learned that aligns nuclear morphology descriptors (eccentricity, curvature, wrinkling, blebs) with time-resolved deformation features, enabling cross-study comparisons and mechanistic interpretation.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working group structure. We will run a community-scale synthesis effort integrating imaging, omics, epigenomics, and perturbation datasets to infer emergent nuclear mechanical regimes. The team will include expertise in mechanobiology, nuclear envelope biology, epigenomics, computer vision, statistical genetics/causal inference, and scientific software engineering. All analyses will use publicly available data only; no new experiments will be performed.

Data sources and inclusion criteria. (1) Imaging: Cell Painting and related image-based profiling datasets with accessible raw images or per-cell features; Human Protein Atlas (HPA) immunofluorescence for lamins/envelope proteins; Image Data Resource (IDR) studies with nuclear morphology phenotypes; and public microfluidic confinement/strain imaging where raw movies are deposited. (2) Molecular: transcriptomics/proteomics from GTEx-like tissue atlases, CCLE-like cell line compendia, and CPTAC tumor proteomics; targeted nuclear envelope proteomes where public. (3) Epigenomics: ENCODE ATAC-seq and histone ChIP-seq (H3K9me3, H3K27me3, H3K27ac) as compaction proxies; where available, Hi-C-derived compartment strength as an auxiliary proxy. (4) Perturbations: CRISPR/RNAi screens affecting lamins, LINC components, chromatin modifiers; GEO/ArrayExpress perturbation transcriptomes; small-molecule epigenetic perturbations with imaging readouts.

Harmonization and metadata. We will create a minimal metadata schema for nuclear mechanics synthesis: cell type/line, perturbation identity/dose/time, imaging modality, segmentation method, deformation context (confinement size/strain), and batch identifiers. We will map genes/proteins to unified identifiers and align cell lines/tissues across resources using ontology terms.

Image analysis and feature standardization. We will develop an open pipeline to (i) segment nuclei (leveraging established tools such as Cellpose/StarDist where compatible with licenses), (ii) compute standardized shape descriptors (area, perimeter, eccentricity, solidity, curvature spectra), (iii) quantify wrinkling/blebbing via multiscale boundary roughness and protrusion statistics, and (iv) extract texture features reflecting chromatin organization (Haralick, radial intensity profiles when DNA channels exist). For deformation movies, we will compute strain, creep/relaxation proxies, and rupture indicators (sudden area change, discontinuities, leakage markers if available).

Mechanical proxy inference and latent representation learning. We will align heterogeneous outputs by learning a latent mechanics space using multi-view methods (e.g., canonical correlation analysis, variational multi-modal factor models) that integrate morphology, deformation trajectories, and molecular/epigenomic covariates. Where direct mechanical measurements exist (e.g., aspiration pressure–deformation curves), we will calibrate latent axes to interpretable parameters (effective stiffness, viscosity, yield threshold).

Integrative modeling and hypothesis testing. (1) Predictive models: regularized regression, gradient boosting, and interpretable neural models to predict mechanical proxies from lamin/envelope modules and chromatin features, with nested cross-validation and strict train/test separation by study to assess generalization. (2) Mechanistic composite modeling: fit simplified shell–core models where lamina features parameterize shell stiffness and chromatin features parameterize core modulus; test for interaction terms and regime shifts using segmented regression and mixture models. (3) Causal inference: use perturbation datasets as instruments—difference-in-differences across perturbation vs control within studies; causal graphs to identify confounders; and meta-analytic aggregation of perturbation effects. We will prioritize estimates that replicate across independent datasets.

Linking to outcomes. We will associate inferred mechanical regimes with DNA damage signatures (transcriptomic modules, imaging micronuclei features), migration-related phenotypes (where available), and stress response programs, using multilevel models controlling for cell type and batch.

Milestones. By month 6: harmonized dataset index and baseline feature pipeline. By month 12: latent mechanics representation and first cross-study predictors. By month 18: regime map + rupture susceptibility catalog. By month 24: Nuclear Mechanics Emergence Atlas release and training materials.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific products. (1) Nuclear Mechanics Emergence Atlas: a harmonized, queryable resource linking standardized nuclear morphology/deformation features to lamin/envelope expression, chromatin compaction proxies, perturbations, and inferred mechanical regimes across diverse cell types and contexts. (2) Generalizable principles: quantitative rules describing when lamina composition dominates mechanics, when chromatin compaction dominates, and when nonlinear interactions produce high deformability coupled to rupture susceptibility. These principles will be expressed as interpretable models, regime diagrams, and validated cross-study predictors.

Methodological products. (3) Open toolkit for nuclear mechanics feature extraction from microscopy: reproducible pipelines for segmentation, shape/bleb/wrinkle quantification, deformation-trajectory summarization, and quality control, designed to work across common imaging modalities and public repositories. (4) Community metadata standard recommendations for nuclear deformation experiments and image-based nuclear mechanics phenotyping, enabling future data reuse and synthesis.

Biological insights and candidate regulators. (5) A prioritized catalog of candidate regulators of nuclear rupture susceptibility and mechanical failure modes, derived from integrative modeling and perturbation meta-analysis, highlighting lamin isoform balances, LINC components, and chromatin modifiers with consistent effects across datasets.

Impact on NCEMS mission. The nucleus is a canonical mesoscale system; this project will demonstrate how emergent mechanical properties arise from coupled molecular networks and chromatin organization. By synthesizing public data at scale, we will address a long-standing mechanobiology puzzle with a transdisciplinary approach that single laboratories cannot execute. The Atlas and tools will lower barriers for the community to connect molecular perturbations to mechanical phenotypes, accelerating discovery in development, cancer, aging, and laminopathies.

Workforce and community impact. The working group will train trainees in integrative image analysis, multi-omics synthesis, causal inference, and open, reproducible computational science. The resulting datasets and workflows will serve as reusable teaching modules and as a foundation for subsequent community-scale synthesis efforts at NCEMS.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support request rationale. This synthesis requires coordinated, in-person and virtual collaboration across mechanobiology, epigenomics, imaging analytics, and causal inference; substantial data curation; and shared compute and software engineering. These needs exceed what a single lab or existing bilateral collaboration typically supports, aligning with NCEMS’s role in catalyzing community-scale synthesis.

Budget categories (illustrative, adaptable to NCEMS guidelines). (1) Working group meetings: support for 2–3 in-person meetings at NCEMS (or designated venue) plus regular virtual meetings, including travel and lodging for geographically distributed participants, with explicit funds to include trainees and participants from under-resourced institutions. (2) Personnel effort: partial support for a dedicated research software engineer/data curator to maintain pipelines, metadata standards, and releases; and partial support for a project coordinator to manage timelines, documentation, and open-science compliance. (3) Trainee support: travel awards and short-term support for graduate students/postdocs to participate in sprints, lead subprojects, and develop training modules. (4) Compute and storage: cloud/HPC allocations for image processing at scale (segmentation, feature extraction), with budget for storage of derived features and intermediate artifacts; use of NCEMS-provided compute where available to reduce cost. (5) Dissemination and training: costs for hosting workshops (materials, accessibility services such as captioning), maintaining a documentation site, and archiving releases (Zenodo/OSF).

Resource plan. NCEMS will provide convening infrastructure, facilitation, and access to collaborative platforms. Participating labs will contribute domain expertise, existing open-source components, and time for co-development and review. We will structure work into cross-lab subteams (Imaging/Features; Omics/Epigenomics; Causal/Mechanistic Modeling; Atlas/Engineering; Training) with clearly defined deliverables and integration milestones.

Sustainability. We will design the Atlas and toolkits for long-term maintenance: modular code, automated tests, semantic versioning, and archived releases. Documentation will enable reuse by the broader community beyond the award period.

title: A Synthesis of Spatially Structured Immune Synapse Formation: Integrating Imaging, Proteomics, and Signaling Perturbation Data
abstract:
The immune synapse is a mesoscale, spatially patterned interface where receptors, adhesion molecules, and cytoskeletal structures self-organize to enable antigen recognition and signaling. Despite extensive study, we lack a unified synthesis connecting molecular composition, spatial patterning, and emergent signaling outcomes across immune cell types and stimulation contexts. Public imaging and omics datasets can now be integrated to address this gap.

This working group will integrate (i) high-resolution imaging datasets of immune synapses (TCR/BCR clustering, actin organization) from IDR and published repositories, (ii) proteomics of immunological synapse fractions and signaling complexes (PRIDE), (iii) phospho-signaling time courses following receptor stimulation (PRIDE/CPTAC/GEO), (iv) interaction networks and curated signaling pathways (SIGNOR, BioGRID), and (v) perturbation datasets (CRISPR screens, inhibitor panels, LINCS-like perturbation transcriptomics in immune contexts). We will standardize stimulation conditions (ligand potency, mechanical context) and extract quantitative spatial metrics (cluster size distributions, radial organization, actin ring integrity).

Scientific aims: (1) Identify conserved spatial organization motifs and relate them to signaling amplitude, duration, and specificity. (2) Determine how cytoskeletal and membrane organization constraints produce emergent thresholds for activation. (3) Compare synapse organization across T cells, B cells, NK cells, and engineered CAR-T contexts to identify generalizable design principles.

Analytical approach: We will develop models that couple spatial statistics from imaging with dynamical signaling models. Graph-based representations of synapse architecture will be linked to phospho-signaling trajectories using multimodal learning. Perturbation data will provide causal anchors to identify regulators controlling spatial patterning and signaling outcomes. A methodological deliverable will be an open, standardized pipeline for immune synapse image quantification.

NCEMS support is essential to convene immunologists, imaging experts, proteomics specialists, and computational modelers, and to coordinate curation and benchmarking across heterogeneous datasets. The project’s community-scale integration is beyond a single lab’s scope.

Deliverables will include an Immune Synapse Emergence Atlas with harmonized spatial metrics, molecular modules, and predicted activation regimes; reproducible workflows for synapse image analysis and signaling integration; and a catalog of candidate targets that modulate synapse organization. Training will be provided through workshops on spatial image analysis, signaling modeling, and open science practices, with trainees leading dataset annotation and tool development. This synthesis will reveal how mesoscale spatial self-organization drives emergent immune decision-making.
background_and_significance:
Immune recognition is governed not only by molecular binding events but by mesoscale self-organization at the cell–cell interface. The immune synapse—classically described for T cells engaging antigen-presenting cells and analogously for B cells, NK cells, and engineered CAR-T cells—exhibits striking spatial patterning: receptor microclusters, adhesion rings, actin-rich lamellae, and organized signaling assemblies. These structures arise from coupled processes spanning membrane mechanics, cytoskeletal dynamics, receptor–ligand kinetics, phase-like clustering, and feedback through kinase/phosphatase networks. The synapse is therefore an archetypal emergence problem in the molecular and cellular biosciences: the collective behavior of many interacting molecules produces new functional properties (sensitivity, specificity, digital/graded responses, and decision thresholds) that cannot be inferred from isolated components.

Despite decades of work, the field lacks a unified, quantitative synthesis that connects (i) synapse molecular composition, (ii) spatial organization motifs, and (iii) emergent signaling dynamics across immune cell types and stimulation contexts. Individual studies often focus on a single cell system, a limited set of markers, and laboratory-specific imaging/analysis pipelines. Proteomic studies of synapse fractions reveal rich molecular repertoires, but are rarely integrated with spatial readouts. Time-resolved phosphoproteomics and transcriptomics capture pathway activation, yet are typically disconnected from the physical organization that conditions signaling. Perturbation studies (CRISPR screens, inhibitor panels, and transcriptional perturbation signatures) identify regulators, but their mechanistic roles in shaping synapse architecture and activation thresholds remain fragmented.

This fragmentation is now addressable because public resources provide unprecedented breadth of relevant data. The Image Data Resource (IDR) and associated repositories host high-resolution microscopy datasets spanning receptor clustering, actin organization, and synapse morphology. PRIDE and CPTAC provide proteomic and phosphoproteomic datasets, including immune receptor stimulation time courses and synapse-enriched fractions. GEO and related archives provide transcriptional responses to immune activation and perturbations. Interaction and pathway resources such as SIGNOR and BioGRID encode mechanistic relationships that can scaffold integrative models. Finally, immune-focused functional genomics screens and perturbation expression compendia can provide causal anchors.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that is beyond any single lab: harmonizing heterogeneous imaging modalities, proteomic quantification strategies, and perturbation designs; developing interoperable representations of synapse architecture; and benchmarking models that link spatial structure to signaling outcomes. This effort aligns tightly with NCEMS’s mesoscale focus by treating the synapse as a mesoscale “material” whose organization governs higher-level cellular decisions. A synthesis that yields generalizable design principles would impact immunology broadly (infection, cancer, autoimmunity) and inform engineering of cell therapies where synapse quality predicts efficacy and toxicity. Just as importantly, the project will produce reusable analytical infrastructure for spatial-omics integration, advancing the methodological toolkit for emergence research in other mesoscale assemblies (e.g., focal adhesions, phase-separated signaling clusters, neuronal synapses).
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This working group will pursue three linked scientific questions that operationalize “emergence” at the immune synapse: how spatial organization arises, how it constrains signaling, and which principles generalize across immune contexts.

Question 1: What conserved spatial organization motifs recur across immune synapses, and how do they map to signaling dynamics?
Hypothesis 1A: Across TCR, BCR, NK activating receptors, and CARs, synapses occupy a low-dimensional “motif space” defined by measurable spatial statistics (e.g., microcluster size distributions, radial segregation indices, actin ring continuity, central–peripheral partitioning) that is conserved despite differences in receptors and ligands.
Hypothesis 1B: Specific motifs predict signaling amplitude and temporal features (peak strength, persistence, oscillations) better than molecular abundance alone, because spatial proximity and segregation modulate effective reaction rates and phosphatase access.

Question 2: How do cytoskeletal and membrane constraints create emergent activation thresholds and decision regimes?
Hypothesis 2A: Emergent thresholds (digital vs graded activation; sharp transitions with ligand potency) arise from coupled positive feedback between actin-driven transport/retention of receptor clusters and kinase activation, producing bistability in signaling trajectories.
Hypothesis 2B: Mechanical context (substrate stiffness, ligand mobility, supported lipid bilayers vs cell–cell contacts) shifts these thresholds by altering the energetic cost of cluster coalescence and actin architecture, leading to predictable changes in motif space and downstream phospho-signatures.

Question 3: Which regulators causally control the coupling between spatial patterning and signaling outcomes, and are these regulators shared across immune cell types?
Hypothesis 3A: A conserved “synapse coupling module” exists—enriched for actin regulators (e.g., Arp2/3, WASP/WAVE), membrane organizers (tetraspanins, lipid kinases), and phosphatase localization factors—that mediates the mapping from spatial motifs to signaling regimes.
Hypothesis 3B: Perturbations of coupling-module components will show concordant effects across modalities: predictable shifts in spatial metrics, coordinated changes in phosphoproteomic trajectories, and consistent perturbation transcriptomic signatures.

Cross-cutting methodological question: Can multimodal models that explicitly encode synapse architecture outperform unimodal approaches for predicting signaling outcomes and perturbation effects?
Hypothesis M1: Graph-based and multimodal representation learning models that integrate spatial graphs with proteomic/phosphoproteomic features will yield improved predictive accuracy and mechanistic interpretability compared to models using only pathway membership or bulk molecular abundance.

Each hypothesis is designed to be testable using exclusively public data, with success criteria defined by quantitative benchmarks: motif reproducibility across datasets, predictive performance for signaling outcomes, and robustness of inferred regulators across perturbation sources and cell types.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working-group structure. We will conduct a synthesis-only, multi-lab integration effort organized into four technical thrusts: (T1) data acquisition and harmonization, (T2) quantitative spatial feature extraction, (T3) multimodal integration and modeling, and (T4) causal inference and benchmarking. All analyses will use publicly available datasets; no new experiments will be performed.

T1: Dataset discovery, inclusion criteria, and harmonization. We will curate imaging datasets from IDR and associated journal repositories that include immune synapse formation with sufficient metadata (cell type, receptor/ligand, time post-stimulation, imaging modality, markers). Proteomics/phosphoproteomics will be sourced from PRIDE and CPTAC; transcriptomics and perturbation expression from GEO and immune-relevant perturbation compendia; functional screens from published CRISPR/RNAi datasets. Inclusion will require raw or minimally processed data availability, clear stimulation conditions, and replicates. We will standardize metadata using controlled vocabularies (cell ontology terms, receptor/ligand identifiers, stimulation potency bins, mechanical context descriptors) and map proteins/genes to unified identifiers (UniProt/Ensembl). Batch effects will be modeled explicitly (ComBat/limma for omics; domain adaptation for imaging features) and assessed via replicate concordance.

T2: Immune synapse image quantification pipeline. We will develop an open pipeline (Napari/CellProfiler/Scikit-image-based) to segment synapse regions, detect receptor microclusters, quantify actin structures, and compute spatial metrics: Ripley’s K/L functions, pair-correlation, cluster size and intensity distributions, radial distribution functions, centralization indices, co-localization/segregation measures, and topology of actin rings (continuity, thickness, anisotropy). Where single-cell segmentation is infeasible, we will use weakly supervised approaches and published annotations; uncertainty will be propagated into downstream models. Output will be a standardized “synapse feature table” with per-cell and per-condition summaries.

T3: Multimodal integration and predictive modeling. We will represent synapse architecture as graphs (nodes: clusters/regions; edges: proximity/contact; attributes: marker intensities, local actin density). These graphs will be integrated with proteomic modules (synapse-enriched proteins, signaling complex composition) and phospho-signaling trajectories (time-series features: peak, area-under-curve, decay). Models will include: (i) hierarchical Bayesian models linking motif space to signaling parameters with dataset-level random effects; (ii) multimodal representation learning (graph neural networks + variational multimodal encoders) to predict signaling outcomes from spatial and molecular inputs; and (iii) mechanistic dynamical models (ODEs/logic models) constrained by pathway knowledge (SIGNOR) where spatial metrics modulate effective rates (e.g., kinase–substrate encounter rates).

T4: Causal anchors from perturbations and benchmarking. Perturbation datasets (CRISPR/inhibitors/perturbation transcriptomics) will be used to infer regulators of motif shifts and signaling regimes. We will apply causal discovery with prior constraints (directed edges from SIGNOR), mediation analysis (perturbation → spatial metrics → signaling), and network propagation to connect screens to spatial modules. Benchmarking will use held-out datasets and cross-cell-type transfer tests: train on T cell synapses, predict B/NK/CAR contexts; evaluate with pre-registered metrics (AUROC for activation classification, RMSE for continuous signaling features, calibration, and stability of regulator rankings).
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific products. (1) A quantitative “Immune Synapse Emergence Atlas” that harmonizes imaging-derived spatial metrics with proteomic composition, phospho-signaling dynamics, and perturbation effects across T cells, B cells, NK cells, and CAR-T contexts. The atlas will include motif definitions, condition annotations (ligand potency, mechanical context), and links to molecular modules and pathways. (2) Evidence-supported design principles describing how mesoscale organization constrains immune decision-making, including: conserved motif space across receptors, mechanistic explanations for emergent activation thresholds, and a prioritized set of coupling-module regulators.

Methodological products. (3) A reusable, open pipeline for immune synapse image quantification with standardized outputs and uncertainty reporting, enabling consistent re-analysis of public datasets and future community contributions. (4) Benchmark datasets and evaluation protocols for multimodal spatial–signaling integration, including reference tasks (predict activation regime; predict phospho-trajectory features; predict perturbation directionality) and baseline models.

Impact on molecular and cellular emergence research. This project will provide a concrete, data-driven bridge between mesoscale architecture and downstream functional outcomes—an essential step toward general theories of emergence in cellular signaling assemblies. The integrative framework (spatial graphs + omics + perturbations) will be transferable to other mesoscale systems where organization and dynamics co-determine function (e.g., focal adhesions, endocytic pits, phase-separated signaling condensates). For immunology and therapeutic engineering, the atlas and inferred regulators will guide hypotheses about why some synapses yield robust activation while others fail or produce exhaustion/toxicity signatures, informing rational design of CAR constructs and interventions that tune synapse quality.

Training and community impact. The working group will train trainees in reproducible spatial analysis, multimodal modeling, and open science, producing a cohort capable of conducting synthesis-based, AI-enabled molecular/cellular research at community scale.
budget_and_resources:
NCEMS support rationale. The project requires intensive, coordinated synthesis across heterogeneous public imaging and multi-omics repositories, plus sustained collaboration among immunologists, imaging analysts, proteomics experts, statisticians, and machine-learning modelers. NCEMS resources are essential to convene this multidisciplinary team, provide neutral coordination, and support shared cyberinfrastructure and open dissemination that exceed the capacity of any single lab or existing bilateral collaboration.

Budget categories (high-level; exact amounts per NCEMS guidelines). (1) Working group meetings: support for 2–3 in-person meetings at NCEMS (or NCEMS-supported venue) plus regular virtual meetings. Costs include participant travel, lodging, and meeting logistics, enabling participation across geography, institution types, and career stages. (2) Personnel effort/time: partial support for a project coordinator/data curator to manage accession tracking, metadata harmonization, and release packaging; and limited support for research software engineering to harden the image-analysis pipeline and workflow automation. (3) Trainee support: travel and per diem for graduate students/postdocs to attend meetings and lead hackathon-style integration sprints; small honoraria for trainee-led tutorial development where allowed. (4) Computing and data services: cloud credits or NCEMS-provided compute for large-scale image feature extraction and model training; storage for derived, shareable artifacts; DOI minting and repository fees if applicable.

Resource plan and roles. Participating labs will contribute complementary expertise: immune synapse biology and receptor signaling; quantitative imaging and spatial statistics; proteomics/phosphoproteomics interpretation; network biology and causal inference; and multimodal ML. NCEMS will provide facilitation, project management support, and access to collaborative platforms.

Milestones and deliverable-linked spending. Year 1 resources prioritize curation, harmonization, and pipeline prototypes; Year 2 emphasizes modeling, benchmarking, and atlas release; final-quarter resources support documentation, workshops, and archival deposition (Zenodo/OSF/GitHub). All spending is tied to synthesis deliverables, not new data generation, ensuring compliance with NCEMS requirements.

title: Emergent Principles of Protein Allostery at Scale: Integrating Structural Ensembles, Mutational Scans, and Functional Genomics
abstract:
Allostery—long-range coupling between sites in proteins—is an emergent property of molecular structure and dynamics. While classic studies focus on individual proteins, public deep mutational scanning (DMS), structural models, and functional genomics now enable a synthesis to identify general rules predicting allosteric coupling and its cellular consequences.

This working group will integrate (i) DMS datasets with publicly available raw/processed scores (MaveDB), (ii) structural data and predicted models (PDB, AlphaFold DB), (iii) molecular dynamics ensemble resources where available, (iv) protein interaction and pathway context (BioGRID, Reactome), and (v) human genetic variation and disease annotations (gnomAD, ClinVar) to connect allosteric sites to phenotypes. We will curate protein families with multiple DMS studies to enable comparative analyses.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify structural and sequence determinants of allosteric sensitivity (e.g., network centrality in residue contact graphs, flexibility, packing frustration). (2) Quantify how allosteric coupling patterns vary across protein classes (enzymes, transcription factors, membrane receptors) and evolutionary distances. (3) Link predicted allosteric sites to cellular phenotypes via pathway integration and genetic dependency data, illuminating why certain distal variants are pathogenic.

Analytical approach: We will compute residue interaction networks from structures and develop models that predict mutational effects at distal sites using graph neural networks and interpretable network metrics. We will meta-analyze DMS across conditions to detect context-dependent allostery. Integrating functional genomics (e.g., dependency scores) will allow prioritization of allosteric sites most relevant to cellular fitness. A methodological deliverable will be an open benchmark suite for allostery prediction using standardized splits across proteins and families.

NCEMS support is required because the synthesis spans structural biology, statistical genetics, ML, and systems biology, and requires coordinated curation of diverse DMS experiments and structural representations. The working group will align on standards for mapping DMS variants to structures and for reporting uncertainty.

Deliverables will include an open Allostery Synthesis Atlas with harmonized DMS-to-structure mappings, predicted allosteric networks, and links to disease variants; reproducible pipelines for feature extraction and modeling; and benchmarks for community method development. Training will include workshops on structural data processing, DMS analysis, and reproducible ML, with trainees leading curation of protein families. The synthesis will uncover general emergent rules of allostery and enable better interpretation of distal variants.
background_and_significance:
Allostery—functional coupling between spatially separated sites in a protein—has long served as a paradigm for emergent biological behavior: collective properties arise from networks of interactions that are not obvious from local chemistry alone. Historically, allostery has been elucidated through intensive, protein-by-protein experimentation, yielding canonical examples (e.g., hemoglobin, kinases, GPCRs) and mechanistic models (MWC, KNF, energy landscape perspectives). Yet decades of work have not produced generalizable, quantitative principles that predict (i) which residues participate in long-range coupling, (ii) how coupling depends on structural context and dynamics, and (iii) which distal variants are likely to perturb cellular phenotypes or human disease.

This gap is increasingly consequential. In human genetics, many pathogenic missense variants occur outside active sites or classical binding interfaces, complicating interpretation and therapeutic targeting. In drug discovery, allosteric modulators offer selectivity advantages, but identifying allosteric sites remains difficult. In protein engineering, distal mutations can strongly influence activity, stability, specificity, and regulation, but rules for predicting beneficial distal substitutions are incomplete. These challenges all reflect the same core scientific problem: allostery is an emergent mesoscale phenomenon linking residue-level perturbations to protein-level conformational ensembles and, ultimately, cellular systems.

NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze a community-scale synthesis that converts the recent explosion of public molecular data into broadly applicable allosteric principles. Three public data streams now make this feasible. First, deep mutational scanning (DMS) has produced quantitative, residue-resolved maps of mutational effects across hundreds of proteins and multiple experimental contexts, with many datasets deposited in MaveDB. These maps implicitly contain signatures of long-range coupling: mutations far from an active site can alter function in systematic, nonlocal patterns. Second, structural resources have expanded dramatically, including high-resolution structures (PDB), predicted models at proteome scale (AlphaFold DB), and, for some proteins, ensembles from NMR, cryo-EM heterogeneity analyses, or public molecular dynamics repositories. Third, functional genomics and network biology resources (BioGRID, Reactome, DepMap/CRISPR dependency screens, expression and pathway annotations) connect proteins to cellular phenotypes, while population and clinical genetics (gnomAD, ClinVar) connect variants to organismal outcomes.

Despite these advances, integration remains a bottleneck. DMS measurements are heterogeneous (assay types, selection regimes, score scales), variant annotation and coordinate mapping are inconsistent, and structural representations vary (single structures vs ensembles; resolved vs predicted regions). Moreover, connecting protein-level allosteric sensitivity to cellular phenotype requires careful synthesis across pathway context, genetic dependencies, and disease annotations. No single lab typically spans the necessary expertise in DMS statistics, structural bioinformatics, molecular simulation, machine learning, and systems genetics.

This working group will address this need by building a harmonized, open “Allostery Synthesis Atlas” and an associated benchmark suite for allostery prediction. By integrating DMS, structures/ensembles, interaction networks, and genotype–phenotype evidence, we will identify general, testable rules of allosteric coupling across protein classes and evolutionary distances. The project aligns with NCEMS’s mission by focusing on emergence at the mesoscale—how distributed residue interactions and conformational variability give rise to long-range functional coupling—and by leveraging AI-enabled synthesis of publicly available data to resolve longstanding puzzles in molecular and cellular biosciences.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This project centers on the premise that allostery can be quantified as a measurable, distributed sensitivity of protein function to distal perturbations, and that this sensitivity is governed by emergent network- and ensemble-level properties rather than only local chemistry. We will pursue three tightly linked research questions, each with explicit hypotheses that can be evaluated using integrated public datasets.

RQ1: Which structural and sequence features best predict allosteric sensitivity at residue resolution? Allosteric sensitivity here is defined operationally as the degree to which mutations at a residue produce functional effects that cannot be explained by local structural disruption alone (e.g., distance to active site, solvent exposure), and that correlate with changes in activity, regulation, or binding measured by DMS.

H1.1 (network mediation): Residues with high centrality in residue–residue contact graphs (betweenness, current flow, communicability) are enriched for distal DMS sensitivity, reflecting their role as conduits for information/energy propagation.

H1.2 (energetic frustration and packing): Sites with high local packing frustration or heterogeneous contact energies show elevated allosteric sensitivity because they facilitate alternative interaction patterns across the ensemble.

H1.3 (ensemble flexibility): Residues with higher predicted or observed conformational variability (B-factors, AlphaFold pLDDT/PAE proxies, NMR ensembles, MD-derived fluctuations where available) are more likely to participate in context-dependent coupling.

RQ2: How do allosteric coupling patterns vary across protein classes and evolutionary distances, and what constitutes a conserved “allosteric architecture”? We will compare families with multiple DMS datasets (across homologs and/or assay contexts) to quantify conserved vs divergent coupling.

H2.1 (class-specific architectures): Enzymes will display coupling concentrated along catalytic networks and substrate channels; transcription factors will show coupling enriched at DNA-binding and regulatory interfaces; membrane receptors will show coupling aligned with transmembrane helix networks and ligand/effector interfaces.

H2.2 (evolutionary constraint on coupling): Distal sites with strong allosteric sensitivity will be more evolutionarily constrained than matched control sites, but the degree of constraint will depend on whether coupling supports core function (highly conserved) versus regulation/adaptation (more lineage-specific).

H2.3 (epistasis as emergent signature): Proteins with stronger distal coupling will exhibit higher-order epistasis patterns in DMS (non-additive effects across sites), reflecting ensemble redistribution rather than independent local disruptions.

RQ3: When and why do distal variants become pathogenic or phenotypically consequential in cells? We will link predicted allosteric sites to cellular phenotypes through pathway context, interaction networks, and gene dependency data, focusing on human proteins with ClinVar/gnomAD annotations and orthologous DMS where available.

H3.1 (network amplification): Distal variants at allosteric sites are more likely to be pathogenic when the protein occupies a high-control position in cellular networks (e.g., hubs, bottlenecks, pathway gatekeepers), because small functional shifts are amplified.

H3.2 (context dependence): Allosteric variant effects will be more condition-specific (assay/environment dependent in DMS; cell-line dependent in dependency screens) than active-site variants, consistent with regulation via shifting interaction equilibria.

H3.3 (predictive integration): Joint models that combine residue-network/ensemble features with pathway and dependency context will outperform structure-only or genetics-only baselines in prioritizing clinically relevant distal variants.

These questions and hypotheses drive a synthesis agenda that is both mechanistic (mesoscale coupling principles) and translationally relevant (variant interpretation), while remaining fully testable using only existing public data and rigorous benchmarking.
methods_and_approach:
Overview and working group structure. We will run an NCEMS-supported working group with coordinated subteams: (A) DMS curation and statistical harmonization, (B) structure/ensemble processing and residue-network feature extraction, (C) predictive modeling and benchmarking, and (D) cellular/clinical integration. The project uses only publicly available datasets and produces no new experimental data.

1) Data acquisition and harmonization (DMS core). We will identify proteins with (i) at least one high-quality DMS dataset in MaveDB and (ii) a mappable structure/model. Priority will be given to families with multiple DMS studies across homologs or conditions (e.g., kinases, nuclear receptors, GPCRs where feasible, transcription factors, metabolic enzymes). For each study, we will extract raw/processed variant scores, uncertainty where available, assay metadata, and selection conditions. We will implement a harmonization framework: (a) map variants to a canonical UniProt sequence; (b) standardize score directionality and scale via robust normalization (e.g., rank-based transforms; z-scoring within study) while preserving interpretability; (c) model measurement error and replicate structure when available; and (d) annotate assay type (activity, binding, abundance, stability proxies) to enable stratified analyses.

2) Mapping variants to structures and ensembles. For each protein, we will map sequence positions to PDB structures and/or AlphaFold DB models using established alignment pipelines (SIFTS where applicable; pairwise alignment with gap handling; isoform resolution). We will annotate structural quality (resolution, missing regions, AlphaFold pLDDT/PAE) and define “analysis-ready” residue sets. Where public ensembles exist (NMR ensembles, multiple PDB conformers, cryo-EM multi-state models, or curated MD trajectories), we will compute ensemble-aware features; otherwise we will use proxies (e.g., AlphaFold confidence, predicted disorder).

3) Residue interaction networks and feature engineering. We will construct residue contact graphs (nodes=residues; edges=contacts weighted by distance, coevolution scores when available, or interaction energy proxies). Features will include classic metrics (degree, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector centrality), current-flow betweenness, community structure, shortest-path distances to functional sites (active site, ligand-binding residues, interfaces), and measures of local packing/frustration (e.g., contact density, clash/void proxies). Flexibility features will include B-factors, ensemble RMSF, and predicted disorder/confidence. We will also compute evolutionary features (conservation, coevolution couplings from public MSAs where permissible) and biochemical context (secondary structure, solvent accessibility).

4) Defining allosteric sensitivity phenotypes from DMS. We will derive residue-level allosteric sensitivity scores by aggregating mutational effects at each position (robust mean/median of non-synonymous effects), then regressing out local confounders (solvent exposure, proximity to functional sites, predicted stability impact where available) to isolate distal coupling signatures. We will quantify context dependence by comparing DMS conditions within the same protein (when multiple environments/ligands are present) using hierarchical models.

5) Predictive modeling and benchmarking. We will train models to predict residue-level allosteric sensitivity and variant-level effects using (i) interpretable baselines (regularized regression, gradient-boosted trees) and (ii) graph neural networks operating on residue graphs with structural/ensemble features. Benchmarking will use standardized splits designed to test generalization: within-protein (held-out residues), across-protein within family (held-out homolog), and across families (held-out class). We will preregister evaluation metrics (Spearman/Pearson for continuous scores; AUROC/AUPRC for classification of high-sensitivity residues; calibration curves) and compare to simple baselines (distance-to-active-site, solvent exposure only).

6) Cellular and clinical integration. We will map proteins to pathways and interaction networks (Reactome, BioGRID) and integrate gene dependency data (e.g., DepMap) to quantify cellular essentiality and context specificity. For human proteins, we will overlay gnomAD constraint metrics and ClinVar variant annotations, testing enrichment of pathogenic variants at predicted allosteric sites while controlling for mutability and exposure. We will build integrative models that combine residue-level predictions with network position to prioritize variants likely to have phenotypic impact.

All analyses will be executed via reproducible, containerized workflows and released as an open atlas and benchmark suite.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
Scientific outcomes. The primary scientific outcome will be a quantitative, cross-protein synthesis of how long-range coupling emerges from residue networks and conformational ensembles. We expect to identify a small set of robust predictors of allosteric sensitivity—combining network centrality/communicability, ensemble flexibility proxies, and packing/frustration measures—that generalize across many proteins better than distance-based heuristics. Comparative analyses across protein classes and families will yield “allosteric architectures”: recurring motifs of coupling (e.g., helix networks in receptors, catalytic communication pathways in enzymes, interface-mediated coupling in transcription factors) and their evolutionary conservation patterns.

Methodological outcomes. We will deliver (i) a harmonized dataset linking DMS variant effects to standardized structural coordinates and ensemble-aware features, (ii) an open benchmark suite with clearly defined train/test splits (within protein, across homologs, across families) to enable fair comparison of allostery prediction methods, and (iii) validated modeling pipelines spanning interpretable baselines through graph neural networks. These resources will lower barriers for the community to develop and test new AI methods for mesoscale emergence.

Translational and cellular impact. By integrating predicted allosteric sites with pathway context, interaction networks, and gene dependency, we will produce a principled framework for prioritizing distal variants most likely to alter cellular fitness or cause disease. We anticipate improved interpretation of ClinVar variants of uncertain significance that lie outside active sites, and clearer hypotheses for why certain distal variants are pathogenic (e.g., network amplification in key pathways; context-dependent regulation). The resulting Allostery Synthesis Atlas will be directly useful to researchers studying disease mechanisms, designing allosteric drugs, or engineering proteins.

Workforce and community impact. The working group will train trainees in cross-disciplinary synthesis: DMS statistics, structural bioinformatics, graph learning, and open/reproducible workflows. By convening diverse experts and producing reusable standards for mapping, uncertainty reporting, and benchmarking, the project will create durable community infrastructure aligned with NCEMS goals—enabling future synthesis efforts on other emergent protein phenomena beyond allostery.
budget_and_resources:
Budget philosophy and NCEMS need. This is a community-scale synthesis requiring coordinated curation, multi-modal integration, and shared compute/software infrastructure beyond a single lab’s scope. NCEMS support is essential for convening a multidisciplinary team (structural biology, DMS analysis, ML/AI, statistical genetics, systems biology), providing neutral coordination, and enabling intensive, in-person/virtual working sessions that accelerate harmonization standards and joint deliverables.

Requested resources (categories). (1) Working group convenings: support for multiple multi-day meetings (hybrid/in-person) to align standards, conduct hands-on curation/modeling sprints, and run trainee-led tutorials. Costs include travel, lodging, and meeting logistics to ensure participation across institutions, career stages, and geographic regions. (2) Personnel support: partial support for a project coordinator/data curator and/or research software engineer time (distributed across participating labs) to maintain pipelines, manage provenance, and implement the atlas and benchmark infrastructure. Trainee support (graduate/postdoc) will be prioritized for curation, reproducibility checks, and tutorial development. (3) Compute and storage: access to NCEMS-supported compute (CPU/GPU) for graph feature extraction and model training, plus scalable storage for intermediate artifacts (structures, mappings, feature matrices) and public hosting of derived products. (4) Dissemination and training: resources for hosting open workshops, producing documentation, and archiving releases (DOIs).

Feasibility and scope control. To ensure deliverables within the award period, we will phase work: Year 1 focuses on a curated set of protein families with strong DMS coverage and reliable structural mapping; Year 2 expands breadth and refines models/benchmarks and cellular/clinical integration. We will set clear inclusion criteria (data quality thresholds, mapping confidence) to avoid uncontrolled scope.

In-kind contributions. Participating labs will contribute domain expertise, existing open-source tools, and effort for code review and mentoring. NCEMS will provide the convening structure, shared infrastructure, and synthesis-centered project management needed to integrate these contributions into coherent, community-usable outputs.

title: Deciphering the Sequence-to-Emergent-Property Grammar of Biomolecular Condensates
abstract: The emergence of biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation represents a paradigm shift in understanding mesoscale cellular organization. Despite extensive single-lab studies, the universal predictive rules governing how diverse protein and RNA sequences encode the physical properties of these condensates remain elusive. This mesoscale phenomenon bridges the gap between nanoscale molecular interactions and macroscale cellular functions, such as stress response and gene expression. Understanding this emergence is critical for solving long-standing puzzles in molecular and cellular biosciences, specifically regarding how non-membrane-bound organelles dynamically assemble and disassemble in response to environmental cues. Current research is highly fragmented, lacking a unified framework to explain how local interactions scale up to form functional, mesoscale structures that dictate global cellular outcomes. To address this, our working group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decipher the sequence-to-emergent-property grammar of phase separation. By integrating publicly available proteomics data, single-molecule biophysics datasets, transcriptomics, and high-throughput imaging repositories from the Protein Data Bank, LLPSDB, and the Image Data Resource, we will employ advanced artificial intelligence and machine learning frameworks to model condensate emergence. Our approach utilizes graph neural networks and deep learning architectures to synthesize these disparate multi-omics and imaging datasets, entirely bypassing the need for new experimental data. This innovative analytical strategy will allow us to map the multidimensional landscape of phase separation, identifying hidden patterns and emergent properties that cannot be observed in isolated datasets. The proposed synthesis goes far beyond the capacity of any individual laboratory, necessitating the dedicated support and resources of NCEMS. We will convene a transdisciplinary team of structural biologists, biophysicists, computational scientists, and cell biologists. Our working group is intentionally assembled to reflect diverse scientific perspectives, career stages, geographic locations, and institutional research levels, ensuring a robust and inclusive approach to this complex problem. This collaborative partnership will break down traditional disciplinary silos, fostering a dynamic environment where diverse new talent can thrive. Crucially, the project serves as a premier training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will be co-mentored across disciplines, gaining hands-on experience in cloud computing, AI-driven data integration, and collaborative research methodologies. In strict adherence to open science principles, all synthesized datasets, AI models, and analytical pipelines will be made freely available to the broader scientific community through open-source repositories like GitHub and Zenodo. Ultimately, this project reveals how the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale influences higher-order cellular functions.
background_and_significance: The emergence of biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) represents one of the most profound paradigm shifts in modern molecular and cellular biology. For decades, the organization of the cytoplasm and nucleoplasm was largely understood through the lens of membrane-bound organelles. However, the discovery that proteins and nucleic acids can spontaneously demix into liquid-like, non-membrane-bound droplets has revolutionized our understanding of mesoscale cellular architecture. This phenomenon bridges the critical gap between nanoscale molecular interactions, such as transient multivalent contacts between intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), and macroscale cellular functions, including stress response, chromatin organization, and gene expression. Despite the explosion of research in this area, the field remains highly fragmented. Individual laboratories have generated vast amounts of specialized data, ranging from single-molecule biophysics and proteomics to high-throughput cellular imaging. Yet, a fundamental puzzle remains unsolved: What are the universal predictive rules, or the 'sequence-to-emergent-property grammar,' that dictate how specific biomolecular sequences encode the physical and functional properties of these condensates? Currently, we lack a unified framework to explain how local, nanoscale interactions scale up to form functional, mesoscale structures that dictate global cellular outcomes. The complexity of these mesoscale phenomena, coupled with the sheer volume of publicly available, yet siloed, datasets, makes this a challenge that cannot be solved by any single laboratory. It requires a community-scale synthesis approach. The National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) is uniquely positioned to support this endeavor. By synthesizing distinct, publicly available datasets from repositories such as the Protein Data Bank (PDB), LLPSDB, and the Image Data Resource (IDR), our proposed working group will leverage advanced artificial intelligence and data science methodologies to uncover the hidden rules of condensate emergence. This project perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission to understand the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale, specifically focusing on the scale between biomolecules and organelles. The lack of a predictive grammar currently hinders both basic biological understanding and therapeutic design, particularly for neurodegenerative diseases where condensate dynamics are dysregulated. By integrating vast, disparate data sources without generating new experimental data, we will transition the field from descriptive, single-gene studies to a predictive, systems-level understanding of mesoscale emergence. This synthesis will solve a long-standing mystery in the molecular and cellular biosciences, illuminating how spatial, temporal, and informational complexities arise in biological systems.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: The proposed synthesis project is driven by three compelling, interconnected research questions designed to uncover the fundamental rules governing mesoscale emergence in biomolecular condensates. Question 1: What constitutes the universal sequence-to-emergent-property grammar that dictates the material state and physical properties of biomolecular condensates? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that a decipherable, universal grammar exists within the primary sequences of proteins and RNAs, specifically within intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and multivalent structured domains, that predictably scales from nanoscale molecular interactions to mesoscale physical properties such as viscosity, surface tension, and network connectivity. By synthesizing biophysical data from LLPSDB with structural data from the PDB, we anticipate identifying hidden sequence motifs, charge patterning, and spacer lengths that act as the fundamental syntax for condensate formation. Question 2: How do emergent condensate properties dynamically adapt to complex, multifactorial environmental cues across different cellular contexts? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the phase separation threshold and subsequent material properties of condensates are not static, but are dynamically tuned by environmental factors (e.g., pH, temperature, ion concentration, and molecular crowding) in a manner that can be predicted by integrating multi-omics data. By synthesizing transcriptomic and proteomic datasets with biophysical phase diagrams, we expect to reveal how cellular states modulate the physical chemistry of the cytoplasm to trigger or dissolve condensates. This will explain how the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale is dynamically regulated by the cellular environment. Question 3: How do the mesoscale material properties of condensates dictate higher-order, macroscale cellular functions and phenotypic outcomes? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the material properties of biomolecular condensates (e.g., liquid-like vs. gel-like states) act as non-linear signal amplifiers that couple local sequence composition to global cellular responses, such as stress granule assembly during environmental stress or transcriptional bursting in the nucleus. By integrating high-throughput imaging data from the Image Data Resource (IDR) with functional genomic datasets, we will map the causal relationships between mesoscale condensate dynamics and macroscale cellular phenotypes. Addressing these questions requires the integration of vastly different data types, ranging from one-dimensional sequence data to multidimensional imaging and multi-omics datasets. These questions are entirely novel in their scope and scale, moving beyond the traditional single-protein focus to establish a generalized, predictive model for phase separation. By answering these questions, this working group will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how non-membrane-bound organelles dynamically assemble and disassemble, providing a unified framework for understanding mesoscale emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences.
methods_and_approach: To decipher the sequence-to-emergent-property grammar of biomolecular condensates, our working group will employ a community-scale synthesis approach, relying exclusively on existing, publicly available data. We will not generate any new experimental data. Instead, our methodological innovation lies in the integration of disparate datasets using advanced artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) frameworks. Data Ingestion and Harmonization: The first phase involves the systematic aggregation and curation of heterogeneous datasets. We will extract sequence, biophysical, and phase diagram data from LLPSDB and PhaSePro. Structural features, including AlphaFold-predicted intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and multivalent contact points, will be sourced from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and UniProt. High-throughput cellular imaging data capturing condensate dynamics will be retrieved from the Image Data Resource (IDR), while corresponding cellular state information will be drawn from public transcriptomic and proteomic repositories (e.g., GEO, PRIDE). Harmonizing these multiscale datasets, spanning 1D sequences, 3D structures, and 4D imaging, will require the development of novel data ontologies to ensure interoperability. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Frameworks: Once harmonized, we will utilize state-of-the-art AI architectures to model condensate emergence. We will deploy Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to represent multivalent molecular interactions, where nodes represent interaction domains (e.g., RNA-binding domains, charged motifs) and edges represent transient physical contacts. GNNs are uniquely suited to capture the complex, non-linear network topologies that give rise to mesoscale phase separation. To predict continuous physical properties such as critical concentration, viscosity, and surface tension, we will utilize deep learning regression models and transformer-based architectures trained on the harmonized biophysical datasets. Image Analysis and Multi-Omics Integration: To bridge the gap between in vitro biophysics and in vivo cellular outcomes, we will apply convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to extract quantitative features from IDR imaging data, such as condensate size, number, and dissolution rates. These imaging features will be correlated with transcriptomic profiles using multi-omics integration algorithms to identify how cellular stress states dictate condensate behavior. Transdisciplinary Collaboration: This methodological approach is beyond the capabilities of any individual research lab. It requires the convergence of diverse scientific perspectives. Our working group will consist of structural biologists to guide feature engineering, biophysicists to validate the physical plausibility of AI predictions, computational scientists to architect the deep learning models, and cell biologists to contextualize the findings within macroscale cellular functions. Through iterative, cross-disciplinary feedback loops, the team will refine the AI models, ensuring they are biologically interpretable and mathematically robust. This synthesis strategy will map the multidimensional landscape of phase separation, extracting hidden patterns that isolated single-lab datasets cannot reveal.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The proposed synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that fundamentally advance the molecular and cellular biosciences. First, we will deliver the first unified, AI-driven predictive model capable of decoding the sequence-to-emergent-property grammar of biomolecular condensates. This model will allow researchers to input any protein or RNA sequence and accurately predict its propensity to phase separate, its resulting material properties, and its sensitivity to environmental cues. This directly solves a long-standing mystery regarding how mesoscale non-membrane-bound organelles dynamically assemble. Second, by mapping the multidimensional landscape of phase separation, we will uncover novel biological insights into how mesoscale emergence influences higher-order cellular functions, such as stress responses and gene regulation. This predictive capability has profound implications beyond basic science, offering new avenues for biotechnology and therapeutic interventions targeting condensate dysregulation in neurodegenerative diseases and cancer. Crucially, this project will have a massive impact on workforce development. It will serve as a premier training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will be cross-trained in molecular biology, cloud computing, and advanced AI methodologies, breaking down traditional disciplinary silos. By convening a transdisciplinary team reflecting diverse scientific perspectives, career stages, geographic locations, and institutional levels, we will tap into diverse new talent and foster a highly collaborative, inclusive research community. Ultimately, the synthesis of these vast, disparate datasets will generate innovative analytical strategies that the broader scientific community can adopt to study other complex emergence phenomena, solidifying NCEMS's vision of understanding mesoscale biological complexity.
budget_and_resources: The proposed community-scale synthesis project demonstrates a clear and compelling need for NCEMS support, as the required integration of massive, multi-modal datasets and the convening of a transdisciplinary team far exceed the resources and capabilities of any single laboratory or existing collaboration. The requested budget is meticulously aligned with the goals of catalyzing team science, leveraging AI, and training the next-generation workforce. A significant portion of the budget will be allocated to support Working Group convenings. Funds will cover travel, lodging, and logistical expenses for intensive, multi-day collaborative meetings at the NCEMS facility. These face-to-face interactions are critical for breaking down disciplinary silos among our diverse team of structural biologists, biophysicists, computational scientists, and cell biologists, fostering the deep intellectual integration necessary to tackle mesoscale emergence. To execute the computationally intensive AI and machine learning workflows, funds are requested for robust cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud). Training complex Graph Neural Networks and deep learning models on vast proteomics, transcriptomics, and high-throughput imaging datasets requires scalable GPU infrastructure that goes beyond standard institutional clusters. Crucially, the budget includes dedicated support for trainees. Stipends and travel allowances will be provided for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, ensuring they can fully participate in working group meetings and cross-disciplinary co-mentoring activities. This investment is vital for fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to train a future data-savvy workforce proficient in both molecular biosciences and advanced data science. Finally, funds are allocated for open science dissemination, including open-access publication fees and data storage costs, ensuring all synthesized datasets and analytical pipelines remain freely accessible to the global scientific community.

title: Emergence of Cellular Morphology from Cytoskeletal Crosstalk and Motor Protein Dynamics
abstract: The dynamic interplay between actin filaments and microtubules drives the emergence of complex cellular morphologies, representing a fundamental example of mesoscale biological organization. While the individual components of the cytoskeleton have been studied exhaustively, the emergent properties arising from their large-scale crosstalk remain a critical puzzle in cellular biomechanics. This mesoscale emergence dictates essential cellular outcomes, including directed migration, division, and mechanosensing. Understanding how these distinct biopolymer networks coordinate via crosslinking proteins and molecular motors to generate global cellular forces is essential for advancing our knowledge of cellular emergence. Currently, the field lacks a comprehensive model that integrates molecular-level motor kinetics with whole-cell morphological changes. To bridge this gap, our working group proposes a transdisciplinary synthesis project to decode the emergent mechanics of cytoskeletal crosstalk. We will aggregate and synthesize publicly available cryo-electron tomography datasets, live-cell super-resolution microscopy archives, and biophysical force-measurement databases from repositories such as EMPIAR and the Cell Image Library. By leveraging topological data analysis and agent-based machine learning models, we will simulate and analyze the emergent network topologies without generating any new experimental data. This data science approach will identify the universal principles by which local cytoskeletal interactions produce global, mesoscale cellular architectures. Addressing this multi-scale problem requires resources and collaborative infrastructure that far exceed the capabilities of a single research group, making NCEMS support indispensable. Our working group will unite a diverse cohort of polymer physicists, structural biologists, computational mechanobiologists, and live-cell imaging experts. We have specifically recruited team members from various geographic locations and institutional backgrounds to ensure a wide range of scientific perspectives. This diversity will stimulate cross-disciplinary innovation, allowing us to tackle this long-standing puzzle from multiple angles. Furthermore, this project is deeply committed to training the next generation of researchers.
