title: Synthesizing the Mechanotransductive Emergence of Focal Adhesion Maturation
abstract: Focal adhesions are highly dynamic, mesoscale protein complexes that physically connect the extracellular matrix to the intracellular actin cytoskeleton. The maturation of these complexes under mechanical tension is a classic example of biological emergence, where local physical forces dictate the large-scale spatial organization and signaling output of the cell. While the individual integrins and scaffolding proteins are well-characterized, how their collective interactions give rise to the emergent property of cellular mechanosensing remains a fundamental question. Understanding this mesoscale phenomenon is critical for explaining how cells adapt their morphology and behavior in response to varied physical environments. Our working group proposes a community-scale data synthesis project to unravel the emergent properties of focal adhesion maturation. We will integrate massive, publicly available datasets encompassing live-cell traction force microscopy, proximity-dependent biotinylation proteomics (BioID), and single-molecule tracking from the Image Data Resource and PRIDE. By utilizing advanced graph neural networks and spatio-temporal clustering algorithms, we will model the dynamic architecture of focal adhesions without generating any new experimental data. This AI-driven synthesis will reveal the hidden biophysical rules that govern how nanoscale protein unfolding events scale up to produce mesoscale mechanotransductive signaling hubs. The integration of complex biomechanical data with proteomics requires a level of transdisciplinary collaboration that can only be supported by NCEMS. Our working group brings together mechanobiologists, computational biophysicists, proteomics experts, and data scientists. We have prioritized diverse scientific perspectives by recruiting team members from varying career stages, geographic locations, and institutional backgrounds. This diversity is essential for fostering the innovative analytical strategies required to tackle mechanobiological emergence. A major focus of our initiative is to train the next generation of researchers in data-intensive biology. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive rigorous cross-training in big data integration, machine learning, and collaborative software development. We are fully committed to gold-standard open science practices; all synthesized datasets, AI models, and codebases will be made publicly available through Zenodo and GitHub. By synthesizing existing biomechanical and molecular data, this project will answer long-standing questions about how cells process physical information, revealing the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale.
background_and_significance: Focal adhesions (FAs) represent a quintessential example of biological emergence at the mesoscale. Bridging the gap between the extracellular matrix (ECM) and the intracellular actin cytoskeleton, these dynamic multi-protein complexes are essential for cellular mechanotransduction—the process by which cells convert mechanical stimuli into biochemical signals. At the nanoscale, individual molecular components such as integrins, talin, vinculin, and focal adhesion kinase (FAK) are well understood. We know that mechanical tension induces conformational changes, such as the unfolding of talin, which exposes cryptic binding sites to recruit additional scaffolding proteins. However, the true scientific mystery lies at the mesoscale: how do these localized, nanoscale protein unfolding events collectively scale up to produce the emergent properties of mature focal adhesions, which ultimately dictate whole-cell behavior, morphology, and fate? Despite decades of research, the biophysical rules governing this emergent assembly remain elusive. Historically, mechanobiology has been constrained by the limitations of single-laboratory approaches, which typically focus on either the biochemical composition of FAs or their biophysical force output, but rarely both simultaneously at a systems level. The recent explosion of publicly available, high-throughput biological data presents an unprecedented opportunity to transcend these limitations. Repositories such as the Image Data Resource (IDR) and the Proteomics Identifications Database (PRIDE) now host vast quantities of live-cell traction force microscopy (TFM) data, single-molecule tracking trajectories, and proximity-dependent biotinylation (BioID) proteomics. Yet, these datasets remain siloed. There has been no community-scale effort to synthesize these disparate data modalities into a cohesive, predictive model of mesoscale emergence. This fragmentation represents a critical barrier to progress in the molecular and cellular biosciences. Our proposed working group directly addresses this challenge by answering the U.S. National Science Foundation National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) call for transdisciplinary synthesis research. We will leverage AI and data science to integrate existing proteomic and biomechanical datasets, strictly adhering to the NCEMS mandate of generating no new experimental data. By synthesizing these diverse data streams, we aim to uncover the hidden architectural dynamics and emergent properties of FA maturation. The significance of this project extends beyond the specific biology of focal adhesions; it serves as a paradigm for understanding mesoscale emergence in any complex biological system. Furthermore, this initiative will catalyze a much-needed cultural shift in mechanobiology, moving the field toward large-scale data synthesis, open science, and cross-disciplinary collaboration. By bringing together mechanobiologists, computational biophysicists, proteomics experts, and data scientists from diverse geographic and institutional backgrounds, we will develop innovative analytical strategies capable of solving long-standing puzzles in cellular mechanosensing. Ultimately, this project will not only illuminate the fundamental principles of biological emergence but also provide rigorous training for the next-generation workforce of data-savvy scientists.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: Our synthesis project is driven by the overarching goal of understanding how mesoscale emergent properties arise from nanoscale molecular interactions during mechanotransduction. To achieve this, we have formulated three compelling, interrelated research questions that can only be answered through the transdisciplinary synthesis of publicly available proteomic, biophysical, and imaging data. Question 1: What are the spatio-temporal topological signatures that define the emergent transition from nascent adhesions to mature focal adhesions? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that focal adhesion maturation is not a linear accumulation of proteins, but rather a phase transition characterized by a distinct shift in the network topology of the complex. By synthesizing single-molecule tracking data with BioID proteomics, we predict the emergence of highly connected, mesoscale 'hub' sub-complexes that only form when local mechanical tension exceeds a critical threshold. We will test this by constructing dynamic protein-protein interaction networks and utilizing graph theory to map topological changes over time and varying force regimes. Question 2: How do specific biophysical parameters (e.g., substrate stiffness, traction force) quantitatively dictate the compositional hierarchy of the focal adhesion interactome? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the recruitment sequence and residence time of specific mechanosensitive proteins are governed by universal biophysical rules that scale predictably with extracellular tension. We anticipate that synthesizing traction force microscopy (TFM) data with time-resolved proteomics will reveal hidden correlations between force application rates and the spatial stratification of the FA core (integrin signaling layer vs. force transduction layer vs. actin regulatory layer). We expect to identify a 'mechanical code' where specific force vectors uniquely predict the recruitment probabilities of downstream signaling effectors. Question 3: Can cross-modal AI-driven data synthesis identify previously uncharacterized molecular players essential for the mesoscale emergence of cellular mechanosensing? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the current inventory of focal adhesion components is incomplete because transient, force-dependent interactions are often lost in traditional, single-modality studies. By employing advanced graph neural networks (GNNs) to bridge the latent spaces of TFM imaging data and proteomic profiles, we predict the discovery of novel, transiently acting 'bridging' proteins. These proteins likely act exclusively at the mesoscale to synchronize the maturation of adjacent adhesion sites, facilitating cell-wide mechanical coordination. These questions address fundamental gaps in our understanding of molecular emergence. They are designed to be entirely independent of new data generation, relying instead on the innovative synthesis of existing, disparate datasets. By testing these hypotheses, our working group will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how cells interpret their physical environment, while simultaneously developing robust, reusable analytical frameworks for the broader molecular and cellular biology community. The answers to these questions will redefine focal adhesions not merely as structural anchors, but as sophisticated, emergent computational hubs that process complex physical information.
methods_and_approach: Our methodological approach is grounded exclusively in the community-scale synthesis of existing, publicly available data, strictly adhering to NCEMS guidelines requiring no new experimental data generation. The project is structured around three core phases: Data Harvesting and Harmonization, AI-Driven Cross-Modal Synthesis, and Mechanistic Modeling of Emergence. Phase 1: Data Harvesting and Harmonization. We will systematically mine the Image Data Resource (IDR) and the Proteomics Identifications Database (PRIDE) to extract high-quality datasets related to focal adhesion dynamics. From IDR, we will aggregate live-cell traction force microscopy (TFM) maps, single-molecule tracking (SMT) trajectories of integrins and scaffolding proteins, and super-resolution localization microscopy data. From PRIDE, we will extract proximity-dependent biotinylation (BioID) and AP-MS proteomic datasets obtained under varying mechanical conditions (e.g., different substrate stiffnesses). The primary challenge in synthesis is data harmonization. We will develop a standardized, open-source metadata ontology to align these diverse datasets. Spatial data will be normalized to a common coordinate system relative to the cell edge, while temporal data will be aligned using dynamic time warping algorithms to synchronize distinct stages of adhesion maturation across different experimental setups. Phase 2: AI-Driven Cross-Modal Synthesis. To bridge the gap between biophysical forces (TFM) and molecular composition (proteomics/SMT), we will employ Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Spatio-Temporal Clustering algorithms. We will represent focal adhesions as dynamic graphs, where nodes represent specific proteins (derived from proteomics) and edges represent physical interactions or spatial proximity (derived from SMT and super-resolution data). Node features will be augmented with localized traction force vectors mapped from TFM data. We will train Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (ST-GCNs) to learn the latent representations of these complex networks. This AI-driven approach will allow us to predict the unobserved proteomic states of a focal adhesion based purely on its biophysical force profile, effectively synthesizing the modalities. Phase 3: Mechanistic Modeling of Emergence. To explicitly study emergence, we will analyze the outputs of our GNNs using topological data analysis (TDA). We will track the evolution of network motifs (e.g., feed-forward loops, highly connected hubs) as a function of increasing mechanical tension. By applying percolation theory to our synthesized networks, we will identify the critical force thresholds at which the nanoscale unfolding of individual mechanosensors triggers the mesoscale phase transition into a mature focal adhesion. Team Structure and Training: Our working group consists of mechanobiologists, computational biophysicists, and data scientists. Collaboration will be facilitated through biannual in-person synthesis meetings and continuous virtual integration via GitHub and Slack. A core component of our approach is the cross-training of postdocs and graduate students. Trainees will participate in intensive hackathons focused on machine learning and big data integration, ensuring they develop the transdisciplinary skills necessary to become the next generation of data-savvy biological scientists.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This community-scale synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that advance the molecular and cellular biosciences, specifically in the realm of mesoscale emergence. Scientifically, the primary outcome will be the first comprehensive, predictive model of focal adhesion maturation that seamlessly integrates biophysical force with spatiotemporal proteomic dynamics. By revealing the hidden biophysical rules and topological network shifts that govern mechanosensing, we will solve the long-standing puzzle of how localized nanoscale protein unfolding scales up to dictate whole-cell behavior. This will fundamentally shift the paradigm of mechanobiology from descriptive, single-molecule observations to predictive, systems-level understanding. Methodologically, we will produce a suite of highly innovative, open-source analytical strategies. Our novel application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (ST-GCNs) to bridge distinct biological data modalities (imaging, biophysics, and proteomics) will serve as a blueprint for future synthesis research across the biological sciences. The metadata ontologies and harmonization pipelines developed by our team will enable other researchers to unlock the latent value in existing public repositories. The broader impacts of this project align directly with the NCEMS mission. By assembling a geographically and institutionally diverse working group, we are tapping into diverse new talent and fostering cross-disciplinary collaboration that transcends the capabilities of any single laboratory. Crucially, this project will serve as a premier training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows will emerge as transdisciplinary leaders, uniquely equipped with deep domain expertise in molecular biology combined with advanced proficiency in AI, big data integration, and collaborative software development. Ultimately, this project will demonstrate the immense power of data synthesis to uncover the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties.
budget_and_resources: The requested budget is strictly tailored to support the collaborative, computational, and synthesis-driven nature of this project, in full compliance with NCEMS guidelines. No funds are requested for wet-lab equipment, reagents, or the generation of new experimental data. The primary budget category is Personnel, which directly supports our objective to train the future data-savvy workforce. Funds are allocated for the stipends, tuition, and benefits of two postdoctoral fellows and three graduate students. These trainees will serve as the computational engine of the project, receiving rigorous cross-training in AI, data science, and mechanobiology under the mentorship of our diverse team of Principal Investigators. The second major category is Collaborative Travel and Meetings. To foster the deep transdisciplinary integration required for this community-scale synthesis, funds are requested for biannual, intensive working group meetings. These multi-day, in-person sessions will bring together our diverse team of mechanobiologists, biophysicists, and data scientists from across different geographic locations and institutions. Additionally, we have budgeted for two trainee-focused hackathons to accelerate software development and model integration. The third category is Computational Infrastructure and Resources. Given the massive scale of the publicly available imaging and proteomic datasets we are synthesizing, we require robust cloud computing resources. Funds are allocated for Amazon Web Services (AWS) or Google Cloud Platform (GCP) instances, specifically high-performance GPU clusters necessary for training our Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (ST-GCNs) and processing large-scale live-cell traction force microscopy data. Finally, a small portion of the budget is reserved for Open Science and Publication costs, covering open-access article processing charges (APCs) and cloud storage fees for hosting our synthesized datasets and Docker containers on platforms like Zenodo. This budget directly addresses the NCEMS requirement for support that goes far beyond the capabilities of a single lab.

title: Decoding the Emergence of Stress Granules and Cellular Resilience Networks
abstract: In response to environmental stress, eukaryotic cells rapidly halt translation and sequester mRNAs and RNA-binding proteins into mesoscale condensates known as stress granules. The formation, maturation, and dissolution of these membrane-less organelles represent a critical survival mechanism driven by emergent phase separation. Despite intense scrutiny, the universal rules governing how different stressors induce distinct stress granule compositions and how these mesoscale structures confer global cellular resilience remain a major puzzle. Understanding this emergence is vital for deciphering cellular adaptation to shifting environmental conditions. Our working group proposes a large-scale data synthesis project to decode the emergent dynamics of stress granule formation. We will integrate diverse, publicly available datasets, including spatial transcriptomics, high-throughput confocal imaging, and dynamic interactome data from repositories such as the Gene Expression Omnibus, BioGRID, and the Cell Image Library. By leveraging advanced natural language processing models adapted for biological sequences and spatio-temporal deep learning, we will synthesize these multi-omics datasets to predict stress granule assembly pathways. This project relies entirely on existing data, using innovative AI strategies to map the complex network of interactions that drive mesoscale condensation. The multifaceted nature of stress granule biology requires a transdisciplinary approach that exceeds the capacity of any single lab, making NCEMS support critical. We will convene a diverse team of RNA biologists, physical chemists, computational toxicologists, and machine learning engineers. Our working group is structured to promote collaborative partnerships across diverse geographic locations, institutional types, and career stages, ensuring a broad range of scientific perspectives. This inclusive environment will stimulate the cross-disciplinary innovation necessary to solve this long-standing cellular mystery. Training the future data-savvy workforce is a core component of our mission. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in a collaborative network, gaining expertise in multi-omics integration, AI-driven data analysis, and open science protocols. We commit to making all findings, integrated databases, and analytical workflows publicly accessible via community-standard repositories like GitHub. By synthesizing these vast public datasets, our project will reveal how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale stress granules influences higher-order cellular survival outcomes, directly supporting the NCEMS vision of understanding biological emergence.
background_and_significance:
The fundamental principles governing how biological systems transition from isolated molecular components to highly organized, functional mesoscale structures remain one of the most profound mysteries in the molecular and cellular biosciences. A quintessential example of this phenomenon is the emergence of stress granules (SGs). In response to adverse environmental conditions—such as oxidative stress, thermal shock, viral infection, or osmotic imbalance—eukaryotic cells rapidly undergo a massive reorganization of their intracellular space. They halt global translation to conserve energy and sequester untranslated mRNAs, RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), and signaling molecules into dynamic, membrane-less condensates. This process, driven by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represents a critical, emergent survival mechanism. Individual biomolecules, which exhibit standard Brownian motion under homeostatic conditions, suddenly engage in multivalent interactions driven by intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and specific RNA architectures, culminating in the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale.

Despite decades of intense scrutiny and the generation of terabytes of multi-omics and imaging data, the field is currently bottlenecked by fragmentation. Individual laboratories have mapped specific stressor pathways or characterized isolated protein behaviors, yet the universal rules governing how different stressors induce distinct SG compositions—and how these mesoscale structures confer global cellular resilience—remain a major puzzle. Are there fundamental, stress-independent biophysical grammars that dictate condensation, or is emergence entirely context-dependent? How do these mesoscale structures influence higher subcellular and cellular outcomes, such as survival versus apoptosis? 

Addressing these questions requires a paradigm shift from reductionist, single-lab experimental approaches to a community-scale data synthesis model. This working group proposal aligns perfectly with the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) mission. We aim to catalyze a multidisciplinary scientific team to leverage artificial intelligence and data science to synthesize existing, publicly available datasets. By integrating spatial transcriptomics, high-throughput confocal imaging, and dynamic interactome data, we will map the complex, multi-dimensional networks that drive mesoscale condensation. 

The significance of this research extends far beyond basic cell biology. Understanding the emergence and dissolution of stress granules is vital for deciphering cellular adaptation to shifting environmental conditions and has profound implications for human health. The failure of SGs to properly dissolve is directly linked to pathological solid phase transitions observed in neurodegenerative diseases, such as Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), while hyper-resilient SGs are implicated in cancer chemoresistance. By synthesizing vast amounts of disparate public data, this project will not only answer long-standing mysteries regarding mesoscale biological emergence but will also provide the foundational, predictive models necessary for future therapeutic innovations. Furthermore, by embedding trainees in this transdisciplinary, synthesis-driven environment, we will cultivate the next-generation workforce of data-savvy scientists equipped to tackle the most complex challenges in the biosciences.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our synthesis project is driven by the overarching goal of understanding the unexpected appearance of mesoscale properties during cellular stress. To decode the emergent dynamics of stress granule formation and their role in cellular resilience, our working group will address four compelling, interrelated research questions through the synthesis of existing public data:

Research Question 1: What is the universal molecular grammar driving stress granule emergence across diverse environmental stressors, and how does it diverge into stressor-specific compositional signatures? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that while upstream signaling cascades (e.g., eIF2alpha phosphorylation) are stressor-specific, the core mesoscale phase transition is governed by a universal, quantifiable 'grammar' of multivalent RNA-protein and protein-protein interactions. By synthesizing diverse transcriptomic and interactome datasets, we predict the identification of a core network of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and RNA structural motifs that are invariant across stressors, decorated by peripheral, stress-specific interactors that tune the biophysical properties of the condensate.

Research Question 2: How do the spatio-temporal dynamics of stress granule assembly, maturation, and dissolution correlate with varying degrees of cellular resilience or vulnerability across different cell lineages?
Hypothesis 2: We posit that the kinetic profiles of mesoscale condensation—specifically the rates of assembly and the latency of dissolution—serve as direct, predictive biomarkers of global cellular survival outcomes. We hypothesize that delayed dissolution, quantifiable through the synthesis of time-lapse imaging and temporal transcriptomic data, strictly correlates with a transition from an adaptive liquid state to a pathological, irreversible solid state, leading to cellular apoptosis.

Research Question 3: Can advanced artificial intelligence architectures, specifically natural language processing (NLP) adapted for biological sequences combined with spatio-temporal deep learning, accurately predict stress granule composition and physical properties solely from foundational multi-omics data?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that transformer-based NLP models trained on protein and RNA sequences, when integrated with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) modeling interactome topologies, will identify cryptic, higher-order interaction motifs that traditional reductionist models overlook. This AI-driven synthesis will enable highly accurate predictions of mesoscale emergent properties without the need for de novo experimental validation.

Research Question 4: To what extent does the baseline cellular transcriptome predetermine the capacity for emergent phase separation under acute stress?
Hypothesis 4: We hypothesize that cell-type-specific transcriptomic landscapes establish a defined stoichiometric ratio of essential scaffolding molecules versus client proteins. By synthesizing baseline RNA-seq data with stress-induced spatial transcriptomics across diverse cell lines, we expect to demonstrate that this pre-existing stoichiometric balance dictates the thermodynamic threshold and capacity for emergent phase separation, explaining why certain cellular lineages are inherently more vulnerable to environmental stressors.

These questions directly address long-standing puzzles in the molecular and cellular sciences. By leveraging AI to interrogate these hypotheses using only existing data, our transdisciplinary team will uncover the fundamental rules of biological emergence at the mesoscale, fulfilling the core mandate of the NCEMS research call.
methods_and_approach:
To achieve our objectives, we will employ a community-scale synthesis approach that strictly utilizes existing, publicly available data, generating no new experimental data. Our methodology relies on the transdisciplinary integration of multi-omics curation, advanced artificial intelligence, and spatio-temporal modeling, executed by a diverse team of RNA biologists, physical chemists, computational toxicologists, and machine learning engineers.

Data Acquisition and Harmonization: We will systematically mine, curate, and harmonize multi-modal datasets from established public repositories. Transcriptomic and spatial transcriptomic data (RNA-seq, CLIP-seq, smFISH) will be sourced from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and ArrayExpress to map the RNA constituents of stress granules across varying stressors (e.g., arsenite, heat shock, viral infection) and cell lines. Protein-protein and RNA-protein interaction networks will be extracted from BioGRID, STRING, and the eCLIP database. High-throughput confocal and super-resolution imaging data capturing the spatio-temporal dynamics of SG formation will be sourced from the Cell Image Library and the Image Data Resource (IDR). A critical first step will be the development of a unified, relational database with standardized metadata ontologies to ensure seamless integration of these disparate data types.

AI-Driven Sequence Analysis (NLP for Molecular Grammar): To decode the molecular grammar of phase separation, we will leverage advanced Natural Language Processing (NLP) models adapted for biological sequences. We will utilize pre-trained transformer architectures (such as ProtBERT and RNA-FM) to generate high-dimensional embeddings of protein Intrinsically Disordered Regions (IDRs) and RNA structural motifs identified in our curated datasets. By applying attention mechanisms, we will extract the cryptic sequence syntax that dictates multivalent interactions, allowing us to predict the propensity of novel proteins and RNAs to partition into mesoscale condensates under specific stress conditions.

Spatio-Temporal Deep Learning: To model the emergent kinetics of SG assembly and dissolution, we will apply spatio-temporal deep learning to our curated imaging and time-series multi-omics data. We will utilize Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to model the dynamic interactome, where nodes represent biomolecules and edges represent interaction strengths modulated by stress. Concurrently, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Vision Transformers will be applied to time-lapse imaging data to extract features related to condensate size, number, and fusion events. 

Multi-Modal Data Integration: The core of our synthesis strategy involves fusing sequence, interaction, and imaging modalities. We will employ Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to map these diverse data types into a shared latent space. This will allow us to correlate specific molecular grammars (from NLP) and network topologies (from GNNs) with the physical properties and kinetic behaviors of the condensates (from CNNs), ultimately linking mesoscale emergence to cellular resilience outcomes.

Training the Data-Savvy Workforce: Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded at the core of this methodology. Trainees will lead specific analytical modules under the joint mentorship of domain experts and data scientists. We will host bi-annual, cross-disciplinary boot camps and hackathons focused on multi-omics integration and AI model training, ensuring the next generation is equipped with the transdisciplinary skills required for modern synthesis research.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This community-scale synthesis project is expected to yield transformative outcomes that fundamentally advance our understanding of mesoscale emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences. The primary deliverable will be the first comprehensive, multi-modal predictive model of stress granule assembly, composition, and dissolution. 

Specifically, our expected outcomes include: 
1) The 'SG-Atlas': A publicly accessible, highly curated, and integrated database harmonizing spatial transcriptomics, interactomics, and imaging data related to stress-induced mesoscale condensates across diverse cell types and environmental stressors. 
2) Novel AI Architectures: The release of custom-trained NLP and spatio-temporal deep learning models optimized for predicting phase separation behaviors and emergent subcellular phenomena solely from sequence and baseline omics data. 
3) Resolution of Long-Standing Puzzles: High-impact publications detailing the universal versus stressor-specific rules of SG composition, definitively linking the kinetics of mesoscale condensation to global cellular resilience and survival pathways.

The impact of this work will be deeply felt across multiple biological disciplines. By shifting the paradigm from descriptive, single-gene studies to predictive, systems-level synthesis, we will provide a robust framework for understanding how the unexpected appearance of new biological properties at the mesoscale influences higher-order cellular outcomes. This foundational knowledge is critical for future translational research, offering new computational avenues to identify therapeutic targets for diseases characterized by aberrant phase transitions, such as neurodegeneration and cancer.

Furthermore, this project will have a profound impact on the scientific workforce. By embedding trainees in a highly collaborative, transdisciplinary environment, we will produce a cohort of early-career scientists who are fluent in both molecular biology and advanced data science. These trainees will be uniquely positioned to lead the future of synthesis research, perfectly embodying the NCEMS vision of cultivating a diverse, data-savvy scientific community.

These multi-day sessions will bring together our diverse team of RNA biologists, physical chemists, computational toxicologists, and ML engineers from distinct geographic locations and institutional types to review progress, troubleshoot analytical bottlenecks, and integrate findings.

title: Emergent Transport Selectivity of the Nuclear Pore Complex Assembly
abstract: The Nuclear Pore Complex (NPC) is one of the largest and most intricate mesoscale structures in the eukaryotic cell, mediating all transport between the nucleus and cytoplasm. The selective permeability of the NPC emerges from the collective behavior of intrinsically disordered proteins (FG-Nups) that line its central channel. However, how the dynamic, nanoscale interactions of these individual proteins scale up to create a robust, mesoscale selective barrier remains a highly debated puzzle in molecular biology. Understanding this emergent property is crucial for explaining how cells maintain compartmentalization while allowing rapid, targeted communication. Our working group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decipher the emergent transport selectivity of the NPC. We will integrate publicly available cryo-electron microscopy maps, single-molecule fluorescence transport data, and interactomic datasets from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank, PRIDE, and specific biophysical repositories. By employing advanced molecular dynamics simulations guided by machine learning and topological data analysis, we will synthesize these disparate datasets to model the dynamic state of the NPC barrier. This approach utilizes only existing public data to develop innovative analytical strategies that reveal the physical rules of mesoscale transport emergence. The sheer scale and complexity of integrating high-resolution structural data with dynamic transport kinetics require the robust collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS. Our transdisciplinary team brings together structural biologists, polymer physicists, computational data scientists, and cell biologists. We have intentionally assembled a working group that reflects diverse scientific perspectives, including researchers from various career stages and geographic locations. This diversity is essential for breaking down disciplinary silos and fostering novel insights into complex biological phenomena. Training the next generation of researchers is a fundamental aspect of our proposal. Trainees will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship, developing critical skills in structural bioinformatics, AI-driven modeling, and collaborative open science. In strict adherence to community policies on reproducible science, all integrated datasets, simulation trajectories, and analytical code will be published openly via Zenodo and GitHub. By synthesizing structural and functional data, this project will illuminate how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale barrier properties influences higher-order cellular compartmentalization, perfectly aligning with the overarching goals of NCEMS.
background_and_significance: The transition from individual biomolecular interactions to complex, functional cellular organelles represents one of the most profound frontiers in modern biological sciences. At the heart of this frontier lies the mesoscale, a critical spatial and temporal domain where the collective behaviors of macromolecules give rise to emergent properties that dictate cellular life. The Nuclear Pore Complex (NPC) serves as the quintessential model for mesoscale emergence. As the sole gateway between the nucleus and the cytoplasm, the NPC is a massive, megadalton-scale macromolecular assembly that tightly regulates the bidirectional flow of genetic information, proteins, and signaling molecules. The structural scaffold of the NPC is well-characterized, yet its most critical functional feature—its selective permeability—arises not from a rigid structural gate, but from the dynamic, collective behavior of intrinsically disordered proteins known as Phenylalanine-Glycine nucleoporins (FG-Nups). These FG-Nups line the central channel of the pore, creating a barrier that is highly permeable to specific transport receptors while strictly excluding inert macromolecules. Despite decades of intense study, the physical mechanism by which the nanoscale interactions of individual FG-Nups scale up to create a robust, mesoscale selective barrier remains a highly debated puzzle. Competing models suggest the barrier functions either as a highly cross-linked hydrogel, a dynamic polymer brush, or a phase-separated liquid condensate. This lack of consensus persists largely because experimental techniques are inherently limited by their spatial and temporal resolution, capturing either static high-resolution snapshots or low-resolution dynamic traces. Consequently, the field has generated vast, but siloed, repositories of publicly available data, including high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) maps, vast interactomic datasets, and single-molecule fluorescence transport kinetics. The complexity and lack of understanding of this mesoscale phenomenon make it an area of research that is ripe for novel discoveries through data synthesis. Addressing this long-standing mystery requires a paradigm shift from reductionist experimentation to holistic, community-scale data integration. By synthesizing these disparate datasets, we can bridge the gap between static architecture and dynamic function. Understanding the emergent transport selectivity of the NPC is not only vital for fundamental cell biology but also holds profound implications for understanding viral infection mechanisms, neurodegenerative diseases, and cancer, where nucleocytoplasmic transport is often dysregulated. Furthermore, elucidating the physical rules of mesoscale transport emergence will inspire the development of novel, bio-inspired nanomaterials and targeted drug delivery systems. This project perfectly aligns with the NCEMS vision by leveraging publicly available data to understand the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale, utilizing a transdisciplinary approach to solve a fundamental biological mystery without generating new experimental data.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: Our community-scale synthesis project is driven by three fundamental research questions designed to decode the emergent properties of the NPC barrier. Question 1: How do the spatial arrangement and grafting density of FG-Nups within the rigid NPC scaffold dictate the emergent phase behavior and topology of the central channel? We hypothesize that the specific architectural confinement and grafting geometry provided by the NPC scaffold drive a density-dependent percolation transition among the FG-Nups. This transition creates a unique, mesoscale barrier topology that cannot be predicted by the behavior of isolated FG-Nups in vitro. By synthesizing static structural constraints from cryo-EM data with polymer physics models, we expect to demonstrate that the emergent barrier is highly heterogeneous, featuring localized regions of liquid-liquid phase separation interspersed with dynamic voids, rather than a uniform hydrogel or simple brush. Question 2: What are the universal scaling laws governing the transit times of active transport receptors compared to inert macromolecules through the dynamic FG-network? We hypothesize that transport efficiency is governed by a dynamic, transient cross-linking network where multivalent, low-affinity interactions between transport receptors and FG-repeats significantly lower the free energy barrier for translocation. We postulate that this multivalent avidity creates an emergent 'lubrication' effect, allowing receptors to glide through the pore orders of magnitude faster than inert molecules of similar size. To test this, we will synthesize single-molecule fluorescence tracking data with interactomic binding affinities, using machine learning to extract the hidden scaling laws that govern transit kinetics as a function of molecular size, surface hydrophobicity, and receptor valency. Question 3: How do structural variations and physiological dilations of the NPC scaffold allosterically modulate the emergent selectivity of the transport barrier? Recent structural data suggest that the NPC scaffold can undergo significant dilation or constriction in response to cellular stress or metabolic states. We hypothesize that these scaffold dynamics allosterically regulate the central FG-network topology, effectively tuning the size-exclusion limit and transport capacity of the pore. We propose that dilation stretches the grafted FG-Nups, altering their collective phase behavior and increasing the probability of large cargo transit. By integrating disparate cryo-EM datasets representing various physiological states of the NPC with our dynamic barrier models, we will map the conformational landscape of the pore. These three interconnected questions address long-standing puzzles in molecular biology. Answering them requires the integration of diverse datasets—ranging from atomic coordinates to cellular transit times—which is beyond the capability of any single research group. Through this transdisciplinary synthesis, we will uncover the fundamental physical rules that govern how nanoscale protein interactions yield mesoscale transport emergence, fulfilling the core mission of NCEMS to catalyze novel discoveries through community-scale collaboration.
methods_and_approach: To answer our research questions, we will employ a transdisciplinary, purely computational approach that synthesizes diverse, publicly available datasets. Our methodology is divided into three integrated phases, entirely dependent on existing data and avoiding any de novo experimental data generation. Phase 1: Community-Scale Data Acquisition and Harmonization. We will systematically mine the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) and the Protein Data Bank (PDB) to extract all high-resolution structural models of the NPC scaffold across various species and physiological states. Concurrently, we will aggregate interactomic datasets from the PRIDE database, specifically focusing on binding affinities and cross-linking mass spectrometry data between FG-Nups and transport receptors. Finally, we will harvest single-molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET) and high-speed particle tracking trajectories from biophysical repositories such as Zenodo and Figshare. The critical first step involves harmonizing these multi-modal datasets. Our computational data scientists will develop automated, open-source pipelines to standardize data formats, ensuring that static structural coordinates can be seamlessly integrated with kinetic transit times and thermodynamic binding affinities. Phase 2: AI-Guided Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics (CG-MD). Modeling the entire NPC barrier at an atomistic level is computationally prohibitive and unnecessary for capturing mesoscale emergence. Instead, we will utilize machine learning algorithms to develop highly optimized, physics-informed coarse-grained models of the FG-Nups. The AI will be trained on the aggregated interactomic and smFRET data to accurately parameterize the intermolecular forces and solvent interactions of the disordered regions. Using these AI-derived parameters, we will perform extensive CG-MD simulations of the FG-network, strictly constrained by the boundary conditions derived from the harmonized cryo-EM scaffold data. By simulating the insertion of transport receptors and inert molecules into this virtual barrier, we will generate massive synthetic trajectories that bridge the gap between structure and function. Phase 3: Topological Data Analysis (TDA) and Kinetic Modeling. To extract meaningful biological insights from the complex simulation trajectories, we will apply Topological Data Analysis. TDA is uniquely suited for studying emergence, as it quantifies the shape, connectivity, and void spaces of dynamic networks over time. By applying TDA to our simulated FG-network, we will map the transient phase separations and percolation networks hypothesized in our research questions. We will then synthesize these topological maps with the empirical single-molecule transport data using Bayesian inference models. This will allow us to rigorously test our hypotheses regarding scaling laws and allosteric modulation, determining how changes in scaffold diameter or receptor valency alter the topological landscape of the barrier. This comprehensive synthesis requires the robust collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS. Structural biologists will interpret the cryo-EM constraints, polymer physicists will define the CG-MD parameters, and computational scientists will execute the AI and TDA workflows. Together, this diverse team will develop innovative analytical strategies that not only solve the NPC puzzle but also establish a new methodological framework for studying mesoscale emergence across the biological sciences.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This community-scale synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that significantly advance the molecular and cellular biosciences. Scientifically, our primary outcome will be the first unified, dynamic, and topologically accurate model of the Nuclear Pore Complex barrier. By synthesizing disparate structural, interactomic, and kinetic datasets, we will resolve the decades-old debate regarding the physical nature of the NPC’s selective permeability, definitively mapping how nanoscale FG-Nup interactions generate mesoscale phase behaviors. We will produce a comprehensive set of universal scaling laws governing nucleocytoplasmic transport, providing a predictive framework for how molecular size, valency, and scaffold dilation influence cargo transit. Beyond the NPC, the innovative analytical strategies developed here—specifically the integration of AI-guided coarse-grained modeling with Topological Data Analysis—will have a profound broader impact. These methodologies will be directly applicable to studying other mesoscale biological condensates and intrinsically disordered protein networks, catalyzing new avenues of research across the scientific community. Furthermore, understanding the physical rules of transport emergence will inform the design of next-generation, bio-inspired selective filters and targeted drug delivery vehicles. Crucially, this project will have a massive impact on workforce development. By deeply integrating trainees into our working group, we will train the future data-savvy workforce. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive unparalleled cross-disciplinary mentorship, gaining highly sought-after expertise in data harmonization, machine learning, polymer physics, and structural bioinformatics. They will learn to communicate across disciplinary boundaries, a vital skill for modern collaborative science. Ultimately, by leveraging the resources of NCEMS to unite diverse scientific perspectives, this project will transform isolated public data into profound biological insights, illuminating the fundamental principles of mesoscale emergence and setting a new standard for transdisciplinary synthesis research.

title: Synthesizing the Emergence of Autophagosomes at ER-Mitochondria Contact Sites
abstract: Autophagy is a highly conserved cellular degradation pathway that relies on the *de novo* formation of double-membrane autophagosomes. The biogenesis of these mesoscale organelles frequently initiates at dynamic contact sites between the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria. How local lipid transfer and protein scaffolding at these nanoscale inter-organelle junctions scale up to drive the large-scale membrane curvature required for autophagosome emergence remains a fundamental, unsolved puzzle in cell biology. Understanding this mesoscale phenomenon is essential for deciphering how cells maintain homeostasis under metabolic stress. Our working group proposes a transdisciplinary synthesis project to decode the emergent biophysics of autophagosome formation. We will systematically integrate publicly available lipidomics data, high-resolution 3D electron tomography, and live-cell imaging datasets from repositories such as the Metabolomics Workbench, EMPIAR, and the Image Data Resource. By leveraging advanced 3D computer vision and generative machine learning models, we will synthesize these multi-modal datasets to reconstruct the spatio-temporal dynamics of membrane curvature. This project relies entirely on existing public data, utilizing AI to extract novel insights into how local molecular interactions dictate the emergence of complex mesoscale organelles. The integration of lipid biochemistry with 3D ultrastructural imaging requires a collaborative effort that far exceeds the capabilities of a single laboratory, necessitating the support of NCEMS. We have assembled a diverse team of lipid biologists, biophysicists, computer vision experts, and cellular ultrastructure specialists. Our working group is intentionally curated to include diverse scientific perspectives, bridging researchers from different institutional tiers and geographic locations. This collaborative environment will drive the innovative analytical strategies needed to solve this long-standing biological mystery. Furthermore, this project serves as a vital training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdocs will gain hands-on experience in multi-omics integration, advanced image analysis, and open science practices. We are fully committed to making all synthesized datasets, AI models, and analytical pipelines freely available to the scientific community through open-source platforms like GitHub. By illuminating the relationship between inter-organelle contact sites and autophagosome biogenesis, this synthesis project will directly advance the NCEMS mission to understand the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale.
background_and_significance: Autophagy is a fundamental, highly conserved cellular degradation and recycling pathway critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis, particularly under metabolic stress. The hallmark of macroautophagy is the de novo biogenesis of the autophagosome, a unique double-membrane mesoscale organelle that engulfs cytoplasmic cargo for subsequent lysosomal degradation. Extensive experimental evidence over the past decade has revealed that autophagosome biogenesis frequently initiates at dynamic, nanoscale inter-organelle junctions, specifically endoplasmic reticulum-mitochondria contact sites (ERMCS). At these junctions, localized lipid synthesis and transfer, coordinated by specialized protein tethers, provide the necessary building blocks for membrane expansion. However, a profound and long-standing mystery in molecular and cellular biology remains: how do these localized, nanoscale molecular events—specifically lipid transfer and protein scaffolding—scale up to drive the large-scale, dramatic membrane curvature required for the emergence of a mature, functional autophagosome? This transition from localized molecular interactions to a structurally distinct mesoscale organelle represents a quintessential example of biological emergence. Understanding this phenomenon is not only crucial for fundamental cell biology but also holds significant implications for understanding diseases linked to autophagic dysfunction, including neurodegeneration and cancer. Historically, investigating this mesoscale emergence has been hindered by the limitations of isolated experimental approaches. Individual laboratories typically focus either on the biochemistry of lipidomics or the ultrastructural analysis of cellular membranes, rarely integrating the two. Consequently, the field is rich with disjointed, publicly available datasets—ranging from mass spectrometry-based lipid profiles to high-resolution 3D electron tomography (ET) and live-cell fluorescence microscopy. The complexity of these multi-modal datasets and the lack of a cohesive framework to synthesize them represent a major bottleneck. Our proposed working group directly addresses this critical gap by leveraging the power of data synthesis and artificial intelligence, aligning perfectly with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). We propose to synthesize vast amounts of existing, publicly available data to decode the emergent biophysics of autophagosome formation. By completely foregoing the generation of new experimental data, we will focus our efforts on extracting deeper, novel insights from the wealth of information already residing in repositories such as the Metabolomics Workbench, EMPIAR, and the Image Data Resource (IDR). This community-scale synthesis project is fundamentally beyond the capabilities of any single research laboratory. It necessitates a highly collaborative, transdisciplinary approach that brings together experts in lipid biochemistry, cellular biophysics, advanced 3D computer vision, and machine learning. Through this diverse collaboration, we will develop innovative analytical strategies to bridge the gap between molecular composition and mesoscale organelle architecture. Ultimately, this research will illuminate the fundamental principles governing the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale, fulfilling the core scientific vision of NCEMS while establishing a new paradigm for data-driven discovery in the molecular and cellular biosciences.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
To decode the emergent biophysics of autophagosome formation at ER-mitochondria contact sites (ERMCS), our working group will address three compelling, interrelated research questions through the synthesis of multi-modal public datasets. These questions are designed to bridge the gap between nanoscale molecular composition and mesoscale structural emergence, directly advancing our understanding of mesoscale phenomena as prioritized by NCEMS.

Question 1: How do localized shifts in lipid composition at ERMCS quantitatively dictate the emergence of complex membrane curvature during early autophagosome biogenesis? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that specific, synergistic alterations in the local concentrations of conical lipids (e.g., phosphatidylethanolamine) and signaling phosphoinositides (e.g., PI3P) act as emergent drivers of membrane deformation. By synthesizing spatial lipidomics data with 3D membrane curvature metrics extracted from electron tomography, we predict that critical thresholds of these lipid species are strictly required to initiate and sustain the severe membrane bending characteristic of the phagophore (the autophagosome precursor).

Question 2: What are the spatio-temporal dynamics of inter-organelle tethering proteins, and how do their structural conformations constrain or facilitate the physical expansion of the autophagosomal membrane? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that ERMCS tethering complexes do not merely act as passive bridges but function as dynamic, mechanical scaffolds that actively guide mesoscale membrane emergence. We anticipate that machine learning-driven synthesis of live-cell imaging and high-resolution ultrastructural data will reveal distinct, temporal conformational states of these tethers that directly correlate with the stages of phagophore expansion, suggesting a coordinated mechanical scaling from protein complex to organelle.

Question 3: Can the integration of multi-omics and 3D ultrastructural data yield a predictive, generative model of mesoscale organelle emergence under varying states of cellular stress? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the biogenesis of autophagosomes follows a conserved, identifiable set of biophysical rules that can be mathematically modeled using deep learning frameworks. By training generative AI models on synthesized datasets spanning varied metabolic conditions (e.g., starvation, oxidative stress), we will uncover a universal "morphological trajectory" of autophagosome emergence. We predict this model will successfully simulate how perturbations in molecular inputs (lipid availability, tether density) non-linearly alter the probability and rate of mesoscale organelle formation.

Addressing these questions requires the integration of diverse datasets, ranging from the Metabolomics Workbench for lipid profiles to EMPIAR for 3D architecture, and the Image Data Resource for temporal dynamics. This transdisciplinary synthesis will resolve long-standing puzzles regarding the biophysical requirements for de novo membrane generation. By shifting the focus from individual molecular players to the holistic, emergent properties of the system, our approach will yield novel insights into how cells orchestrate complex spatial and temporal events to maintain homeostasis. Furthermore, the development of predictive generative models will provide the broader scientific community with innovative analytical strategies to explore other instances of organelle emergence and membrane dynamics, thereby catalyzing future research across the molecular and cellular biosciences.
methods_and_approach:
Our transdisciplinary working group will employ a purely data-driven synthesis approach, strictly utilizing existing, publicly available datasets to decode autophagosome emergence. This project requires no new experimental data generation; instead, it relies on the innovative integration of disparate data types through advanced artificial intelligence and data science methodologies. Our approach is structured into three integrated phases: Data Aggregation and Curation, Multi-Modal AI Integration, and Generative Biophysical Modeling.

Phase 1: Data Aggregation and Curation. We will systematically mine, curate, and standardize high-quality datasets from established public repositories. From the Metabolomics Workbench, we will extract lipidomics data detailing the compositional profiles of cellular fractions enriched for ER, mitochondria, and autophagosomal membranes under varying metabolic states. From the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR), we will aggregate high-resolution 3D electron tomography (ET) datasets capturing the ultrastructure of ERMCS and phagophores. Concurrently, we will source live-cell fluorescence microscopy datasets from the Image Data Resource (IDR) to track the temporal dynamics of established ERMCS tethers and early autophagic markers. A dedicated team of trainees will harmonize these datasets, mapping temporal metadata and standardizing spatial resolutions to create a unified, multi-modal database.

Phase 2: Multi-Modal AI Integration and 3D Computer Vision. To bridge the gap between lipid biochemistry and ultrastructure, we will develop bespoke 3D computer vision algorithms. Using deep learning-based segmentation architectures (e.g., modified 3D U-Nets), we will automate the extraction of precise membrane curvature metrics, tether distances, and contact site surface areas from the EMPIAR ET datasets. We will then employ multi-modal canonical correlation analysis (CCA) and graph neural networks (GNNs) to map the structured lipidomics data onto these extracted 3D architectural features. The GNNs will model the ERMCS as dynamic networks, where nodes represent localized membrane domains and edges represent lipid transfer pathways. This will allow us to statistically correlate specific lipid signatures with distinct stages of mesoscale membrane curvature, effectively synthesizing biochemical and structural data.

Phase 3: Generative Biophysical Modeling. In the final phase, we will leverage generative machine learning models, specifically 3D Generative Adversarial Networks (3D-GANs) and diffusion models, to synthesize the temporal data from IDR with the static, high-resolution structural data from EMPIAR. By training these models on our integrated database, we aim to reconstruct the continuous spatio-temporal dynamics of membrane curvature during autophagosome biogenesis. The generative models will simulate the physical expansion of the phagophore over time, allowing us to predict how targeted molecular perturbations (e.g., altering lipid concentrations in silico) impact the emergent mesoscale architecture.

This ambitious methodological framework requires a diverse synthesis of expertise. Our team integrates lipid biologists to interpret biochemical profiles, cellular ultrastructure specialists to validate 3D segmentations, and computer vision experts to architect the AI pipelines. This cross-disciplinary collaboration, supported by NCEMS, will push the boundaries of current analytical strategies, providing a robust, reproducible pipeline for investigating mesoscale biological emergence strictly through the lens of existing public data.

Scientifically, our primary outcome will be the first comprehensive, AI-driven biophysical model of de novo organelle emergence. This model will reveal the precise quantitative thresholds of lipid composition and mechanical tethering necessary to drive mesoscale membrane deformation. These insights will fundamentally shift the paradigm of autophagy research from qualitative molecular descriptions to predictive, systems-level biophysics, offering new avenues for understanding cellular homeostasis and metabolic stress responses.

title: Emergent Cargo Sorting Dynamics in Extracellular Vesicle Biogenesis
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs), including exosomes and microvesicles, are mesoscale lipid-bound particles that mediate critical intercellular communication. The biogenesis of EVs involves the highly selective sorting of proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids into budding membranes. However, the physical and molecular rules governing how local, nanoscale clustering of specific cargoes drives the emergent macroscopic budding and release of these vesicles remain poorly understood. Deciphering this mesoscale emergence is crucial for understanding how cells package complex molecular information for systemic delivery. Our working group proposes a community-scale data synthesis project to unravel the emergent properties of EV cargo sorting and biogenesis. We will aggregate and synthesize massive, publicly available datasets, including EV proteomics, transcriptomics, and high-resolution imaging data from specialized repositories like Vesiclepedia, EVpedia, and the PRIDE database. By employing advanced graph neural networks and multi-modal deep learning architectures, we will model the dynamic networks of cargo-lipid interactions without generating any new experimental data. This innovative data science approach will identify the universal principles by which local molecular crowding leads to the mesoscale emergence of functional extracellular vesicles. The complexity of EV biogenesis requires the integration of multi-omics data with membrane biophysics, a task that demands the collaborative infrastructure provided by NCEMS. Our transdisciplinary working group unites exosome biologists, computational systems biologists, lipidomics experts, and machine learning engineers. We have prioritized diverse scientific perspectives by recruiting team members from various career stages, geographic locations, and institutional backgrounds. This diversity will foster a dynamic environment capable of generating novel insights into complex cellular communication networks. Training the next generation of researchers is a central focus of our initiative.
