background_and_significance: Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs), exemplified by carboxysomes and metabolosomes, represent a pinnacle of evolutionary engineering. These mesoscale, proteinaceous organelles are ubiquitous across diverse bacterial phyla, serving to encapsulate sensitive or toxic metabolic pathways, thereby enhancing catalytic efficiency and protecting the cellular environment. Composed of thousands of individual shell proteins—hexamers, pentamers, and trimers—that self-assemble around a condensed enzymatic core, BMCs form geometrically precise polyhedral structures. The spontaneous organization of these macromolecular components into a functional, spatially defined compartment is a paradigmatic example of biological emergence at the mesoscale. Despite decades of research yielding high-resolution structural data for individual BMC components, a fundamental mystery remains: what are the predictive rules governing the dynamic self-organization of these disparate parts into functional mesoscale compartments? Currently, our understanding is fragmented. Structural biologists have deposited thousands of protein structures into the Protein Data Bank (PDB), microbiologists have sequenced countless bacterial genomes housed in NCBI, and biochemists have generated extensive interactome data available in PRIDE. However, these datasets remain siloed. The lack of a unified, synthesized perspective limits our ability to predict assembly pathways, understand the evolutionary trajectory of BMCs, or rationally design synthetic microcompartments for bioengineering applications. This project addresses this critical knowledge gap by proposing a massive, community-scale data synthesis initiative. Aligning directly with the U.S. National Science Foundation National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) mandate, we will leverage existing, publicly available data to decode the emergent properties of BMC assembly. By integrating comparative genomics, structural biology, and proteomics, we will move beyond reductionist views of individual proteins to understand the system-level phenomena that dictate mesoscale organelle formation. The significance of this work is twofold. First, it will solve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology regarding how transient, weak protein-protein interactions collectively drive the robust, deterministic assembly of complex biological architectures. Second, it will establish a novel computational paradigm for studying mesoscale emergence, utilizing advanced artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning-based kinetic modeling. This transdisciplinary approach—requiring the combined expertise of structural biologists, microbiologists, computational biophysicists, and machine learning engineers—exceeds the capabilities of any single laboratory. By synthesizing these diverse data streams, we will elucidate how the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale influences higher-order subcellular and cellular metabolic outcomes. Furthermore, this project will serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists, equipping them with the skills necessary to navigate and synthesize vast biological datasets. Ultimately, unlocking the design principles of BMCs will not only deepen our fundamental understanding of microbial ecology and cellular organization but will also catalyze breakthroughs in synthetic biology, enabling the development of custom nanoreactors for sustainable biomanufacturing, carbon fixation, and targeted drug delivery.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: To decode the emergent assembly of Bacterial Microcompartments (BMCs), our working group will focus on three primary research questions, each addressing a critical facet of mesoscale biological emergence. These questions are designed to be answered exclusively through the synthesis and integration of existing, publicly available datasets, utilizing advanced AI and computational modeling. Question 1: What are the universal sequence-to-structure-to-assembly rules that govern the formation of diverse BMC classes across different bacterial phyla? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that despite significant sequence divergence among shell proteins across evolutionary lineages, a conserved set of geometric and thermodynamic interaction motifs dictates the emergent assembly of the polyhedral shell. By synthesizing genomic data (NCBI) with structural databases (PDB) and utilizing AlphaFold-multimer predictions, we expect to identify cryptic, pan-BMC interaction interfaces that drive the initial nucleation and subsequent propagation of the protein shell. We postulate that specific, identifiable amino acid co-evolutionary networks act as thermodynamic switches that guide the system toward a closed polyhedral state rather than an open-ended aggregate. Question 2: How do the kinetic pathways of core enzyme condensation and shell encapsulation coordinate to prevent misassembly and the formation of kinetic traps? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the emergent assembly of BMCs relies on a tightly regulated, hierarchical kinetic pathway where the liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) or condensation of core enzymes acts as a necessary scaffold for the ordered recruitment and multimerization of shell proteins. By integrating proteomics and interactomics data (PRIDE) with deep learning-based kinetic modeling, we predict that the interaction affinities between core enzymes and specific shell proteins are evolutionarily tuned to synchronize condensation and encapsulation. We anticipate that synthesizing these datasets will reveal distinct kinetic checkpoints that prevent the premature closure of empty shells or the failure to encapsulate critical metabolic intermediates. Question 3: Can we predict the emergent mesoscale properties (e.g., shell permeability, stability, and size) of uncharacterized BMCs based solely on their genomic operon architecture and predicted protein interactomes? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the higher-order structural and functional properties of BMCs are encoded not just in individual protein sequences, but in the stoichiometric ratios and interaction networks of the entire BMC operon. By training machine learning models on synthesized multi-omics datasets, we expect to develop a predictive framework that links operon architecture to the physical properties of the assembled organelle. We hypothesize that variations in the ratio of hexameric to pentameric shell proteins, driven by differential expression patterns inferred from transcriptomic data, directly modulate the emergent size and permeability of the microcompartment. Addressing these questions will solve long-standing mysteries regarding how molecular parts dynamically self-organize into functional mesoscale compartments. By answering these questions through a purely synthetic, data-driven approach, our working group will establish new methodological standards for investigating biological emergence. This transdisciplinary inquiry will yield profound insights into the physical principles of self-assembly, providing a comprehensive blueprint of how molecular interactions scale up to produce complex, functional cellular subsystems.
methods_and_approach: Our methodological approach is rooted in the large-scale synthesis of publicly available multi-omics, structural, and biophysical data, strictly adhering to the NCEMS mandate of generating no new experimental data. Our workflow is divided into three interconnected phases: Data Aggregation and Curation, AI-Driven Structural Synthesis, and Deep Learning-Based Kinetic Modeling. Phase 1: Data Aggregation and Curation. We will construct a comprehensive, unified database of BMC components by mining existing repositories. Genomic data and operon architectures will be extracted from the NCBI RefSeq database. High-resolution structural data for individual BMC proteins will be sourced from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Furthermore, we will integrate mass spectrometry-based proteomics and protein-protein interaction (PPI) data from the PRIDE database to establish empirical baselines for protein abundances and interaction networks. This phase requires rigorous data harmonization, utilizing automated pipelines to standardize metadata, resolve nomenclature inconsistencies, and map genomic sequences to structural models. Phase 2: AI-Driven Structural Synthesis. To bridge the gap between individual protein structures and mesoscale assemblies, we will employ advanced AI-driven structural bioinformatics. We will utilize AlphaFold-Multimer and RoseTTAFold to predict the structures of multi-protein complexes and interaction interfaces that have not been experimentally resolved. By running massive, parallelized structure predictions on high-performance computing clusters, we will map the complete interactome of BMC shell and core proteins. We will apply Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to analyze these predicted interaction networks, identifying conserved structural motifs and co-evolutionary patterns across thousands of diverse bacterial species. This will allow us to synthesize a comprehensive atlas of the structural rules governing BMC facet formation and vertex closure. Phase 3: Deep Learning-Based Kinetic Modeling. To understand the dynamic emergence of BMCs, we will transition from static structural models to dynamic kinetic simulations. We will synthesize our structural interactome data with empirical proteomics data to parameterize deep learning-based kinetic models. Utilizing frameworks like reinforcement learning, we will simulate the assembly pathways of BMCs under varying stoichiometric and thermodynamic conditions. These models will explore the massive phase space of possible assembly trajectories, identifying the most probable pathways that lead to functional, closed polyhedra while avoiding kinetic traps. We will specifically model the interplay between core enzyme condensation (using predictive phase-separation algorithms) and shell protein encapsulation. Transdisciplinary Collaboration: This ambitious synthesis requires a diverse working group. Our team integrates structural biologists (to validate AI structural predictions), microbiologists (to provide ecological and evolutionary context), computational biophysicists (to design kinetic models), and machine learning engineers (to optimize deep learning pipelines). We will host bi-monthly virtual synthesis sessions and bi-annual in-person hackathons at the NCEMS facility to foster intensive cross-disciplinary collaboration. By combining these diverse perspectives and utilizing cutting-edge AI to synthesize disparate datasets, our approach will transcend traditional reductionist methodologies, providing a holistic, systems-level understanding of mesoscale biological emergence that is impossible to achieve within a single laboratory setting.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The proposed synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that fundamentally advance our understanding of mesoscale biological emergence. First, we will produce the 'BMC-SynthAtlas', the first comprehensive, publicly accessible database integrating genomic, structural, and interactomic data for thousands of bacterial microcompartments across diverse phyla. This resource will serve as a foundational tool for the global molecular and cellular biology community. Second, we will deliver a validated suite of AI-driven predictive models capable of mapping the assembly pathways and emergent physical properties of BMCs based solely on genomic sequence data. This will solve the long-standing puzzle of how complex, multi-protein organelles self-assemble with high fidelity. The impact of these outcomes extends far beyond basic science. By elucidating the design principles of BMCs, this project will catalyze significant advancements in synthetic biology. Researchers will be able to leverage our predictive rules to engineer bespoke nanoreactors for targeted drug delivery, enhanced carbon fixation, and the sustainable biomanufacturing of high-value chemicals. Furthermore, understanding BMC emergence will provide deeper insights into microbial ecology, particularly how bacteria adapt to specific metabolic niches through subcellular compartmentalization. Crucially, this project will have a profound impact on workforce development. By embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers within a highly collaborative, transdisciplinary network, we will train the next generation of data-savvy scientists. These trainees will gain invaluable, hands-on experience in structural data integration, advanced machine learning, and collaborative coding. Ultimately, by successfully synthesizing disparate public datasets to reveal the mechanisms of mesoscale emergence, this project will strongly validate the NCEMS vision, demonstrating the immense power of community-scale data synthesis to answer the most fundamental and complex questions in the molecular and cellular biosciences.
budget_and_resources: The successful execution of this community-scale synthesis project requires strategic financial and infrastructural support from NCEMS, as the scope vastly exceeds the capacity of any individual laboratory. Our budget is meticulously structured to facilitate transdisciplinary collaboration, support high-performance computing, and train the next-generation workforce. These gatherings are critical for fostering the deep, cross-disciplinary integration required to merge structural biology with machine learning. Additionally, we request funding to support bi-monthly virtual collaboration platforms and collaborative software licenses. A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to workforce development. We request stipend and salary support for two postdoctoral researchers and three graduate students who will execute the core data harmonization and AI modeling tasks. These trainees will be co-mentored by our diverse team of principal investigators, receiving unparalleled training in team science and biological data synthesis. To support our computational needs, we require funding for cloud computing resources and access to high-performance GPU clusters necessary for running massive AlphaFold-Multimer predictions and deep learning kinetic simulations. While we will leverage existing university clusters, dedicated cloud resources are essential for the rapid, parallelized processing of our synthesized datasets. Finally, we allocate funds for open science initiatives, including article processing charges (APCs) for open-access publications, cloud hosting fees for the 'BMC-SynthAtlas' database, and costs associated with maintaining open-source software repositories. This budget directly aligns with the NCEMS mission by investing in collaborative infrastructure, advanced computational resources, and trainee development, ensuring the successful synthesis of publicly available data to decode mesoscale biological emergence.

title: Emergence of Lipid Homeostasis through Peroxisome Biogenesis Networks
abstract: Peroxisomes are highly dynamic mesoscale organelles essential for cellular lipid metabolism and reactive oxygen species detoxification. Unlike mitochondria, peroxisomes can form de novo from the endoplasmic reticulum or multiply by fission, creating a highly adaptable, emergent metabolic network. The precise molecular rules governing how local protein import and membrane lipid sorting dictate the global abundance, size, and metabolic capacity of the peroxisomal compartment remain a major unresolved puzzle in cell biology. Understanding this mesoscale emergence is vital for deciphering how cells maintain lipid homeostasis under varying environmental stresses. Our working group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decipher the emergent properties of peroxisome biogenesis. We will systematically integrate publicly available lipidomics data, high-throughput fluorescence microscopy, and interactomic datasets from the Metabolomics Workbench, the Image Data Resource, and BioGRID. By employing advanced computer vision algorithms and spatial network analysis tools powered by machine learning, we will synthesize these disparate datasets to model the dynamic state of the peroxisome network. This approach utilizes only existing public data to develop innovative analytical strategies that reveal the physical rules of mesoscale metabolic emergence. The sheer scale and complexity of integrating spatial imaging with functional lipidomics require the robust collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS. Our transdisciplinary team brings together cell biologists, lipid biochemists, computational data scientists, and systems biologists. We have intentionally assembled a working group that reflects diverse scientific perspectives, including researchers from various career stages and geographic locations. This diversity is essential for breaking down disciplinary silos and fostering novel insights into complex biological phenomena. Training the next generation of researchers is a fundamental aspect of our proposal. Trainees will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship, developing critical skills in spatial bioinformatics, AI-driven modeling, and collaborative open science. In strict adherence to community policies on reproducible science, all integrated datasets, network models, and analytical code will be published openly via Zenodo and GitHub. By synthesizing structural and functional data, this project will illuminate how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale organelle networks influences higher-order cellular metabolism, perfectly aligning with the overarching goals of NCEMS.
background_and_significance: Peroxisomes represent a quintessential example of mesoscale biological emergence. Unlike mitochondria, which only divide from pre-existing organelles, peroxisomes possess the remarkable ability to form de novo from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) or multiply via fission. This duality allows cells to rapidly and dynamically scale their peroxisomal networks in response to metabolic demands, environmental stresses, and developmental cues. As crucial hubs for cellular lipid metabolism—particularly the beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids—and the detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS), the emergent properties of peroxisome biogenesis are foundational to cellular homeostasis. Despite decades of study, the precise molecular rules governing how local events, such as peroxisomal membrane protein (PMP) import and lipid sorting at the ER, dictate the global abundance, spatial distribution, size, and metabolic capacity of the peroxisomal compartment remain a major unresolved puzzle in molecular and cellular biology. Understanding this mesoscale emergence is vital for deciphering how cells maintain lipid homeostasis under varying environmental stresses and why peroxisome biogenesis disorders are so devastating. Currently, the field is rich with publicly available but isolated datasets. The Metabolomics Workbench houses extensive functional lipidomics data detailing metabolic states across various cell types and conditions. The Image Data Resource (IDR) contains massive repositories of high-throughput fluorescence microscopy images capturing the spatial distribution and morphological dynamics of peroxisomes. BioGRID and other interaction databases catalog the complex protein-protein interactomes underlying peroxisome assembly and fission. However, these datasets have never been systematically integrated to model the emergent properties of the peroxisome network. This fragmentation represents a critical missed opportunity. By synthesizing these disparate data streams, we can bridge the gap between molecular interactions (nanoscale) and cellular metabolic states (microscale), focusing precisely on the mesoscale organelle network. This proposed community-scale synthesis project aligns perfectly with the NCEMS mission. It addresses a fundamental question of emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences by leveraging only existing, publicly available data. It moves beyond the capabilities of a single laboratory by demanding a convergence of expertise in cell biology, lipid biochemistry, computational data science, and systems biology. By integrating spatial imaging with functional lipidomics and interactomic data, we will elucidate the physical and molecular rules of mesoscale metabolic emergence. This synthesis will not only solve long-standing puzzles regarding peroxisome network scaling but will also develop innovative computational strategies for multi-omics and spatial data integration. Furthermore, this project addresses the critical need to understand how mesoscale structures decouple or couple with other cellular networks, such as the ER and mitochondria, during metabolic stress. The dynamic interplay between these organelles forms a meta-network essential for cellular survival. By utilizing advanced machine learning and network analysis, we will map these interactions, providing a holistic view of cellular lipid homeostasis. This synthesis will catalyze a new era of organelle biology, shifting the focus from isolated components to emergent, system-wide properties, thereby fulfilling the core vision of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: Our synthesis project is driven by three overarching research questions that aim to decode the emergent properties of peroxisome biogenesis networks. By integrating multi-modal public datasets, we will test specific hypotheses regarding the mesoscale organization and metabolic capacity of these organelles. Question 1: How do local protein-protein interaction networks at the ER-peroxisome interface dictate the global spatial distribution and morphological heterogeneity of the peroxisome network? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the topology of the peroxisome interactome, specifically the abundance and connectivity of Pex3/Pex19 docking complexes and fission factors (e.g., Fis1/Mff), serves as a predictive blueprint for the emergent spatial architecture of the peroxisome network. We expect that specific interactomic signatures will correlate with distinct morphological states (e.g., hyper-fission vs. de novo biogenesis dominance) captured in high-throughput imaging datasets. By mapping interactomic data from BioGRID onto spatial features extracted from the Image Data Resource (IDR), we anticipate identifying critical network nodes that act as master regulators of mesoscale organelle emergence. Question 2: What are the mathematical rules governing the scaling relationship between peroxisome network morphology (size, number, distribution) and global cellular lipid homeostasis? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that peroxisome networks do not scale linearly with cellular lipid load; rather, they exhibit non-linear, emergent scaling behaviors optimized for specific metabolic stress states. We predict that integrating spatial network metrics (derived from computer vision analysis of microscopy data) with functional lipidomics profiles (from the Metabolomics Workbench) will reveal distinct 'metabolic-morphological attractors.' For instance, conditions characterized by high very-long-chain fatty acid accumulation will correspond to highly specific, emergent spatial configurations of peroxisomes that maximize membrane contact sites with lipid droplets and mitochondria, thereby optimizing metabolic flux. Question 3: Can machine learning models trained on integrated multi-omics and spatial datasets accurately predict the emergent metabolic state of a cell based solely on the structural dynamics of its peroxisome network? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the structural configuration of the mesoscale peroxisome network is fundamentally deterministic of its metabolic output. Therefore, AI-driven spatial network analysis tools can be trained to predict complex lipidomic profiles from fluorescence microscopy images alone. We posit that by synthesizing these diverse datasets, we can develop a robust computational framework that uncovers the hidden physical rules linking organelle architecture to metabolic function. This will solve the long-standing puzzle of how cells dynamically balance de novo biogenesis and fission to maintain lipid homeostasis under varying environmental conditions. Together, these questions challenge the traditional, reductionist view of organelle biology. Instead of studying individual peroxisomal proteins in isolation, our hypotheses focus on the emergent properties that arise when these components interact at the mesoscale. By answering these questions through data synthesis, we will establish a new paradigm for understanding how dynamic, highly adaptable organelle networks self-organize to regulate cellular metabolism, directly addressing the NCEMS call for transdisciplinary research into molecular and cellular emergence.
methods_and_approach: To investigate the emergent properties of peroxisome biogenesis, our working group will employ a purely data-driven, synthesis-based approach, rigorously adhering to the constraint of generating no new experimental data. Our methodology relies on the systematic integration of three distinct, publicly available data streams: functional lipidomics (Metabolomics Workbench), high-throughput fluorescence microscopy (Image Data Resource, IDR), and protein-protein interactions (BioGRID and STRING). Phase 1: Data Curation and Harmonization. The first major hurdle in community-scale synthesis is standardizing disparate datasets. Our computational data scientists will develop automated pipelines to extract and curate lipidomic profiles of wild-type and peroxisome-deficient/stressed cell lines from the Metabolomics Workbench. Concurrently, we will retrieve corresponding high-throughput imaging datasets from the IDR that feature fluorescently tagged peroxisomal markers (e.g., PMP70, GFP-SKL). Interactomic data detailing peroxisome biogenesis factors will be pulled from BioGRID. We will utilize semantic web technologies and biological ontologies to create a unified, harmonized meta-database linking specific cellular conditions across these three modalities. Phase 2: Computer Vision and Spatial Feature Extraction. To quantify the mesoscale emergence of peroxisome networks, we will apply advanced computer vision algorithms to the IDR imaging datasets. Using deep learning-based segmentation models (e.g., Cellpose adapted for organelle detection), we will extract highly granular spatial features for millions of individual cells. These features will include peroxisome count, volume, spatial distribution (e.g., clustering vs. dispersion), and proximity to the nucleus or other organelles. This will transform qualitative image data into quantitative, high-dimensional structural profiles representing the emergent physical state of the network. Phase 3: Spatial Network Analysis and Interactome Mapping. We will construct spatial network models where individual peroxisomes are treated as nodes, and their spatial proximities are treated as edges. By integrating BioGRID interactomic data, we will overlay molecular interaction probabilities onto these spatial networks. This will allow us to model how local protein complex formations (e.g., at the ER) propagate to influence global network topology. We will utilize graph neural networks (GNNs) to identify emergent structural motifs within these spatial interactomes. Phase 4: Multi-Modal Synthesis and Machine Learning. The final phase involves synthesizing the structural profiles (Phase 2 & 3) with the functional lipidomic data (Phase 1). We will employ multi-omics integration frameworks, such as Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (MOFA), to identify latent factors that drive the co-variation between peroxisome network architecture and cellular lipid homeostasis. Furthermore, we will train predictive machine learning models (e.g., Random Forests, Gradient Boosting) to forecast lipidomic states based entirely on spatial network metrics. This transdisciplinary approach requires the collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS. The sheer computational scale of processing IDR images, combined with the biochemical expertise needed to interpret complex lipidomic shifts, is beyond any single laboratory. By leveraging diverse scientific perspectives, we will develop innovative analytical strategies that synthesize existing data into a cohesive model of mesoscale organelle emergence, solving long-standing puzzles in cellular metabolism.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: This community-scale synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes for the molecular and cellular biosciences, directly fulfilling the NCEMS mission. Scientifically, our primary outcome will be the first comprehensive, multi-scale model of peroxisome biogenesis as an emergent network. By elucidating the mathematical rules that link local protein interactions to mesoscale organelle architecture and macroscale cellular lipid homeostasis, we will solve the long-standing puzzle of how cells dynamically scale their metabolic compartments. This will provide unprecedented insights into cellular adaptation, aging, and the etiology of peroxisomal biogenesis disorders. Methodologically, we will deliver a suite of innovative, open-source analytical strategies and computational pipelines. Our novel application of graph neural networks and computer vision to integrate spatial imaging with functional lipidomics will establish a new gold standard for multi-modal data synthesis. These tools will be broadly applicable to other researchers studying emergent phenomena in different organelle systems, thereby amplifying the impact of our work across the biological sciences. Crucially, this project will have a profound impact on workforce development. By bringing together a transdisciplinary team of cell biologists, lipid biochemists, and computational scientists across various career stages and geographic locations, we will break down traditional academic silos. Our working group will serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Graduate students and postdoctoral trainees will receive intensive, cross-disciplinary mentorship, acquiring highly sought-after skills in spatial bioinformatics, AI-driven modeling, and collaborative data synthesis. The resulting predictive models will not only advance basic science but also offer potential new avenues for identifying therapeutic targets in metabolic diseases characterized by lipid dysregulation, ensuring a lasting legacy for this NCEMS-funded initiative. Ultimately, this project will demonstrate the immense untapped potential of publicly available data, proving that community-scale synthesis is a powerful engine for discovery.
budget_and_resources: The proposed synthesis project requires the unique collaborative infrastructure and resources provided by NCEMS, as it significantly exceeds the capabilities and funding scope of any single laboratory. Crucially, in accordance with NCEMS guidelines, no funds are requested for the generation of new experimental data. The primary budget allocation will support the convening of our transdisciplinary working group. We request funding for four in-person, multi-day synthesis meetings to be held at the NCEMS facility over the two-year project period. These intensive collaborative sessions are essential for bridging disciplinary vocabularies, integrating diverse scientific perspectives, and driving the conceptual synthesis of our data. The budget will cover travel, lodging, and per diem expenses for all working group members, ensuring equitable participation across different geographic locations and career stages. A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to training and workforce development. We request stipend and tuition support for two graduate students and partial salary support for one postdoctoral fellow. These trainees will be the primary engines of data integration and will benefit immensely from the cross-disciplinary mentorship network established by the working group. To support the heavy computational demands of processing high-throughput IDR imaging data and training machine learning models, we request resources for secure, high-performance cloud computing infrastructure (e.g., AWS or similar platforms). This includes costs for data storage, GPU-accelerated computing instances, and software licensing necessary for advanced computer vision and spatial network analysis. Finally, funds are requested for open science dissemination, including open-access publication fees and costs associated with hosting our harmonized datasets and Docker containers on public repositories. This budget directly empowers our team to leverage existing public data, develop innovative analytical strategies, and foster the transdisciplinary collaboration required to unravel the emergent properties of mesoscale organelle networks.

title: Decoding the Emergent Membrane Scission Dynamics of the ESCRT Machinery
abstract: The Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport (ESCRT) machinery is a highly conserved set of proteins that drive membrane remodeling and scission away from the cytoplasm. This machinery functions in diverse cellular processes, including multivesicular body biogenesis, viral budding, and cytokinesis. The sequential assembly of ESCRT components into mesoscale helical filaments that constrict and cleave membranes represents a profound example of biophysical emergence. However, the universal rules governing how local, nanoscale protein-lipid interactions translate into the generation of massive, mesoscale mechanical forces for membrane scission remain highly contested. Our working group proposes a transdisciplinary synthesis project to decode the emergent biophysics of ESCRT-mediated membrane scission. We will aggregate and synthesize massive, publicly available datasets, including cryo-electron microscopy structures, single-molecule biophysics data, and cellular imaging from repositories such as the Electron Microscopy Data Bank and the Image Data Resource. By utilizing advanced molecular dynamics simulations guided by machine learning and topological data analysis, we will synthesize these multi-modal datasets to reconstruct the spatio-temporal dynamics of membrane constriction. This project relies entirely on existing public data, utilizing AI to extract novel insights into how local molecular interactions dictate the emergence of complex mesoscale forces. The integration of structural biophysics with cellular imaging requires a collaborative effort that far exceeds the capabilities of a single laboratory, necessitating the support of NCEMS. We have assembled a diverse team of structural biologists, biophysicists, computer vision experts, and cellular ultrastructure specialists. Our working group is intentionally curated to include diverse scientific perspectives, bridging researchers from different institutional tiers and geographic locations. This collaborative environment will drive the innovative analytical strategies needed to solve this long-standing biological mystery. Furthermore, this project serves as a vital training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdocs will gain hands-on experience in structural data integration, advanced image analysis, and open science practices. We are fully committed to making all synthesized datasets, AI models, and analytical pipelines freely available to the scientific community through open-source platforms like GitHub. By illuminating the relationship between protein assembly and membrane scission, this synthesis project will directly advance the NCEMS mission to understand the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale.
background_and_significance: The Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport (ESCRT) machinery is a highly conserved biological apparatus responsible for driving topologically unique membrane remodeling and scission events away from the cytoplasm. This machinery is indispensable for a myriad of critical cellular processes, including multivesicular body (MVB) biogenesis, the budding of enveloped viruses such as HIV-1, and the final abscission step of cytokinesis. The sequential recruitment and assembly of ESCRT-I, -II, and -III complexes, culminating in the polymerization of ESCRT-III into mesoscale helical filaments, represents a profound and elegant example of biophysical emergence. At the nanoscale, individual ESCRT-III monomers interact with specific lipid geometries; however, it is the collective, higher-order assembly and subsequent ATP-dependent remodeling by the AAA+ ATPase Vps4 that generates the massive, mesoscale mechanical forces required to constrict and cleave the membrane neck. Despite decades of intense study, the universal rules governing this emergent translation of local protein-lipid interactions into mesoscale force generation remain highly contested. Current models debate whether scission is driven by a buckling spring mechanism, a sliding filament mechanism, or a dome-like structural collapse. This fundamental knowledge gap persists largely because traditional, single-laboratory experimental approaches are limited in their spatial and temporal resolution, often capturing only static snapshots or isolated in vitro phenomena. The complexity of this mesoscale phenomenon necessitates a community-scale synthesis approach, perfectly aligned with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). Over the past decade, an unprecedented volume of structural and cellular data has been deposited into public repositories. High-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of ESCRT filaments are available in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB), while dynamic, single-molecule biophysics trajectories and live-cell imaging datasets reside in repositories such as the Image Data Resource (IDR) and BioImage Archive. However, these multi-modal datasets remain siloed. Our proposed synthesis project will aggregate, integrate, and synthesize these massive, publicly available datasets to decode the emergent biophysics of ESCRT-mediated membrane scission. By leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) and data science, our transdisciplinary working group will bridge the gap between structural biophysics and cellular ultrastructure. This project does not seek to generate new experimental data; rather, it harnesses the untapped potential of existing data to solve a long-standing puzzle in the molecular and cellular sciences. The synthesis of such disparate data types—ranging from sub-nanometer structural coordinates to micron-scale cellular phenotypes—far exceeds the computational and analytical capabilities of any single research group. It requires the convergence of structural biologists, biophysicists, computer vision experts, and cellular ultrastructure specialists. By illuminating the relationship between ESCRT protein assembly and membrane scission, this project will directly advance the NCEMS vision of understanding the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale, ultimately providing a predictive framework for emergent mechanobiology that can be applied to other complex macromolecular machines.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
To unravel the emergent biophysics of the ESCRT machinery, our working group has formulated a series of interconnected research questions and hypotheses that can only be addressed through the systematic synthesis of existing multi-modal data. Our inquiry is guided by the overarching premise that the mesoscale mechanical forces required for membrane scission are not inherent to any single ESCRT component, but rather emerge dynamically from the spatiotemporal integration of nanoscale protein-protein and protein-lipid interactions.

Question 1: What are the universal geometric and thermodynamic rules governing the transition of ESCRT-III filaments from flat spirals to 3D helical funnels across different cellular contexts?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that a conserved, sequence-independent topological mechanism drives ESCRT-III filament buckling. By synthesizing static cryo-EM structures with dynamic single-molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET) data, we predict that the emergence of mesoscale buckling is dictated by a critical threshold of membrane curvature and specific electrostatic lipid interactions, which will be universally identifiable across MVB biogenesis, viral budding, and cytokinesis datasets.

Question 2: How does the AAA+ ATPase Vps4 coordinate the continuous turnover of ESCRT-III subunits to generate the mechanical work required for membrane constriction and ultimate scission?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that Vps4 does not act merely as a disassembly factor, but functions as an active mechanochemical motor that drives a "sliding filament" mechanism within the ESCRT-III polymer. By integrating existing high-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM) datasets with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we expect to reveal that Vps4-mediated extraction of specific ESCRT-III subunits induces a global, emergent conformational change in the filament network, constricting the membrane neck to the critical hemifission radius.

Question 3: In what ways do local membrane lipid compositions (e.g., PI(3)P, cholesterol, and ceramide) modulate the emergent mechanical properties of the ESCRT-III/Vps4 complex?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that local lipid sorting acts as an allosteric regulator of mesoscale ESCRT assembly. By synthesizing lipidomics data with cellular imaging and structural models, we anticipate finding that specific lipid microdomains lower the activation energy barrier for filament buckling, thereby dictating the spatial precision and timing of scission.

Question 4: Can machine learning models predict the emergent scission efficiency of novel or mutant ESCRT assemblies based solely on their nanoscale structural parameters?
Hypothesis 4: We hypothesize that artificial intelligence, specifically graph neural networks (GNNs) trained on synthesized structural and phenotypic data, can accurately predict mesoscale scission outcomes. We expect that topological data analysis of the ESCRT-membrane interface will identify a minimal set of geometric features that define the "scission-competent" state.

Addressing these questions perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mandate to tackle compelling scientific questions using publicly available data. By testing these hypotheses through data synthesis, we will resolve long-standing debates regarding the ESCRT mechanism. Furthermore, answering these questions requires the cross-disciplinary expertise of our team, combining structural biology, computational biophysics, and AI, to acquire novel, deeper, and broader insights into how complex mesoscale forces emerge in cellular biology.
methods_and_approach:
Our transdisciplinary working group will employ a purely computational, data-driven synthesis approach to decode ESCRT-mediated membrane scission. In strict adherence to NCEMS guidelines, this project will not generate any new experimental data. Instead, we will aggregate, harmonize, and synthesize massive, publicly available datasets from diverse repositories, utilizing advanced artificial intelligence (AI) and computational biophysics to extract novel mesoscale insights.

Data Aggregation and Harmonization: We will systematically mine the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) for all available high-resolution structures of ESCRT-III and Vps4 complexes. Concurrently, we will extract dynamic single-molecule biophysics data (smFRET, HS-AFM) from the BioImage Archive and cellular imaging datasets (live-cell fluorescence, electron tomography) from the Image Data Resource (IDR). Because these datasets exist in disparate formats and spatiotemporal scales, our first critical step is data harmonization. We will develop automated, open-source Python pipelines to standardize coordinate frames, normalize intensity values, and annotate metadata using standardized biological ontologies.

AI-Guided Structural Synthesis and Topological Data Analysis (TDA): To bridge the gap between static nanoscale structures and dynamic mesoscale assemblies, we will employ Topological Data Analysis (TDA). TDA will allow us to extract shape-based, scale-invariant features from the aggregated cryo-EM and electron tomography datasets. We will train Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on these topological features to predict intermediate conformational states of the ESCRT-III filament that have not been experimentally captured. The GNNs will map the trajectory of filament buckling, identifying the structural transition states that define the emergence of mechanical force.

Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics (CG-MD) Simulations: To test our hypotheses regarding force generation and lipid interactions, we will integrate our AI-predicted intermediate structures into highly scalable Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics (CG-MD) simulations using the Martini 3 force field. By parameterizing these simulations with aggregated lipidomics data, we will model the mesoscale dynamics of the entire ESCRT-membrane scission neck (comprising millions of particles) over microsecond timescales. This will allow us to calculate the mechanical work generated by Vps4-mediated subunit turnover and observe the emergent membrane constriction forces in silico.

Cross-Disciplinary Collaborative Workflow: The complexity of synthesizing structural biophysics, computer vision, and cellular ultrastructure requires a robust collaborative framework. Our working group will utilize cloud-based computational infrastructure to enable real-time, multi-institutional data sharing and analysis. Bi-weekly virtual synthesis meetings and bi-annual in-person hackathons will ensure continuous cross-pollination of ideas between our structural biologists, biophysicists, and AI experts.

Training the Data-Savvy Workforce: This project is designed as a premier training ground. Graduate students and postdocs will be co-mentored by PIs from different disciplines, gaining hands-on expertise in multi-modal data integration, machine learning, and advanced MD simulations. Trainees will lead the development of the data harmonization pipelines and AI models, equipping them with highly sought-after skills in the modern, data-driven biological sciences. This comprehensive approach ensures that we not only solve a fundamental biological puzzle but also build the collaborative and analytical infrastructure necessary for future mesoscale synthesis research.

title: Synthesizing the Emergent Architecture of the Cellular Glycocalyx Meshwork
abstract: The glycocalyx is a dense, mesoscale meshwork of glycoproteins and glycolipids that coats the surface of nearly all eukaryotic cells. This complex sugar barrier mediates critical cellular outcomes, including immune recognition, mechanotransduction, and pathogen entry. Despite its importance, the glycocalyx remains one of the least understood cellular structures due to its immense structural complexity. How the nanoscale biosynthesis of diverse glycan chains scales up to produce the emergent, biophysical properties of this mesoscale meshwork is a major unsolved puzzle in glycobiology. Our working group proposes a community-scale data synthesis project to unravel the emergent properties of glycocalyx architecture. We will integrate publicly available glycomics, spatial transcriptomics, and super-resolution imaging datasets from specialized repositories like GlyTouCan, the Gene Expression Omnibus, and the Image Data Resource. By employing advanced graph neural networks and spatio-temporal deep learning architectures, we will model the dynamic network of glycan interactions without generating any new experimental data. This innovative data science approach will identify the universal principles by which local sugar biosynthesis leads to the mesoscale emergence of functional cellular barriers. The complexity of glycobiology requires the integration of chemical biology with multi-omics data, a task that demands the collaborative infrastructure provided by NCEMS. Our transdisciplinary working group unites glycobiologists, computational biophysicists, multi-omics experts, and machine learning engineers. We have prioritized diverse scientific perspectives by recruiting team members from various career stages, geographic locations, and institutional backgrounds. This diversity will foster a dynamic environment capable of generating novel insights into complex cellular surface networks. Training the next generation of researchers is a central focus of our initiative. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive rigorous cross-training in big data integration, AI-driven pattern recognition, and collaborative open science workflows. We commit to making all analytical pipelines, synthesized datasets, and predictive models publicly accessible via Zenodo and GitHub, ensuring full reproducibility. By synthesizing existing public data, this project will answer fundamental questions about how cells orchestrate the unexpected appearance of mesoscale surface barriers, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS mission to catalyze discoveries in cellular emergence.
background_and_significance:
The cellular glycocalyx represents one of the most compelling and enigmatic examples of mesoscale emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences. Coating the surface of nearly all eukaryotic cells, this dense meshwork of glycoproteins, glycolipids, and proteoglycans serves as the primary interface between the cell and its environment. It mediates highly critical cellular outcomes, including immune system recognition, cellular mechanotransduction, and the entry of viral and bacterial pathogens. Despite its undeniable biological significance, the glycocalyx remains one of the least understood cellular structures. This knowledge gap is primarily driven by the immense structural complexity and dynamic nature of glycan networks, which cannot be fully captured by traditional, single-discipline experimental approaches. The fundamental mystery lies in emergence: how does the nanoscale biosynthesis of diverse, localized glycan chains scale up to produce the highly organized, biophysical properties of a mesoscale meshwork? 

Currently, the molecular and cellular sciences are rich with isolated datasets that capture fragments of this process. Repositories such as GlyTouCan house vast amounts of structural glycomics data; the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) contains extensive spatial transcriptomic profiles of glycosyltransferases and related enzymes; and the Image Data Resource (IDR) archives high-fidelity super-resolution imaging of cellular surfaces. However, these datasets exist in silos. The lack of integration across scales—from the molecular sequence of sugars to the spatial organization of the cellular surface—has prevented a holistic understanding of glycocalyx architecture. 

This proposal directly addresses the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) call by executing a community-scale data synthesis project that requires no new experimental data generation. We propose to synthesize these disparate, publicly available datasets to uncover the rules governing the mesoscale emergence of the glycocalyx. This synthesis is beyond the capabilities of any single research laboratory; it requires a transdisciplinary approach that merges chemical biology, computational biophysics, and advanced artificial intelligence. By leveraging this wealth of untapped data, our working group will solve a long-standing puzzle in glycobiology: the translation of molecular-level sugar modifications into cellular-level barrier functions. 

Furthermore, this project aligns seamlessly with the NCEMS vision of understanding the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at different scales of composition and space. The mesoscale—the critical nexus between individual biomolecules and whole organelles—is precisely where the glycocalyx operates. By integrating AI and data science with molecular biology, we will catalyze multidisciplinary scientific discovery, stimulate novel questions regarding cellular surface dynamics, and recruit and train a new generation of data-savvy scientists. Ultimately, this research will transform our understanding of cellular barriers, providing foundational insights that will impact fields ranging from developmental biology to immunology and infectious disease, all while adhering strictly to the highest standards of open and reproducible science.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our synthesis project is driven by three primary research questions that seek to decode the emergent properties of the glycocalyx. These questions are designed to bridge the gap between nanoscale molecular data and mesoscale cellular phenomena, relying entirely on the computational synthesis of existing public datasets. 

Question 1: How do nanoscale glycan linkages and chemical modifications scale to dictate the emergent mesoscale properties (e.g., thickness, density, and charge) of the glycocalyx? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that specific, identifiable combinatorial patterns of nanoscale glycan structures act as 'molecular blueprints' that predictably generate distinct mesoscale biophysical states. Rather than a random assortment of sugars, the glycocalyx architecture is governed by emergent topological rules where localized clustering of specific glycoproteins (e.g., heavily sialylated mucins) disproportionately drives the macroscopic rigidity and porosity of the cellular barrier. 

Question 2: What are the universal emergent topological motifs of the glycocalyx meshwork across diverse eukaryotic cell types, and how do these motifs reorganize during pathogenic transitions? 
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that emergent topological motifs within the glycocalyx are evolutionarily conserved across diverse cell types to maintain baseline barrier integrity, but undergo predictable, systemic reorganization during disease states (such as viral infection or malignant transformation). By synthesizing super-resolution imaging with glycomic profiles, we expect to identify 'glyco-architectural signatures'—mesoscale structural shifts that correlate with cellular vulnerability or resilience to external pathogens. 

Question 3: How can spatial transcriptomic profiles of the cellular biosynthetic machinery predict the emergent biophysical properties of the surface barrier? 
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the spatial co-expression networks of glycosyltransferases and glycosidases within the Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum directly correlate with the localized emergent architecture of the glycocalyx. We predict that by mapping transcriptomic data to surface imaging data, we can build a predictive AI model that accurately forecasts the mesoscale physical properties of the glycocalyx based solely on the transcriptional state of the cell. 

These research questions are highly novel because they shift the focus of glycobiology from the mere cataloging of sugar structures to the understanding of systemic, emergent physical properties. By addressing these questions, our working group will solve the long-standing puzzle of how cells dynamically tune their surface barriers in response to environmental cues. The hypotheses challenge the traditional, linear view of glycan biosynthesis, proposing instead a complex systems perspective where non-linear interactions between diverse molecules give rise to entirely new physical properties at the mesoscale. Testing these hypotheses requires the integration of multi-modal omics and imaging data, demanding a sophisticated data science approach that perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission to foster deep, transdisciplinary insights into molecular and cellular emergence.
methods_and_approach:
To answer our research questions without generating new experimental data, our working group will employ a robust, multi-phased computational methodology centered on data harmonization, advanced machine learning, and collaborative synthesis. 

Phase 1: Multi-Modal Data Acquisition and Harmonization 
We will systematically mine publicly available repositories to construct a unified meta-database. Structural glycomics data will be extracted from GlyTouCan and UniCarbKB. Spatial transcriptomics targeting the cellular biosynthetic machinery will be sourced from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Super-resolution microscopy and cryo-electron tomography images of cellular surfaces will be aggregated from the Image Data Resource (IDR) and the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR). Our multi-omics experts will develop standardized pipelines to harmonize these disparate data types, mapping transcriptomic identifiers to glycan structures and correlating these with morphological features extracted from imaging datasets. 

Phase 2: AI-Driven Feature Extraction and Synthesis 
To bridge the molecular and mesoscale levels, our machine learning engineers will deploy spatio-temporal deep learning architectures. We will utilize convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to extract quantitative, mesoscale topological features (e.g., mesh density, filament length, spatial clustering) from the super-resolution imaging data. Concurrently, we will implement Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to model the nanoscale interactions between diverse glycan chains. GNNs are uniquely suited for this task, as they can represent glycans as nodes and their chemical linkages as edges, capturing the complex, non-linear topology of the sugar networks. 

Phase 3: Modeling Mesoscale Emergence 
The core synthesis will involve fusing the GNN-derived molecular models with the CNN-derived mesoscale imaging features. We will train multi-modal transformer models to identify correlations between the transcriptomic expression of glyco-enzymes, the predicted nanoscale glycan structures, and the observed mesoscale architecture of the glycocalyx. This AI-driven approach will allow us to reverse-engineer the universal principles of glycocalyx emergence, testing our hypotheses by predicting macroscopic barrier properties based on localized molecular inputs. 

Phase 4: Working Group Dynamics and Training 
This project is fundamentally beyond the scope of a single lab. Our transdisciplinary working group—comprising glycobiologists, computational biophysicists, and AI researchers—will meet bi-weekly virtually and convene for three intensive, in-person synthesis hackathons over the grant period. We have strategically recruited members from diverse geographic locations, career stages, and institutional research levels to ensure a rich variety of scientific perspectives. A critical component of our approach is the cross-training of the future data-savvy workforce. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will be embedded in all phases of the project. Through structured mentorship and hands-on workshops during our hackathons, trainees with biological backgrounds will learn advanced AI and data integration techniques, while computational trainees will gain deep domain expertise in molecular and cellular biophysics. This methodology ensures scientific rigor while fulfilling the NCEMS mandate for collaborative, transdisciplinary synthesis.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This community-scale synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission to decode emergent phenomena in the molecular and cellular biosciences. First, by identifying the universal rules that govern how nanoscale glycan biosynthesis scales into mesoscale barrier properties, we will solve a major, long-standing puzzle in glycobiology. This will fundamentally shift the paradigm from viewing the glycocalyx as a static coating to understanding it as a dynamic, emergent system. 

Second, the project will yield highly innovative analytical strategies. The multi-modal AI architectures—specifically the integration of Graph Neural Networks with spatio-temporal deep learning to bridge omics and imaging data—will establish a new methodological gold standard for mesoscale biology. These computational pipelines will be adaptable to other complex cellular networks, amplifying the project's impact far beyond glycobiology. 

Third, the insights generated will have profound implications for human health. Understanding the emergent architecture of the glycocalyx will uncover new mechanisms of viral entry, cancer metastasis, and immune evasion, providing a foundational biophysical context for future therapeutic interventions. 

Finally, the impact on workforce development will be substantial. By bringing together a diverse, transdisciplinary working group, we will tap into diverse new talent across geographic and institutional boundaries. Our rigorous cross-training program will produce a cohort of graduate students and postdoctoral fellows uniquely equipped to navigate the intersection of big data, artificial intelligence, and cellular biology. These newly trained, data-savvy scientists will be perfectly positioned to lead the next generation of synthesis research, ensuring a lasting legacy of multidisciplinary collaboration and innovation in the molecular sciences.

The proposed synthesis project requires NCEMS support because it necessitates a collaborative, computational infrastructure and dedicated personnel that far exceed the resources of any single laboratory. The budget is specifically designed to facilitate transdisciplinary integration, large-scale data synthesis, and workforce training, with absolutely no funds allocated for experimental data generation. 

Personnel costs represent the core of our budget. We request stipend and tuition support for two graduate students and salary for two postdoctoral fellows. These trainees are the engine of the synthesis project and the focus of our workforce development goals. They will conduct the day-to-day data harmonization and machine learning tasks while receiving invaluable cross-disciplinary training. 

Travel and meeting logistics are critical for our transdisciplinary working group. We request funds to support three intensive, in-person 'synthesis hackathons' over the funding period. These funds will cover travel, lodging, and hosting expenses for our diverse team of researchers, ensuring that members from various geographic locations and institutional backgrounds can collaborate effectively, build trust, and integrate their distinct expertise. 

Cloud computing and data storage resources are essential for handling the massive volume of multi-omics and super-resolution imaging data. We request funding for cloud infrastructure (e.g., AWS or Azure) to train our computationally intensive Graph Neural Networks and deep learning models, as well as to host our synthesized meta-databases for public access. 

Finally, we have allocated funds for Open Science and Publication fees to ensure that all manuscripts are published in high-impact, open-access journals. This budget perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission, providing the critical resources needed to catalyze a multidisciplinary team, synthesize vast public datasets, and train the next generation of data-savvy scientists.

title: Emergent Contractility from Myosin II Thick Filament Assembly in Non-Muscle Cells
abstract: In non-muscle cells, the dynamic assembly of non-muscle myosin II into mesoscale bipolar thick filaments is essential for generating the contractile forces that drive cell migration, adhesion, and cytokinesis. The transition from individual, auto-inhibited myosin motors to highly ordered, force-generating mesoscale ensembles represents a classic example of biophysical emergence. However, the precise spatio-temporal rules governing how localized phosphorylation events and actin network architecture coordinate to drive this large-scale filament assembly remain a highly debated puzzle in mechanobiology. Understanding this emergence is vital for deciphering how cells dynamically alter their shape and exert physical force. Our working group proposes a comprehensive data synthesis project to decode the emergent properties of myosin filament assembly. We will integrate diverse, publicly available datasets, including live-cell super-resolution microscopy, biophysical force measurements, and phosphoproteomics from repositories such as the Cell Image Library, PRIDE, and specific mechanobiology databases. By utilizing advanced spatio-temporal data mining and unsupervised machine learning algorithms, we will synthesize these distinct datasets to identify the universal principles of mesoscale contractility. This approach relies entirely on existing data, leveraging AI to uncover the hidden rules of how local molecular motors scale up to produce global cellular forces. The multifaceted nature of cellular biomechanics requires a collaborative partnership that transcends individual lab capabilities, making NCEMS support essential. We will convene a transdisciplinary team of mechanobiologists, structural biophysicists, computational modelers, and data scientists. Our working group is structured to promote diverse scientific perspectives, incorporating researchers from various geographic locations, institutional types, and career stages. This inclusive environment will stimulate the cross-disciplinary innovation necessary to solve this critical biological mystery. Training the future data-savvy workforce is a core component of our mission. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in a collaborative network, gaining expertise in multi-modal data integration, AI-driven network analysis, and open science protocols. We commit to making all findings, integrated databases, and analytical workflows publicly accessible via community-standard repositories like GitHub. By synthesizing these vast public datasets, our project will reveal how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale contractile structures influences higher-order cellular morphology, directly supporting the NCEMS vision of understanding biological emergence.
background_and_significance: Non-muscle myosin II (NMII) is a fundamental molecular motor responsible for generating contractile forces in non-muscle cells, driving essential processes such as cell migration, adhesion, tissue morphogenesis, and cytokinesis. At the core of these dynamic cellular behaviors lies a classic, yet poorly understood, example of biophysical emergence: the transition of individual, auto-inhibited NMII molecules into highly ordered, force-generating mesoscale ensembles known as bipolar thick filaments. While the structural biology of the myosin motor domain is well characterized at the nanoscale, and the macroscopic consequences of cellular contractility are observable at the phenotypic level, the mesoscale dynamics bridging these scales remain a profound mystery. Specifically, the spatio-temporal rules governing how localized phosphorylation events, biochemical signaling cascades, and the physical architecture of the surrounding actin network coordinate to drive large-scale filament assembly are highly debated. Understanding this emergence is critical, as it dictates how cells dynamically alter their morphology and exert physical force on their microenvironment. Currently, the field of mechanobiology is rich with disparate datasets spanning multiple scales. High-throughput phosphoproteomics capture the biochemical states of regulatory light chains; live-cell super-resolution microscopy provides spatial snapshots of filament assembly; and traction force microscopy (TFM) quantifies the resulting macroscopic mechanical outputs. However, these data are highly siloed. The complexity of mesoscale phenomena requires a paradigm shift from isolated, single-lab experimental approaches to community-scale synthesis. This project directly addresses the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) mission by leveraging existing, publicly available data to solve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences. By synthesizing proteomics, advanced imaging, and biophysical force measurements, we aim to uncover the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties, specifically, how local molecular interactions scale up to produce global cellular forces. The mesoscale, defined here as the scale between individual myosin biomolecules and higher-order subcellular contractile networks, is exactly where this emergent property manifests. Our transdisciplinary working group will bridge the gap between structural biophysics, cell biology, and computational data science. We will utilize advanced AI and unsupervised machine learning to mine repositories such as the Cell Image Library, PRIDE, and mechanobiology-specific databases. This synthesis will not generate new experimental data but will extract unprecedented value from existing resources, answering fundamental questions about the rules of emergent contractility. The significance of this work extends beyond basic cell biology; it provides a foundational understanding of mechanotransduction that is applicable to cancer metastasis, developmental disorders, and cardiovascular diseases. By mapping the mesoscale emergence of NMII filaments, this project will catalyze novel research strategies, establish new analytical methodologies for multi-modal data integration, and set a gold standard for transdisciplinary synthesis in the molecular and cellular sciences.
research_questions_and_hypotheses: To decode the emergent properties of non-muscle myosin II (NMII) thick filament assembly, our working group will address three compelling, interconnected scientific questions. These questions are specifically designed to be answered through the synthesis of existing, multi-modal datasets, moving beyond the capabilities of any single experimental approach to reveal the hidden rules of mesoscale contractility. Question 1: What are the spatio-temporal thresholds of NMII regulatory light chain (RLC) phosphorylation required to trigger the emergent assembly of mesoscale bipolar thick filaments? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that NMII filament assembly is not a linear response to kinase activity but rather a highly cooperative, threshold-driven emergent phenomenon. By synthesizing phosphoproteomic time-series data from the PRIDE database with live-cell super-resolution imaging from the Cell Image Library, we predict the identification of specific, localized phosphorylation density thresholds that serve as nucleation points. We expect machine learning models to reveal that cooperative phosphorylation kinetics, previously masked in bulk assays, dictate the sudden appearance of ordered mesoscale ensembles. Question 2: How does the pre-existing topological architecture of the actin cytoskeleton constrain or facilitate the spatial organization and scaling of NMII thick filaments? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the actin network acts as a physical template that dictates the emergent scaling of NMII filaments, where specific actin geometries (e.g., anti-parallel bundles versus branched networks) lower the energetic barrier for myosin ensemble formation. By integrating super-resolution structural datasets with biophysical modeling, we anticipate uncovering a set of geometric rules governing how local actin topologies guide the spatial distribution and maximum size of NMII bipolar filaments. We predict that AI-driven spatial point pattern analysis of synthesized imaging data will demonstrate that mesoscale filament emergence is strictly dependent on cross-linker-mediated actin architecture. Question 3: What are the quantitative transfer functions that map the structural parameters of mesoscale NMII assemblies to the macroscopic generation of cellular traction forces? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the macroscopic traction forces exerted by a cell are not simply the sum of individual motor forces, but are an emergent property dictated by the higher-order spatial arrangement and connectivity of the mesoscale NMII filaments. By coupling structural imaging datasets with corresponding Traction Force Microscopy (TFM) data available in mechanobiology repositories, we aim to train deep learning algorithms to predict cellular force outputs solely from the topological features of the NMII mesoscale network. We expect to find that specific mesoscale network configurations exhibit non-linear force amplification, representing a true emergent property of the cellular system. These questions directly align with the NCEMS objective to understand the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties across scales of space, time, and motion. By framing our hypotheses around the integration of distinct data types, we ensure that our synthesis project will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how local molecular inputs are translated into global cellular mechanics.
methods_and_approach: Our approach is strictly computational and synthesis-driven, adhering to the NCEMS mandate of utilizing only existing, publicly available data without generating new experimental results. The complexity of integrating multi-modal datasets spanning biochemistry, structure, and mechanics necessitates a transdisciplinary working group comprising mechanobiologists, structural biophysicists, computational modelers, and data scientists. Our methodology is divided into three integrated phases: Data Aggregation and Curation, AI-Driven Spatio-Temporal Synthesis, and Predictive Mechanistic Modeling. Phase 1: Data Aggregation, Standardization, and Curation. We will systematically mine disparate public repositories to build a unified, multi-scale database of NMII dynamics. Phosphoproteomic data detailing NMII regulatory light chain states will be sourced from the PRIDE archive and PeptideAtlas. High-resolution spatial data, including live-cell super-resolution microscopy and electron microscopy of actin-myosin networks, will be extracted from the Cell Image Library, BioImage Archive, and EMPIAR. Cellular force measurements, specifically Traction Force Microscopy (TFM) maps, will be gathered from specialized mechanobiology databases and published supplementary datasets. A significant methodological innovation of our working group will be the development of a standardized metadata ontology to align these diverse data types across common temporal and spatial coordinates, enabling cross-modal synthesis. Phase 2: AI-Driven Spatio-Temporal Synthesis. To uncover the rules of mesoscale emergence, we will employ advanced data science and artificial intelligence techniques. We will utilize unsupervised machine learning, specifically spatial clustering algorithms and topological data analysis (TDA), to identify hidden structural patterns in super-resolution imaging data. TDA is particularly suited for detecting emergent mesoscale structures, such as filament nodes and bundles, that are not apparent at the single-molecule level. To link phosphorylation kinetics with structural assembly, we will develop spatio-temporal data mining pipelines that map temporal proteomic profiles onto spatial assembly rates using dynamic time warping and cross-correlation analyses. This will allow us to test our hypothesis regarding cooperative phosphorylation thresholds driving emergent assembly. Phase 3: Predictive Mechanistic Modeling. To bridge the gap between mesoscale structure and macroscopic force, we will implement deep learning frameworks. We will train Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on paired structural and mechanical datasets. The GNNs will represent the actin-myosin network as a mathematical graph, where nodes are NMII filaments and edges are actin cross-links. By training these models to predict traction forces based on network topology, we will extract the quantitative transfer functions that define emergent contractility. To ensure biological interpretability, we will employ Explainable AI (XAI) techniques to identify which specific mesoscale architectural features most significantly contribute to force generation. Throughout this process, our working group will utilize collaborative cloud computing environments to facilitate seamless data sharing and model development among our geographically diverse team members, developing innovative analytical strategies broadly applicable to the wider biosciences community.
expected_outcomes_and_impact: The proposed synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission to understand biological emergence at the mesoscale. First, we will deliver a paradigm-shifting mechanistic understanding of non-muscle myosin II (NMII) thick filament assembly. By identifying the precise spatio-temporal phosphorylation thresholds and actin topological constraints that govern this process, we will solve a long-standing puzzle in mechanobiology, explaining how local molecular interactions scale up to produce global cellular forces. Second, we will produce a highly curated, integrated, and standardized multi-modal database linking phosphoproteomics, super-resolution microscopy, and cellular biomechanics. This unprecedented resource will overcome current data silos, providing the broader scientific community with a powerful tool for future mechanobiological research. Third, we will develop and validate novel, open-source AI and machine learning pipelines specifically designed for cross-modal data synthesis and the detection of emergent topological features in biological networks. These analytical strategies will be highly transferable, enabling researchers to investigate mesoscale emergence in other complex macromolecular systems. Beyond scientific discovery, this project will have a profound impact on workforce development. By embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in a highly collaborative, geographically diverse, and transdisciplinary working group, we will train the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Trainees will gain invaluable, hands-on experience in cloud computing, multi-modal data integration, advanced AI techniques, and open science practices. Ultimately, by decoding the emergent properties of cellular contractility, our findings will provide crucial insights into the physical mechanisms underlying cell migration and tissue morphogenesis, offering new theoretical frameworks that could eventually inform therapeutic strategies for diseases characterized by aberrant mechanotransduction, such as cancer metastasis and fibrotic disorders.

Crucially, the budget includes robust support for workforce training. We are requesting dedicated funding for graduate student and postdoctoral fellowships.
