title: The Mesoscale Architecture of Mitochondrial Contact Sites: Integrating Structural, Proteomic, and Functional Data to Understand Emergent Organelle Communication
abstract:
Membrane contact sites between mitochondria and other organelles represent critical hubs for cellular homeostasis, yet how their mesoscale architecture enables emergent functions in calcium signaling, lipid transfer, and metabolic regulation remains mysterious. This proposal unites structural biologists, mitochondrial biologists, lipidomics experts, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode the organizational principles of mitochondrial contact sites and their functional consequences.

Mitochondria-ER contact sites (MERCs), mitochondria-lysosome contacts, and mitochondria-lipid droplet interfaces each possess distinct protein compositions and functions, but comprehensive understanding of their architecture-function relationships is lacking. We will integrate cryo-electron tomography data from EMPIAR revealing contact site ultrastructure, proteomics data from proximity labeling studies, lipidomics datasets, calcium imaging data, and metabolomics measurements. Cross-referencing with disease-associated variants from ClinVar and GWAS catalogs will connect molecular architecture to physiological relevance.

Our first aim develops an integrated structural model of mitochondrial contact sites by synthesizing tomography data with protein structural predictions from AlphaFold and experimentally determined structures from PDB. We will map protein complexes to contact site architectures and identify organizational principles. Our second aim connects contact site composition to function by integrating proteomics, lipidomics, and metabolomics data across cell types and conditions. Machine learning approaches will identify compositional signatures predicting functional outcomes. Our third aim examines how contact site dysfunction contributes to disease by linking architectural and compositional features to disease phenotypes.

This project exemplifies the need for NCEMS support. Understanding contact sites requires expertise spanning membrane biology, structural biology, metabolism, and computational modeling that no single laboratory encompasses. Data integration across imaging, proteomics, and metabolomics modalities requires specialized computational approaches. The collaborative framework enables synthesis impossible through traditional single-laboratory efforts.

Our team includes researchers from seven institutions, spanning structural biology, mitochondrial biology, computational biology, and metabolism. Career stages range from assistant professors to senior investigators, with strong participation from underrepresented groups and primarily undergraduate institutions.

Expected outcomes include: (1) an integrated database of mitochondrial contact site architecture and composition, (2) predictive models linking contact site features to cellular functions, (3) identification of disease-relevant contact site alterations, and (4) new hypotheses for experimental validation. All data integration workflows, analysis code, and findings will be publicly released.

Training is embedded throughout the project. Graduate students will gain experience in multi-modal data integration through collaborative research. Postdocs will develop leadership skills through aim coordination. We will develop educational modules on contact site biology and data synthesis methods for the broader community. This project will establish principles for understanding how mesoscale organelle interfaces enable emergent cellular functions.
background_and_significance:
Mitochondria do not function in isolation. Rather, they engage in dynamic physical and functional interactions with virtually every other membrane-bound compartment in the cell through specialized structures called membrane contact sites (MCS). These nanometer-scale interfaces—typically spanning 10-30 nm gaps between organelles—represent quintessential mesoscale phenomena where molecular components organize into higher-order assemblies that enable emergent cellular functions impossible to predict from individual protein properties alone. Mitochondria-ER contact sites (MERCs) facilitate calcium transfer critical for ATP production and apoptotic signaling. Mitochondria-lysosome contacts regulate mitochondrial fission and metabolite exchange. Mitochondria-lipid droplet interfaces coordinate fatty acid trafficking during metabolic stress. Despite decades of research, we lack integrated understanding of how the mesoscale architecture of these contact sites enables their diverse emergent functions.

The significance of this knowledge gap extends beyond basic cell biology. Dysfunction at mitochondrial contact sites is implicated in neurodegeneration, metabolic disease, and cancer. Mutations in MERC proteins cause Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and hereditary spastic paraplegia. Altered mitochondria-lysosome contacts contribute to Parkinson's disease pathogenesis. Yet without understanding the organizational principles governing contact site architecture and function, we cannot develop rational therapeutic strategies targeting these interfaces.

The time is ripe for synthesis research addressing this challenge. The past decade has witnessed an explosion of publicly available data relevant to mitochondrial contact sites. The Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR) now contains hundreds of cryo-electron tomography datasets revealing contact site ultrastructure at unprecedented resolution. Proximity labeling proteomics studies using BioID and APEX have mapped contact site protein compositions across multiple cell types and conditions, with data deposited in ProteomeXchange and PRIDE databases. The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database provides predicted structures for essentially all human proteins, including poorly characterized contact site components. Lipidomics datasets in MetaboLights and Metabolomics Workbench capture lipid compositions relevant to contact site function. Calcium imaging datasets document signaling dynamics at MERCs. Disease variant databases including ClinVar and the GWAS Catalog link contact site genes to human pathology.

However, these data exist in silos. Structural biologists analyze tomography data without integrating proteomics. Biochemists study protein interactions without spatial context. Metabolic researchers examine lipid transfer without architectural information. No single laboratory possesses the expertise to synthesize across these domains. This fragmentation prevents answering fundamental questions: How do protein complexes organize within contact sites? What compositional features predict functional capacity? How do architectural perturbations cause disease?

This proposal directly addresses NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale. Contact sites exemplify emergence—their functions in calcium signaling, lipid transfer, and metabolic regulation arise from the collective organization of molecular components in ways unpredictable from studying isolated proteins. By synthesizing structural, proteomic, lipidomic, and functional data, we will decode the organizational principles enabling these emergent properties, establishing paradigms applicable to other mesoscale cellular structures.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses three interconnected research questions that progressively build from structural characterization through functional understanding to disease relevance.

Research Question 1: What are the organizational principles governing mitochondrial contact site architecture?

We hypothesize that mitochondrial contact sites exhibit hierarchical organization, with core tethering complexes establishing baseline architecture and accessory proteins creating functional microdomains within contact zones. Specifically, we predict that: (H1a) Contact sites of different types (MERC, mitochondria-lysosome, mitochondria-lipid droplet) share conserved architectural motifs despite distinct protein compositions, reflecting common biophysical constraints on membrane apposition. (H1b) Protein complexes within contact sites exhibit non-random spatial distributions, clustering into functional modules visible in tomographic reconstructions. (H1c) Contact site dimensions and protein densities correlate with cellular metabolic states, suggesting dynamic architectural remodeling.

Research Question 2: How does contact site composition predict functional capacity?

We hypothesize that specific compositional signatures—combinations of structural proteins, lipid species, and regulatory factors—determine the functional repertoire of individual contact sites. Our specific predictions include: (H2a) Distinct protein-lipid compositional states correspond to contact sites specialized for calcium transfer versus lipid exchange versus metabolic signaling. (H2b) Cell type-specific contact site compositions explain differential reliance on mitochondrial contacts across tissues. (H2c) Machine learning models trained on compositional features can predict functional outcomes including calcium transfer efficiency, lipid flux rates, and metabolic coupling strength.

Research Question 3: How do alterations in contact site architecture and composition contribute to disease?

We hypothesize that disease-associated variants in contact site proteins cause pathology through specific architectural or compositional perturbations rather than simple loss of function. Specifically: (H3a) Pathogenic variants cluster at protein-protein interfaces critical for contact site assembly, disrupting architectural integrity. (H3b) Disease severity correlates with the magnitude of predicted architectural disruption. (H3c) Different diseases affecting the same contact site proteins cause distinct architectural alterations, explaining phenotypic heterogeneity.

These hypotheses are testable through data synthesis approaches. For H1a-c, we will analyze tomographic reconstructions across contact site types, quantifying architectural parameters and correlating with metadata on cellular conditions. For H2a-c, we will integrate proteomics and lipidomics datasets, applying machine learning to identify compositional predictors of function. For H3a-c, we will map disease variants onto structural models and correlate predicted effects with clinical phenotypes.

Importantly, these questions cannot be answered through traditional single-laboratory approaches. Testing H1 requires synthesizing tomography data across multiple studies using different cell types and conditions—data that no single laboratory has generated. Testing H2 demands integration of proteomics, lipidomics, and functional datasets using computational approaches beyond typical experimental laboratory capabilities. Testing H3 requires connecting structural predictions to clinical databases, necessitating collaboration between basic scientists and those with clinical informatics expertise.

Our questions directly address the NCEMS focus on mesoscale emergence. Contact sites represent mesoscale structures where molecular components organize into functional assemblies. Understanding how architecture enables function—and how architectural perturbations cause disease—exemplifies the emergence phenomena NCEMS seeks to illuminate.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates multi-modal data synthesis with advanced computational analysis, organized around three synergistic aims.

Aim 1: Develop Integrated Structural Models of Mitochondrial Contact Sites

We will systematically retrieve cryo-electron tomography datasets from EMPIAR containing mitochondrial contact sites, currently comprising over 150 relevant depositions. Using standardized segmentation pipelines developed by our computational team, we will extract contact site geometries including membrane separation distances, contact zone areas, and protein density distributions. We will integrate these measurements with protein structural information by: (1) retrieving experimentally determined structures of contact site proteins from the PDB, (2) obtaining AlphaFold predictions for proteins lacking experimental structures, and (3) using AlphaFold-Multimer to predict structures of known contact site complexes. Molecular fitting approaches will dock protein complexes into tomographic densities, generating integrated structural models. We will apply graph-based network analysis to identify recurring architectural motifs across contact site types. Statistical analysis will test whether architectural parameters differ significantly between contact site types and cellular conditions.

Aim 2: Connect Contact Site Composition to Function Through Multi-Omics Integration

We will compile proteomics datasets from proximity labeling studies (BioID, APEX, TurboID) targeting contact site proteins, retrieving data from ProteomeXchange and PRIDE. Standardized reanalysis using MaxQuant and MSstats will enable cross-study comparison. We will integrate lipidomics data from MetaboLights capturing lipid compositions of mitochondria and partner organelles. Metabolomics datasets documenting metabolic fluxes at contact sites will be retrieved from Metabolomics Workbench. Calcium imaging datasets from public repositories will provide functional readouts of MERC activity.

For data integration, we will develop a unified data model representing contact site composition across molecular types. Multi-omics factor analysis (MOFA) will identify latent factors capturing coordinated variation across data types. Machine learning approaches including random forests and neural networks will be trained to predict functional outcomes from compositional features. Cross-validation across cell types will test model generalizability. Feature importance analysis will identify compositional signatures most predictive of specific functions.

Aim 3: Link Contact Site Features to Disease Phenotypes

We will retrieve disease-associated variants in contact site genes from ClinVar, HGMD, and the GWAS Catalog. Structural mapping will position variants within our integrated contact site models, using FoldX and Rosetta to predict effects on protein stability and interactions. We will categorize variants by predicted mechanism: interface disruption, stability perturbation, or regulatory alteration. Statistical analysis will test whether pathogenic variants show non-random distributions within contact site structures. title: Emergent Properties of the Cellular Crowding Landscape: Synthesizing Biophysical, Structural, and Systems Data to Understand Macromolecular Organization
abstract:
The cellular interior is extraordinarily crowded, with macromolecules occupying 20-40% of cytoplasmic volume, yet how this crowding influences molecular behavior and gives rise to emergent cellular properties remains poorly understood. This proposal assembles biophysicists, structural biologists, systems biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode how crowding shapes cellular organization and function at the mesoscale.

Macromolecular crowding affects protein folding, diffusion, interaction kinetics, and phase behavior, but these effects have been studied in isolation. We hypothesize that integrating diverse data types will reveal emergent organizational principles arising from crowding that cannot be understood from any single data source. Our synthesis will integrate protein abundance data from PaxDb and proteomics repositories, structural data from PDB and AlphaFold, diffusion measurements from FRAP and single-molecule tracking studies, and spatial proteomics data from the Human Protein Atlas and subcellular fractionation studies.

Our first aim constructs a quantitative map of the cellular crowding landscape by integrating protein abundance, size, and localization data to estimate local crowding across subcellular compartments. We will develop computational models predicting how crowding varies spatially and temporally. Our second aim synthesizes biophysical measurements to understand how crowding affects molecular behavior, integrating diffusion coefficients, binding constants, and reaction rates measured under different crowding conditions. Our third aim connects crowding to emergent cellular phenomena including phase separation, reaction compartmentalization, and metabolic channeling.

This project requires NCEMS support because it demands integration of biophysical, structural, and systems-level data requiring expertise no single laboratory possesses. The challenge of connecting molecular-scale crowding effects to cellular-scale organization requires collaborative efforts spanning multiple disciplines. Computational infrastructure for modeling crowded cellular environments exceeds typical laboratory capabilities.

Our team spans eight institutions across four countries, including biophysicists, structural biologists, systems biologists, and computational scientists. We include researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions and community colleges, ensuring broad participation and training opportunities.

Deliverables include: (1) a publicly available database of cellular crowding parameters across cell types and conditions, (2) computational tools for predicting crowding effects on molecular behavior, (3) models connecting crowding to emergent cellular organization, and (4) educational resources on crowding biology. All analysis workflows and findings will be openly shared.

Training opportunities include graduate student exchanges between biophysics and systems biology laboratories, workshops on integrating biophysical and omics data, and research experiences for undergraduate students. This project addresses a fundamental question: how does the crowded cellular environment shape emergent biological organization? By synthesizing diverse data types, we will establish principles for understanding mesoscale cellular organization.
background_and_significance:
The cellular interior represents one of the most complex physicochemical environments in nature. Unlike the dilute conditions typically used in biochemical experiments, the cytoplasm contains 200-400 mg/mL of macromolecules, creating an extraordinarily crowded environment where proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and metabolites compete for limited space. This macromolecular crowding fundamentally alters the thermodynamics and kinetics of virtually every cellular process, yet our understanding of how crowding shapes emergent cellular properties remains fragmented across disciplines.

Historically, the study of macromolecular crowding has proceeded along parallel but disconnected tracks. Biophysicists have characterized how synthetic crowding agents affect protein stability, folding kinetics, and diffusion in vitro. Structural biologists have determined the shapes and sizes of individual macromolecules in isolation. Systems biologists have catalogued protein abundances and localizations across cell types and conditions. Single-molecule researchers have measured diffusion coefficients and reaction kinetics in living cells. However, these data streams have rarely been integrated to understand how crowding operates as an organizing principle at the mesoscale—the critical interface between individual molecules and cellular-scale organization that represents NCEMS's core scientific focus.

The significance of understanding crowding extends far beyond basic science. Crowding profoundly influences protein aggregation diseases including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, where pathological aggregates form in the crowded cellular milieu. Cancer cells exhibit altered crowding landscapes due to changes in cell volume, protein expression, and organelle organization. Aging is accompanied by systematic changes in proteome composition that alter the crowding environment. Understanding how crowding shapes cellular organization is therefore essential for both fundamental biology and translational applications.

Recent advances have created an unprecedented opportunity for synthesis research in this area. The AlphaFold revolution has provided structural predictions for essentially all human proteins, enabling estimation of molecular volumes and shapes at proteome scale. Quantitative proteomics databases like PaxDb now contain protein abundance measurements across hundreds of cell types and conditions. Spatial proteomics initiatives including the Human Protein Atlas have mapped protein localizations to subcellular compartments. Single-molecule tracking studies have generated thousands of diffusion measurements in living cells. Phase separation databases catalogue proteins that undergo liquid-liquid phase separation under crowded conditions.

Despite this data abundance, no systematic effort has integrated these resources to understand crowding as an emergent cellular property. Individual laboratories lack the multidisciplinary expertise required to bridge biophysics, structural biology, systems biology, and computational science. The computational infrastructure needed to model crowded cellular environments at realistic scales exceeds typical laboratory capabilities. This synthesis project addresses a fundamental gap in our understanding of cellular organization by leveraging NCEMS resources to unite diverse expertise and data types.

The mesoscale focus of this proposal directly addresses NCEMS's scientific vision. Crowding effects manifest precisely at the mesoscale—between individual biomolecules and organelle-scale organization. Understanding how molecular-scale crowding interactions give rise to emergent cellular properties such as phase separation, metabolic channeling, and spatial organization of biochemical reactions represents a quintessential emergence problem. Our synthesis approach will reveal organizational principles invisible from any single data perspective, advancing fundamental understanding of how cells achieve functional organization in their crowded interiors.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses three interconnected research questions that span scales from individual molecules to cellular organization, each supported by testable hypotheses derived from preliminary analysis of publicly available data.

Research Question 1: How does macromolecular crowding vary across subcellular space and time, and what factors determine local crowding landscapes?

We hypothesize that cellular crowding is highly heterogeneous, with distinct subcellular compartments exhibiting characteristic crowding signatures determined by their protein composition, organelle density, and cytoskeletal organization. Preliminary integration of Human Protein Atlas localization data with PaxDb abundance measurements suggests that crowding in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen may exceed cytoplasmic crowding by 30-50%, while nuclear crowding varies dramatically with chromatin state. We further hypothesize that crowding landscapes are dynamic, changing systematically during cell cycle progression, stress responses, and differentiation. Testing these hypotheses requires integration of spatial proteomics, protein structure data, and temporal expression profiles that no single laboratory possesses.

Research Question 2: How do crowding effects on individual molecular behaviors—diffusion, binding, folding, and reaction kinetics—scale and interact to produce emergent cellular properties?

We hypothesize that crowding effects are non-additive and context-dependent, such that predictions based on studies of individual proteins in synthetic crowders fail to capture behavior in complex cellular environments. Specifically, we predict that the size distribution and surface properties of endogenous crowders create emergent effects distinct from those produced by uniform synthetic crowding agents. We further hypothesize that crowding effects exhibit threshold behaviors, where gradual changes in crowding density produce abrupt transitions in molecular organization—a hallmark of emergence. Our preliminary meta-analysis of published diffusion coefficients reveals systematic discrepancies between in vitro crowding predictions and in vivo measurements, supporting the existence of emergent crowding phenomena.

Research Question 3: How does crowding drive emergent cellular organization including biomolecular condensate formation, metabolic channeling, and reaction compartmentalization?

We hypothesize that crowding serves as a master regulator of mesoscale organization, with local crowding conditions determining which proteins undergo phase separation, which metabolic pathways exhibit channeling, and how reaction networks achieve spatial organization. We predict that proteins exhibiting phase separation in cells share characteristic features—intrinsically disordered regions, multivalent interaction domains, and specific surface properties—that make their phase behavior exquisitely sensitive to local crowding conditions. Furthermore, we hypothesize that metabolic enzymes catalyzing sequential reactions co-localize under crowded conditions to enable substrate channeling, and that this channeling emerges from crowding-dependent protein-protein interactions rather than stable complex formation.

These hypotheses generate specific, testable predictions. For Question 1, we predict that crowding maps will reveal conserved organizational principles across cell types despite differences in proteome composition. For Question 2, we predict that machine learning models trained on integrated biophysical data will outperform physics-based models assuming simple excluded volume effects. For Question 3, we predict that phase-separating proteins will cluster in crowding-sensitivity space, enabling prediction of phase behavior from sequence and structural features.

Our synthesis approach is essential for addressing these questions because the relevant data span multiple disciplines and databases. Answering Question 1 requires integration of structural (PDB, AlphaFold), abundance (PaxDb, PRIDE), and localization (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell) data. Question 2 demands synthesis of biophysical measurements scattered across thousands of publications with varying experimental conditions. Question 3 necessitates connecting phase separation databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS) with metabolic network data (KEGG, Reactome) and protein interaction databases (STRING, BioGRID). This integration challenge exceeds any single laboratory's capabilities and represents precisely the type of community-scale synthesis NCEMS was created to enable.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach comprises three integrated aims, each employing rigorous data synthesis strategies, computational modeling, and validation frameworks appropriate for community-scale synthesis research.

Aim 1: Constructing Quantitative Crowding Maps

We will systematically integrate protein abundance data from PaxDb (covering >100 organisms and thousands of conditions), structural data from PDB and AlphaFold Database (providing volumes and shapes for >200 million proteins), and localization data from Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, and subcellular fractionation proteomics studies. Our data integration pipeline will: (1) harmonize protein identifiers across databases using UniProt as the reference; (2) estimate molecular volumes from structural data using Voronoi tessellation and solvent-accessible surface calculations; (3) map abundances to subcellular compartments using machine learning classifiers trained on validated localization data; (4) calculate local volume fractions accounting for organelle volumes from electron microscopy morphometry databases.

We will develop Bayesian hierarchical models to estimate crowding parameters while propagating uncertainty from underlying measurements. These models will incorporate prior knowledge from biophysical theory while learning crowding distributions from integrated data. Temporal dynamics will be incorporated using cell cycle proteomics data from multiple published studies, enabling construction of time-resolved crowding maps.

Aim 2: Synthesizing Biophysical Crowding Effects

We will conduct systematic literature mining and database integration to compile the most comprehensive collection of crowding-dependent biophysical measurements ever assembled. Data sources include: diffusion coefficients from FRAP, FCS, and single-particle tracking studies; binding constants measured under varying crowding conditions; protein stability measurements from thermal and chemical denaturation studies; reaction kinetics from enzyme assays with crowding agents.

Our text mining pipeline will extract quantitative measurements from published literature using natural language processing tools optimized for scientific text. Extracted data will undergo manual validation by domain experts in our working group. We will develop standardized ontologies for describing experimental conditions, enabling meaningful comparison across studies.

Machine learning models will be trained to predict crowding effects from molecular features including size, shape, surface charge distribution, and intrinsic disorder content. We will employ gradient boosting, neural networks, and Gaussian process regression, with model selection based on cross-validation performance. Feature importance analysis will reveal which molecular properties most strongly determine crowding sensitivity.

Aim 3: Connecting Crowding to Emergent Organization

We will integrate our crowding maps and biophysical models with databases of emergent cellular phenomena. Phase separation analysis will combine data from PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, and LLPSDB with our crowding predictions to identify conditions favoring condensate formation. Metabolic channeling analysis will integrate KEGG pathway data with protein localization and interaction data to identify enzyme clusters potentially exhibiting substrate channeling. We will develop agent-based models simulating molecular behavior in crowded environments, parameterized by our synthesized data.

Validation Strategy

Our predictions will be validated against independent datasets withheld from model training. We will collaborate with experimentalist members of our working group who can test specific predictions using existing unpublished data. Cross-validation across cell types and organisms will assess generalizability. Sensitivity analyses will identify predictions robust to data uncertainty.

Computational Infrastructure

This project requires substantial computational resources for data integration, model training, and simulation. We will utilize NCEMS computational infrastructure for large-scale data processing and model training. All code will be developed using reproducible workflows with version control, containerization, and automated testing.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will generate transformative outcomes advancing both fundamental understanding and practical capabilities in molecular and cellular biology.

Primary Deliverables:

First, we will produce the Cellular Crowding Atlas, a comprehensive, publicly accessible database providing quantitative crowding parameters across subcellular compartments, cell types, organisms, and conditions. This resource will include estimated volume fractions, crowder size distributions, and temporal dynamics, enabling researchers worldwide to incorporate realistic crowding conditions into their studies.

Second, we will deliver CrowdPredict, a computational toolkit for predicting how crowding affects molecular behavior. This software suite will enable researchers to estimate diffusion coefficients, binding affinities, and reaction rates under specified crowding conditions, parameterized by our integrated biophysical data.

Third, we will produce validated computational models connecting molecular-scale crowding effects to emergent cellular organization, including phase separation propensity, metabolic channeling efficiency, and reaction compartmentalization.

Fourth, we will create educational resources including tutorials, workshops materials, and undergraduate teaching modules on crowding biology suitable for diverse educational contexts.

Scientific Impact:

Our synthesis will establish crowding as a quantitative, predictable organizing principle in cell biology. By revealing how local crowding conditions shape emergent properties, we will provide a new framework for understanding mesoscale cellular organization—directly advancing NCEMS's scientific mission. Our integrated models will generate testable predictions guiding future experimental research, potentially revealing novel regulatory mechanisms operating through crowding modulation.

Broader Impacts:

Our open resources will democratize access to crowding biology, enabling researchers at institutions lacking specialized biophysics infrastructure to incorporate crowding considerations into their work. Training activities will develop data science capabilities in the next generation of molecular and cellular biologists. Inclusion of researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions ensures broad participation and dissemination of synthesis research approaches. Our findings may inform therapeutic strategies for protein aggregation diseases and improve understanding of how cellular organization changes in cancer and aging.

title: Deciphering the Emergence of Cellular Polarity: Multi-Scale Data Synthesis Across Molecular, Mesoscale, and Cellular Organization
abstract:
Cellular polarity—the asymmetric organization of cellular components—is essential for development, tissue function, and disease prevention, yet how molecular interactions give rise to this emergent mesoscale organization remains incompletely understood. This proposal brings together cell biologists, developmental biologists, physicists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data spanning molecular interactions to tissue-level organization to decode the principles underlying polarity emergence.

Polarity establishment involves coordinated action of conserved protein modules including PAR proteins, Rho GTPases, and phosphoinositides, but how these molecular components self-organize into stable asymmetric distributions is poorly understood. We will integrate protein interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct, structural data from PDB and AlphaFold, imaging data from public repositories, single-cell transcriptomics from GEO and Human Cell Atlas, and spatial transcriptomics datasets. Cross-species comparisons will identify conserved principles.

Our first aim synthesizes molecular interaction networks underlying polarity, integrating protein-protein interactions, lipid-protein interactions, and post-translational modifications to construct comprehensive polarity networks. Our second aim examines mesoscale organization by integrating super-resolution imaging data, electron microscopy datasets, and proximity labeling proteomics to understand how molecular interactions produce asymmetric protein distributions. Our third aim connects molecular and mesoscale organization to cellular and tissue-level polarity phenotypes by integrating imaging, transcriptomics, and phenotypic data.

This synthesis project requires NCEMS support for multiple reasons. Understanding polarity emergence requires expertise spanning molecular biology, cell biology, developmental biology, physics, and computational modeling. Data integration across imaging modalities, proteomics, and transcriptomics demands specialized computational approaches. The collaborative framework enables insights impossible through individual laboratory efforts.

Our team includes researchers from six institutions spanning cell biology, developmental biology, biophysics, and computational biology. We include faculty from primarily undergraduate institutions and researchers at various career stages, ensuring diverse perspectives and training opportunities.

Expected outcomes include: (1) comprehensive polarity interaction networks across species, (2) models linking molecular interactions to mesoscale organization, (3) identification of conserved principles and species-specific adaptations, and (4) predictions for experimental validation. All integrated datasets, analysis workflows, and findings will be publicly released following FAIR principles.

Training is central to our project. Graduate students will participate in cross-laboratory research, gaining experience in diverse methodologies. We will develop educational modules on polarity biology and multi-scale data integration. Summer workshops will train the broader community in synthesis approaches. This project will establish foundational principles for understanding how molecular interactions give rise to emergent cellular asymmetry.
background_and_significance:
Cellular polarity represents one of the most fundamental examples of biological emergence, where molecular interactions give rise to macroscopic asymmetries essential for virtually all aspects of cellular and organismal function. From the first asymmetric division of the fertilized egg to the maintenance of epithelial barrier function in adult tissues, polarity underpins development, homeostasis, and disease prevention. Despite decades of research identifying key molecular players, the field lacks a unified understanding of how molecular-scale interactions produce stable, self-organizing asymmetric distributions at the mesoscale—the critical intermediate scale between individual biomolecules and organelles where emergent properties first manifest.

The molecular machinery of polarity is remarkably conserved across eukaryotes. The PAR (partitioning defective) protein network, first discovered in C. elegans, establishes anterior-posterior polarity through mutual antagonism between anterior (PAR-3, PAR-6, aPKC) and posterior (PAR-1, PAR-2) complexes. Rho family GTPases, including Cdc42, Rac, and RhoA, provide spatial cues through localized activation cycles. Phosphoinositide lipids, particularly PIP2 and PIP3, create membrane domains that recruit and organize cytoplasmic polarity factors. Post-translational modifications, especially phosphorylation, create feedback loops that reinforce asymmetry. While individual interactions are well-characterized, how these components collectively generate robust, self-correcting polarity remains poorly understood.

The mesoscale represents a critical knowledge gap in polarity biology. At this scale (10-500 nm), polarity proteins form clusters, condensates, and membrane domains that bridge molecular interactions and cellular-scale asymmetry. Recent advances in super-resolution microscopy and proximity labeling proteomics have revealed unexpected complexity at this scale, including phase-separated polarity condensates, nanoscale membrane domains, and dynamic protein clusters. However, these observations remain fragmented across different model systems, cell types, and experimental approaches, preventing synthesis into coherent mechanistic understanding.

The significance of understanding polarity emergence extends beyond basic biology. Polarity loss is a hallmark of epithelial cancers, where disruption of apical-basal organization promotes invasion and metastasis. Polarity defects underlie developmental disorders including neural tube defects and polycystic kidney disease. Understanding the principles governing polarity emergence could reveal therapeutic targets and predictive biomarkers.

This synthesis project is timely because publicly available data now span the full range of scales relevant to polarity emergence. Protein interaction databases contain thousands of polarity-relevant interactions. AlphaFold provides structural predictions for polarity proteins across species. Public imaging repositories contain super-resolution and electron microscopy data revealing mesoscale organization. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics datasets capture polarity gene expression across tissues and developmental stages. However, these datasets remain siloed within disciplines and have never been systematically integrated to address emergence.

NCEMS support is essential because understanding polarity emergence requires transdisciplinary synthesis beyond any single laboratory's capability. Physicists bring expertise in self-organization and phase transitions; developmental biologists understand tissue-level polarity; cell biologists characterize molecular mechanisms; computational scientists develop integration approaches. Only through collaborative synthesis can we decode how molecular interactions produce emergent cellular asymmetry, establishing principles applicable across biological scales and systems.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses three interconnected research questions spanning molecular, mesoscale, and cellular scales, unified by the central theme of understanding how emergence produces cellular polarity.

Research Question 1: What are the complete molecular interaction networks underlying polarity establishment, and how do network properties predict emergent behavior?

Hypothesis 1a: Polarity networks exhibit conserved topological features across species—including feedback loops, mutual inhibition motifs, and hub proteins—that are necessary for robust symmetry breaking. We hypothesize that network analysis will reveal that polarity-competent networks share specific architectural features distinguishing them from non-polarizing protein interaction networks.

Hypothesis 1b: Post-translational modification networks create temporal ordering of polarity establishment. We predict that integrating phosphorylation, ubiquitination, and lipid modification data will reveal sequential activation cascades where early modifications enable subsequent interactions, creating the temporal dynamics necessary for symmetry breaking.

Hypothesis 1c: Lipid-protein interactions define spatial boundaries essential for polarity. We hypothesize that systematic integration of lipid-binding domains, membrane localization data, and lipid distribution information will reveal that membrane lipid asymmetry templates protein asymmetry through specific lipid-protein interaction modules.

Research Question 2: How do molecular interactions produce mesoscale organization, and what physical principles govern polarity protein clustering, condensation, and domain formation?

Hypothesis 2a: Polarity proteins form biomolecular condensates through phase separation, and condensate properties (size, composition, dynamics) are predictable from molecular interaction data. We will test whether proteins identified as condensate components share sequence features (intrinsically disordered regions, multivalent interaction domains) and interaction network positions that predict condensate formation.

Hypothesis 2b: Mesoscale polarity organization follows universal scaling relationships across cell types and species. We hypothesize that despite molecular diversity, the physical dimensions of polarity domains, cluster sizes, and spatial gradients follow predictable scaling laws related to cell size, enabling cells of different sizes to establish proportional polarity.

Hypothesis 2c: Membrane curvature and cortical actin organization provide mesoscale templates for polarity protein localization. We predict that integrating structural data on curvature-sensing domains with imaging data on membrane geometry will reveal that physical membrane properties constrain polarity protein distributions.

Research Question 3: How do mesoscale polarity structures determine cellular and tissue-level phenotypes, and can we predict polarity outcomes from molecular and mesoscale features?

Hypothesis 3a: Quantitative features of mesoscale polarity organization (domain size, protein concentration gradients, temporal dynamics) predict cellular outcomes including asymmetric division, directed migration, and epithelial organization. We will test whether machine learning models trained on mesoscale features can predict phenotypic outcomes across cell types.

Hypothesis 3b: Tissue-level polarity emerges from cell-cell communication that coordinates individual cell polarity. We hypothesize that integrating spatial transcriptomics with tissue imaging data will reveal signaling networks that align polarity across cells, with disruption of these networks explaining tissue polarity defects in disease.

Hypothesis 3c: Species-specific adaptations in polarity mechanisms reflect ecological and developmental constraints. Cross-species synthesis will test whether variations in polarity network architecture correlate with differences in developmental timing, cell size, or tissue organization.

These hypotheses are testable through data synthesis and will generate specific predictions for future experimental validation, ensuring our synthesis work advances mechanistic understanding rather than remaining purely descriptive.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates diverse publicly available datasets through a structured workflow designed to address each research aim while maintaining rigorous data provenance and reproducibility.

Aim 1 Methods - Molecular Network Synthesis: We will construct comprehensive polarity interaction networks by integrating data from BioGRID (>2 million interactions), IntAct, and STRING databases. Polarity-relevant proteins will be identified through Gene Ontology annotations, literature curation, and orthology mapping across model organisms (H. sapiens, M. musculus, D. melanogaster, C. elegans, S. cerevisiae). Network construction will employ Cytoscape and custom Python pipelines using NetworkX. We will integrate post-translational modification data from PhosphoSitePlus and UniProt, mapping modifications onto network nodes and identifying modification-dependent interactions. Lipid-protein interactions will be extracted from databases including STITCH and literature mining using natural language processing. Structural data from PDB and AlphaFold will inform interaction interfaces and predict novel interactions through structural complementarity analysis. Network analysis will identify topological features including motifs, modules, and hubs using algorithms implemented in graph-tool and igraph. Cross-species network comparison will use orthology mappings from InParanoid and OMA to identify conserved network cores and species-specific elaborations.

Aim 2 Methods - Mesoscale Organization Analysis: We will aggregate super-resolution microscopy data from public repositories including the Image Data Resource (IDR), BioImage Archive, and Cell Image Library. Standardized image analysis pipelines using Python (scikit-image, cellpose) will extract quantitative features including cluster sizes, spatial distributions, and colocalization metrics. Electron microscopy data from EMPIAR will provide ultrastructural context for mesoscale organization. Proximity labeling proteomics datasets (BioID, APEX) from ProteomeXchange will define local protein environments around polarity factors. We will develop machine learning approaches to integrate imaging and proteomics data, using graph neural networks to model spatial relationships. Physical modeling will employ reaction-diffusion frameworks and phase-field models to test whether molecular interaction parameters predict observed mesoscale organization. Collaboration with physicist team members will ensure rigorous application of soft matter physics principles.

Aim 3 Methods - Multi-Scale Integration: Single-cell RNA sequencing data from GEO, Human Cell Atlas, and Tabula Muris will provide expression profiles across polarized cell types. Spatial transcriptomics data from repositories including Spatial Research and published datasets will map polarity gene expression within tissue contexts. We will develop integration frameworks using multi-modal data analysis approaches including MOFA+ and Seurat for connecting molecular, imaging, and transcriptomic data. Machine learning models (random forests, neural networks) will predict cellular phenotypes from molecular and mesoscale features, with rigorous cross-validation to assess predictive power. Phenotypic data from genome-wide screens (DepMap, GenomeRNAi) will connect polarity network perturbations to cellular outcomes.

Computational Infrastructure: Analysis will utilize NCEMS computational resources supplemented by institutional high-performance computing. We will implement containerized workflows (Docker/Singularity) ensuring reproducibility. Version control through GitHub will track all analysis code. Regular virtual meetings and annual in-person workshops will coordinate team efforts and ensure methodological consistency across institutions.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will generate multiple transformative outcomes advancing understanding of polarity emergence while establishing resources and approaches benefiting the broader scientific community.

Primary Scientific Outcomes: First, we will produce comprehensive, multi-species polarity interaction networks integrating protein-protein interactions, lipid-protein interactions, and post-translational modifications—the most complete molecular maps of polarity machinery to date. These networks will identify novel polarity regulators and predict functional interactions for experimental validation. Second, we will establish quantitative relationships between molecular interaction parameters and mesoscale organization, generating predictive models for how protein properties (binding affinities, concentrations, modification states) determine clustering, condensation, and domain formation. Third, we will identify conserved principles and species-specific adaptations in polarity mechanisms, revealing which features represent universal requirements for symmetry breaking versus evolutionary elaborations. Fourth, we will develop predictive models connecting molecular and mesoscale features to cellular phenotypes, enabling prediction of polarity outcomes from measurable parameters.

Methodological Advances: Our project will develop novel computational approaches for multi-scale biological data integration, creating pipelines applicable beyond polarity to other emergence phenomena. Machine learning models for predicting mesoscale organization from molecular data will establish new paradigms for connecting scales in cell biology.

Community Resources: All integrated datasets will be released through public repositories with comprehensive metadata. Analysis workflows will be shared as documented, containerized pipelines. We will create a web portal enabling researchers to query polarity networks and access analysis tools without computational expertise.

Broader Impact: Understanding polarity emergence has implications for cancer biology, developmental disorders, and regenerative medicine. Our findings will generate testable hypotheses for experimental laboratories, accelerating discovery beyond our synthesis work. Training outcomes will produce data-savvy scientists equipped for modern biological research, while educational materials will enhance polarity biology instruction broadly. This project exemplifies how synthesis research can transform fragmented observations into mechanistic understanding of biological emergence.

title: The Grammar of Intrinsically Disordered Regions: Synthesizing Sequence, Structure, and Function Data to Predict Emergent Behaviors
abstract:
Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) comprise approximately 30% of eukaryotic proteomes and are central to cellular regulation, signaling, and organization, yet predicting their functional behaviors from sequence remains challenging. This proposal unites structural biologists, bioinformaticians, biophysicists, and cell biologists to synthesize publicly available data to decode the sequence-function grammar of IDRs and predict their emergent behaviors including phase separation, protein interactions, and regulatory functions.

IDRs lack stable three-dimensional structures but adopt transient conformational ensembles that enable diverse functions. Current understanding of IDR function is fragmented across disparate studies. We will integrate sequence databases, structural ensembles from NMR and molecular dynamics simulations, phase separation propensity data, post-translational modification annotations, interaction data, and cellular localization information. This comprehensive synthesis will reveal principles connecting IDR sequence features to functional outcomes.

Our first aim develops a comprehensive IDR feature database by synthesizing sequence annotations, predicted and experimental structural ensembles, and biophysical properties. We will apply machine learning to identify sequence patterns associated with specific functions. Our second aim connects IDR features to interaction behaviors by integrating protein-protein interaction data, binding site annotations, and structural data on IDR-mediated complexes. Our third aim links IDR properties to emergent cellular behaviors including condensate formation, signaling hub function, and transcriptional regulation.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding IDR function requires expertise spanning bioinformatics, structural biology, biophysics, and cell biology that no single laboratory possesses. The data integration challenge—connecting sequence features to cellular functions—requires diverse computational approaches and biological insights. The scale of analysis exceeds typical laboratory capabilities.

Our team includes researchers from seven institutions spanning structural biology, bioinformatics, biophysics, and cell biology. We include early-career investigators, researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions, and international collaborators, ensuring diverse perspectives.

Deliverables include: (1) a comprehensive IDR feature database with visualization tools, (2) predictive models for IDR function from sequence, (3) identification of IDR grammar rules for specific functions, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released with comprehensive documentation.

Training opportunities include graduate student rotations between computational and experimental laboratories, workshops on IDR analysis methods, and research experiences for undergraduates. This project addresses a fundamental challenge in molecular biology: predicting protein function from sequence for the substantial fraction of proteins containing disordered regions. By synthesizing diverse data types, we will establish principles for understanding how IDR sequences encode emergent functional behaviors.
background_and_significance:
Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) represent one of the most significant paradigm shifts in molecular biology over the past two decades. Unlike classical protein domains that fold into stable three-dimensional structures, IDRs exist as dynamic conformational ensembles, challenging the structure-function paradigm that has guided protein science for over a century. Approximately 30% of eukaryotic proteomes contain substantial disordered regions, with this fraction increasing to over 50% in signaling and regulatory proteins. Despite their prevalence and functional importance, our ability to predict IDR function from sequence remains remarkably limited, representing a fundamental gap in our understanding of the molecular basis of life.

IDRs are central to emergent cellular behaviors that align directly with NCEMS's focus on mesoscale phenomena. These regions drive liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), the process underlying membraneless organelle formation including stress granules, P-bodies, and nucleoli. Phase separation represents a quintessential emergent property: individual IDR-containing proteins exhibit specific sequence features, but their collective behavior produces higher-order cellular compartments with distinct physicochemical properties and biological functions. Understanding how IDR sequence features encode phase separation propensity is essential for deciphering mesoscale cellular organization.

Beyond phase separation, IDRs serve as interaction hubs, binding multiple partners through short linear motifs embedded within disordered sequences. These interactions are often transient and multivalent, enabling the formation of dynamic signaling networks that respond rapidly to cellular stimuli. IDRs also serve as substrates for post-translational modifications (PTMs), with phosphorylation, methylation, acetylation, and other modifications modulating IDR conformation, interactions, and phase behavior. The integration of PTM information with IDR sequence features represents an unexplored frontier for understanding cellular regulation.

Current knowledge of IDR function is fragmented across disparate databases, publications, and computational predictions. Sequence databases such as DisProt and MobiDB catalog disorder annotations, while structural databases including the Protein Ensemble Database (PED) and BMRB contain conformational ensemble data from NMR spectroscopy and molecular dynamics simulations. Phase separation databases such as PhaSepDB and DrLLPS document proteins involved in condensate formation, while interaction databases including BioGRID and IntAct catalog protein-protein interactions. PTM databases such as PhosphoSitePlus provide modification annotations. However, no systematic effort has integrated these diverse data sources to establish comprehensive principles connecting IDR sequence features to functional outcomes.

This fragmentation creates a critical barrier to progress. Individual laboratories possess expertise in specific aspects of IDR biology—sequence analysis, structural characterization, phase separation biophysics, or cellular function—but lack the breadth to synthesize across these domains. The data integration challenge requires computational infrastructure, diverse analytical approaches, and biological insights that exceed the capabilities of any single research group. NCEMS provides the ideal framework for assembling the multidisciplinary team and resources necessary to address this challenge.

The significance of this work extends beyond basic science. IDRs are implicated in numerous diseases, including neurodegeneration (where aberrant phase separation drives pathological aggregation), cancer (where disordered transcription factors are frequently mutated), and viral infection (where viral IDRs hijack cellular condensates). Establishing predictive principles for IDR function will accelerate therapeutic development targeting these regions. Furthermore, IDRs represent an untapped resource for synthetic biology, where their modular and tunable properties could enable novel cellular engineering applications.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses three overarching research questions that progressively connect IDR sequence features to emergent cellular behaviors, each supported by specific testable hypotheses derived from preliminary observations in the literature.

**Research Question 1: What sequence features define the functional grammar of IDRs?**

We hypothesize that IDR sequences contain identifiable grammatical elements—analogous to syntax in language—that encode specific functional properties. These elements include: (a) compositional biases (amino acid frequencies and distributions), (b) patterning features (charge distribution, hydrophobic clustering, aromatic spacing), (c) short linear motifs (SLiMs) that mediate specific interactions, and (d) context-dependent features where the same motif exhibits different functions depending on surrounding sequence.

*Hypothesis 1a*: IDRs with similar functions share identifiable sequence signatures that can be extracted through machine learning analysis of comprehensive feature databases, even when overall sequence similarity is low.

*Hypothesis 1b*: The spacing and arrangement of functional elements within IDRs (grammar) is as important as the elements themselves (vocabulary) for determining function, analogous to how word order determines meaning in language.

*Hypothesis 1c*: Evolutionary conservation patterns within IDRs reflect functional constraints on grammatical elements rather than overall sequence, enabling identification of functionally critical features.

**Research Question 2: How do IDR sequence features determine interaction behaviors?**

IDRs mediate diverse interactions ranging from high-affinity binding to transient, multivalent contacts. We hypothesize that distinct sequence grammars encode these different interaction modes and that integration of interaction data with sequence features will reveal predictive principles.

*Hypothesis 2a*: IDRs that function as interaction hubs (binding multiple partners) exhibit distinct sequence features from IDRs that bind single partners with high specificity, including higher SLiM density and greater conformational flexibility.

*Hypothesis 2b*: The conformational ensemble properties of IDRs (compactness, transient secondary structure, dynamics) encoded by sequence features determine binding kinetics and thermodynamics in predictable ways.

*Hypothesis 2c*: PTM sites within IDRs are positioned to maximally modulate interaction behaviors, with modification-induced changes in local sequence properties (charge, hydrophobicity) altering binding partner selectivity.

**Research Question 3: How do IDR properties give rise to emergent cellular behaviors?**

Phase separation, signaling hub function, and transcriptional regulation represent emergent behaviors arising from IDR properties. We hypothesize that specific sequence grammars encode propensity for these behaviors and that integration of cellular-scale data with sequence features will establish predictive models.

*Hypothesis 3a*: Phase-separating IDRs exhibit characteristic sequence grammars involving aromatic residue spacing, charge patterning, and prion-like composition that can be quantified and used for prediction with higher accuracy than current single-feature approaches.

*Hypothesis 3b*: IDRs that function as signaling hubs exhibit sequence features that balance interaction promiscuity with specificity, including optimal SLiM density and conformational properties that enable rapid partner exchange.

*Hypothesis 3c*: The relationship between IDR sequence features and cellular function is modulated by cellular context (PTM state, expression level, available binding partners), and integration of expression and localization data will improve functional predictions.

*Hypothesis 3d*: Certain IDR sequence grammars are associated with specific subcellular localizations and condensate types, reflecting the physicochemical requirements of different cellular environments.

These hypotheses are designed to be testable through synthesis of existing data and will generate specific predictions for experimental validation by the broader community. The hierarchical structure—from sequence features to interaction behaviors to cellular functions—enables systematic investigation of how molecular-level properties give rise to emergent mesoscale and cellular outcomes, directly addressing NCEMS's scientific vision.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates data synthesis, computational analysis, and machine learning within a collaborative framework designed to leverage the diverse expertise of our working group.

**Aim 1: Comprehensive IDR Feature Database Development**

We will construct a unified database integrating IDR annotations from DisProt, MobiDB, and IDEAL with sequence-derived features, structural ensemble data, and biophysical properties. Data acquisition will utilize established APIs and bulk downloads from public repositories. For each IDR, we will compute comprehensive sequence features including amino acid composition, charge distribution metrics (NCPR, FCR, kappa), hydropathy profiles, complexity measures, and predicted secondary structure propensities using established algorithms (IUPred3, PONDR, metapredict).

Structural ensemble data from the Protein Ensemble Database and BMRB will be processed to extract conformational properties including radius of gyration distributions, end-to-end distances, secondary structure populations, and contact maps. For IDRs lacking experimental ensembles, we will integrate predictions from AlphaFold2 confidence scores and molecular dynamics simulations deposited in public repositories. PTM annotations from PhosphoSitePlus, dbPTM, and UniProt will be mapped onto IDR sequences with functional annotations where available.

Machine learning analysis will employ both supervised and unsupervised approaches. Unsupervised clustering using UMAP and hierarchical methods will identify natural groupings of IDRs based on feature profiles. Supervised classification using random forests, gradient boosting, and neural networks will identify features predictive of specific functions. Feature importance analysis will reveal which sequence properties most strongly associate with functional outcomes. Cross-validation and held-out test sets will ensure model generalizability.

**Aim 2: IDR-Interaction Relationship Mapping**

We will integrate protein-protein interaction data from BioGRID, IntAct, and STRING with IDR annotations to identify interactions mediated by disordered regions. The Eukaryotic Linear Motif (ELM) database and SLiMSearch will provide SLiM annotations that will be mapped onto IDR sequences. Structural data on IDR-mediated complexes from the PDB will be analyzed to characterize binding modes, including disorder-to-order transitions and fuzzy complex formation.

Network analysis will identify IDRs functioning as interaction hubs versus those with limited partners. Graph-theoretic measures including degree, betweenness centrality, and clustering coefficient will characterize IDR positions within interaction networks. Integration with structural ensemble data will test whether conformational properties correlate with interaction network position.

Statistical modeling will relate IDR sequence features to interaction properties including partner number, binding affinity (where available from curated databases), and interaction dynamics. Regression models will predict interaction properties from sequence features, with model performance evaluated through cross-validation.

**Aim 3: Linking IDR Properties to Emergent Cellular Behaviors**

Phase separation data from PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, and LLPSDB will be integrated with IDR feature profiles to identify sequence determinants of condensate formation. We will develop improved phase separation predictors by combining multiple sequence features using ensemble machine learning methods, benchmarking against existing tools (catGRANULE, PSPredictor).

Transcription factor IDRs will be analyzed by integrating data from UniProt, TFClass, and ChIP-seq databases to connect IDR properties to regulatory functions. Expression data from the Human Protein Atlas and GTEx will provide cellular context, enabling analysis of how IDR function varies with expression level and tissue type.

Subcellular localization data from the Human Protein Atlas and UniProt will be integrated to test whether IDR features predict localization patterns. Condensate-specific localization (stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli) will be analyzed using curated datasets from the literature.

**Collaborative Integration**

Biweekly virtual meetings will coordinate analysis across working group members. Annual in-person workshops at NCEMS will enable intensive collaborative analysis and training. A shared computational infrastructure using cloud resources will ensure reproducibility and enable collaborative code development. All analyses will be implemented in documented, version-controlled workflows.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will generate transformative outcomes advancing our understanding of IDR function and establishing resources for the broader scientific community.

**Primary Deliverables:**

The IDR Grammar Database will provide the most comprehensive resource for IDR analysis, integrating sequence features, structural ensembles, interaction data, and functional annotations for over 50,000 IDRs across model organisms. Interactive visualization tools will enable researchers to explore relationships between features and functions, query specific IDRs, and compare sequences against established functional classes.

Predictive models for IDR function will achieve substantially improved accuracy over existing single-feature approaches by integrating multiple sequence properties. We anticipate developing models predicting phase separation propensity, interaction hub function, and regulatory activity with AUC values exceeding 0.85, representing significant advances over current methods.

IDR grammar rules will be formalized as interpretable sequence patterns associated with specific functions. These rules will be published as a comprehensive catalog enabling researchers to annotate newly identified IDRs and generate functional hypotheses.

**Scientific Impact:**

This work will establish foundational principles for understanding how IDR sequences encode emergent functional behaviors, addressing a fundamental challenge in molecular biology. The integration of data across scales—from sequence to cellular function—directly advances NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale.

Our findings will generate specific, testable hypotheses for experimental validation, catalyzing follow-up studies by the broader community. The predictive models will accelerate discovery by enabling prioritization of IDRs for functional characterization.

**Broader Impact:**

Training activities will develop data science skills in the next generation of scientists, with at least 15 trainees (graduate students, postdocs, undergraduates) participating directly in research activities. Workshop materials will be publicly released, extending training impact beyond direct participants.

The methodological framework—integrating diverse data types to understand emergent properties—will serve as a template for future synthesis projects addressing other biological systems.
