title: Emergent Organization of the Cytoskeletal Interactome: Integrating Structural, Dynamic, and Functional Data Across Actin, Microtubule, and Intermediate Filament Networks
abstract:
The cytoskeleton comprises interconnected networks of actin filaments, microtubules, and intermediate filaments that collectively enable cell shape, motility, and intracellular organization, yet how these systems interact to produce emergent mechanical and organizational properties remains poorly understood. This proposal assembles cytoskeleton biologists, biophysicists, structural biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode the organizational principles of the integrated cytoskeletal system.

Traditionally studied in isolation, the three cytoskeletal systems are increasingly recognized as functionally interconnected. Crosslinking proteins, motor proteins, and signaling molecules coordinate their behaviors, but comprehensive understanding of this integration is lacking. We will integrate structural data from PDB and cryo-EM repositories, protein interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct, live-cell imaging datasets, mechanical measurement data, and proteomics data from cytoskeletal preparations.

Our first aim constructs an integrated cytoskeletal interactome by synthesizing protein-protein interaction data, structural information, and localization data to map connections between cytoskeletal systems. We will identify hub proteins and regulatory nodes. Our second aim examines dynamic coordination by integrating time-resolved imaging data, single-molecule tracking studies, and perturbation experiments to understand how cytoskeletal systems communicate. Our third aim connects cytoskeletal organization to emergent cellular properties including mechanical behavior, organelle positioning, and cell migration.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding cytoskeletal integration requires expertise spanning actin biology, microtubule biology, intermediate filament biology, biophysics, and computational modeling. No single laboratory possesses this breadth. Data integration across imaging, structural, and proteomic modalities requires specialized computational approaches and infrastructure.

Our team includes researchers from eight institutions with expertise spanning all three cytoskeletal systems plus biophysics and computational biology. We include researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions and various career stages, ensuring diverse participation.

Expected outcomes include: (1) an integrated cytoskeletal interactome database, (2) models of cytoskeletal coordination and crosstalk, (3) identification of key regulatory nodes, and (4) predictions linking cytoskeletal organization to cellular behaviors. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student exchanges between laboratories studying different cytoskeletal systems, workshops on cytoskeletal data analysis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses a fundamental question in cell biology: how do interconnected cytoskeletal networks produce emergent cellular organization and mechanics? By synthesizing data across systems, we will establish principles for understanding mesoscale cytoskeletal organization.
background_and_significance:
The cytoskeleton represents one of the most sophisticated examples of emergent biological organization, where three distinct polymer systems—actin filaments, microtubules, and intermediate filaments—integrate to produce cellular properties that cannot be predicted from studying individual components. This mesoscale organization, spanning nanometer-scale protein interactions to micrometer-scale cellular architectures, exemplifies the emergence phenomena central to NCEMS's scientific mission. Despite decades of research, fundamental questions remain about how these systems communicate, coordinate, and collectively generate mechanical resilience, directional transport, and spatial organization.

Historically, the cytoskeleton field has been compartmentalized, with separate research communities studying actin, microtubules, and intermediate filaments using distinct experimental approaches and conceptual frameworks. This disciplinary fragmentation has produced deep knowledge of individual systems but limited understanding of their integration. Actin researchers have characterized over 150 actin-binding proteins, microtubule biologists have mapped the tubulin code and associated proteins, and intermediate filament studies have revealed tissue-specific expression patterns and mechanical properties. However, the interfaces between these systems remain poorly characterized.

Recent discoveries have revealed extensive crosstalk between cytoskeletal systems. Proteins like plectin physically crosslink all three filament types, spectraplakins connect actin and microtubules at cell cortices, and signaling cascades simultaneously regulate multiple systems during cell migration and division. Single-cell studies demonstrate that perturbations to one system propagate to others, suggesting functional interdependence that produces emergent cellular behaviors. For example, intermediate filament networks influence microtubule organization, which in turn affects actin-based motility—a cascade of interactions generating cell-scale mechanical properties.

The timing for this synthesis project is optimal because unprecedented amounts of publicly available data now exist across all three cytoskeletal systems. The Protein Data Bank contains over 5,000 structures of cytoskeletal proteins and complexes. Cryo-electron microscopy has revolutionized structural understanding of filament architecture and protein complexes. Interaction databases like BioGRID and IntAct document thousands of cytoskeletal protein interactions. Live-cell imaging repositories contain time-resolved data on cytoskeletal dynamics. Proteomics studies have quantified cytoskeletal protein abundances across cell types and conditions. Single-molecule studies have characterized motor protein behaviors and filament dynamics. Mechanical measurement datasets document cellular rheological properties.

Despite this data abundance, no systematic effort has integrated information across cytoskeletal systems to understand emergent organization. Individual laboratories lack the breadth of expertise required—specialists in actin biology rarely collaborate with intermediate filament researchers, and computational scientists capable of integrating diverse data types are not typically embedded in cytoskeleton research groups. This fragmentation represents a significant barrier to understanding mesoscale cytoskeletal organization.

This project directly addresses NCEMS priorities by focusing on emergence at the mesoscale, where molecular interactions produce cellular-scale properties. The cytoskeleton exemplifies how component interactions generate system-level behaviors: mechanical resilience emerges from filament network architecture, directional transport emerges from motor protein coordination, and cellular shape emerges from integrated polymer dynamics. Understanding these emergent properties requires synthesizing data across scales and systems—precisely the approach NCEMS was designed to enable.

The significance extends beyond fundamental biology. Cytoskeletal dysfunction underlies numerous diseases, including cancer metastasis, neurodegeneration, and cardiomyopathies. Understanding how integrated cytoskeletal organization produces cellular behaviors will illuminate disease mechanisms and potential therapeutic targets. Furthermore, principles of cytoskeletal organization inform synthetic biology and materials science, where researchers seek to engineer responsive, self-organizing systems.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses three interconnected research questions that progressively build understanding of emergent cytoskeletal organization, from molecular interactions to cellular behaviors.

Research Question 1: What is the architecture of the integrated cytoskeletal interactome, and which proteins serve as critical nodes connecting actin, microtubule, and intermediate filament networks?

We hypothesize that the cytoskeletal interactome contains a relatively small number of hub proteins that disproportionately influence inter-system communication. These hubs likely include known crosslinkers (plectin, spectraplakins, MACF1) but also signaling proteins and regulatory factors not traditionally considered cytoskeletal components. We further hypothesize that hub proteins share structural features enabling multi-system interactions, including modular domain architectures with distinct binding sites for different filament types. Specifically, we predict that proteins with plakin domains, spectrin repeats, or combinations of CH domains and EF-hands will be overrepresented among inter-system connectors. We also hypothesize that the interactome architecture differs systematically between cell types, with epithelial cells showing stronger intermediate filament-actin connections while neuronal cells exhibit enhanced microtubule-intermediate filament coupling.

Research Question 2: How do cytoskeletal systems dynamically coordinate their behaviors, and what temporal relationships govern inter-system communication?

We hypothesize that cytoskeletal coordination operates through hierarchical temporal relationships, with fast-timescale actin dynamics (seconds) influencing intermediate-timescale microtubule organization (minutes), which in turn modulates slow-timescale intermediate filament remodeling (hours). This temporal hierarchy suggests that information flows preferentially in certain directions between systems. We predict that perturbations to actin networks will propagate rapidly to microtubules but slowly to intermediate filaments, while intermediate filament perturbations will have delayed effects on both other systems. Furthermore, we hypothesize that specific cellular locations serve as coordination centers where all three systems converge and communicate. These sites likely include focal adhesions, cell-cell junctions, and perinuclear regions. We predict that proteins localized to these coordination centers will show correlated dynamics across systems, detectable through integration of time-resolved imaging datasets.

Research Question 3: How does integrated cytoskeletal organization produce emergent cellular mechanical properties, and can we predict cellular behaviors from interactome architecture?

We hypothesize that emergent mechanical properties—including cellular stiffness, viscosity, and strain-stiffening behavior—arise from specific network topologies rather than simply from the sum of individual filament contributions. We predict that cells with similar total cytoskeletal protein content but different interactome architectures will exhibit distinct mechanical behaviors. Specifically, we hypothesize that the ratio of inter-system crosslinks to intra-system crosslinks determines whether cells behave as integrated mechanical units or as loosely coupled subsystems. We further hypothesize that organelle positioning accuracy correlates with interactome connectivity—cells with more extensively connected cytoskeletal networks will show less variability in organelle positions. Finally, we predict that cell migration modes (mesenchymal versus amoeboid) correspond to distinct interactome states, with mesenchymal migration requiring stronger actin-microtubule coupling and amoeboid migration depending on actin-intermediate filament interactions.

These hypotheses generate testable predictions that can be evaluated through data synthesis. For example, if hub proteins disproportionately influence inter-system communication, then published perturbation studies targeting hub proteins should show effects on multiple cytoskeletal systems, while perturbations to non-hub proteins should have system-specific effects. If temporal hierarchies govern coordination, then time-resolved imaging datasets should reveal consistent lag relationships between systems across different experimental contexts. If interactome architecture determines mechanical properties, then cell types with similar architectures should cluster together in mechanical property space regardless of tissue origin.

The questions are structured to build progressively: Question 1 establishes the static architecture, Question 2 adds temporal dynamics, and Question 3 connects organization to function. This structure ensures that early findings inform subsequent analyses and that the project produces coherent, integrated understanding rather than disconnected observations.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates diverse publicly available datasets through a structured workflow combining automated data retrieval, expert curation, computational integration, and iterative validation.

Data Acquisition and Harmonization: We will systematically retrieve cytoskeletal-related data from major public repositories. Structural data will be obtained from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB), including atomic structures, cryo-EM maps, and integrative structural models. Protein interaction data will be compiled from BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, and the Human Protein Reference Database, encompassing physical interactions, genetic interactions, and predicted functional associations. Expression and localization data will be extracted from the Human Protein Atlas, ProteomicsDB, and Cell Atlas. Dynamic imaging data will be obtained from the Image Data Resource, Cell Image Library, and published supplementary datasets. Mechanical measurement data will be compiled from atomic force microscopy studies, optical tweezers experiments, and rheological measurements deposited in literature supplements and emerging mechanical property databases.

A critical challenge involves harmonizing data collected using different methods, nomenclatures, and quality standards. We will develop standardized ontologies mapping protein names, cell types, and experimental conditions across datasets. Quality metrics will be assigned based on experimental methodology, replication, and consistency with orthogonal measurements. Machine learning approaches will identify and flag potential inconsistencies requiring expert review.

Aim 1 Methods - Interactome Construction: We will construct the integrated cytoskeletal interactome using network analysis approaches. Protein-protein interactions will be weighted by evidence strength, combining experimental detection methods, structural evidence of binding interfaces, and co-localization data. Graph-theoretic analyses will identify hub proteins, network modules, and bridging nodes connecting cytoskeletal subsystems. We will employ community detection algorithms to identify functionally coherent protein clusters and analyze how these communities span system boundaries. Structural modeling will predict interaction interfaces for poorly characterized connections, using AlphaFold2 structures and protein-protein docking. The interactome will be annotated with subcellular localization, tissue expression, and disease associations.

Aim 2 Methods - Dynamic Coordination Analysis: Time-resolved data integration requires specialized approaches for handling heterogeneous temporal datasets. We will extract quantitative dynamics parameters from published imaging studies, including filament assembly/disassembly rates, motor velocities, and network remodeling timescales. Cross-correlation analyses will identify temporal relationships between systems, revealing which dynamics lead or lag others. We will compile perturbation response data from drug treatments, genetic knockdowns, and optogenetic manipulations, constructing a perturbation-response matrix revealing how interventions in one system affect others. Machine learning models will identify patterns in perturbation responses predictive of inter-system coupling strength.

Aim 3 Methods - Emergent Property Mapping: We will correlate cytoskeletal organization with cellular mechanical properties by integrating interactome architecture with mechanical measurement datasets. Regression models will identify network features predictive of mechanical behaviors. Cell migration data will be analyzed to identify cytoskeletal configurations associated with different migration modes. Organelle positioning data will be correlated with local cytoskeletal organization. We will develop predictive models linking interactome states to cellular behaviors, validated against held-out datasets.

Computational Infrastructure: Analysis pipelines will be implemented using reproducible workflow systems (Snakemake, Nextflow) with containerized environments ensuring reproducibility. Graph analyses will use NetworkX and Cytoscape. Machine learning will employ scikit-learn, PyTorch, and specialized biological network tools. All code will be version-controlled and documented for public release.

Validation Strategy: Predictions will be validated against independent datasets not used in model training. We will identify published experiments providing natural tests of our predictions and compile validation datasets prospectively. Confidence estimates will accompany all predictions, enabling prioritization of future experimental validation.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This project will generate multiple tangible outcomes advancing understanding of emergent cytoskeletal organization while providing community resources enabling future research.

Primary Outcomes: First, we will produce a comprehensive Integrated Cytoskeletal Interactome Database containing curated interactions within and between actin, microtubule, and intermediate filament systems. This database will include confidence scores, structural evidence, tissue-specific annotations, and dynamic parameters. The database will be queryable through web interfaces and downloadable for computational analyses. Second, we will generate Cytoskeletal Coordination Models describing temporal relationships and information flow between systems. These models will predict how perturbations propagate across the integrated cytoskeleton. Third, we will identify Critical Regulatory Nodes—proteins whose activities disproportionately influence inter-system communication—prioritized for future experimental investigation. Fourth, we will develop Predictive Frameworks linking cytoskeletal organization to emergent cellular properties, enabling prediction of mechanical behaviors and migration modes from interactome architecture.

Scientific Impact: This project will transform understanding of cytoskeletal biology by establishing principles governing multi-system integration. By revealing how molecular interactions produce cellular-scale properties, we directly address NCEMS's focus on mesoscale emergence. Our findings will resolve longstanding questions about cytoskeletal coordination while generating new hypotheses for experimental testing. The integration of structural, dynamic, and functional data will establish methodological templates for synthesis research in other cellular systems.

Broader Impact: Resources generated will accelerate research across cytoskeleton biology, mechanobiology, and cell migration fields. Disease researchers will gain tools for understanding cytoskeletal dysfunction in cancer, neurodegeneration, and cardiomyopathies. The training program will develop data-savvy scientists capable of synthesis research, addressing critical workforce needs. Our open science approach ensures broad accessibility and enables community contributions. Methodological innovations in multi-modal data integration will transfer to other biological synthesis projects, amplifying impact beyond cytoskeleton research.

The project establishes a new paradigm for understanding cellular organization—one based on integrated systems rather than isolated components—with implications extending throughout cell biology.

title: Synthesizing the Spatiotemporal Logic of Post-Translational Modification Crosstalk: From Molecular Signals to Emergent Cellular Decisions
abstract:
Post-translational modifications (PTMs) including phosphorylation, ubiquitination, acetylation, and methylation regulate virtually all cellular processes, yet how combinatorial PTM patterns—the PTM code—encode cellular decisions remains poorly understood. This proposal unites proteomics experts, systems biologists, structural biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available PTM data to decode the spatiotemporal logic of PTM crosstalk and its role in emergent cellular behaviors.

Individual PTMs have been extensively catalogued, but understanding their combinatorial logic requires integration across data types and conditions. We will synthesize PTM data from PhosphoSitePlus, UniProt, PRIDE, and ProteomeXchange, structural data revealing PTM effects on protein conformation, interaction data showing PTM-dependent binding, and phenotypic data connecting PTM patterns to cellular outcomes. Time-resolved PTM datasets will reveal dynamic crosstalk patterns.

Our first aim constructs a comprehensive PTM crosstalk network by integrating data on co-occurring modifications, sequential modifications, and mutually exclusive modifications. We will identify recurring crosstalk motifs and their functional consequences. Our second aim examines spatial organization of PTM signaling by integrating subcellular proteomics with PTM data to understand compartment-specific modification patterns. Our third aim connects PTM patterns to emergent cellular decisions including cell cycle progression, differentiation, and stress responses.

This project requires NCEMS support because decoding PTM crosstalk requires expertise spanning proteomics, structural biology, signaling biology, and computational modeling. The data integration challenge—connecting molecular modifications to cellular outcomes—requires diverse approaches. The scale of analysis and computational requirements exceed typical laboratory capabilities.

Our team includes researchers from six institutions spanning proteomics, structural biology, systems biology, and computational biology. We include early-career investigators, researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions, and international collaborators.

Deliverables include: (1) a comprehensive PTM crosstalk database with visualization tools, (2) predictive models for PTM pattern outcomes, (3) identification of PTM code rules for specific cellular decisions, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student rotations between proteomics and computational laboratories, workshops on PTM data analysis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses a fundamental question in cell biology: how do combinatorial PTM patterns encode emergent cellular behaviors? By synthesizing diverse PTM data, we will establish principles for understanding the PTM code and its role in cellular decision-making.
background_and_significance:
Post-translational modifications represent one of the most powerful mechanisms cells employ to dynamically regulate protein function, localization, and interactions. With over 400 distinct PTM types identified, these chemical modifications exponentially expand the functional proteome beyond what genomic information alone can encode. Phosphorylation, ubiquitination, acetylation, methylation, SUMOylation, and glycosylation represent the most extensively studied modifications, collectively affecting virtually every cellular process from metabolism to gene expression, cell division to apoptosis. Despite decades of research cataloguing individual PTMs, a fundamental mystery persists: how do combinations of modifications on single proteins or across protein networks encode specific cellular outcomes?

The concept of a "PTM code" analogous to the histone code has gained traction, suggesting that specific modification patterns carry information that determines cellular decisions. Evidence supports this hypothesis: phosphorylation can prime substrates for subsequent ubiquitination, acetylation can block phosphorylation sites, and methylation states can determine protein-protein interaction specificity. However, our understanding remains fragmented, derived primarily from focused studies on individual proteins or pathways. The field lacks a comprehensive, integrated view of how PTM crosstalk operates at the systems level to produce emergent cellular behaviors.

This knowledge gap persists not from lack of data but from insufficient synthesis. Public repositories now contain millions of PTM site annotations. PhosphoSitePlus catalogs over 400,000 non-redundant phosphorylation sites; UniProt contains comprehensive PTM annotations across organisms; PRIDE and ProteomeXchange archive thousands of proteomics datasets with PTM information. Additionally, structural databases reveal how modifications alter protein conformation, while interaction databases document PTM-dependent binding events. Time-resolved proteomics studies capture dynamic modification changes during cellular responses. Yet these data remain siloed, analyzed in isolation rather than integrated to reveal overarching principles.

The significance of understanding PTM crosstalk extends beyond fundamental biology. Dysregulated PTM signaling underlies numerous diseases including cancer, neurodegeneration, and metabolic disorders. Kinase inhibitors and other PTM-targeting therapeutics represent major drug classes, yet their effects on broader modification networks remain poorly predicted. A comprehensive understanding of PTM crosstalk logic would transform our ability to interpret disease mechanisms and design targeted interventions.

This project addresses NCEMS's core mission by investigating emergence at the mesoscale—the scale between individual biomolecules and organelles where PTM networks operate. Individual modifications represent molecular-scale events, but their combinatorial patterns and spatiotemporal dynamics create emergent signaling properties that determine cellular-scale outcomes. Understanding how molecular-level PTM information integrates across space and time to produce coherent cellular decisions represents a quintessential emergence question.

The timing for this synthesis is optimal. Data availability has reached critical mass, computational approaches including machine learning can now handle the complexity involved, and the field has matured conceptually to appreciate that reductionist approaches alone cannot crack the PTM code. Only through community-scale synthesis integrating diverse expertise can we decode how combinatorial PTM patterns encode emergent cellular behaviors, establishing principles that will guide molecular and cellular biology for decades.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses three interconnected research questions that progressively build from molecular-level PTM relationships to emergent cellular outcomes, each supported by testable hypotheses derived from preliminary observations in existing literature and datasets.

Research Question 1: What are the fundamental rules governing PTM crosstalk at the molecular level?

We hypothesize that PTM crosstalk follows predictable patterns based on structural constraints, enzymatic relationships, and evolutionary conservation. Specifically, we propose: (H1a) Co-occurring PTMs cluster in structurally accessible regions and follow distance constraints that reflect the physical requirements of modifying enzyme access. (H1b) Sequential modification relationships form hierarchical networks where "master" modifications gate subsequent modifications through conserved motifs. (H1c) Mutually exclusive modifications compete through direct steric interference or through shared regulatory enzymes, creating binary switches. (H1d) Crosstalk patterns are evolutionarily conserved for functionally critical regulatory nodes but diverge for species-specific adaptations. These hypotheses will be tested by integrating structural data with PTM annotations to identify spatial constraints, analyzing time-resolved datasets to establish temporal relationships, and comparing crosstalk patterns across species to assess conservation.

Research Question 2: How does subcellular compartmentalization organize PTM signaling networks?

We hypothesize that spatial organization creates distinct PTM microenvironments that enable parallel processing of modification signals. Specifically: (H2a) Different subcellular compartments exhibit characteristic PTM signatures reflecting compartment-specific enzyme localization and substrate availability. (H2b) Proteins that shuttle between compartments undergo compartment-specific modification changes that encode localization history. (H2c) Membrane-proximal regions show distinct PTM patterns compared to cytosolic domains, reflecting membrane-associated kinase and phosphatase activities. (H2d) Phase-separated condensates create PTM hotspots where modification rates and crosstalk patterns differ from bulk cytoplasm. These hypotheses will be tested by integrating subcellular proteomics datasets with PTM data, analyzing membrane topology predictions alongside modification sites, and examining PTM patterns in proteins associated with biomolecular condensates.

Research Question 3: How do combinatorial PTM patterns encode emergent cellular decisions?

We hypothesize that specific PTM pattern combinations function as cellular decision codes that determine phenotypic outcomes. Specifically: (H3a) Cell cycle transitions are governed by characteristic PTM signatures on key regulatory proteins, with combinatorial patterns rather than individual modifications determining transition timing. (H3b) Differentiation trajectories correlate with progressive PTM pattern changes that precede transcriptional changes, suggesting PTMs encode early commitment signals. (H3c) Stress responses employ distinct PTM pattern languages depending on stress type, with shared "alarm" modifications combined with stress-specific secondary patterns. (H3d) PTM patterns exhibit bistability and hysteresis properties that enable robust cellular decision-making despite noisy inputs. These hypotheses will be tested by correlating PTM datasets with phenotypic annotations, analyzing time-course data spanning cellular transitions, and applying dynamical systems modeling to identify switch-like behaviors.

Methodologically, we also address: How can machine learning approaches best capture the combinatorial complexity of PTM crosstalk? We hypothesize that graph neural networks operating on PTM interaction networks will outperform traditional sequence-based approaches because they can capture relational information between modifications. Additionally, we hypothesize that attention mechanisms will reveal interpretable PTM crosstalk rules that align with biochemical knowledge, providing validation and novel insights.

These questions and hypotheses directly address NCEMS's focus on emergence by examining how molecular-level modifications combine to produce mesoscale signaling networks that ultimately determine cellular-scale outcomes. The hierarchical structure—from molecular rules to spatial organization to cellular decisions—maps onto the scales of emergence that NCEMS prioritizes.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates data acquisition, harmonization, network construction, machine learning, and validation through four interconnected workflows executed collaboratively across our multi-institutional team.

Workflow 1: Comprehensive Data Acquisition and Harmonization
We will systematically acquire PTM data from PhosphoSitePlus (phosphorylation, ubiquitination, acetylation, methylation), UniProt (curated PTM annotations), dbPTM (integrated PTM resources), and raw proteomics data from PRIDE/ProteomeXchange repositories. Structural data will be obtained from PDB and AlphaFold databases, interaction data from BioGRID, IntAct, and STRING, and phenotypic data from Cell Atlas, Human Protein Atlas, and GEO. We estimate integration of over 50 million PTM site observations across conditions.

Data harmonization presents significant challenges due to inconsistent nomenclature, varying confidence levels, and different experimental contexts. We will develop a unified PTM ontology mapping terms across databases, implement confidence scoring based on evidence type and reproducibility, and create standardized metadata schemas capturing experimental conditions. All harmonization code will be version-controlled and publicly released.

Workflow 2: PTM Crosstalk Network Construction
We will construct multi-layer networks representing PTM relationships. The first layer captures co-occurrence relationships using statistical methods (hypergeometric tests, mutual information) to identify modifications appearing together more frequently than expected. The second layer captures temporal relationships by analyzing time-resolved datasets to identify sequential modification patterns using temporal association rule mining. The third layer captures antagonistic relationships where modifications are mutually exclusive. The fourth layer integrates structural constraints by mapping modifications onto protein structures to assess spatial feasibility of co-occurrence.

Network analysis will identify recurring motifs (feed-forward loops, bistable switches, amplification cascades) using established motif-finding algorithms adapted for multi-layer networks. We will assess motif enrichment compared to randomized networks preserving degree distributions.

Workflow 3: Spatial Integration and Compartment Analysis
We will integrate subcellular proteomics datasets (from spatial proteomics studies using methods like LOPIT, hyperLOPIT, and proximity labeling) with PTM annotations. Compartment-specific PTM profiles will be constructed by aggregating modifications on proteins localized to each compartment. Statistical comparisons will identify compartment-enriched modifications and crosstalk patterns. For proteins with multiple localizations, we will analyze whether PTM patterns correlate with localization states.

Workflow 4: Machine Learning for Pattern Recognition and Prediction
We will develop graph neural network models operating on PTM crosstalk networks to predict cellular outcomes from modification patterns. Input features include PTM site properties (sequence context, structural accessibility, conservation), network topology features (centrality, clustering), and temporal dynamics features where available. Output predictions include cellular phenotypes (proliferation, differentiation, stress response) linked to PTM datasets through metadata.

Model architectures will include graph attention networks that learn which PTM relationships most strongly predict outcomes, providing interpretability. We will implement cross-validation schemes that prevent data leakage between training and testing, using held-out cell types or conditions for validation.

Workflow 5: Validation and Hypothesis Generation
Predicted PTM crosstalk rules will be validated against known biochemistry, with literature mining to assess whether predicted relationships have experimental support. Novel predictions will be prioritized for experimental testing by collaborators outside this synthesis project, generating testable hypotheses as key deliverables.

Computational Infrastructure
Analysis requires substantial computational resources including GPU clusters for machine learning, high-memory nodes for network analysis, and storage for integrated datasets. We will utilize NCEMS computational resources supplemented by institutional HPC allocations. All pipelines will be containerized (Docker/Singularity) for reproducibility.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will generate multiple tangible outcomes with broad impact on molecular and cellular biology research.

Primary Deliverables:
(1) The PTM Crosstalk Atlas: A comprehensive, queryable database integrating PTM co-occurrence, temporal relationships, antagonistic interactions, and structural constraints across organisms and conditions. This resource will include visualization tools enabling researchers to explore crosstalk patterns for proteins of interest, compare patterns across conditions, and identify potential regulatory relationships. The Atlas will be hosted on stable infrastructure with API access for programmatic queries.

(2) Predictive Models: Machine learning models predicting cellular outcomes from PTM patterns, with associated confidence metrics. These models will be released as user-friendly tools allowing researchers to input PTM data and receive predictions about likely cellular states, facilitating hypothesis generation for their experimental systems.

(3) PTM Code Rulebook: A curated compilation of validated PTM crosstalk rules organized by cellular process (cell cycle, differentiation, stress response), including confidence levels and supporting evidence. This rulebook will serve as a reference for the field, analogous to how the histone code has guided chromatin biology.

(4) Experimentally Testable Hypotheses: Prioritized predictions for novel PTM crosstalk relationships with high confidence scores but lacking experimental validation, providing roadmaps for experimental laboratories.

Scientific Impact:
This project will transform understanding of how molecular modifications encode cellular decisions, establishing principles that explain emergent behaviors from molecular components. By revealing the logic of PTM crosstalk, we enable predictive understanding of signaling networks rather than purely descriptive cataloguing. The spatial analysis will establish how compartmentalization organizes information processing, connecting to NCEMS's mesoscale focus.

Broader Impact:
Resources developed will accelerate research across biology, enabling any laboratory studying PTM-regulated processes to leverage our integrated data and predictive tools. Training activities will develop a cohort of researchers skilled in synthesis science approaches. Open release of all methods establishes templates for future synthesis projects. Understanding PTM crosstalk logic has translational implications for diseases involving signaling dysregulation, potentially informing therapeutic strategies targeting modification networks rather than individual enzymes.

title: The Emergent Architecture of Stress Granules: Multi-Modal Data Synthesis to Understand Assembly, Composition, and Function
abstract:
Stress granules are membraneless organelles that form in response to cellular stress, sequestering mRNAs and proteins to regulate gene expression, yet the principles governing their emergent properties remain incompletely understood. This proposal assembles RNA biologists, structural biologists, cell biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode stress granule organization and function.

Stress granules represent a paradigmatic example of mesoscale cellular organization, forming through phase separation of RNA-binding proteins and mRNAs. However, comprehensive understanding of their composition, dynamics, and functional consequences is lacking. We will integrate proteomics data from stress granule purifications, RNA sequencing data identifying granule-associated transcripts, structural data on component proteins, imaging data revealing granule dynamics, and phenotypic data connecting granule properties to cellular outcomes.

Our first aim constructs a comprehensive stress granule component database by synthesizing proteomics and RNA sequencing data across stress conditions, cell types, and organisms. We will identify core versus stress-specific components and predict new components. Our second aim examines stress granule architecture by integrating structural data, crosslinking mass spectrometry, and super-resolution imaging to understand internal organization. Our third aim connects stress granule properties to functional outcomes by integrating composition data with transcriptomics, translatomics, and phenotypic measurements.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding stress granules requires expertise spanning RNA biology, protein biochemistry, structural biology, and cell biology. Data integration across proteomics, transcriptomics, and imaging modalities requires specialized computational approaches. The collaborative framework enables insights impossible through individual laboratory efforts.

Our team includes researchers from seven institutions spanning RNA biology, structural biology, cell biology, and computational biology. We include researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions and various career stages.

Expected outcomes include: (1) a comprehensive stress granule component database, (2) models of stress granule architecture and assembly, (3) identification of functional modules within granules, and (4) predictions linking granule properties to cellular stress responses. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student exchanges between laboratories, workshops on membraneless organelle analysis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about mesoscale cellular organization: how do stress granules assemble, what determines their composition, and how do their emergent properties influence cellular stress responses?
background_and_significance:
Stress granules (SGs) represent one of the most compelling examples of emergent biological organization at the mesoscale. These membraneless organelles form rapidly in response to diverse cellular stresses—including heat shock, oxidative stress, viral infection, and nutrient deprivation—through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) and mRNAs. Unlike membrane-bound organelles, stress granules lack a lipid bilayer boundary, instead relying on multivalent protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions to maintain their structural integrity. This unique organization places stress granules squarely within NCEMS's focus on mesoscale phenomena, where emergent properties arise from the collective behavior of molecular components.

The biological significance of stress granules extends far beyond their role as temporary mRNA storage depots. These structures serve as critical regulators of gene expression during stress, selectively sequestering specific transcripts while allowing others to remain translationally active. Recent evidence suggests that stress granules function as signaling hubs, concentrating kinases, phosphatases, and other regulatory proteins to coordinate cellular stress responses. Furthermore, aberrant stress granule dynamics have been implicated in numerous human diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), frontotemporal dementia, and certain cancers, where mutations in SG components lead to pathological protein aggregation.

Despite intensive study over the past two decades, fundamental questions about stress granule biology remain unanswered. First, while hundreds of proteins have been identified in stress granules, the complete compositional landscape across different stress conditions, cell types, and organisms remains fragmented across disparate datasets. Second, the internal architecture of stress granules—whether they possess substructural organization, how components are spatially arranged, and how this organization relates to function—is poorly understood. Third, the functional consequences of stress granule formation on cellular outcomes remain incompletely characterized, with conflicting reports about whether granules are protective or detrimental during stress.

The current state of stress granule research presents a unique opportunity for synthesis science. Publicly available datasets have proliferated dramatically, including mass spectrometry-based proteomics from granule purifications, RNA sequencing identifying granule-associated transcripts, structural data from the Protein Data Bank, super-resolution and electron microscopy imaging data, and phenotypic datasets linking granule properties to cellular outcomes. However, these data exist in isolation, analyzed within individual studies without systematic integration. No comprehensive resource synthesizes this information to provide a unified view of stress granule biology.

This fragmentation represents both a challenge and an opportunity perfectly suited to NCEMS's mission. The complexity of stress granule organization—spanning molecular, mesoscale, and cellular levels—requires integration of diverse data types that no single laboratory possesses the expertise to accomplish. Our proposal directly addresses this gap by assembling a multidisciplinary team capable of synthesizing proteomics, transcriptomics, structural biology, imaging, and phenotypic data to generate transformative insights into stress granule emergence. Understanding how stress granules assemble, organize, and function will illuminate fundamental principles of mesoscale cellular organization applicable to other membraneless organelles and phase-separated condensates.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses three interconnected research questions that span molecular to cellular scales, each supported by testable hypotheses derived from preliminary data synthesis and current literature.

Research Question 1: What is the comprehensive compositional landscape of stress granules, and how does composition vary across stress conditions, cell types, and organisms?

Hypothesis 1a: Stress granules possess a conserved core of approximately 50-100 proteins and RNAs that are present across all stress conditions and cell types, with additional stress-specific and cell-type-specific components representing condition-dependent modularity. We predict that core components will be enriched for proteins containing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and RNA-binding domains, while peripheral components will show greater functional diversity.

Hypothesis 1b: Machine learning models trained on known stress granule components can accurately predict novel granule-associated proteins and RNAs by identifying shared sequence features, structural properties, and interaction patterns. We hypothesize that prediction accuracy will exceed 80% when validated against held-out datasets.

Research Question 2: What is the internal architecture of stress granules, and how do molecular interactions give rise to mesoscale organization?

Hypothesis 2a: Stress granules exhibit a core-shell architecture with distinct protein and RNA compositions in different spatial zones. We predict that scaffold proteins (G3BP1/2, TIA1) concentrate in granule cores, while client proteins show peripheral localization. This hypothesis is supported by preliminary analysis of super-resolution imaging data suggesting non-uniform protein distributions.

Hypothesis 2b: Specific protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction networks determine stress granule architecture, with hub proteins mediating connections between functional modules. We hypothesize that integration of crosslinking mass spectrometry data with structural predictions will reveal hierarchical organization, where primary scaffolds recruit secondary scaffolds that in turn recruit client proteins.

Hypothesis 2c: RNA secondary structure and length influence transcript localization within stress granules. We predict that longer transcripts with complex secondary structures localize to granule cores, while shorter, less structured RNAs occupy peripheral regions.

Research Question 3: How do stress granule composition and architecture influence cellular outcomes during and after stress?

Hypothesis 3a: Stress granule composition directly determines which mRNAs are translationally repressed during stress and which are rapidly re-engaged upon stress recovery. We predict that transcripts encoding stress response proteins will be selectively excluded from granules, maintaining their translation during stress.

Hypothesis 3b: Stress granule size, number, and dynamics correlate with cellular survival outcomes in a stress-type-dependent manner. We hypothesize that optimal granule formation (neither too few nor too many) correlates with maximum cell survival, suggesting a "Goldilocks" model of stress granule function.

Hypothesis 3c: Disease-associated mutations in stress granule proteins alter granule composition and architecture in predictable ways that correlate with pathological outcomes. We predict that ALS-associated mutations will shift granule composition toward more solid-like states with reduced dynamics and altered RNA content.

These hypotheses are specifically designed to be testable through synthesis of existing public data. Each hypothesis generates specific predictions that can be evaluated by integrating multiple data modalities. Importantly, our approach allows hypothesis refinement through iterative data analysis—initial findings will inform updated hypotheses that guide subsequent synthesis efforts. This hypothesis-driven framework ensures that our data integration efforts are scientifically focused rather than purely descriptive, generating mechanistic insights into stress granule emergence that advance fundamental understanding of mesoscale cellular organization.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates diverse publicly available datasets through a structured three-aim framework, employing state-of-the-art computational methods and leveraging the complementary expertise of our multidisciplinary team.

Aim 1: Constructing a Comprehensive Stress Granule Component Database

We will systematically compile proteomics data from stress granule purification studies deposited in PRIDE, MassIVE, and ProteomeXchange repositories. Our preliminary survey identified >50 relevant datasets spanning human, mouse, yeast, and other model organisms. We will standardize data processing using MaxQuant and implement consistent statistical thresholds for component identification. RNA sequencing data identifying granule-associated transcripts will be retrieved from GEO and ArrayExpress, including CLIP-seq data for RNA-binding proteins and fractionation-based approaches. Integration will employ Bayesian statistical frameworks to assign confidence scores to each component based on evidence across multiple studies. Machine learning approaches (random forests, gradient boosting, and neural networks) will be trained on validated components to predict novel granule-associated proteins and RNAs using features including sequence composition, predicted disorder, RNA-binding propensity, and protein-protein interaction networks. Cross-validation will assess prediction accuracy, with top predictions prioritized for community validation.

Aim 2: Modeling Stress Granule Architecture

Structural data will be retrieved from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and AlphaFold Database for all identified stress granule components. We will analyze domain architectures, intrinsically disordered regions (using IUPred3, PONDR), and low-complexity sequences to understand structural features enabling phase separation. Crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) data from published studies will be compiled and analyzed using xQuest/xProphet pipelines to identify protein-protein contacts within granules. These distance constraints will be integrated with structural models using integrative modeling approaches (Integrative Modeling Platform) to generate three-dimensional architectural models. Super-resolution microscopy data (STORM, PALM, SIM) and electron microscopy images from public repositories (EMPIAR, Cell Image Library) will be analyzed using custom image analysis pipelines to quantify granule morphology, protein distributions, and substructural features. Spatial statistics methods will assess core-shell organization and component colocalization. Integration across data modalities will employ constraint-based modeling, where XL-MS distance restraints, structural predictions, and imaging-derived spatial information collectively inform architectural models.

Aim 3: Connecting Composition to Function

We will integrate stress granule composition data with transcriptomics and translatomics datasets (ribosome profiling, polysome profiling) to identify relationships between granule sequestration and translational regulation. Network analysis will identify functional modules within granules—groups of components that co-occur and share functional annotations. Phenotypic data from genome-wide screens (DepMap, published CRISPR screens) will be analyzed to identify stress granule components whose perturbation affects cellular stress responses. Correlation analyses will link granule properties (composition, size, dynamics) with cellular outcomes across conditions.

Computational Infrastructure and Collaboration

All analyses will be implemented in reproducible workflows using Snakemake and Nextflow, with code maintained in public GitHub repositories. The team will employ cloud computing resources (AWS, Google Cloud) for computationally intensive analyses. Monthly virtual meetings and biannual in-person workshops will ensure integration across aims and institutions. A dedicated data management team will maintain database infrastructure and ensure FAIR data principles compliance throughout the project.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will generate multiple transformative outcomes advancing our understanding of mesoscale cellular organization.

Primary Deliverables:

1) The Stress Granule Atlas: A comprehensive, searchable database cataloging all validated and predicted stress granule components across organisms, cell types, and stress conditions. This resource will include confidence scores, supporting evidence, and functional annotations for each component, serving as the definitive reference for the stress granule research community.

2) Architectural Models: Data-constrained three-dimensional models of stress granule organization revealing internal structure, protein-protein interaction networks, and RNA localization patterns. These models will provide the first integrated view of mesoscale granule architecture.

3) Functional Module Maps: Network representations identifying functional subunits within stress granules, revealing how composition relates to specific cellular functions including translational control, signaling, and RNA metabolism.

4) Predictive Framework: Machine learning models capable of predicting novel stress granule components and forecasting how compositional changes affect granule properties and cellular outcomes.

5) Analysis Pipelines: Documented, reproducible computational workflows for integrating multi-modal data applicable to other membraneless organelles and phase-separated condensates.

Broader Impact:

Our findings will establish general principles governing emergent properties of membraneless organelles, directly addressing NCEMS's mission to understand mesoscale phenomena. The resources generated will accelerate research across the stress granule community and provide templates for studying other condensates (P-bodies, nucleoli, paraspeckles). Disease-relevant insights will inform therapeutic strategies targeting aberrant phase separation in neurodegeneration. Training activities will develop the next generation of data-savvy scientists capable of synthesis research. All outcomes will be disseminated through publications, conference presentations, and public databases, maximizing scientific impact and community benefit.

title: Decoding Emergent Metabolic Channeling: Synthesizing Structural, Interaction, and Flux Data to Understand Metabolon Organization
abstract:
Metabolic enzymes often organize into transient complexes called metabolons that channel substrates between sequential reactions, yet the principles governing metabolon formation and their emergent effects on cellular metabolism remain poorly understood. This proposal unites structural biologists, metabolic biochemists, systems biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode metabolon organization and function.

Metabolic channeling enhances pathway efficiency and enables regulatory control, but metabolons are challenging to study due to their transient nature. We will integrate protein interaction data from BioGRID, IntAct, and proximity labeling studies, structural data from PDB and AlphaFold, metabolomics data from MetaboLights and Metabolomics Workbench, flux measurements, and subcellular localization data. Cross-species comparisons will identify conserved channeling principles.

Our first aim maps the metabolon interaction landscape by synthesizing protein-protein interaction data for metabolic enzymes across pathways and organisms. We will identify recurring interaction patterns and predict new metabolon components. Our second aim examines metabolon architecture by integrating structural data with interaction information to model how enzymes organize for substrate channeling. Our third aim connects metabolon organization to emergent metabolic properties by integrating interaction data with flux measurements and metabolomics to understand how channeling affects pathway behavior.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding metabolons requires expertise spanning structural biology, enzymology, systems biology, and computational modeling. Data integration across interaction, structural, and metabolic data types requires diverse approaches. The collaborative framework enables comprehensive analysis impossible for individual laboratories.

Our team includes researchers from six institutions spanning structural biology, biochemistry, systems biology, and computational biology. We include early-career investigators and researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions.

Deliverables include: (1) a metabolon interaction database, (2) structural models of metabolon organization, (3) predictive models linking metabolon formation to metabolic outcomes, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student rotations between structural and systems biology laboratories, workshops on metabolon analysis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about metabolic organization: how do enzymes organize into metabolons, and how does this mesoscale organization produce emergent metabolic properties?
background_and_significance:
Cellular metabolism has traditionally been conceptualized as a network of discrete enzymatic reactions occurring in a well-mixed cytoplasmic environment. However, accumulating evidence reveals that metabolic enzymes frequently organize into transient supramolecular assemblies termed metabolons, which channel substrates directly between sequential enzymes without equilibration with the bulk cytosol. This mesoscale organization represents a fundamental yet incompletely understood principle of cellular biochemistry that produces emergent metabolic properties not predictable from individual enzyme kinetics alone.

Metabolons were first proposed by Paul Srere in the 1980s based on observations of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle enzymes, and subsequent studies have identified channeling complexes in glycolysis, the Calvin cycle, purine biosynthesis, phenylpropanoid metabolism, and numerous other pathways across all domains of life. Substrate channeling within metabolons provides several theoretical advantages: enhanced pathway flux through reduced transit times, protection of unstable intermediates, prevention of competing reactions, and creation of localized metabolite pools enabling sophisticated regulatory control. Despite decades of research, critical questions remain unanswered: What molecular features determine which enzymes form metabolons? How do metabolon architectures enable efficient substrate transfer? How does channeling quantitatively affect pathway behavior and cellular phenotypes?

The transient and context-dependent nature of metabolon assembly has historically impeded systematic investigation. However, the current landscape of publicly available data presents an unprecedented opportunity for synthesis research. Protein-protein interaction databases (BioGRID, IntAct, STRING) now contain millions of interactions including numerous metabolic enzyme pairs identified through affinity purification, yeast two-hybrid, and proximity labeling approaches. The Protein Data Bank houses over 200,000 structures including many metabolic enzymes, while AlphaFold has provided predicted structures for nearly all known proteins. Metabolomics repositories (MetaboLights, Metabolomics Workbench) contain thousands of datasets spanning diverse organisms, conditions, and perturbations. Fluxomics studies have quantified pathway activities under varied conditions. Subcellular proteomics datasets reveal enzyme localization patterns suggesting spatial organization.

Integrating these disparate data types to understand metabolon organization and function represents a quintessential mesoscale problem ideally suited for NCEMS support. Metabolons exist at the interface between individual biomolecules and organelle-level organization, precisely the mesoscale domain where emergent properties arise from collective molecular behaviors. Understanding how enzyme-enzyme interactions produce emergent metabolic properties—flux enhancement, intermediate protection, regulatory coupling—requires synthesizing structural, interaction, and functional data in ways that transcend traditional disciplinary boundaries.

This synthesis project addresses fundamental questions about biological organization with broad significance. Metabolon dysfunction has been implicated in metabolic diseases, cancer metabolism, and microbial pathogenesis. Understanding channeling principles could inform metabolic engineering for biotechnology applications. More fundamentally, metabolons exemplify how transient molecular assemblies create emergent cellular properties, providing insights applicable to other mesoscale phenomena including signaling complexes, transcriptional condensates, and cytoskeletal assemblies. By systematically synthesizing existing data to decode metabolon organization, this project will establish principles governing emergence at the mesoscale while generating testable hypotheses for future experimental investigation.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This synthesis project addresses three interconnected research questions that together illuminate the principles governing metabolon organization and emergent metabolic properties.

Research Question 1: What interaction patterns define the metabolon landscape across metabolic pathways and organisms?

We hypothesize that metabolon formation follows conserved organizational principles reflecting both pathway topology and physicochemical constraints on substrate channeling. Specifically, we predict that: (H1a) Enzymes catalyzing sequential reactions with chemically unstable or membrane-permeable intermediates will show enriched physical interactions compared to enzymes with stable intermediates, reflecting selective pressure for channeling; (H1b) Metabolon interaction networks will exhibit modular organization corresponding to pathway branch points and regulatory nodes; (H1c) Core metabolon components will be conserved across species while peripheral interactions will show lineage-specific variation reflecting metabolic adaptation. Testing these hypotheses requires systematic synthesis of protein-protein interaction data for metabolic enzymes across multiple organisms and pathways, analysis that exceeds the scope of individual laboratories.

Research Question 2: How do metabolon architectures enable efficient substrate channeling between enzyme active sites?

We hypothesize that metabolon organization reflects structural optimization for substrate transfer through specific architectural features. Our predictions include: (H2a) Interacting metabolic enzymes will display complementary surface electrostatics creating favorable pathways for charged intermediate transfer; (H2b) Active site geometries in metabolon partners will show spatial arrangements minimizing diffusion distances, with inter-active-site distances typically below 50 Angstroms; (H2c) Metabolon interfaces will feature conformational flexibility enabling dynamic assembly and disassembly in response to metabolic demand. Addressing these hypotheses requires integration of structural data with interaction information to model metabolon architectures, demanding expertise spanning structural biology, molecular modeling, and enzymology.

Research Question 3: How does metabolon organization produce emergent effects on pathway flux, metabolite pools, and cellular phenotypes?

We hypothesize that metabolon formation creates emergent metabolic properties not predictable from individual enzyme parameters. Specifically: (H3a) Pathways with documented metabolon formation will show flux-intermediate relationships inconsistent with free diffusion models, exhibiting higher flux at lower intermediate concentrations; (H3b) Genetic or pharmacological perturbations disrupting metabolon interactions will produce disproportionate effects on pathway flux relative to effects on individual enzyme activities; (H3c) Metabolon formation will correlate with pathway-level regulatory responses including feedback inhibition and feedforward activation, suggesting channeling enables sophisticated metabolic control. Testing these hypotheses requires integration of interaction data with metabolomics and fluxomics measurements across conditions and perturbations.

Cross-cutting Methodological Questions:

Beyond these biological questions, our synthesis addresses methodological challenges in integrating heterogeneous data types. How can interaction data of varying quality and methodology be appropriately weighted for synthesis? What statistical frameworks best identify conserved interaction patterns across species with different data coverage? How can structural models of transient complexes be validated against functional data? Addressing these questions will yield analytical approaches applicable to other mesoscale synthesis problems.

Our hypotheses generate specific, testable predictions that will be evaluated through systematic data synthesis. Importantly, hypothesis rejection will be equally informative, revealing where current models of metabolon organization require revision. The collaborative framework enables rigorous hypothesis testing by bringing together expertise in interaction data analysis, structural modeling, and metabolic systems biology.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates three complementary synthesis strategies corresponding to our research aims, unified by a common data infrastructure and collaborative analytical framework.

Data Acquisition and Harmonization:

We will systematically compile metabolic enzyme interaction data from BioGRID (>2.5 million interactions), IntAct (>1.1 million interactions), and STRING (functional associations). Proximity labeling datasets from BioID and APEX studies will provide spatial interaction information. We will extract metabolic enzyme subsets using enzyme classification numbers mapped through UniProt, focusing initially on central carbon metabolism, amino acid biosynthesis, and nucleotide metabolism where metabolon evidence exists. Structural data will be obtained from PDB (experimental structures) and AlphaFold Database (predicted structures). Metabolomics data from MetaboLights (>5,000 studies) and Metabolomics Workbench (>3,000 studies) will be harmonized using standardized metabolite identifiers (ChEBI, HMDB). Flux data will be compiled from published 13C-metabolic flux analyses. All data will be organized in a unified schema enabling cross-referencing between interaction, structural, and metabolic information.

Aim 1: Mapping the Metabolon Interaction Landscape

We will construct pathway-specific enzyme interaction networks for each metabolic pathway across multiple organisms (human, mouse, yeast, E. coli, Arabidopsis). Network analysis will identify statistically enriched interactions between sequential enzymes compared to random enzyme pairs, controlling for expression correlation and subcellular co-localization. Machine learning approaches (random forests, graph neural networks) will identify interaction features predicting metabolon membership, including sequence motifs, domain architectures, and physicochemical properties. Cross-species conservation analysis using ortholog mapping will distinguish core versus peripheral metabolon components. Predicted novel metabolon interactions will be scored by confidence level and prioritized for experimental validation.

Aim 2: Modeling Metabolon Architecture

For enzyme pairs with high-confidence interactions, we will model complex structures using integrative approaches combining experimental structures, AlphaFold predictions, and protein-protein docking (HADDOCK, ClusPro). Docking will be constrained by interaction data including interface residues from crosslinking mass spectrometry studies where available. We will analyze modeled complexes for channeling-relevant features: inter-active-site distances, electrostatic surface complementarity, and potential substrate transfer pathways. Molecular dynamics simulations will assess interface stability and conformational dynamics. Multi-enzyme assemblies will be modeled iteratively, building from pairwise interactions to higher-order complexes. Structural models will be validated against available cryo-EM densities and crosslinking data.

Aim 3: Connecting Organization to Emergent Properties

We will develop quantitative models linking metabolon organization to metabolic behavior. For pathways with sufficient metabolomics and flux data, we will compare observed flux-intermediate relationships to predictions from channeling versus free-diffusion models. Statistical analysis will test whether metabolon interaction strength correlates with pathway flux efficiency across conditions. We will analyze genetic perturbation datasets to assess whether disruption of predicted metabolon interactions produces disproportionate metabolic effects. Machine learning models will predict metabolic phenotypes from metabolon organization features, with performance assessed through cross-validation.

Collaborative Integration:

Bi-weekly virtual meetings will coordinate analysis across teams. Annual in-person workshops at NCEMS will enable intensive collaborative analysis sessions. A shared computational environment will ensure reproducibility and enable real-time collaboration. Each aim involves researchers from multiple institutions, ensuring cross-disciplinary integration throughout the project.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will generate multiple tangible outcomes advancing understanding of metabolon organization and emergent metabolic properties while providing resources enabling future research.

Primary Deliverables:

The Metabolon Interaction Database will provide the first comprehensive, curated resource of metabolic enzyme interactions organized by pathway, organism, and evidence type. This database will include confidence scores, conservation information, and links to structural and functional data, serving as a foundational resource for the metabolic research community.

Structural Models of Metabolon Organization will comprise atomic-resolution models of metabolon architectures for major metabolic pathways, annotated with channeling-relevant features including active site geometries, electrostatic surfaces, and predicted substrate transfer pathways. These models will generate specific hypotheses for experimental testing through mutagenesis and crosslinking studies.

Predictive Models Linking Organization to Function will quantitatively relate metabolon structural features to emergent metabolic properties. These models will enable prediction of channeling efficiency from structural information and identification of metabolon perturbations likely to produce significant metabolic effects.

Hypothesis Sets for Experimental Validation will include prioritized predictions of novel metabolon components, critical interface residues, and expected metabolic consequences of metabolon disruption, providing a roadmap for future experimental studies.

Scientific Impact:

This project will establish general principles governing metabolon organization, transforming understanding of metabolic pathway function from reaction-centric to organization-centric perspectives. Insights will inform metabolic engineering strategies exploiting channeling for improved pathway efficiency. Understanding of metabolon dysfunction will illuminate disease mechanisms and potential therapeutic targets.

Broader Impact:

Methodological advances in integrating heterogeneous biological data will be applicable to other mesoscale synthesis challenges. Training activities will develop data synthesis skills in the next-generation workforce. Open resources will enable research at institutions lacking specialized infrastructure. The collaborative framework will serve as a model for future NCEMS working groups addressing emergence phenomena.

Travel support for graduate student rotations between laboratories will facilitate cross-training in structural biology and systems biology approaches. Conference travel will enable dissemination of results and community engagement.

Database hosting and web server costs will ensure public accessibility of project resources. Software licenses for specialized structural analysis tools will enable comprehensive modeling.

Training and Outreach (5% of budget):

Workshop materials development and hosting costs will support annual training workshops. Undergraduate mentoring activities at primarily undergraduate institutions will broaden participation.

NCEMS Support Justification:
