title: The Emergence of Synaptic Organization: Integrating Proteomic, Structural, and Functional Data Across Synaptic Compartments
abstract:
Synapses are highly organized structures enabling neuronal communication, yet how molecular components organize to produce emergent synaptic properties remains incompletely understood. This proposal assembles neuroscientists, structural biologists, proteomics experts, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode synaptic organization principles.

Synapses contain thousands of proteins organized into presynaptic and postsynaptic compartments with distinct functions. We will integrate synaptic proteomics data, structural data on synaptic protein complexes, super-resolution imaging data, electrophysiology measurements, and disease-associated variant information from psychiatric and neurological conditions.

Our first aim maps synaptic protein organization by synthesizing proteomics data across synaptic compartments, developmental stages, and brain regions. We will identify organizational modules and their compositional variation. Our second aim examines synaptic architecture by integrating structural data with localization information to understand nanoscale organization. Our third aim connects synaptic organization to emergent functional properties by integrating compositional and structural data with electrophysiological measurements.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding synaptic organization requires expertise spanning neuroscience, structural biology, and proteomics. Data integration across proteomic, structural, and functional data types requires diverse approaches. The collaborative framework enables comprehensive analysis impossible for individual laboratories.

Our team includes researchers from eight institutions spanning neuroscience, structural biology, and computational biology. We include researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions and various career stages.

Expected outcomes include: (1) an integrated synaptic organization database, (2) models of synaptic architecture, (3) predictions linking organization to function, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student exchanges, workshops on synaptic biology, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about neural organization: how does molecular organization produce emergent synaptic properties?
background_and_significance:
Synapses represent one of the most striking examples of emergent biological organization, where thousands of molecular components assemble into functional units capable of information processing, plasticity, and adaptation. The postsynaptic density alone contains over 1,500 distinct proteins, while the presynaptic active zone harbors hundreds of additional components essential for neurotransmitter release. Despite decades of research characterizing individual synaptic proteins, we lack a comprehensive understanding of how these components organize spatially and temporally to produce emergent functional properties such as synaptic strength, plasticity, and reliability.

This knowledge gap exists precisely at the mesoscale—the interface between individual biomolecules and functional organelles—that NCEMS prioritizes. Synapses operate through emergent properties that cannot be predicted from individual protein functions alone. For example, the precise stoichiometry of AMPA receptors, scaffolding proteins like PSD-95, and regulatory enzymes determines synaptic strength, yet how this stoichiometry is established and maintained remains unclear. Similarly, the nanoscale alignment between presynaptic vesicle release sites and postsynaptic receptor clusters—termed trans-synaptic nanocolumns—represents an emergent organizational principle discovered only recently through super-resolution microscopy.

The timing for this synthesis project is optimal because multiple large-scale datasets have become publicly available in recent years. Synaptic proteomics studies have catalogued thousands of proteins across different brain regions, developmental stages, and disease states. The Protein Data Bank contains structural information for hundreds of synaptic protein complexes. Super-resolution imaging studies have deposited localization data revealing nanoscale synaptic architecture. Electrophysiology databases contain functional measurements from thousands of synapses. Crucially, genome-wide association studies and exome sequencing have identified disease-associated variants in synaptic genes linked to autism, schizophrenia, and intellectual disability. However, these datasets remain siloed within their respective disciplines, preventing integrative analyses that could reveal organizational principles.

The significance of understanding synaptic organization extends beyond basic neuroscience. Synaptic dysfunction underlies numerous neurological and psychiatric conditions, yet therapeutic development is hampered by incomplete understanding of synaptic organization. By identifying how molecular organization produces emergent synaptic properties, this project will generate testable hypotheses about how disease-associated variants disrupt synaptic function.

This project addresses a long-standing puzzle in neuroscience: how do synapses achieve their remarkable functional diversity despite sharing a common molecular toolkit? Different synapse types exhibit distinct functional properties—from the high-fidelity transmission at neuromuscular junctions to the highly plastic synapses in hippocampus—yet utilize largely overlapping protein components. We hypothesize that emergent synaptic properties arise from variations in protein stoichiometry, spatial organization, and dynamic interactions rather than from unique molecular components. Testing this hypothesis requires integrating data across multiple scales and modalities, precisely the type of synthesis research that NCEMS enables.

The proposed working group brings together expertise that no single laboratory possesses: synaptic proteomics, structural biology, super-resolution imaging, computational modeling, and clinical genetics. This transdisciplinary collaboration will generate insights impossible through traditional single-laboratory approaches, addressing NCEMS's mission to catalyze community-scale synthesis research.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our overarching research question is: How does molecular organization at synapses produce emergent functional properties? We decompose this into three interconnected questions with specific, testable hypotheses.

Research Question 1: What organizational modules exist within synaptic proteomes, and how do they vary across compartments, brain regions, and development?

Hypothesis 1a: Synaptic proteins organize into discrete functional modules that are conserved across brain regions but vary in stoichiometry. We predict that network analysis of co-expression patterns across proteomics datasets will reveal 15-25 core modules corresponding to distinct functional processes (vesicle cycling, receptor trafficking, cytoskeletal organization, signaling cascades).

Hypothesis 1b: Module stoichiometry, rather than module presence/absence, distinguishes synapse types. We hypothesize that excitatory versus inhibitory synapses, and synapses from different brain regions, will contain the same core modules but with systematically different protein ratios that correlate with functional properties.

Hypothesis 1c: Developmental maturation involves coordinated shifts in module stoichiometry following predictable trajectories. We predict that immature synapses will show elevated ratios of plasticity-related modules relative to stability modules, with this ratio inverting during maturation.

Research Question 2: How does nanoscale spatial organization of synaptic proteins relate to their modular organization and structural properties?

Hypothesis 2a: Proteins within the same functional module exhibit correlated spatial distributions at the nanoscale. We predict that super-resolution localization data will show that co-modular proteins cluster together, while proteins from different modules occupy distinct nanoscale domains.

Hypothesis 2b: Structural constraints predict spatial organization. We hypothesize that protein complex structures from crystallography and cryo-EM will predict observed nanoscale distances between interacting proteins, allowing us to build spatially accurate models of synaptic architecture.

Hypothesis 2c: Trans-synaptic nanocolumn organization reflects coordinated pre- and postsynaptic module alignment. We predict that specific presynaptic modules (vesicle release machinery) align with specific postsynaptic modules (receptor clusters) through trans-synaptic adhesion protein bridges.

Research Question 3: How does synaptic organization produce emergent functional properties, and how do disease-associated variants disrupt this relationship?

Hypothesis 3a: Synaptic strength correlates with receptor module stoichiometry and nanoscale clustering. We predict that integrating proteomics data with electrophysiology measurements will reveal quantitative relationships between AMPA receptor abundance, PSD-95 levels, and miniature excitatory postsynaptic current amplitudes.

Hypothesis 3b: Synaptic plasticity capacity depends on the ratio of plasticity-promoting to stability-promoting modules. We hypothesize that synapses with higher ratios of CaMKII and related signaling proteins to structural scaffolds will show greater long-term potentiation magnitude.

Hypothesis 3c: Disease-associated variants cluster within specific organizational modules and disrupt module stoichiometry or spatial organization. We predict that autism-associated variants will preferentially affect plasticity modules, while schizophrenia-associated variants will target receptor trafficking modules, providing mechanistic explanations for distinct clinical phenotypes.

These hypotheses are testable through synthesis of existing data and generate specific predictions for future experimental validation. By connecting molecular organization to emergent properties, we address fundamental questions about how biological complexity arises from component interactions.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates diverse publicly available datasets through a unified computational framework, organized around three complementary aims.

Aim 1: Mapping Synaptic Protein Organization

Data Sources: We will compile proteomics data from SynaptomeDB, G2C database, and published synaptic fractionation studies encompassing over 50 datasets spanning mouse and human samples, multiple brain regions, developmental timepoints, and disease states. Data will be standardized using common protein identifiers (UniProt) and normalized using established proteomics pipelines.

Analytical Approach: We will apply weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) adapted for proteomics data to identify conserved protein modules across datasets. Module preservation analysis will quantify conservation across brain regions and species. Stoichiometric analysis will use intensity-based absolute quantification (iBAQ) values to estimate protein copy numbers within modules. Machine learning approaches (random forests, gradient boosting) will identify features distinguishing synapse types.

Aim 2: Integrating Structural and Spatial Data

Data Sources: Structural data will be obtained from the Protein Data Bank (PDB), including over 500 structures of synaptic protein complexes. AlphaFold predictions will supplement experimental structures. Super-resolution imaging data will be compiled from published studies using STORM, PALM, and STED microscopy, including datasets from the Image Data Resource and individual laboratory repositories.

Analytical Approach: We will construct a synaptic protein interaction network integrating physical interactions from structural data with functional associations from proteomics. Distance constraints from structures will be used to build spatial models using integrative modeling approaches developed for nuclear pore complex studies. Super-resolution localization data will be analyzed using cluster analysis algorithms (DBSCAN, Ripley's K-function) to quantify nanoscale organization. We will develop a probabilistic framework integrating structural constraints with localization data to generate ensemble models of synaptic architecture.

Aim 3: Connecting Organization to Function

Data Sources: Electrophysiology data will be obtained from NeuroElectro database, Allen Brain Atlas, and published patch-clamp studies. Disease variant data will be compiled from ClinVar, SFARI Gene, and psychiatric GWAS catalogs. We will integrate these with our organizational models from Aims 1-2.

title: Emergent Properties of the Glycocalyx: Synthesizing Glycomic, Proteomic, and Functional Data to Understand Cell Surface Organization
abstract:
The glycocalyx—the carbohydrate-rich layer coating cell surfaces—mediates cell-environment interactions, yet how glycan composition produces emergent cellular properties remains poorly understood. This proposal unites glycobiologists, cell biologists, structural biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode glycocalyx organization and function.

The glycocalyx comprises glycoproteins and glycolipids with diverse glycan structures, but comprehensive understanding of glycocalyx organization and its functional consequences is lacking. We will integrate glycomics data from GlyGen and GlyTouCan, glycoproteomics data, structural data on glycan-protein interactions, cell surface proteomics, and functional measurements of adhesion, signaling, and immune recognition.

Our first aim maps glycocalyx composition by synthesizing glycomics and glycoproteomics data across cell types and conditions. We will identify compositional patterns and their variation. Our second aim examines glycocalyx architecture by integrating structural data to understand how glycans are organized on cell surfaces. Our third aim connects glycocalyx properties to emergent cellular functions by integrating compositional data with functional measurements.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding the glycocalyx requires expertise spanning glycobiology, cell biology, and structural biology. Data integration across glycomic, proteomic, and functional data types requires specialized approaches. The collaborative framework enables comprehensive analysis impossible for individual laboratories.

Our team includes researchers from six institutions spanning glycobiology, cell biology, and computational biology. We include early-career investigators and researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions.

Deliverables include: (1) a comprehensive glycocalyx database, (2) models of glycocalyx architecture, (3) predictions linking composition to function, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student rotations, workshops on glycobiology data analysis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about cell surface organization: how does glycocalyx composition produce emergent cellular properties?
background_and_significance:
The glycocalyx represents one of the most complex and least understood structures in cell biology, functioning as the primary interface between cells and their environment. This dense, carbohydrate-rich layer extends 50-500 nanometers from the plasma membrane and comprises glycoproteins, proteoglycans, and glycolipids decorated with diverse oligosaccharide chains. Despite its critical roles in cell adhesion, immune recognition, mechanosensing, and signaling, the glycocalyx exemplifies a mesoscale structure where emergent properties arise from molecular complexity in ways that remain poorly characterized.

The significance of understanding glycocalyx organization extends across multiple biological and medical domains. In cancer biology, altered glycosylation patterns contribute to metastasis and immune evasion, with aberrant sialylation serving as both a biomarker and therapeutic target. In cardiovascular disease, endothelial glycocalyx degradation precedes atherosclerosis and contributes to vascular dysfunction. In infectious disease, pathogens exploit glycan structures for cell entry, as demonstrated by influenza virus binding to sialic acids and SARS-CoV-2 interactions with heparan sulfate proteoglycans. Despite this biomedical importance, we lack integrated understanding of how glycocalyx composition produces these diverse functional outcomes.

The glycocalyx presents a paradigmatic example of biological emergence at the mesoscale. Individual glycan structures have defined biochemical properties, yet collective glycocalyx behavior cannot be predicted from individual components. Emergent properties include the formation of protective physical barriers, the creation of microenvironments with distinct pH and ion concentrations, the generation of mechanosensitive responses to fluid shear stress, and the establishment of cell-type-specific recognition signatures. These properties arise from the spatial organization, density, and dynamic interactions of thousands of glycan structures, representing precisely the type of mesoscale emergence that NCEMS seeks to understand.

Recent advances have generated unprecedented publicly available data relevant to glycocalyx biology. The GlyGen database now contains comprehensive glycomics data spanning multiple organisms and cell types. GlyTouCan provides standardized glycan structure representations enabling cross-database integration. UniCarb-DB offers curated glycan fragmentation data. The Protein Data Bank contains thousands of glycoprotein structures revealing glycan-protein interactions. Cell surface proteomics studies deposited in ProteomeXchange quantify glycoprotein abundance across conditions. Functional genomics databases including Gene Expression Omnibus contain measurements linking glycosylation to cellular phenotypes.

Despite this data abundance, no systematic effort has integrated these diverse resources to understand glycocalyx organization and emergence. This gap exists because the data span multiple disciplines—glycobiology, structural biology, cell biology, and systems biology—each with distinct data standards, nomenclatures, and analytical approaches. Individual laboratories lack the breadth of expertise required for meaningful integration. Furthermore, the computational challenges of linking glycan structures to protein carriers to spatial organization to functional outcomes require specialized approaches beyond typical bioinformatics pipelines.

This proposal directly addresses NCEMS priorities by focusing on mesoscale emergence—how molecular-level glycan diversity produces cellular-level properties through glycocalyx organization. The project exemplifies community-scale synthesis, requiring integration of distinct data types impossible for individual laboratories. Our transdisciplinary team brings together the diverse expertise essential for success, while our commitment to open science ensures broad impact.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our overarching research question addresses a fundamental mystery in cell biology: How does the molecular complexity of the glycocalyx generate emergent cellular properties that cannot be predicted from individual glycan structures? We decompose this central question into three interconnected aims, each with specific hypotheses testable through data synthesis.

Aim 1 Research Question: What are the compositional principles governing glycocalyx organization across cell types and physiological states?

Hypothesis 1.1: Cell-type-specific glycocalyx signatures exist as coherent glycan-glycoprotein modules rather than random combinations. We predict that synthesis of glycomics and glycoproteomics data will reveal conserved co-occurrence patterns where specific glycan structures preferentially decorate particular protein carriers, forming functional modules that distinguish cell types.

Hypothesis 1.2: Glycocalyx composition follows predictable trajectories during cellular state transitions. By integrating temporal glycomics data from differentiation, activation, and disease progression studies, we hypothesize that glycocalyx remodeling follows ordered sequences reflecting underlying regulatory programs rather than stochastic variation.

Hypothesis 1.3: Glycocalyx complexity scales with cellular functional requirements. We predict that cells requiring sophisticated environmental interactions (immune cells, endothelial cells) exhibit greater glycan structural diversity than cells with simpler interaction requirements, testable through comparative analysis across cell type databases.

Aim 2 Research Question: How does three-dimensional glycocalyx architecture emerge from molecular components, and what organizational principles govern spatial arrangement?

Hypothesis 2.1: Glycan density and distribution on protein carriers follow biophysical constraints that limit possible architectures. By integrating structural data on glycosylation site occupancy, glycan conformational dynamics, and protein surface accessibility, we hypothesize that glycocalyx architecture is constrained to a limited ensemble of configurations rather than representing random decoration.

Hypothesis 2.2: Glycocalyx architecture exhibits hierarchical organization with distinct structural features at different length scales. We predict that integration of atomic-resolution structural data with mesoscale modeling will reveal emergent organizational features—clustering, layering, domain formation—not apparent from molecular-level analysis alone.

Hypothesis 2.3: Inter-glycan interactions contribute to glycocalyx mechanical properties. Through synthesis of glycan-glycan interaction data with mechanical measurements, we hypothesize that specific glycan structural features (branching, charge, length) predict collective mechanical behaviors including stiffness and permeability.

Aim 3 Research Question: How do glycocalyx compositional and architectural features produce emergent cellular functions?

Hypothesis 3.1: Glycocalyx composition predicts cell adhesion specificity through combinatorial lectin recognition. By integrating glycomics data with lectin binding profiles and adhesion measurements, we hypothesize that adhesion outcomes can be predicted from glycan structural features using machine learning models trained on synthesized datasets.

Hypothesis 3.2: Glycocalyx architecture modulates receptor accessibility and signaling pathway activation. We predict that glycan density and organization around signaling receptors, derivable from structural and proteomics data integration, correlates with signaling sensitivity measurements across conditions.

Hypothesis 3.3: Immune recognition outcomes emerge from glycocalyx patterns rather than individual glycan epitopes. Through synthesis of glycomics data with immune cell interaction measurements, we hypothesize that pattern-level features (glycan diversity indices, spatial clustering metrics) better predict immune outcomes than single-epitope presence/absence.

These hypotheses are specifically designed to be testable through synthesis of existing public data, generating predictions that can guide future experimental validation while advancing fundamental understanding of glycocalyx emergence.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach employs systematic data integration, computational modeling, and machine learning to synthesize diverse public datasets into coherent understanding of glycocalyx emergence.

Data Acquisition and Harmonization: We will systematically retrieve glycomics data from GlyGen, GlyTouCan, and UniCarb-DB, extracting glycan structures, abundances, and cell type annotations. Glycoproteomics data from ProteomeXchange and PRIDE will provide glycan-protein linkages. Structural data from PDB and AlphaFold will inform glycoprotein architectures. Functional data from GEO, ArrayExpress, and published studies will supply phenotypic measurements. A critical challenge involves harmonizing nomenclature across databases; we will implement automated translation between IUPAC, GlycoCT, and WURCS glycan representations using established conversion tools. Metadata standardization will follow MIRAGE guidelines for glycomics data reporting.

Aim 1 Methods—Compositional Mapping: We will construct a unified glycocalyx composition matrix spanning cell types, tissues, and conditions. Dimensionality reduction (UMAP, t-SNE) will identify compositional clusters. Network analysis will detect glycan-glycoprotein co-occurrence modules using weighted correlation network analysis (WGCNA) adapted for glycomics data. Trajectory inference methods (Monocle, RNA velocity adaptations) will model compositional dynamics during state transitions. Statistical frameworks will quantify compositional complexity using diversity indices (Shannon, Simpson) and structural complexity metrics.

Aim 2 Methods—Architectural Modeling: We will integrate glycoprotein structures with glycan conformational ensembles from molecular dynamics simulations deposited in public repositories. Glycan density mapping will use glycoproteomics quantification combined with structural glycosylation site data. We will develop coarse-grained models of glycocalyx architecture using mesoscale simulation approaches, parameterized by structural data synthesis. These models will predict emergent properties including thickness, density profiles, and permeability. Validation will compare predictions against published biophysical measurements.

Aim 3 Methods—Function Prediction: Machine learning models will link compositional and architectural features to functional outcomes. We will construct feature matrices encoding glycan structural descriptors (branching, charge, linkages), compositional metrics (diversity, abundance), and architectural parameters (density, organization). Supervised learning (random forests, gradient boosting, neural networks) will predict adhesion, signaling, and immune recognition outcomes from published functional datasets. Model interpretation using SHAP values will identify predictive features, generating mechanistic hypotheses. Cross-validation across independent datasets will assess generalizability.

Computational Infrastructure: Analysis pipelines will be implemented in Python and R, utilizing established bioinformatics packages (glycowork for glycan analysis, Biopython for structural analysis, scikit-learn for machine learning). Workflows will be containerized using Docker for reproducibility. Large-scale computations will utilize NCEMS computational resources and XSEDE allocations.

Team Coordination: Monthly virtual meetings will coordinate activities across institutions. Annual in-person workshops at NCEMS will facilitate intensive collaborative analysis. A shared computational environment will enable real-time collaboration on analyses. Project management tools (GitHub, Slack, shared documentation) will maintain coordination.

Quality Control: All data integration steps will include provenance tracking. Statistical analyses will employ appropriate multiple testing corrections. Machine learning models will use held-out test sets and cross-validation. Results will be validated against independent datasets where available.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This project will generate multiple transformative outcomes advancing understanding of glycocalyx emergence while providing lasting resources for the scientific community.

Primary Deliverables: First, we will create the Integrated Glycocalyx Atlas (IGA), a comprehensive database linking glycan structures, protein carriers, cellular contexts, and functional annotations across cell types and conditions. This resource will enable researchers to query glycocalyx composition for any characterized cell type and identify compositional changes associated with biological processes. Second, we will develop Glycocalyx Architecture Models providing computational representations of glycocalyx organization at multiple scales, from individual glycoproteins to mesoscale surface organization. These models will predict physical properties including thickness, density, and permeability. Third, we will produce Composition-Function Prediction Tools implementing machine learning models linking glycocalyx features to cellular outcomes, enabling researchers to predict functional consequences of glycocalyx alterations. Fourth, we will generate Testable Hypotheses providing specific, experimentally addressable predictions about glycocalyx organization and function derived from our synthesis analyses.

Scientific Impact: This project addresses fundamental questions about biological emergence at the mesoscale, directly advancing NCEMS scientific priorities. Our findings will establish principles governing how molecular complexity generates cellular properties, applicable beyond glycobiology to other mesoscale systems. The integrated datasets will enable hypothesis generation across glycobiology, cell biology, immunology, and biomedical research.

Broader Impacts: All resources will be publicly released following open science principles, maximizing community benefit. Training activities will develop data science capabilities in glycobiology, an underserved area. Our diverse team composition, including early-career researchers and PUI faculty, promotes inclusive participation in synthesis science. The methodological frameworks developed will serve as templates for similar integration efforts in other biological domains.

Long-term Legacy: Beyond immediate deliverables, this project establishes sustainable infrastructure for glycocalyx research, including data standards, analysis pipelines, and collaborative networks that will persist beyond the funding period.

title: The Emergence of Enhancer-Promoter Specificity: Synthesizing Chromatin, Transcription, and 3D Genome Data
abstract:
Enhancers activate specific promoters despite genomic distances, yet how enhancer-promoter specificity emerges from molecular interactions remains a fundamental puzzle. This proposal assembles gene regulation experts, chromatin biologists, computational scientists, and systems biologists to synthesize publicly available data to decode enhancer-promoter communication principles.

Enhancer-promoter specificity involves chromatin looping, transcription factor binding, and compatibility rules, but comprehensive understanding is lacking. We will integrate Hi-C and Capture-C data, ChIP-seq data for transcription factors and chromatin marks, ATAC-seq data, eQTL data, and transcription measurements from ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, and GTEx.

Our first aim maps enhancer-promoter connections by synthesizing chromatin conformation data across cell types. We will identify connection patterns and their cell-type specificity. Our second aim examines molecular determinants of specificity by integrating transcription factor binding, chromatin state, and sequence features with connection data. Our third aim develops predictive models of enhancer-promoter communication by integrating multi-omic data to predict functional connections.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding enhancer-promoter specificity requires expertise spanning gene regulation, chromatin biology, and computational modeling. Data integration across conformation, binding, and expression data types requires specialized approaches. The collaborative framework enables comprehensive analysis impossible for individual laboratories.

Our team includes researchers from seven institutions spanning gene regulation, chromatin biology, and computational biology. We include researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions and various career stages.

Expected outcomes include: (1) an integrated enhancer-promoter connection database, (2) models predicting enhancer-promoter pairs, (3) identification of specificity rules, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student exchanges, workshops on gene regulation data analysis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about gene regulation: how does enhancer-promoter specificity emerge from molecular interactions?
background_and_significance:
The precise regulation of gene expression is fundamental to cellular identity, development, and disease. Enhancers—distal regulatory elements that activate gene transcription—represent a critical mechanism through which cells achieve context-specific gene expression programs. Despite decades of research, a fundamental mystery persists: how do enhancers selectively communicate with their target promoters while ignoring thousands of other potential targets within the three-dimensional nuclear space? This question of enhancer-promoter specificity represents a quintessential emergence problem at the mesoscale, where molecular interactions give rise to higher-order regulatory properties that cannot be predicted from individual components alone.

Enhancers can be located hundreds of kilobases from their target genes, yet they exhibit remarkable specificity in their regulatory targets. Current models propose that specificity emerges from the integration of multiple factors: chromatin looping mediated by architectural proteins like CTCF and cohesin, transcription factor binding patterns, chromatin accessibility states, histone modifications, and sequence-encoded compatibility rules between enhancers and promoters. However, these factors have largely been studied in isolation, and a comprehensive understanding of how they collectively determine enhancer-promoter specificity remains elusive.

The significance of this problem extends beyond basic biology. Disease-associated genetic variants identified through genome-wide association studies (GWAS) are predominantly located in non-coding regions, with many presumed to affect enhancer function. Understanding enhancer-promoter specificity is therefore essential for interpreting how genetic variation contributes to disease risk and for developing therapeutic strategies targeting gene regulation.

The timing for this synthesis project is optimal due to the unprecedented availability of relevant public datasets. The ENCODE Consortium has generated comprehensive chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) data for hundreds of transcription factors and histone modifications across numerous cell types. The Roadmap Epigenomics Project has mapped chromatin states across 127 human tissues and cell types. High-resolution chromatin conformation capture data (Hi-C, Capture-C, HiChIP) are now available for dozens of cell types, providing direct measurements of chromatin looping. The GTEx project offers expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data linking genetic variants to gene expression across 54 human tissues, providing functional evidence for regulatory connections. Additionally, ATAC-seq datasets mapping chromatin accessibility are abundantly available.

Despite this data wealth, no systematic effort has integrated these diverse data types to comprehensively address enhancer-promoter specificity. Individual laboratories have examined specific aspects—chromatin loops, transcription factor binding, or sequence features—but the field lacks an integrated framework explaining how specificity emerges from molecular interactions. This gap exists because such integration requires expertise spanning chromatin biology, gene regulation, computational biology, and systems biology, along with computational infrastructure for handling terabyte-scale datasets.

This project directly addresses NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale. Enhancer-promoter specificity exemplifies emergence: the regulatory outcome cannot be predicted from any single molecular feature but arises from the integration of chromatin architecture, protein binding, and sequence information. By synthesizing existing data through collaborative, transdisciplinary approaches, we will decode the principles governing this fundamental aspect of gene regulation, generating insights impossible for any single laboratory to achieve.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
This proposal addresses the overarching question: How does enhancer-promoter specificity emerge from the integration of chromatin architecture, transcription factor binding, chromatin state, and DNA sequence features? We decompose this into three interconnected research questions, each with testable hypotheses.

**Research Question 1: What are the patterns and principles of enhancer-promoter connectivity across cell types and genomic contexts?**

Hypothesis 1a: Enhancer-promoter connections exhibit a hierarchical organization, with a subset of "hub" promoters receiving inputs from multiple enhancers while most promoters connect to few enhancers. We predict that hub promoters regulate genes with cell-type-specific functions requiring precise expression control.

Hypothesis 1b: The cell-type specificity of enhancer-promoter connections follows predictable patterns related to developmental lineage relationships. We hypothesize that closely related cell types share more enhancer-promoter connections than distantly related types, and that lineage-specific connections emerge at defined developmental branch points.

Hypothesis 1c: Genomic distance constraints on enhancer-promoter communication vary systematically with chromatin domain organization. We predict that topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries impose strong constraints, but that enhancer strength and promoter properties modulate these constraints.

**Research Question 2: What molecular features determine which enhancers communicate with which promoters?**

Hypothesis 2a: Enhancer-promoter specificity is encoded in transcription factor binding compatibility. We hypothesize that functionally connected enhancer-promoter pairs share transcription factor binding motifs and that the overlap in bound transcription factors predicts connection probability.

Hypothesis 2b: Chromatin state compatibility contributes to specificity beyond transcription factor binding. We predict that enhancers and promoters with compatible histone modification signatures (e.g., shared H3K27ac patterns, compatible H3K4 methylation states) preferentially connect, independent of transcription factor occupancy.

Hypothesis 2c: Core promoter sequence elements influence enhancer responsiveness. Different core promoter types (TATA-containing, CpG island, DPE-containing) may exhibit differential compatibility with enhancer classes, contributing to specificity.

Hypothesis 2d: The presence and configuration of insulator elements (CTCF binding sites) and their orientation relative to enhancers and promoters systematically influence connection probability, with convergent CTCF orientations facilitating connections within loops.

**Research Question 3: Can we develop predictive models that accurately forecast functional enhancer-promoter connections from molecular features?**

Hypothesis 3a: Integrative machine learning models incorporating chromatin conformation, transcription factor binding, chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, and sequence features will outperform single-feature models in predicting enhancer-promoter connections, demonstrating the emergent nature of specificity.

Hypothesis 3b: Model feature importance analysis will reveal that different genomic contexts (e.g., gene-dense versus gene-poor regions, different TAD types) rely on different feature combinations for specificity, indicating context-dependent emergence rules.

Hypothesis 3c: Models trained on one cell type will show reduced but measurable predictive performance in related cell types, with transferability correlating with developmental relatedness. This will reveal conserved versus cell-type-specific specificity rules.

Hypothesis 3d: eQTL data will validate predicted enhancer-promoter connections, with genetic variants in predicted enhancers showing significant associations with expression of predicted target genes at rates exceeding background expectations.

These hypotheses are designed to be testable through synthesis of existing public data, with clear predictions that can be validated using independent datasets. The hierarchical structure—from mapping connections, to identifying determinants, to building predictive models—ensures systematic progress toward understanding enhancer-promoter specificity as an emergent property.
methods_and_approach:
**Data Acquisition and Harmonization**

We will systematically compile publicly available datasets from ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, GTEx, 4D Nucleome, and GEO. Chromatin conformation data will include Hi-C datasets from over 100 cell types, Capture-C data for targeted loci, and HiChIP data linking histone modifications to chromatin contacts. ChIP-seq data will encompass transcription factor binding for 300+ factors and histone modifications (H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K4me3, H3K27me3, H3K9me3) across matched cell types. ATAC-seq data will provide chromatin accessibility maps, while RNA-seq data will enable expression quantification. eQTL summary statistics from GTEx will link genetic variants to gene expression.

Data harmonization presents significant challenges given heterogeneous processing pipelines across consortia. We will establish standardized processing workflows using established tools (BWA, STAR, MACS2, HiC-Pro, Juicer) with uniform parameters. All datasets will be mapped to GRCh38, with liftover from earlier assemblies where necessary. Quality metrics will be computed for all datasets, with minimum thresholds for inclusion.

**Aim 1: Mapping Enhancer-Promoter Connectivity**

We will identify enhancer-promoter connections using complementary approaches. For Hi-C data, we will call significant interactions using multiple algorithms (HOMER, FitHiC2, Mustache) and retain connections identified by at least two methods. Loop anchor annotations will classify connections as enhancer-promoter based on chromatin state annotations. For higher-resolution Capture-C and HiChIP data, we will use CHiCAGO and FitHiChIP for interaction calling.

To address technical variability, we will develop a meta-analysis framework that weights connections by data quality and reproducibility across biological replicates. We will construct cell-type-specific enhancer-promoter networks and quantify network properties including degree distributions, clustering coefficients, and modularity. Cross-cell-type comparisons will identify conserved versus cell-type-specific connections.

**Aim 2: Molecular Determinants of Specificity**

For each enhancer-promoter pair (connected and non-connected controls), we will extract molecular features: transcription factor binding profiles (presence/absence and signal intensity for all available factors), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq signal), histone modification patterns, DNA sequence features (motif occurrences, GC content, repeat content), and genomic context (distance, TAD membership, CTCF site configuration).

Statistical analysis will employ logistic regression, random forests, and gradient boosting to identify features associated with connectivity. We will use SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values for interpretable feature importance. Interaction terms will capture combinatorial effects. Cell-type-specific analyses will reveal context-dependent rules.

**Aim 3: Predictive Modeling**

We will develop machine learning models predicting enhancer-promoter connections from molecular features. Training data will comprise connected pairs (positive examples) and distance-matched non-connected pairs (negative examples). We will implement multiple architectures: gradient boosting (XGBoost), deep neural networks, and graph neural networks capturing chromatin topology.

Models will be evaluated using held-out test sets (10% of data), cross-cell-type prediction (train on one cell type, test on another), and external validation using eQTL data (predicted connections should be enriched for significant eQTL associations). We will perform systematic ablation studies removing feature classes to quantify their contributions.

**Computational Infrastructure**

Analysis will require substantial computational resources. We will utilize NCEMS computational infrastructure supplemented by institutional high-performance computing clusters. All workflows will be implemented in Snakemake/Nextflow for reproducibility, with containerization (Docker/Singularity) ensuring portability.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will generate multiple high-impact outcomes advancing our understanding of enhancer-promoter specificity as an emergent property.

**Primary Outcomes:**

1. **Integrated Enhancer-Promoter Connection Database:** A comprehensive, standardized database of enhancer-promoter connections across 50+ human cell types, incorporating data from multiple chromatin conformation technologies. This resource will include confidence scores, cell-type specificity annotations, and associated molecular features, serving as a foundational resource for the gene regulation community.

2. **Predictive Models:** Machine learning models achieving high accuracy in predicting functional enhancer-promoter connections from molecular features. These models will be deployable tools enabling researchers to predict regulatory connections in cell types lacking chromatin conformation data.

3. **Specificity Rules Catalog:** A systematic characterization of molecular rules governing enhancer-promoter specificity, including transcription factor compatibility codes, chromatin state requirements, and sequence features. This knowledge will transform our mechanistic understanding of gene regulation.

4. **Testable Hypotheses:** Specific predictions for experimental validation, including candidate enhancer-promoter pairs for CRISPR-based perturbation studies and transcription factor combinations predicted to confer specificity.

**Scientific Impact:**

This project addresses a fundamental question in molecular biology with implications spanning development, disease, and evolution. Understanding specificity rules will enable interpretation of disease-associated non-coding variants, rational design of synthetic regulatory circuits, and prediction of regulatory consequences of genomic alterations. The emergence framework developed here—understanding how higher-order properties arise from molecular interactions—will serve as a template for addressing similar questions throughout biology.

**Community Impact:**

All resources will be publicly released, maximizing community benefit. The database will serve researchers studying gene regulation, chromatin biology, and disease genetics. Predictive models will enable hypothesis generation for laboratories worldwide. Training materials developed through workshops will build capacity for synthesis research in gene regulation.

**Training Impact:**

This project will train 8-10 graduate students and postdocs in transdisciplinary synthesis research, creating a cohort of researchers skilled in integrating diverse data types to address fundamental biological questions.

title: Decoding the Emergent Organization of the Endoplasmic Reticulum: Multi-Scale Synthesis of Structure, Function, and Dynamics
abstract:
The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) forms a continuous membrane network with distinct functional domains, yet how ER organization produces emergent functions in protein synthesis, lipid metabolism, and calcium signaling remains poorly understood. This proposal unites ER biologists, structural biologists, lipidomics experts, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode ER organization principles.

The ER comprises sheets, tubules, and contact sites with other organelles, each with distinct compositions and functions. We will integrate proteomics data on ER subdomains, lipidomics data, structural data from cryo-ET, calcium imaging data, and protein synthesis measurements. Cross-species comparisons will identify conserved organizational principles.

Our first aim maps ER subdomain composition by synthesizing proteomics and lipidomics data across ER regions. We will identify domain-specific components and their variation across cell types. Our second aim examines ER architecture by integrating structural data to understand how ER morphology relates to function. Our third aim connects ER organization to emergent functions by integrating compositional and structural data with functional measurements.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding ER organization requires expertise spanning ER biology, structural biology, and lipidomics. Data integration across proteomic, lipidomic, and structural data types requires diverse approaches. The collaborative framework enables comprehensive analysis impossible for individual laboratories.

Our team includes researchers from six institutions spanning ER biology, structural biology, and computational biology. We include early-career investigators and researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions.

Deliverables include: (1) an integrated ER organization database, (2) models of ER architecture-function relationships, (3) predictions linking organization to cellular outcomes, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student rotations, workshops on ER biology, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about organelle organization: how does ER architecture produce emergent functional properties?
background_and_significance:
The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) represents one of biology's most remarkable examples of emergent organization at the mesoscale. Comprising approximately 50% of total cellular membrane, the ER forms a continuous network that extends throughout the cytoplasm while maintaining functionally distinct domains—rough ER sheets studded with ribosomes for protein synthesis, smooth ER tubules specialized for lipid metabolism, and membrane contact sites that facilitate inter-organelle communication. Despite decades of research, fundamental questions persist: How do molecular components self-organize into these distinct functional domains? How does the physical architecture of the ER network give rise to emergent properties that individual components cannot achieve alone?

This knowledge gap represents a critical barrier to understanding cellular function. The ER serves as the primary site for synthesis and folding of approximately one-third of the proteome, produces most cellular lipids, and orchestrates calcium signaling cascades that regulate diverse cellular processes from muscle contraction to apoptosis. Dysfunction in ER organization underlies numerous diseases, including neurodegeneration, metabolic disorders, and cancer. Yet we lack integrated models explaining how ER organization produces these emergent functional capabilities.

The scientific challenge is inherently multiscale and multidisciplinary. ER organization spans from nanometer-scale protein complexes to micrometer-scale network architecture. Understanding emergence at this mesoscale requires synthesizing data across molecular composition (proteomics, lipidomics), structure (cryo-electron tomography, fluorescence microscopy), and function (calcium dynamics, protein synthesis rates). No single laboratory possesses the expertise or resources to integrate these diverse data types.

The timing for this synthesis project is optimal. Publicly available datasets have reached critical mass: proteomics databases contain thousands of ER-localized proteins across multiple species and cell types; lipidomics studies have characterized ER membrane composition; cryo-ET studies have revealed ER ultrastructure at unprecedented resolution; and functional imaging datasets capture ER dynamics in living cells. These data exist in isolation, analyzed within disciplinary boundaries, awaiting synthesis to reveal emergent organizational principles.

This project directly addresses NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale. The ER exemplifies mesoscale emergence: individual proteins and lipids self-organize into membrane domains that collectively produce functions impossible for isolated components. Our synthesis approach will identify principles governing this organization, with implications extending to other organelles and membrane systems.

The significance extends beyond basic science. Understanding ER organization principles will inform therapeutic strategies for diseases involving ER dysfunction. Computational models developed through this synthesis will enable predictions about how perturbations—genetic mutations, drug treatments, metabolic stress—alter ER function. Furthermore, principles discovered may generalize to other membrane-bound organelles, advancing our understanding of cellular organization broadly.

This project exemplifies community-scale synthesis: it requires integration of publicly available data across multiple types, demands collaboration between laboratories with distinct expertise, and will generate insights impossible through traditional single-laboratory approaches. The emergent organization of the ER represents a fundamental puzzle in cell biology that synthesis research is uniquely positioned to address.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our overarching research question addresses a fundamental puzzle in cell biology: How does the molecular composition of ER subdomains give rise to emergent architectural and functional properties that individual components cannot achieve alone? We decompose this into three interconnected research questions with testable hypotheses.

Research Question 1: What are the compositional signatures that define distinct ER subdomains, and how are these conserved across cell types and species?

Hypothesis 1a: ER subdomains (sheets, tubules, contact sites) possess distinct proteome and lipidome signatures that are maintained despite continuous membrane connectivity. We predict that synthesis of proteomics data will reveal core protein modules—sets of co-localizing proteins—that define each subdomain.

Hypothesis 1b: Subdomain compositional signatures are evolutionarily conserved at the module level rather than individual protein level. Cross-species analysis will identify functional protein families that substitute across evolution while maintaining subdomain identity.

Hypothesis 1c: Cell type-specific ER functions emerge from quantitative variation in conserved compositional modules rather than qualitatively distinct components. Comparative analysis across cell types will reveal how module stoichiometry relates to specialized functions.

Research Question 2: How does ER membrane architecture emerge from molecular composition, and what structural features enable functional specialization?

Hypothesis 2a: ER sheet versus tubule identity emerges from the ratio of curvature-generating proteins (reticulons, REEPs) to curvature-stabilizing proteins and specific lipid compositions. Integration of structural data with compositional data will reveal quantitative relationships between molecular components and membrane geometry.

Hypothesis 2b: ER network topology—branch points, three-way junctions, fenestrations—follows predictable organizational rules that optimize material transport and functional compartmentalization. Analysis of cryo-ET and light microscopy data will identify conserved topological features and their relationship to function.

Hypothesis 2c: ER-organelle contact sites represent compositionally and structurally distinct domains whose architecture predicts functional capacity. Synthesis of contact site proteomics with structural data will reveal design principles governing inter-organelle communication.

Research Question 3: How do compositional and architectural features of ER subdomains produce emergent functional properties in protein synthesis, lipid metabolism, and calcium signaling?

Hypothesis 3a: Ribosome density on ER sheets correlates with local concentrations of translocon components and specific lipid environments, creating emergent translational microdomains. Integration of ribosome profiling data with sheet composition will reveal how molecular organization enhances protein synthesis efficiency.

Hypothesis 3b: Calcium signaling dynamics emerge from the spatial organization of calcium channels, pumps, and buffers within the ER network. Synthesis of calcium imaging data with ER composition maps will identify how molecular organization shapes calcium wave propagation.

Hypothesis 3c: Lipid synthesis capacity in smooth ER tubules emerges from the co-localization of biosynthetic enzymes with specific membrane curvatures and lipid environments. Integration of lipidomics with enzyme localization data will reveal organizational principles underlying metabolic function.

These hypotheses are testable through data synthesis and will generate specific predictions for experimental validation. Each addresses emergence at the mesoscale—how molecular components produce higher-order properties through organization. The hypotheses are interconnected: compositional signatures (Q1) determine architecture (Q2), which enables emergent functions (Q3). This logical framework ensures our synthesis efforts build toward integrated understanding rather than isolated observations.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach employs a systematic data synthesis pipeline integrating diverse publicly available datasets through computational frameworks designed for heterogeneous biological data.

Data Acquisition and Curation: We will systematically compile datasets from public repositories including PRIDE/ProteomeXchange (proteomics), LIPID MAPS and MetaboLights (lipidomics), EMDB and EMPIAR (cryo-ET structures), and GEO/ArrayExpress (functional genomics). For calcium imaging and protein synthesis measurements, we will access datasets from published studies with deposited raw data. Our team includes experts in each data type who will apply domain-specific quality control criteria. We estimate integration of >50 proteomics datasets, >20 lipidomics studies, >100 cryo-ET tomograms, and >30 functional imaging datasets spanning multiple species (human, mouse, yeast, plant) and cell types.

Aim 1 Methods—Compositional Mapping: We will develop a unified ER protein atlas by harmonizing proteomics data across studies using standardized protein identifiers and quantification normalization. Machine learning approaches will identify protein modules that co-localize across datasets, revealing subdomain signatures. For lipidomics integration, we will map lipid species to ER subdomains using spatial lipidomics data and correlate with protein composition. Cross-species orthology mapping using established databases (OrthoDB, PANTHER) will identify conserved modules. Statistical frameworks will distinguish core subdomain components from cell type-specific variations.

Aim 2 Methods—Architectural Analysis: Cryo-ET data will be processed using standardized segmentation pipelines to extract ER membrane geometry, including curvature measurements, network topology, and contact site architecture. We will develop computational tools to correlate structural features with compositional data, testing hypotheses about curvature-composition relationships. Network analysis algorithms will quantify ER topology across conditions and cell types. Integration with super-resolution microscopy data from public repositories will bridge structural scales.

Aim 3 Methods—Function Integration: We will synthesize ribosome profiling data to map translation activity across ER regions, correlating with sheet composition. Calcium imaging datasets will be analyzed to extract signaling dynamics parameters (wave velocity, amplitude, spatial patterns) and correlated with ER network features. Machine learning models will identify compositional and structural predictors of functional outputs.

Computational Infrastructure: Analysis pipelines will be implemented in Python and R, utilizing established bioinformatics packages and custom tools. We will employ cloud computing resources through NCEMS for computationally intensive analyses. All code will be version-controlled on GitHub with comprehensive documentation.

Integrative Modeling: We will develop multi-layer network models representing ER organization across scales. Graph-based approaches will capture relationships between molecular components, structural features, and functional outputs. Bayesian frameworks will quantify uncertainty and identify high-confidence organizational principles.

Validation Strategy: Model predictions will be validated through: (1) cross-validation using held-out datasets, (2) comparison with published experimental perturbation studies, and (3) generation of specific testable predictions for future experimental work. Our team includes experimentalists who will assess prediction feasibility and biological plausibility.

Timeline: Year 1 focuses on data acquisition, curation, and Aim 1 analysis. Year 2 addresses Aims 2-3 and integrative modeling. Quarterly working group meetings and continuous virtual collaboration ensure coordinated progress.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will generate transformative outcomes advancing our understanding of emergent organelle organization while providing resources benefiting the broader scientific community.

Primary Deliverables: (1) The Integrated ER Organization Database (iERO)—a publicly accessible, queryable resource containing harmonized proteomics, lipidomics, and structural data mapped to ER subdomains across species and cell types. This database will serve as a foundational resource for ER research. (2) Quantitative models of ER architecture-function relationships, including predictive frameworks linking molecular composition to membrane geometry and functional capacity. (3) A catalog of conserved ER organizational modules with evolutionary analysis revealing core versus specialized components. (4) Specific, experimentally testable hypotheses about ER organization mechanisms, prioritized by confidence and feasibility.

Scientific Impact: This project will establish general principles governing mesoscale organization in membrane systems. By revealing how molecular components self-organize into functional domains, we address fundamental questions about biological emergence applicable beyond the ER. Our findings will inform understanding of other organelles with analogous organizational challenges.

Biomedical Relevance: ER dysfunction underlies numerous diseases. Our organizational maps will identify candidate therapeutic targets and predict how mutations disrupt ER function. Models developed will enable in silico testing of perturbation effects.

Methodological Contributions: Novel computational approaches for integrating heterogeneous biological data types will be applicable to other synthesis challenges. Our frameworks for cross-species comparison and multi-scale modeling will serve as templates for future NCEMS projects.

Workforce Development: This project will train 6-8 graduate students and postdocs in transdisciplinary synthesis research, data science, and collaborative science practices. Undergraduate researchers from partner institutions, including primarily undergraduate institutions, will gain research experience through summer programs and academic-year projects. Workshops developed for the working group will be adapted for broader dissemination.

Community Building: By bringing together researchers across disciplines, career stages, and institution types, this project strengthens the ER research community and establishes collaborative networks that will persist beyond the project period.
