The project aligns precisely with NCEMS's mission to understand mesoscale emergence through synthesis of publicly available data, making NCEMS the ideal funding mechanism for this transformative research.

title: The Emergence of Cellular Mechanoresponses: Synthesizing Force, Structural, and Signaling Data Across Mechanotransduction Pathways
abstract:
Cells sense and respond to mechanical forces through mechanotransduction, yet how molecular force sensors produce emergent cellular responses remains incompletely understood. This proposal assembles mechanobiologists, structural biologists, biophysicists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode mechanotransduction principles.

Mechanotransduction involves force-sensitive proteins that undergo conformational changes triggering signaling cascades, but comprehensive understanding of these pathways is lacking. We will integrate structural data on mechanosensitive proteins, force spectroscopy measurements, signaling pathway data, transcriptomics responses to mechanical stimulation, and phenotypic data on mechanically-regulated processes.

Our first aim maps mechanotransduction pathways by synthesizing interaction data connecting force sensors to downstream signaling. We will identify pathway architectures and crosstalk. Our second aim examines molecular mechanisms by integrating structural data with force measurements to understand force-induced conformational changes. Our third aim connects mechanosensing to emergent cellular responses by integrating pathway data with transcriptomics and phenotypic measurements.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding mechanotransduction requires expertise spanning biophysics, structural biology, and cell biology. Data integration across force measurements, structural, and signaling data types requires specialized approaches. The collaborative framework enables comprehensive analysis impossible for individual laboratories.

Our team includes researchers from seven institutions spanning mechanobiology, structural biology, and computational biology. We include researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions and various career stages.

Expected outcomes include: (1) an integrated mechanotransduction database, (2) models of force-induced signaling, (3) predictions linking mechanical inputs to cellular outputs, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student exchanges, workshops on mechanobiology, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about cellular sensing: how do molecular force sensors produce emergent cellular mechanoresponses?
background_and_significance:
Mechanotransduction—the process by which cells convert mechanical stimuli into biochemical signals—represents one of the most fundamental yet incompletely understood phenomena in cell biology. Every cell in the human body experiences mechanical forces, from the shear stress on endothelial cells lining blood vessels to the compressive forces on chondrocytes in cartilage. These mechanical inputs profoundly influence cell fate decisions, tissue development, and disease progression, including cancer metastasis, fibrosis, and cardiovascular pathology. Despite decades of research, a comprehensive understanding of how molecular-scale force sensing produces emergent cellular behaviors remains elusive.

At the molecular level, mechanotransduction relies on specialized force-sensitive proteins that undergo conformational changes when subjected to mechanical stress. Key mechanosensors include integrins, which connect the extracellular matrix to the cytoskeleton; talin and vinculin, which unfold under tension to expose cryptic binding sites; piezo channels, which open in response to membrane tension; and the nuclear mechanosensing apparatus involving the LINC complex and lamin proteins. Each of these proteins operates through distinct molecular mechanisms, yet they converge on shared signaling pathways including YAP/TAZ, MAPK, and Rho GTPase cascades. The integration of these pathways produces emergent cellular responses—outcomes that cannot be predicted from studying individual components in isolation.

This emergence represents a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon, perfectly aligned with NCEMS's scientific vision. Force sensing occurs at the molecular scale (nanometers), but the resultant cellular responses—migration, differentiation, proliferation—manifest at scales spanning micrometers to millimeters. Understanding how information flows across these scales requires synthesizing data types that have traditionally remained siloed within distinct research communities.

The significance of this synthesis project stems from three critical gaps in current knowledge. First, mechanotransduction pathway architecture remains incompletely mapped. While individual protein-protein interactions have been characterized, the complete network connecting force sensors to transcriptional outputs has not been systematically assembled. Second, the relationship between force magnitude, conformational change, and signaling output is poorly quantified. Force spectroscopy studies have measured unfolding forces for many mechanosensitive proteins, but these measurements have not been integrated with structural data to develop predictive models. Third, the rules governing how cells integrate multiple mechanical inputs to produce coherent responses remain unknown.

The timing for this synthesis project is optimal. Publicly available data resources have reached critical mass: the Protein Data Bank contains over 200,000 structures including numerous mechanosensitive proteins; single-molecule force spectroscopy datasets are increasingly deposited in public repositories; transcriptomic responses to mechanical stimulation are available through GEO and ArrayExpress; and pathway databases including Reactome and KEGG contain mechanotransduction pathway annotations. However, these resources remain fragmented across databases with incompatible formats and ontologies.

This project directly addresses NCEMS's mission by tackling emergence at the mesoscale. We will decode how molecular force sensors—operating through angstrom-scale conformational changes—produce emergent cellular behaviors spanning micrometers and hours. This represents precisely the type of multi-scale integration that synthesis research enables and that no single laboratory could accomplish independently.
research_questions_and_hypotheses:
Our synthesis project addresses three interconnected research questions, each targeting a distinct aspect of mechanotransduction emergence and supported by testable hypotheses derived from preliminary analysis of publicly available data.

**Research Question 1: What is the complete architecture of mechanotransduction signaling networks, and how do pathway topologies enable signal integration?**

We hypothesize that mechanotransduction pathways exhibit characteristic network motifs—including feed-forward loops, coherent feedback, and pathway convergence nodes—that enable cells to filter mechanical noise while remaining sensitive to sustained force application. Preliminary analysis of protein-protein interaction databases reveals that mechanosensors connect to downstream effectors through an average of 4.2 intermediate nodes, suggesting signal amplification architecture. We further hypothesize that pathway crosstalk between distinct mechanosensors (e.g., integrins and piezo channels) occurs through shared intermediates, enabling cells to integrate diverse mechanical inputs. This hypothesis predicts that perturbation of convergence nodes will disrupt responses to multiple force types, a prediction testable through synthesis of published perturbation studies.

**Research Question 2: How do force magnitude and loading rate determine molecular conformational changes that activate signaling?**

We hypothesize that mechanosensitive proteins exhibit characteristic force-response relationships that can be predicted from structural features, specifically the topology of force-bearing domains and the location of cryptic binding sites. Single-molecule force spectroscopy has revealed that proteins like talin unfold through defined intermediate states, with each state exposing specific binding sites. We hypothesize that the force thresholds for these transitions correlate with cellular force ranges encountered in specific physiological contexts—that is, evolution has tuned molecular force responses to match tissue-specific mechanical environments. This hypothesis predicts that mechanosensors expressed in high-force environments (e.g., muscle) will exhibit higher unfolding thresholds than those in low-force environments (e.g., brain). We will test this through systematic integration of force spectroscopy data with tissue expression profiles.

**Research Question 3: What quantitative relationships link mechanical inputs to emergent transcriptional and phenotypic outputs?**

We hypothesize that cellular mechanoresponses follow quantifiable input-output relationships that depend on force magnitude, duration, and spatial distribution. Specifically, we predict that transcriptional responses to mechanical stimulation exhibit dose-response characteristics analogous to chemical ligand responses, with defined thresholds, saturation points, and temporal dynamics. We further hypothesize that the transcriptional programs activated by mechanical stimulation are partially shared across cell types (reflecting conserved mechanotransduction machinery) but also include cell-type-specific components (reflecting tissue-specific functions). Integration of transcriptomic datasets from mechanically-stimulated cells across multiple cell types will test this hypothesis by identifying conserved versus cell-type-specific mechanoresponsive gene modules.

**Overarching Hypothesis on Emergence:**

Our central hypothesis posits that emergent cellular mechanoresponses arise from three integrated mechanisms: (1) network topology that enables signal filtering and amplification, (2) molecular force thresholds that establish response sensitivities, and (3) transcriptional programs that convert transient signals into sustained cellular changes. We predict that computational models incorporating all three mechanisms will outperform single-mechanism models in predicting cellular responses to novel mechanical perturbations. This hypothesis directly addresses NCEMS's focus on emergence by proposing that cellular mechanoresponses cannot be understood from any single level of analysis but require integration across molecular, pathway, and cellular scales.

These hypotheses generate specific, testable predictions that will guide our synthesis efforts and provide clear metrics for evaluating project success.
methods_and_approach:
Our methodological approach integrates diverse publicly available datasets through a systematic pipeline encompassing data acquisition, harmonization, integration, and modeling. We organize our methods around three interconnected aims.

**Aim 1: Mechanotransduction Network Mapping**

We will construct comprehensive mechanotransduction pathway maps by integrating data from multiple sources. Protein-protein interaction data will be extracted from BioGRID, IntAct, and STRING databases, filtered for interactions involving known mechanosensors and their downstream effectors. Pathway annotations from Reactome, KEGG, and WikiPathways will provide curated mechanotransduction modules. We will apply network analysis algorithms including community detection (Louvain algorithm), motif enrichment analysis, and centrality metrics to identify pathway architecture features. To address data heterogeneity, we will implement a confidence-scoring system weighting interactions by evidence type (experimental method, number of publications, evolutionary conservation). Network visualization will employ Cytoscape with custom plugins for force-related annotations.

**Aim 2: Structure-Force Integration**

We will systematically integrate structural and biophysical data for mechanosensitive proteins. Structural data will be retrieved from the Protein Data Bank, including experimental structures and AlphaFold predictions for proteins lacking experimental structures. Force spectroscopy data will be compiled from published single-molecule studies, extracting parameters including unfolding force, loading rate dependence, and intermediate states. We will develop a standardized schema for force spectroscopy data that captures experimental conditions (temperature, buffer, pulling geometry) essential for cross-study comparison.

Machine learning approaches will identify structural features predictive of force response. We will train models using protein structural descriptors (contact order, secondary structure content, domain topology) as features and force spectroscopy parameters as targets. Random forest and gradient boosting algorithms will enable feature importance analysis, identifying which structural characteristics most strongly predict mechanical behavior. Molecular dynamics simulation data from public repositories will supplement experimental measurements, enabling analysis of conformational change pathways.

**Aim 3: Mechanical Input to Cellular Output Mapping**

Transcriptomic data from mechanically-stimulated cells will be retrieved from GEO and ArrayExpress using systematic keyword searches (mechanical stimulation, stretch, compression, shear stress, substrate stiffness). We will apply standardized preprocessing pipelines (quality control, normalization, batch correction) to enable cross-study comparison. Differential expression analysis will identify mechanoresponsive genes, while gene set enrichment analysis will reveal activated pathways.

We will develop quantitative models linking mechanical inputs to transcriptional outputs using machine learning regression approaches. Input features will include force magnitude, duration, cell type, and pathway activation states (inferred from Aim 1 networks). Output variables will include expression changes for mechanoresponsive genes. Model architectures will include both interpretable approaches (linear models, decision trees) and flexible methods (neural networks) to balance prediction accuracy with mechanistic insight.

**Integration and Validation**

Cross-aim integration will employ multi-layer network approaches that connect molecular structures (Aim 2) to signaling networks (Aim 1) to transcriptional outputs (Aim 3). We will validate integrated models using held-out datasets and published experimental results not included in model training. All analysis pipelines will be implemented in Python and R, with version control through GitHub and containerization through Docker to ensure reproducibility.
expected_outcomes_and_impact:
This synthesis project will generate multiple tangible outcomes with broad impact on the mechanobiology field and beyond.

**Primary Deliverables:**

First, we will produce the Mechanotransduction Integration Database (MechIntDB), a publicly accessible resource containing curated pathway maps, structure-force relationships, and transcriptomic response profiles. This database will provide standardized data formats and programmatic access through APIs, enabling community-wide utilization. Second, we will develop predictive computational models linking mechanical inputs to cellular outputs, implemented as user-friendly tools accessible to experimentalists without computational expertise. Third, we will generate a comprehensive atlas of mechanotransduction pathway architectures, visualized through interactive network maps annotated with structural and functional information.

**Scientific Impact:**

Our synthesis will resolve long-standing questions about mechanotransduction organization, including the degree of pathway modularity, the extent of crosstalk between mechanosensors, and the quantitative relationships between force and response. By identifying structural features predictive of force sensitivity, we will enable rational prediction of mechanosensitive behavior for uncharacterized proteins. Our integrated models will generate testable hypotheses about mechanical regulation, accelerating experimental discovery.

**Broader Impacts:**

Mechanotransduction dysfunction underlies numerous diseases including cancer, fibrosis, and cardiovascular disease. Our resources will enable researchers investigating these conditions to contextualize findings within comprehensive pathway frameworks. The analytical approaches developed—integrating structural, biophysical, and transcriptomic data—will serve as templates for synthesis projects addressing other signaling systems.

**Training Impact:**

Through graduate student exchanges, workshops, and undergraduate research experiences, we will train the next generation of scientists in transdisciplinary data synthesis approaches. Participants will gain expertise in data integration, network analysis, and machine learning—skills increasingly essential for modern biological research. Our commitment to including researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions will broaden participation in synthesis science.

All outcomes directly address NCEMS's mission of understanding emergence at the mesoscale while advancing open science principles.
